7: Here, we begin Chapter 1, Agricultural Marketing, the first unit of Paper 2's Specific Paper. This chapter covers the meaning and significance of marketing, market classification, approaches to studying marketing, marketing functions and utilities, methods of sale, channels and intermediaries, marketing risks, market information, research institutions, the structure conduct performance framework, costs and price spread, marketable and marketed surplus, regulated markets and the Karnataka APMC system, cooperative marketing, price policy, market reforms and digital platforms, and retailing. Let us start with definitions. A market, in common use, is a place where goods are bought and sold, but in economics it is wider, meaning the whole body of buyers and sellers of a commodity together with the process by which they arrive at a price. The word market comes from the Latin mercatus, meaning trade. The essential elements of a market are a commodity, buyers and sellers, a place or means of contact, and a price determination process. This tendency towards one price is called the law of one price. A market has four dimensions, place, commodity, time and volume. Marketing means the performance of all business activities in the flow of goods from production to the final consumer, including assembling, grading, storage, transport, processing, financing, pricing and sale. Agricultural marketing covers both moving farm produce to the consumer and moving farm inputs to the farmer. Remember, selling is only the narrow act of transferring goods for money, while marketing is the wide process beginning before production and continuing through grading, storage and distribution.
8: On this page, we compare selling and marketing directly. Selling has a narrow scope, the act of sale, and begins only after the good is produced, focusing on disposing of what is produced, with the goal of converting goods into cash. Marketing has a wide scope, covering the whole flow of goods, beginning before production with planning, focusing on satisfying consumer demand, with the goal of securing the best net return through the chain. Next, distinguish input marketing, output marketing and agricultural marketing. Input marketing deals with the supply of farm inputs, such as seed, fertiliser, plant protection chemicals, machinery and credit, moving from industry to the farmer. Output marketing deals with the disposal of farm produce, moving from farmer to consumer, such as paddy, tomato or milk. Agricultural marketing is the umbrella term covering both sides together. Marketing evolved through stages, starting with village barter, then periodic weekly markets called santhe or haat, then regulated markets and wholesale mandis, then cooperative marketing, and now electronic and direct marketing through platforms such as eNAM and the Unified Market Platform. Each stage solved a problem of the previous one. We also distinguish subsistence farming, where the household grows mainly for its own consumption and sells only a small surplus, from commercial farming, where the household grows mainly for sale and marketing decisions guide what to grow. An efficient marketing system widens the market, raises farm income, guides production through price signals, reduces waste, and stabilises prices between surplus and deficit regions.
9: Let us understand why agricultural marketing is harder than industrial marketing. There are three structural reasons. Farm produce is bulky and perishable, raising transport and storage costs. Supply is seasonal and concentrated at harvest, while demand is steady through the year. And output is scattered across millions of small holdings, leaving the individual farmer a weak bargaining party. Further difficulties include varying quality from lot to lot, which makes grading essential and difficult, inelastic demand and supply causing large price swings from small quantity changes, and many farmers lacking holding capacity, forcing them to sell at once at harvest and depress the price. For an Agricultural Officer, these three handicaps, perishability, seasonality and scattered small holdings, are exactly what State schemes try to offset. Grading and cold storage fight perishability, warehouse receipts and Minimum Support Price fight seasonal price crashes, and Farmer Producer Organisations and cooperatives fight the weakness of the scattered small farmer. Now, moving to classification of markets, markets are classified on several bases. By nature of commodities, we have produce, manufactured-goods, capital and bullion markets. By location, village, primary or mandi, secondary or wholesale, terminal, and seaboard markets. By area, local, regional, national and international markets. By time span, short-period, long-period and secular markets. By nature of transactions, spot or cash and forward or future markets. By number of commodities, general and specialised markets. By degree of competition, perfect and imperfect types including monopoly, oligopoly, monopsony and monopolistic. By stage, producing and consuming markets. By extent of public intervention, regulated and unregulated markets.
10: On this page, we look at classification by location, which forms a marketing chain. A village market handles small local sales. A primary or assembling market is the mandi where producers bring produce for first sale, such as a taluk APMC yard. A secondary or wholesale market regroups produce in bulk, such as a district wholesale mandi. A terminal market is the final assembly point, often a metropolis or port, from which produce is exported or distributed. Produce typically climbs this ladder from village to terminal. By degree of competition, markets range from perfect, with many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and full knowledge, to imperfect types. Monopoly is a single seller, monopsony a single buyer, oligopoly a few sellers, oligopsony a few buyers, and monopolistic competition many sellers of slightly differentiated products. A spot market settles a deal for immediate delivery and cash, while a forward market settles a contract now for delivery at a future date and price. A producing market lies in the area where the crop is grown, and a consuming market lies in a demand centre. Remember, agricultural markets are almost never perfectly competitive, the realistic structure is oligopsony or imperfect competition, so if a question asks the typical competition in an agricultural market, perfect competition is the trap answer, not the correct one. Next, approaches to studying marketing problems include functional, institutional, commodity, behavioural-system, structural, and managerial or decision approaches, each identified by trigger words in exam questions.
11: Now, students, let us compare the functional and commodity approaches, which are most often confused. The commodity approach follows the product on its journey from farm to consumer, while the functional approach follows the activities performed on any product, such as buying, selling, storage and grading. The institutional approach studies the people and bodies in the chain, such as the village trader, commission agent, wholesaler, cooperative and regulated market. The systems approach, the most modern, treats marketing as one large system with sub-systems exchanging goods, money and information with feedback. The managerial approach views marketing from inside a firm, centred on the marketing mix, the four P's, Product, Price, Place and Promotion. Even a Farmer Producer Organisation selling under a brand uses this approach. Moving to marketing functions, a marketing function is a major specialised activity performed in moving produce from producer to consumer. Functions are grouped into three classes as shown in Figure 1.1. Exchange functions are buying, or assembling, and selling, or dispersion. Physical functions are transport, storage, processing and packaging. Facilitating functions are grading and standardisation, financing, risk-bearing, and market information. Each function creates a utility, the capacity of a good to satisfy a want. The utilities are time from storage, place from transport, form from processing, and possession from selling. Exchange functions transfer ownership and create possession utility, the value gained when goods pass to the person who wants them.
12: On this page, physical functions are explained further. Transportation moves produce from farm to market and creates place utility, bridging the distance between a surplus farm and a deficit city. Storage and warehousing hold produce until wanted and create time utility, bridging the gap between a single harvest and year-round demand. Processing and packaging change produce into a usable, protected form and create form utility, converting a raw, perishable crop into a stable product, such as paddy into rice, milk into powder, or cane into sugar. Facilitating functions do not handle the produce themselves but make the exchange and physical functions work smoothly. These are standardisation and grading, fixing uniform quality so trade can happen by grade name, financing, supplying working capital, risk-bearing, accepting the chance of loss from spoilage or price fall, and market information, collecting and supplying data on prices, arrivals and stocks. A memorable worked example, a farmer harvests onion in February when prices are low. He grades it, stores it, and sells in June at a higher price in a distant city. Storage created time utility, transport created place utility, grading made it tradable, and the final sale created possession utility, four functions adding value to one bag of onion. Remember this mapping, time equals storage, place equals transport, form equals processing, possession equals selling. Next, we move to methods of sale and types of buying. Farm produce is disposed of by several traditional methods, including open auction where buyers bid openly and the highest bid wins, the under-cover or Hatha method where price is settled secretly under a cloth, private agreement by quoting samples, Dara or heap sale where mixed qualities are sold at one flat rate, close or sealed tender system used in government purchase, and Moghum sale settled verbally and kept secret.
13: Let us continue with methods of sale. These methods split into two groups. The open auction and the sealed tender are transparent, since the basis of price is recorded or witnessed, protecting the farmer. The Hatha, Moghum and private-negotiation methods are secret, settled by signals or whispered figures, which lets a trader exploit an uninformed farmer. Regulated markets therefore make the open auction compulsory. In a worked example, two traders bid on a farmer's wheat. In an open auction one shouts rupees 2,300 and another rupees 2,350, so the farmer knows he got the higher public bid. In the Hatha method the price is pressed out under a cloth, and the farmer cannot tell if he got the true market rate, which is exactly why regulation banned it. Buying is also classified by purpose. Buying for consumption is purchase by a household or firm to use or eat the produce. Buying for sale, or resale, is purchase by a trader intending to sell again at a profit. Speculative buying is purchase made purely in hope of a price rise. Now, moving to marketing channels, a marketing channel is the route or chain of intermediaries through which produce passes from producer to final consumer. A channel with many intermediaries is a long channel, one with few is a short channel. The length of the channel directly affects the producer's share, a long channel adds cost and margin at every stage, reducing the farmer's share, while a short channel, such as producer to Farmer Producer Organisation to consumer, raises that share. Figure 1.2 shows three channels, Channel one is direct, producer to consumer, giving the highest producer share. Channel two adds a retailer. Channel three is longest, with village trader, wholesaler and retailer, giving the lowest producer share.
14: On this page, the table confirms that the shortest channel, producer direct to consumer, gives the highest producer share, while the longest channel, producer through village trader, wholesaler and retailer to consumer, gives the lowest share. Next, market functionaries, or middlemen, are classified by whether they take title, meaning ownership, of the goods. Merchant middlemen, such as wholesalers and retailers, take title, buying and reselling on their own account and bearing price risk. Agent middlemen, such as commission agents and brokers, do not take title, they negotiate sale on behalf of others for a commission. Speculative middlemen take title, buying and holding purely to gain from a price rise. Processors and manufacturers take title, buying produce as raw material. Facilitative organisations like the APMC do not take title, they provide the place, rules and price-discovery setting. Among agent middlemen, a kachha arhatiya works for the seller, the farmer, while a pacca arhatiya works for the buyer. A broker only brings the two parties together and never handles the goods. A dalal is a local broker, and a beopari or village trader buys at the village and resells in the mandi. Middlemen are often blamed for the wide gap between farm and retail prices, yet they perform real services, assembling scattered produce, financing the farmer, bearing risk, and supplying market knowledge. The aim of reform is not to abolish them but to reduce their number and regulate their charges. Remember, the single discriminating test for any middleman is whether he takes title, merchants, speculators and processors do, but commission agents, brokers and the APMC do not. Now we move to management of marketing risks, which the syllabus classifies as economic, natural, human, business, price and credit risks.
15: Now, students, here is the table of risk types. Natural or physical risk is loss from spoilage, fire, pest, flood or deterioration in storage. Price or market risk is loss from an adverse price change between purchase and sale. Economic or business risk is loss from changes in demand, competition or trade conditions. Human risk is loss from theft, careless handling, dishonesty or negligence. Credit risk is loss from a buyer's failure to pay for goods sold on credit. Risks are minimised by several devices, grading and scientific storage to cut physical loss, insurance to transfer natural risk, forward and futures contracts to lock a price and transfer price risk, reliable market information to reduce uncertainty, and spreading sales over time rather than dumping the whole crop at harvest. Hedging means protecting against a price fall by taking an opposite position in the futures market, so a loss on the physical crop is offset by a gain on the contract. In a worked example, a trader buys 100 quintals of soybean expecting to sell after two months but fears a price fall. He sells an equal quantity of soybean futures today. If the price falls, he loses on the physical stock but gains on the futures, and the two largely cancel out, that is hedging against price risk. An Agricultural Officer reduces a farmer's risk on two fronts at once, enrolling the crop under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana to cover natural risk, and using warehouse receipts plus eNAM price trends to spread sales and soften price risk. Next, we separate market information, the current data on prices, arrivals, stocks and demand, from market intelligence, the analysis of past and present information to forecast future prices, and market news, the regular reporting and dissemination of this information.
16: On this page, we learn that good marketing information must be complete, accurate, timely, reliable, comparable across markets, and easily understood. Information that is late or unreliable widens the price gap between farmer and consumer and lets the better-informed trader exploit the farmer. Portals such as AGMARKNET shift bargaining power towards the producer by spreading daily prices to every farmer. Remember, market information equals today's price, the data, for example today's price of tur in Kalaburagi mandi. Market intelligence equals next month's likely price, the forecast, for example tur price likely to rise next month. AGMARKNET is the national portal that disseminates daily mandi prices and arrivals as market news. Next, we cover marketing research and training institutions. DMI is the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, which grades and certifies AGMARK quality. SAMBs are State Agricultural Marketing Boards that coordinate regulated markets in a State. ICAR is the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, handling research and education. NCAER is the National Council of Applied Economic Research, doing economic and market research. SAUs are State Agricultural Universities, handling teaching, research and extension. CAM is the Centre for Agricultural Marketing, a national-level marketing training body. ISAM or CCS NIAM is the National Institute of Agricultural Marketing at Jaipur, the apex training body. NAFED is the National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation, doing price-support buying. SFAC is the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium, which promotes Farmer Producer Organisations and operates eNAM. KSAMB is the Karnataka State Agricultural Marketing Board, the apex body over the State's APMCs.
17: Let us understand how these institutions group by role. The DMI and marketing boards regulate and grade. ICAR, NCAER and the SAUs research and teach. NIAM and CAM train marketing officers. NAFED and SFAC act in the field, NAFED buying under price support and SFAC promoting Farmer Producer Organisations and running eNAM. For an Agricultural Officer, Jaipur's National Institute of Agricultural Marketing trains marketing officers, while KSAMB is the body to which a Karnataka Agricultural Officer actually reports market data. Remember that SFAC, not the APMC, is the national agency operating eNAM, a frequent point of confusion in exams. Now, the structure-conduct-performance framework, or SCP, links three connected ideas. Structure is the number and size of buyers and sellers, degree of product differentiation, and entry conditions. Conduct is how firms actually behave, pricing, collusion, trade practices. Performance is the result, efficiency, the producer's share, price stability and progress. The framework reads in one direction, structure shapes conduct, and conduct shapes performance. A concentrated structure with few large buyers allows collusive conduct, yielding poor performance, a low producer's share, while a competitive structure improves performance. Reform therefore attacks structure first, by widening the number of buyers. We also define marketing cost, the actual expenses in performing marketing functions, such as transport, loading, commission, storage and losses, marketing margin, the difference between the price received and paid by a seller, and price spread, the difference between the price paid by the consumer and received by the producer, equal to marketing costs plus all intermediary margins. Producer's share is the price received by the farmer as a percentage of the price paid by the consumer, higher meaning more efficiency. Figure 1.3 shows vegetables, a perishable, have a 40 percent producer share, versus foodgrain, a durable, with a 70 percent producer share.
18: On this page, two worked examples clarify price spread. If a consumer pays rupees 40 per kilogram for tomatoes while the farmer received rupees 16, the price spread is rupees 24, made up of rupees 14 marketing costs and rupees 10 intermediary margins. The producer's share is 16 divided by 40, or 40 percent, typical for a perishable, far below the 70 percent a foodgrain farmer keeps. In the second example, a wheat farmer is paid rupees 21 per kilogram while the consumer pays rupees 30. The price spread is rupees 9, and the producer's share is 21 divided by 30, or 70 percent, a narrower spread and larger share, the standard contrast the examiner wants. Marketing efficiency is the ratio of the output of the marketing system to the resources used. Shepherd's formula treats efficiency as the value of goods marketed divided by total marketing cost, while Acharya's Modified Marketing Efficiency index relates the producer's net price to the total marketing cost and margin. Efficiency has two sides, technical or operational efficiency means performing physical functions at least cost, and pricing or allocative efficiency means the price paid to the farmer fairly reflects the price paid by the consumer. Market integration means prices in different markets move together, spatially across places, temporally over time, and vertically across chain stages. Remember, a wide price spread and high marketing cost both mean low efficiency and a low producer's share, while high market integration is good, showing markets are well connected. Next, marketable surplus is the quantity left with the farmer after meeting the family's own requirements, while marketed surplus is the quantity actually sold, whatever the level of marketable surplus.
19: Now, students, this table shows how marketable and marketed surplus relate for different farmers. For a large farmer, marketed roughly equals marketable, since he sells the true surplus and holds nothing extra. For a small or distress farmer, marketed exceeds marketable, since he sells even produce he needs and buys it back later. For a commercial cash crop, marketed roughly equals marketable, since almost all output is grown for sale. In a worked example, a small paddy farmer produces 20 quintals and his family needs 8 quintals for food and seed, giving a marketable surplus of 12 quintals. Pressed for cash, he sells 15 quintals at harvest and buys back 3 quintals months later at a higher price. His marketed surplus of 15 exceeds his marketable surplus of 12, the mark of distress sale. Remember, marketable equals what can be sold after own needs, marketed equals what is actually sold. Now we move to regulation of agricultural marketing and the APMC system. Unregulated markets bred malpractices such as wrong weighment, arbitrary deductions, unauthorised charges, secret price settlement and adulteration, all falling on the weaker farmer. The objectives of market regulation are to remove malpractices, ensure correct weighment, fix and publicly display fair charges, provide open price discovery through auction, settle disputes quickly, and supply reliable market information. In Karnataka, regulated markets operate under the Karnataka Agricultural Produce Marketing Regulation and Development Act, 1966. Each market is governed by an Agricultural Produce Market Committee, or APMC, which notifies commodities, licenses traders and commission agents, fixes and publishes the market fee, provides yard infrastructure and weighment, and settles disputes. The apex body is the Karnataka State Agricultural Marketing Board, KSAMB, and the State has roughly 162 main market committees besides many sub-yards.
20: Here, Figure 1.4 shows the regulated market structure in Karnataka, with KSAMB, the State apex board, at the top, overseeing the APMC or Market Committee, which notifies commodities, licenses traders, fixes and publishes fees, provides yard and weighment, and settles disputes. This structure operates under the Karnataka APM Regulation and Development Act, 1966, with about 162 APMCs. The market committee runs the regulated yard day to day, issuing and cancelling licences to traders, agents and weighmen for misconduct, enforcing open auction and correct weighment, collecting the notified market fee, maintaining the yard and godowns, publishing daily prices and arrivals, and deciding disputes. A good market has correct weighing, open and competitive price discovery, low and publicly known charges, prompt cash payment, quick dispute settlement and reliable market information. An ideal marketing system secures for the producer the largest possible share of the consumer's rupee. For an Agricultural Officer, when a farmer complains of short-weighment by a trader, the first step is to refer it to the APMC secretary under the 1966 Act. Now, cooperative marketing lets farmers pool produce and bargain collectively, capturing the margin a private trader would otherwise take. NAFED is the national apex agency for price-support purchase of pulses and oilseeds. Karnataka has strong institutions, HOPCOMS markets fruits and vegetables, KAPPEC handles processing and export promotion, and the Karnataka Milk Federation runs the Nandini brand on the three-tier Anand pattern. Cooperative marketing strengthens bargaining power, removes the chain of middlemen, provides credit against pooled stock, offers grading, storage and transport, and returns surplus to members as bonus. Under the three-tier Anand pattern, a village society collects milk, a district union processes it, and a State federation markets it, exemplified by the Karnataka Milk Federation selling as Nandini.
21: On this page, we cover price policy. The Minimum Support Price, or MSP, is the floor price the government promises for notified crops, protecting the farmer from a price crash at harvest. It is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, CACP, and approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. Three prices must be kept distinct, the MSP protects the farmer, the procurement price is what agencies actually pay to build the buffer stock, and the issue price is the subsidised price at which the public distribution system sells. The Food Corporation of India procures cereals, while NAFED procures pulses and oilseeds. MSP currently covers 23 crops. The CACP weighs the cost of production, demand and supply, price trends, input-output price parity, and effects on the consumer and economy before recommending the MSP, which then goes to the Cabinet Committee for final decision. Scientific marketing means planning the entire marketing sequence in advance, covering proper harvesting at the right maturity, grading and standardisation, suitable packaging, scientific storage, choice of the right market, use of price information, and timing of sale to secure the best net return, the highest price after deducting all marketing costs. In a worked example, a grower is offered rupees 2,000 per quintal locally and rupees 2,200 in a distant city, but transport, loading and commission to the city cost rupees 250 per quintal, giving a net of rupees 1,950 from the city, below the local rupees 2,000. Scientific marketing tells him to sell locally, since the higher gross price gives the lower net return. Remember, CACP only recommends the MSP, the Cabinet approves it. Next, market reforms, the Model APMC Act of 2003 recommended private markets, direct marketing and contract farming, and Karnataka adopted these early. Contract farming is an arrangement where a farmer agrees in advance to supply a buyer a stated quantity and quality at an agreed price.
22: Now, students, two digital platforms are central to market reform. eNAM, the National Agriculture Market, was launched on 14 April 2016 and is operated by SFAC, linking mandis across the country into one online market. Karnataka had already built its own Unified Market Platform through Rashtriya e-Market Services, a 2014 joint venture of the State Government and NCDEX, making Karnataka the first State to run a state-wide online unified trading platform. The Karnataka APMC Amendment of 2020 further allowed trade outside notified yards under a licence valid for three years. These digital platforms benefit the farmer directly, a single online auction draws buyers from many districts, widening competition and raising the bid, quality is fixed by assaying so a graded lot earns a premium, payment is made online cutting delay, and the platform leaves a price record improving market information. Remember, two dates win marks, ReMS or the Unified Market Platform equals 2014, Karnataka with NCDEX, while eNAM equals 2016, national, 14 April, with SFAC, and Karnataka's platform came first. Next, grading, standardisation and warehousing. Grading is sorting produce into lots of uniform quality according to recognised standards of size, colour, moisture and purity. Standardisation is establishing fixed and recognised norms of quality, weight and measure, so produce can be traded by grade name without physical inspection. AGMARK is the quality certification mark managed by the DMI. Grading benefits every party, the farmer earns a premium for better grade, the buyer can purchase from a distance by grade name, and the market trades faster with fewer disputes. Scientific warehousing cuts post-harvest loss and lets a farmer wait for a better price. The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority, WDRA, regulates Negotiable Warehouse Receipts, which a farmer can pledge to a bank for a loan while the stock remains in store, converting storage from a holding cost into a source of finance.
23: On this page, a worked example completes the warehousing point, a farmer stores 50 quintals of maize in a WDRA-accredited warehouse and receives a Negotiable Warehouse Receipt, pledges it to a bank for a loan covering immediate cash needs, avoids a distress sale, and sells three months later when the price has risen, repaying the loan from the higher proceeds. Now, retailing, the final stage of marketing, is the sale of goods in small quantities directly to the final consumer. Traditional retailing is carried on through small, unorganised outlets, the local kirana shop, the weekly santhe, hawkers and street vendors, with advantages of low cost, proximity, personal relationship and credit to known customers, but disadvantages of absent grading, quality assurance or cold chain, limited variety and small scale. Modern or organised retailing operates through supermarkets, hypermarkets, chain stores and online platforms with standard pricing, grading, branding and cold chains, offering quality assurance, lower waste, wider choice and a steadier market for graded produce, but requiring high investment and squeezing small shops, with strict supply standards that an individual small farmer struggles to meet alone. For an Agricultural Officer, when a modern retail chain wants a steady supply of graded vegetables, the officer steers the contract to a Farmer Producer Organisation rather than a lone farmer, turning the chain's demand for quality and volume into an opportunity for the cooperative rather than a barrier for the individual. This closes the theory portion of the Agricultural Marketing chapter.

27: Now, students, we continue through methods of sale and types of market middlemen. The Hatha method settles price by pressing or twisting fingers under a cloth, a secretive system. Question 15 explains the Dara method, where produce of different qualities is mixed into one heap and sold at a single flat rate. Question 16 introduces Moghum sale, where the price is agreed verbally in secret between two parties. Question 17 identifies open auction as the most transparent method of sale, promoted by market regulation, since bids are made publicly. Question 18 defines a commission agent, or arhatiya, as a middleman who does not take title to the goods and works only on commission for someone else. Question 19 distinguishes a kachha arhatiya, who represents the seller or farmer, from a pacca arhatiya, who represents the buyer. Question 20 clarifies that among broker, commission agent, wholesaler and APMC, only the wholesaler, a merchant middleman, actually takes title or ownership of the goods. 28: Here we continue through the different types of marketing risk and key institutions. 32: Now, students, we begin Chapter 2, Input Marketing, part of Unit 2 of Paper 2's Specific Paper. This chapter covers the full theory of input marketing, its nature, scope and significance, how it differs from output marketing, the theory of factor pricing under perfect competition, monopoly, monopsony and oligopoly, the demand and supply of farm inputs, owned versus purchased inputs, fertiliser marketing including NPK nutrients and channels like MARKFED, seed marketing including seed classes and certification tags, the seed replacement rate, plant-protection chemicals and the Insecticides Act 1968, groundwater marketing and power pricing, the agricultural labour market and MGNREGA, and farm-machinery marketing with custom-hiring centres. Section 2.1 begins with input marketing, defined as the set of all activities, agencies and policies involved in moving farm inputs, seed, fertiliser, plant-protection chemicals, machinery, credit, water and labour, from the point of manufacture or supply to the farmer who uses them. Input marketing is the supply side of agricultural marketing, carrying the means of production backward to the farm gate, and its scope covers production planning, distribution networks, pricing and subsidies, quality control, demand forecasting and timely delivery. Its significance lies in making Green Revolution technology reach the farmer, determining the cost of cultivation, and influencing timeliness of farm operations.
33: Here we look at a figure classifying farm inputs into owned, or internal, inputs like family labour, farm-saved seed, farmyard manure and owned land and water, and purchased, or external, inputs like fertiliser, certified seed, plant-protection chemicals, machinery, and hired labour and credit. The key point is that purchased inputs pass through input-marketing channels, while owned inputs do not. An Agri Officer Lens box reminds us that an Agricultural Officer is, in practice, a node in this input-marketing system, recommending fertiliser doses, certifying seed dealer licences, and ensuring subsidised inputs reach genuine farmers on time. Section 2.2 then compares input marketing with output marketing across several bases. Input marketing flows from industry to farmer, moving seed, fertiliser, chemicals and machinery, with the farmer as buyer of factory-made, fairly uniform goods, facing derived and seasonal demand, and common subsidy or MRP control. Output marketing flows the opposite way, from farmer to consumer, moving variable produce that must be graded, facing steady final consumer demand, with MSP and APMC regulation being common. The page closes by introducing derived demand, defined as demand for an input arising not for its own sake but because of demand for the final product it helps produce, illustrated by fertiliser demand being derived from foodgrain demand.
34: On this page, we finish the input-output marketing comparison with a key reminder: in input marketing the farmer is the buyer, in output marketing the farmer is the seller, since input demand is derived and seasonal, never independent of crop prices. Section 2.3 then explains the theoretical framework of factor pricing under different market types. In equilibrium, an input is hired up to the point where the value it adds equals the price paid for it, though the exact rule changes with market structure. Marginal Revenue Product, MRP, is the addition to a firm's total revenue from employing one more unit of an input, while Value of Marginal Product, VMP, is the marginal physical product multiplied by the market price of output; under perfect competition in the product market, VMP equals MRP. Under perfect competition in the factor market, many buyers and sellers exist, the firm is a price-taker, and value of marginal product equals input price. Under monopoly in the product market, marginal revenue is below price, so the monopolist pays less than the value of marginal product, called monopolistic exploitation. Under monopsony, a single buyer of an input faces many sellers, its marginal factor cost rises above the input price, and it pays a price below the value of marginal product, called monopsonistic exploitation, illustrated by a single dominant sugar mill buying cane from many growers. Oligopoly, few large sellers, and oligopsony, few large buyers, involve interdependent behaviour, as seen in India's fertiliser and tractor industries.
35: Let us continue with the market-type summary table, noting oligopsony, where few large buyers depress the input price. An Agri Officer Lens box explains that factor-pricing theory explains real grievances, such as when one mill or a few traders act as monopsony buyers of a perishable crop, paying below its true value, which is why cooperatives and Farmer Producer Organisations are promoted to restore competition. Section 2.4 covers demand and supply of agricultural inputs. Input demand is derived from crop demand, joint since inputs are used together in fixed proportions, highly seasonal peaking at sowing and top-dressing, and price-elastic with respect to output price. Its determinants include expected output price, input price itself, prices of complementary and substitute inputs, subsidy level, cropping pattern, rainfall and irrigation, and new technology. Input supply depends on domestic manufacturing capacity, raw material availability and imports, government licensing and price policy, and distribution network reach; supply is often less flexible than demand in the short run, causing peak-season shortages. Section 2.5 then distinguishes owned, or internal, inputs, like family labour, farm-saved seed, farmyard manure and owned land and water, which carry no cash outlay, from purchased, or external, inputs like chemical fertiliser, certified seed, plant-protection chemicals, machinery, hired labour and credit, which involve cash payment and pass through input-marketing channels.
36: Now, students, Section 2.6 begins fertiliser marketing. Subsection 2.6.1 covers nutrients, NPK, straight and complex fertilisers. Plants need seventeen essential nutrients, but nitrogen, N, phosphorus, P, and potassium, K, are needed in the largest quantity and are always quoted in the order N-P-K. Nitrogen supports vegetative growth, green colour and protein, commonly carried by urea at 46 percent nitrogen. Phosphorus, as P2O5, supports root growth, flowering and energy transfer, commonly carried by DAP and SSP. Potassium, as K2O, supports grain filling and disease and drought resistance, commonly carried by muriate of potash, MOP. A straight fertiliser supplies only one primary nutrient, like urea for nitrogen only, while a complex fertiliser chemically combines two or more primary nutrients in each granule, like DAP at 18-46-0 or the NPK grade 10-26-26; a physical blend of straight fertilisers is merely a mixture, not a true complex. Urea is India's most widely used fertiliser at 46 percent nitrogen, the highest of any solid straight fertiliser, DAP is the leading phosphatic fertiliser at 18 percent N and 46 percent P2O5, and muriate of potash is almost entirely imported. The ideal NPK use ratio is roughly 4:2:1, though actual use skews toward nitrogen because urea is the most subsidised. Subsection 2.6.2 then covers production, consumption and distribution, noting India is a large producer and consumer of fertiliser yet remains import-dependent for raw materials, with consumption concentrated in irrigated States and peaking in the kharif and rabi seasons. Subsection 2.6.3 introduces fertiliser marketing channels and MARKFED.
37: Here a figure shows the fertiliser marketing channel, from manufacturer or importer to wholesaler or MARKFED, to retailer or cooperative society, to farmer, with the government's Nutrient Based Subsidy flowing in parallel to lower the price the farmer pays; the maximum retail price is printed on every bag. MARKFED is defined as a State Cooperative Marketing Federation, the apex cooperative body that wholesales agricultural inputs, chiefly fertiliser, and markets produce for primary cooperative societies. In the cooperative channel, the apex federation buys fertiliser in bulk from manufacturers and distributes it down to district and primary agricultural cooperative societies, which sell to member farmers; nationally IFFCO and KRIBHCO are giant cooperative manufacturers, and in Karnataka the Karnataka State Cooperative Marketing Federation and its network of primary cooperatives play this role. The private channel runs from manufacturer through distributors to licensed retail dealers, usually quicker and more aggressive in promotion, while the cooperative channel is valued for reaching remote and small farmers. Subsection 2.6.4 covers import of fertiliser materials, noting India imports almost all its muriate of potash, since it has no domestic potash reserves, and imports much of the raw materials and finished product for phosphatic fertilisers and urea too, since even urea production depends on imported natural gas. Subsection 2.6.5 then begins government policies on fertiliser pricing, starting with the Retention Price Scheme.
38: Let us understand the key fertiliser policy milestones on this page. The Retention Price Scheme, introduced in 1977 for nitrogenous fertilisers, was a cost-plus subsidy scheme assuring each manufacturer a fixed retention price covering cost plus a reasonable return, while the farmer paid a uniform low controlled price and government paid the difference; but it rewarded high-cost, inefficient producers and ballooned the subsidy bill, so it was gradually replaced. The Nutrient Based Subsidy, NBS, in force since April 2010, fixes a subsidy per kilogram of each nutrient, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and sulphur, rather than per product, with decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilisers having their retail price set by the market within that frame; however, urea was kept outside NBS and remains tightly price-controlled and heavily subsidised, which actually worsened the imbalance toward nitrogen. Decontrol means the removal of government control over price and distribution, and phosphatic and potassic fertilisers were decontrolled in 1992, while urea remains under statutory price control. Direct Benefit Transfer, introduced around 2017-18, releases subsidy to the manufacturer only after the actual retail sale is recorded on a point-of-sale machine, reducing diversion. Remember these key dates: Retention Price Scheme, 1977, cost-plus per product; decontrol of phosphatic and potassic fertilisers, 1992; Nutrient Based Subsidy, 2010, per nutrient; urea staying outside NBS is the single most frequently tested fact. Section 2.7 then begins seed marketing, covering types and classes of seed, where certified seed production follows a strict three-generation multiplication chain, each class tagged with a fixed colour.
39: On this page, a figure shows the seed multiplication chain and certification tag colours. Breeder seed, with highest genetic purity, carries a golden-yellow tag; foundation seed, grown from breeder seed with very high purity, carries a white tag; certified seed, grown from foundation seed with high purity and sold to farmers, carries a blue, or azure, tag. A separate category, Truthfully Labelled seed, which is not certified but self-declared by the producer, carries an opal-green tag. Breeder seed is directly controlled by the originating plant breeder or institution and is the source for foundation seed. Foundation seed is the progeny of breeder seed, produced on State Seed Farms or by the Seeds Corporations under strict supervision. Certified seed is the progeny of foundation seed, produced by registered growers under field and laboratory inspection, and is the class actually sold to ordinary farmers for sowing. Truthfully Labelled seed is sold under the producer's own guarantee of crop, variety and minimum quality, governed by the Seeds Act. Remember the tag colours for exam marks, breeder equals golden-yellow, foundation equals white, certified equals blue, truthfully labelled equals opal-green, with genetic purity falling and quantity rising as you move from breeder to certified. Subsection 2.7.2 then begins seed production and contract seed production, describing seed production as a specialised activity needing isolation distances, roguing of off-types, field inspections and post-harvest germination testing, carried out by public agencies like the National Seeds Corporation and State Seeds Corporations as well as private companies for proprietary hybrids.
40: Let us understand contract seed production, an arrangement where a seed company supplies foundation seed, technical guidance and a buy-back guarantee to selected farmers, who grow the seed crop and sell the entire produce back to the company at a pre-agreed price; this is widely used for hybrid maize, cotton, sunflower and vegetable seeds, with Karnataka's irrigated belts being important production areas, though the farmer risks rejection of the lot if quality standards are not met. Subsection 2.7.3 covers seed certification, labelling, packing and distribution. Seed certification is a legally recognised system of quality control under which a designated State Seed Certification Agency verifies, through field inspection and laboratory testing, that a seed lot meets prescribed standards of genetic and physical purity, germination and health before it is tagged and sold. In Karnataka, the Karnataka State Seed Certification Agency performs this role. Each certified bag carries a tag giving the crop, variety, lot number, germination percentage, physical purity, date of testing and validity period, and distribution follows both a public channel through the Seeds Corporations and cooperatives, and a private channel through company dealers. Remember that a seed tag is a legal certificate, not a sticker, and selling expired-validity or untagged certified seed is an offence under the Seeds Act. Subsection 2.7.4 then covers public and private seed companies, noting the National Seeds Corporation and State Seeds Corporations dominate supply of self-pollinated crop seed like wheat and paddy, while private companies and multinationals concentrate on high-value hybrids like cotton, maize, sunflower and vegetables. Subsection 2.7.5 begins institutional arrangements, listing the National Seeds Corporation, founded 1963, and the State Farms Corporation of India.
41: Here we complete the institutional arrangements table, covering State Seeds Corporations, which produce and market certified seed within a State, for example the Karnataka State Seeds Corporation, or KSSC; State Seed Farms, which multiply foundation seed; the State Seed Certification Agency, which certifies seed lots and issues coloured tags; and the State Seed Testing Laboratory, which tests purity, germination and seed health. The National Seeds Corporation, set up in 1963, is the central public-sector agency holding a national buffer of seed against crop failure, while each State has its own Seeds Corporation, in Karnataka the KSSC, backed by State Seed Farms, a Certification Agency and a Testing Laboratory, with the University of Agricultural Sciences supplying much of the breeder seed of new varieties. Subsection 2.7.6 covers demand-supply forecasting and the Seed Replacement Rate, SRR, defined as the percentage of total cropped area sown with certified or quality seed in a season, as against farm-saved seed; a worked example shows that for 50,000 hectares of paddy at a seed rate of 30 kilograms per hectare, gross requirement is 1,500 tonnes, and at a 40 percent target SRR, the market must supply 600 tonnes of certified seed. Hybrids have an SRR of nearly 100 percent since farmers cannot save hybrid seed without losing vigour. Subsection 2.7.7 then covers government policies, import-export and the National Seed Policy 2002, listing the Seeds Act 1966, Seed Rules 1968, Seeds Control Order 1983, and the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001, which protects both breeders' rights and farmers' age-old right to save, use and exchange seed.
42: Now, students, we finish the National Seed Policy 2002, which liberalised the Indian seed sector, encouraging private and foreign investment, easing import of vegetable and flower seed, strengthening certification and plant-variety protection, and aiming to raise the seed replacement rate. Import of seed is allowed under quarantine to bring in new germplasm, and India also exports hybrid vegetable and flower seed, with Karnataka a leading producing and exporting State. Remember these key seed law dates: Seeds Act, 1966; Seed Rules, 1968; Seeds Control Order, 1983; Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001; National Seed Policy, 2002; and note that certification is voluntary but labelling is compulsory under the Seeds Act. Section 2.8 then begins plant protection chemicals, or pesticides. Subsection 2.8.1 covers types, pesticide being the broad umbrella term for any chemical or biological agent used to prevent, destroy or control a pest, with sub-classes named by their target: insecticides control insect pests, for example chlorpyriphos and imidacloprid; fungicides control fungal diseases, for example mancozeb and copper oxychloride; herbicides, or weedicides, control weeds, for example glyphosate, 2,4-D and atrazine; rodenticides control rodents, for example zinc phosphide; nematicides control nematodes, for example carbofuran; and acaricides, or miticides, control mites, for example dicofol. In India, insecticides have traditionally had the largest share of pesticide consumption, though herbicide use is rising fast as farm labour becomes scarcer and costlier. Pesticides are classified by toxicity into colour-coded bands, red triangle being most toxic, then yellow, blue and green being least toxic, appearing on every label. Subsection 2.8.2 then begins production, consumption and industry structure.
43: Let us continue with the pesticide industry structure. It has two stages, manufacture of the technical-grade active ingredient, and its formulation into ready-to-use products by mixing with carriers and solvents; India is a major producer and exporter of technical-grade pesticides, with the industry moderately concentrated, giving it an oligopolistic character. Indian pesticide consumption per hectare is low by world standards but concentrated on cotton, paddy and vegetables in irrigated States. Subsection 2.8.3 covers brands, quality control and distribution, noting plant-protection chemicals are sold under heavily promoted brand names even though the same active ingredient is offered by many firms, making dealer network quality important; a licence is compulsory to sell pesticides, and government insecticide testing laboratories draw and analyse market samples, since the sale of misbranded or sub-standard products is an offence. Subsection 2.8.4 covers government policies and the Insecticides Act 1968, the central law regulating import, manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use of insecticides in India, requiring every pesticide to be registered and every manufacturer, distributor and dealer to be licensed. Under the Insecticides Act 1968 and Insecticides Rules 1971, no pesticide may be made, imported or sold unless first registered with the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee, every dealer must hold a licence, every label must carry the toxicity colour and antidote, and Insecticide Inspectors may draw samples and prosecute for misbranding. Section 2.9 then begins groundwater marketing, defining a groundwater market as an informal arrangement where a well or borewell owner sells water to neighbouring farmers, usually on an hourly, per-crop or share basis. Subsection 2.9.2 begins power pricing and its effects, noting electricity price is the single most important influence on groundwater markets since pumping cost is mostly power cost, and free or flat-rate power encourages over-extraction.
44: On this page, we finish power pricing's effects on groundwater, remembering that free or flat-rate farm power makes the marginal cost of pumping almost zero, encouraging over-extraction and falling water tables, while metered, per-unit power pricing is the main tool to make groundwater use efficient and sustainable. Subsection 2.9.3 covers equity, sustainability and pricing of groundwater. On equity, these informal markets can help landless and small farmers gain access to water they could never afford to pump themselves, but where one or a few well-owners dominate a hamlet, the market becomes a local monopoly charging high prices. On sustainability, cheap power combined with unregulated selling drives the water table down and dries up shallow wells, ultimately harming even the seller. Pricing of groundwater is set by local bargaining, depending on water scarcity, pumping cost, the number of competing sellers, and the crop's value; sound policy combines rational power pricing, recharge and watershed works, regulation of well spacing and depth, and promotion of micro-irrigation. In hard-rock Karnataka, falling water tables make this a live field issue, and an Agricultural Officer promotes drip and sprinkler systems and watershed recharge to keep these informal water markets fair and the aquifer alive. Section 2.10 then begins the agricultural labour market. Subsection 2.10.1 lists types of labour, family labour, unpaid and owned; attached or permanent labour on a long-term yearly contract; casual or daily-wage labour hired by the day at peak operations; seasonal migrant labour following the cropping calendar; and skilled labour like tractor drivers and sprayer operators. Subsection 2.10.2 then begins wage differentials, demand and supply, and MGNREGA, noting wages differ by region, season and mechanisation, peaking at harvest and transplanting.
45: On this page we look at the MGNREGA effect on the rural labour market, and then move into farm machinery marketing. MGNREGA, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act of 2005, guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work, at a notified minimum wage. By guaranteeing employment at a statutory wage, MGNREGA sets a floor under rural wages and tightens the farm labour supply, especially in the slack season. As a result, farm wages have risen and labour has become scarcer and costlier at peak operations, pushing farmers toward mechanisation and herbicides to economise on labour. Remember, this link between the labour market and demand for machinery and chemicals is a favourite examination point. Next, under section 2.11 on farm machinery marketing, machinery is classified by the stage of crop production at which it is used. Pre-harvest machines cover tillage, sowing and care, such as the tractor, plough, cultivator, rotavator, seed drill, transplanter and sprayer. Harvesting machines include the reaper, combine harvester and harvester-binder. Post-harvest machines, used for processing, include the thresher, winnower, dryer, cleaner-grader, decorticator and mill. The tractor is the central power source and the most important single machine in the market.
46: Let us understand the constraints, pricing and government policy around farm machinery today. Undulating or terraced terrain limits machine use in many regions, and cheap family labour in some areas also weakens the incentive to mechanise. On pricing, farm machinery is priced as a durable capital good, with the dealer's margin, transport, financing cost and after-sales service built into the price. Because the machine is bought once in several years, the farmer weighs not just the price but the cost per hour of use over the machine's life, which is why custom hiring, by spreading that cost over many farms, is so attractive to small holders. Now, on government policy, a Custom Hiring Centre, or CHC, is a unit run by an entrepreneur, cooperative or Farmer Producer Organisation that owns a fleet of farm machines and hires them out to farmers on a per-hour or per-acre basis, giving small farmers access to machinery they cannot afford to buy. Government policy promotes mechanisation through capital subsidy on machine purchase and, above all, through Custom Hiring Centres established under the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation, known as SMAM. Karnataka has actively promoted custom-hiring through cooperatives and private operators, including app-based booking of machines. As the Agri Officer Lens box explains, Custom Hiring Centres are the policy answer to the small-holding constraint, converting an unaffordable purchase into an affordable hire, and linking the machinery market back to the labour scarcity created by MGNREGA.
