An interesting note for officers, Karnataka is roughly seventy per cent dryland, with red soils in the south and east and black cotton soils in the north, and its flagship watershed programmes are the Sujala projects and the Integrated Watershed Management Programme.
155: Let us understand building materials on this page, starting with bricks and tiles. Bricks are moulded clay units burnt in a kiln, and the standard modular brick size in India is 190 by 90 by 90 millimetres, becoming 200 by 100 by 100 with a 10 millimetre mortar joint. Good bricks are well-burnt, uniform in colour, give a clear metallic ring when struck, and absorb less than about twenty per cent of their weight in water. The Bureau of Indian Standards grades bricks by crushing strength, first class bricks need at least 10.5 newtons per square millimetre and under 20 per cent water absorption, used for permanent superior work. Second class needs at least 7.0, under 22 per cent absorption, for plastered ordinary buildings. Third class needs at least 3.5, under 25 per cent, for temporary work. Fourth class, called jhama, is over-burnt and distorted, used only as broken aggregate or road metal. Tiles are thin burnt-clay or cement units for roofing, flooring and paving, and Mangalore tiles, made from coastal laterite-belt clays around Mangaluru, are interlocking and famous across south India. Field tests for bricks and tiles include hardness by scratch, soundness by ring, structure on fracture, and water absorption. The next section moves into lime, cement, sand, mortar and concrete.
156: Here, students, we continue with cement properties and then move into other building materials. Cement testing properties include fineness, tested by sieve or Blaine air-permeability with a limit of at least 225 square metres per kilogram, initial setting time of at least 30 minutes by the Vicat apparatus, final setting time of at most 600 minutes or 10 hours, soundness by the Le-Chatelier or autoclave test with at most 10 millimetres expansion, and compressive strength tested on cubes with a 1 to 3 mortar mix, giving 33, 43, or 53 newtons per square millimetre at 28 days depending on grade. Sand must be sharp, clean and well-graded, with silt content below about eight per cent. Concrete mixes range from nominal M5, meaning a ratio of 1 to 5 to 10, up to M25, and from M30 onward concrete must be design-mixed. Remember, gypsum is added to cement to retard, or slow down, the initial set, not to accelerate it, a very common trap in exams. Also, the M in M20 stands for Mix, and the number is the strength in newtons per square millimetre, not the mix ratio itself. A lower water-cement ratio always gives higher concrete strength, known as Abram's law. The chapter then moves on to timber, metals, glass, rubber and plastics, covering seasoned timber like teak, and metals such as mild steel, which is the standard structural and reinforcement material.
157: Now, students, this page finishes the materials section and introduces building components. Glass is made by fusing silica sand, soda and lime, and is brittle but rigid, used for glazing. Rubber is elastic and waterproof, used in bearings, joints and water stops, while plastics are polymers, thermoplastics like PVC and polythene soften on heating and can be remoulded, while thermosetting plastics like bakelite set permanently. PVC pipes have largely replaced metal pipes in farm water supply because they resist corrosion and are cheap and light. The chapter then introduces building components, a lintel is a horizontal beam placed across a door or window opening, working mainly in bending, while an arch performs the same function but as a curved structure transferring load mainly through compression, using wedge-shaped units called voussoirs meeting at the central keystone. Key arch terms include the keystone, the central topmost voussoir that locks the arch, the springer, the lowest voussoir resting on the support, and the abutment, the support resisting the arch's thrust. Remember, an arch works by compression while a lintel works by bending, and the keystone is the very last unit placed, locking the whole arch together. The page also introduces staircases, with tread, riser, going, flight, landing and headroom as key terms, and floors with their sub-base, base concrete and finishing layer.
158: Let us continue, students, with finishing works and building design. Damp-proofing prevents moisture from rising into walls and floors, using a damp-proof course, or DPC, a layer of dense cement concrete, bitumen, or a polythene membrane laid at plinth level. Plastering is a thin mortar coat, typically cement to sand ratio of 1 to 4 up to 1 to 6, about 12 to 20 millimetres thick, giving walls a smooth protective surface. Pointing finishes exposed mortar joints in brick or stone masonry, in patterns like flush, keyed, weathered and V-pointing. White-washing uses a slaked-lime wash for a cheap hygienic finish, especially useful for dairy and poultry sheds since lime is mildly disinfectant. Distempering uses whiting with a binder for interior decoration, while painting protects and decorates timber, metal and plastered surfaces, made of a base, a vehicle, a pigment, a solvent and a drier. Building design must satisfy strength, stability, serviceability, economy, durability and functional needs, considering dead load, live load, wind load, snow load and earthquake load as specified by Bureau of Indian Standards codes. Agricultural buildings are designed around the needs of the produce or animal housed, cattle and dairy sheds need ventilation, floor drainage, and manger and feeding space, as shown at the start of a new table continuing onto the next page.
159: On this page, students, we see more agricultural building types and then move into construction economics. Poultry houses need temperature and ventilation control, lighting and biosecurity. Grain and seed godowns need to be dry, rodent-proof, ventilated, with a damp-proof floor. Farm stores and implement sheds need enough span for machinery and a durable hard floor. Greenhouses and polyhouses need light transmission with controlled temperature and humidity. Silos and bins need structural strength for the pressure of stored grain. Sloped roofs are preferred in high-rainfall areas like coastal and Malnad Karnataka, while flat roofs suit drier districts and can double as drying yards. This directly connects to schemes like the Rural Godown or Gramin Bhandaran Yojana, where correct floor slope, ventilation and damp-proofing prevent post-harvest losses. The chapter then moves into construction economics, covering estimates and investment appraisal. A preliminary estimate gives a rough cost early using rates per square metre of plinth area, useful for feasibility, while a detailed estimate measures every item of work and multiplies quantities by rates from a Schedule of Rates, forming the basis for tendering. Analysis of rates breaks down a rate into material, labour, machinery cost, and contractor's profit and overheads, while contingencies are an allowance of about three to five per cent for unforeseen items.
160: Now, students, we finish construction economics and begin structural analysis. Investment appraisal methods include cost-in-use, which looks at whole-life cost covering first cost plus running and maintenance, the benefit-to-cost ratio, where a value greater than one means the project is economically viable, the savings-to-investment ratio, rate of return, net benefit, and the payback period, meaning the years needed for savings to recover the investment. Remember, cost-in-use deliberately looks beyond just the first construction cost, and a shorter payback period is always better. This is a practical skill for officers preparing watershed and farm-structure scheme proposals, which must show a benefit-to-cost ratio above one to win sanction. The chapter then begins Block B, Structural Analysis, starting with slope and deflection of beams. When a beam bends under load, it deflects, and the governing relation is the elastic or flexure equation, where bending moment equals flexural rigidity, EI, times curvature. Three standard methods find slope and deflection, the double-integration method, the moment-area theorems, and the conjugate-beam method. The two moment-area theorems are central, the first gives the change in slope between two points as the area of the M over EI diagram between them, and the second gives deflection using the moment of that area.
161: Here, students, we look at standard deflection formulae and then columns and struts. Four standard cases are given, a cantilever with a point load W at the free end deflects by WL cubed over 3EI, a cantilever with a uniformly distributed load w deflects by wL to the fourth over 8EI, a simply supported beam with a central point load W deflects by WL cubed over 48EI, and a simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load deflects by 5wL to the fourth over 384EI. These four formulae are direct one-mark answers worth memorising, especially the 5 over 384 coefficient and the 1 over 48 coefficient. The chapter then covers columns and struts, a column is a vertical compression member, a strut is any compression member, often inclined. Short columns fail by crushing, while long, slender columns fail by buckling, a sudden lateral instability. Euler's theory gives the critical buckling load, Pcr equals pi squared times EI divided by effective length squared, where the effective length depends on end conditions, both ends hinged gives length L, both ends fixed gives 0.5L, one fixed and one hinged gives 0.707L, and one fixed with the other free, like a cantilever, gives 2L. Remember, fixed-fixed columns carry the highest buckling load with the shortest effective length, while cantilever columns carry the lowest with the longest effective length, a common point of confusion.
162: Let us understand riveted and welded connections, and then masonry dams, on this page. Steel members are joined by riveted, bolted or welded connections. A riveted joint may be a lap joint or a butt joint, and rivets can fail by shearing, by bearing or crushing, or the plate can fail by tearing, the joint strength is the least of these values. Pitch is the centre-to-centre distance of rivets in a row, gauge is the distance between adjacent rivet rows, and joint efficiency is the joint strength divided by the strength of the solid plate, expressed as a percentage. Welded connections fuse members with molten metal, common types are the butt weld and the fillet weld, whose strength is based on its throat thickness, about 0.707 times the leg size. Welding gives a cleaner, lighter, often stronger joint than riveting, though it needs skilled workmanship. The chapter then covers stability of masonry or gravity dams, which resist water mainly by their own weight, checked against four failure modes, overturning about the toe, sliding along the base, crushing where compressive stress exceeds the safe limit, and tension developing in the masonry, since masonry is weak in tension and no tension is permitted at the base. The factor of safety against overturning is usually about 1.5 to 2.
163: Now, students, we learn the middle-third rule and statically indeterminate beams. Uplift pressure under the dam's base reduces its effective weight and therefore reduces stability, which is why drainage galleries are provided to relieve it. The middle-third rule states that the resultant of all forces must pass through the middle third of the base for no tension to develop, since masonry is weak in tension. This is highly relevant to Karnataka, since the Krishnaraja Sagar dam across the Cauvery near Mysuru is a gravity dam built largely of surki, or lime-mortar, masonry, and the Tungabhadra and Almatti dams also serve Karnataka's irrigation. The chapter then covers statically indeterminate beams. A beam is statically determinate when the three equations of statics suffice to find all reactions, and indeterminate when there are more unknown reactions than equations. A propped cantilever is one degree indeterminate, a fixed beam is two degrees indeterminate since both ends are restrained, and a continuous beam over multiple supports is indeterminate depending on the number of spans. Standard solving methods include the method of superposition, Clapeyron's three-moment equation for continuous beams, and the moment-distribution or Hardy Cross method, an iterative procedure that is the most popular hand method for continuous beams and frames.
164: On this page we begin Block C, Soil Mechanics, with the phase diagram and index properties. Soil mechanics is the branch of engineering studying the physical properties and behaviour of soil masses under stress, water and load, forming the foundation of all earthwork, foundations, bunds, dams and farm ponds. Soil is a three-phase system of solids, water and air, and the phase diagram in Figure 6.1 separates these volumes and weights to define basic index relations. Void ratio, e, is the volume of voids divided by the volume of solids. Porosity, n, is the volume of voids divided by total volume. Water content, w, is the weight of water divided by the weight of solids, expressed as a percentage. Degree of saturation, S, is the volume of water divided by the volume of voids. Specific gravity, G, of soil solids is typically about 2.65 to 2.70. Key formulas link these, void ratio e equals G times gamma-w over gamma-d, minus one, and S times e equals w times G, while dry unit weight gamma-d equals bulk unit weight divided by one plus water content. These three relations solve most phase-diagram numerical problems. For coarse-grained soils the key index is particle-size distribution from sieving, while for fine-grained soils the key indices are the Atterberg limits, the liquid limit, the plastic limit, and the shrinkage limit, continuing on the next page with the plasticity index.
165: On this page we finish the plasticity index and move into soil classification. The plasticity index, PI, equals the liquid limit minus the plastic limit, and it tells you the range of water content over which a soil stays plastic. A high PI means a highly plastic, expansive clay, like Karnataka's black cotton or regur soil, which swells when wet and cracks when dry, damaging foundations, canal linings and farm ponds. Now, students, let us understand classification. Soils are classified using the Indian Standard Soil Classification System, ISSCS, IS 1498, closely related to the Unified Soil Classification System, USCS. Soils are split first into coarse-grained, gravels G and sands S, classified by grain size and gradation, and fine-grained, silts M and clays C, classified using the plasticity chart. Highly organic soils are grouped as peat, Pt. Suffixes matter too. W means well-graded, P means poorly-graded. L means low compressibility, liquid limit below 35, H means high compressibility. On the plasticity chart, the A-line separates clay above from silt below. A high-plasticity clay is called CH, a low-plasticity silt is ML. Field identification uses dilatancy, toughness and dry-strength tests. Remember, land-capability and irrigation-suitability assessments depend on this texture knowledge: a coarse sand drains fast but holds little water, while a CH black clay holds water but waterlogs easily.
166: Let us understand effective stress, the cornerstone of soil mechanics, given to us by Karl Terzaghi. The key formula is sigma-prime equals sigma minus u, where sigma is total stress, u is pore-water pressure, also called neutral stress, and sigma-prime is effective stress. Only effective stress controls the strength and volume change of soil, because pore water carries none of the soil's strength. Now, when a load is applied at the ground surface, the vertical stress spreads and reduces with depth. Boussinesq's analysis gives the stress increase for a point load in a homogeneous, isotropic, elastic soil. Westergaard's analysis suits layered or stratified soils with thin stiff partings. Newmark's influence chart is a graphical tool that finds vertical stress under any loaded area of any shape by counting influence units on a plan. There is also a quick 2:1 approximate method for average stress spread. Remember, raising the water table increases pore pressure and reduces effective stress and hence strength. Do not interchange Boussinesq, for uniform soil, and Westergaard, for layered soil. For an agriculture officer, this explains why a farm-pond embankment or foundation that is firm when drained can become weak and even fail when saturated after heavy monsoon rain, because the effective stress supporting it has dropped.
167: Here we look at shear strength, the Mohr circle, and shear tests. The key formula, Mohr-Coulomb, is tau-f equals c plus sigma times tan phi in total stress terms, or c-prime plus sigma-prime tan phi-prime in effective stress terms. Here, c is cohesion and phi is the angle of internal friction. For pure sand, cohesion c is zero; for pure clay under undrained conditions, phi is zero. Four laboratory tests measure these parameters. The direct shear or shear box test is simple and used mainly for sands, though its failure plane is fixed and drainage is hard to control. The triaxial compression test is the most versatile and reliable, especially for clays, because it controls drainage and pore pressure. The vane shear test measures the in-situ or laboratory undrained strength of soft, saturated clays by twisting a cruciform vane. The unconfined compression test gives a quick undrained strength for cohesive soil where phi equals zero. In a triaxial test, the confining cell pressure is the minor principal stress, and the added axial stress at failure gives the major principal stress. Shear strength decides whether a farm-pond bund, canal bank or terrace stands or slumps. Saturated clay loses friction, phi approaching zero, which is exactly why embankments fail during prolonged monsoon saturation, making compaction and drainage so important.
168: This page continues into compaction and then moves to consolidation. Compaction densifies soil by expelling air through mechanical effort like rolling, ramming or vibration, increasing dry density, shear strength and bearing capacity while reducing settlement and permeability. Four compaction tests are listed. Standard Proctor uses a 2.6 kilogram rammer with a 310 millimetre drop, three layers and 25 blows. Modified Proctor uses a heavier 4.9 kilogram rammer and greater effort, giving a higher maximum dry density at a lower optimum moisture content, matching modern heavy rollers. The Abbot compaction test uses a drop-weight, Harvard or Abbot apparatus, and the Jodhpur mini-compaction test is a small-sample rapid dynamic test. In the field, quality is checked by comparing field dry density, using sand-replacement or core-cutter methods, against the laboratory maximum, expressed as relative or percentage compaction. Now, students, let us understand consolidation, which is completely different from compaction. Consolidation is the slow, time-dependent squeezing out of pore water from saturated fine-grained soil under sustained load, causing long-term settlement. Terzaghi's spring analogy pictures soil as a spring in a water-filled cylinder: load is first carried by water, high pore pressure, which then drains, transferring load onto the spring, effective stress. Key terms include coefficient of compressibility av, coefficient of volume change mv, compression index Cc, coefficient of consolidation cv, and pre-consolidation pressure, the maximum past effective stress a soil has experienced. Sheepsfoot rollers suit clays, vibratory rollers suit sands. For officers, earthen bunds and farm-pond embankments must be compacted near optimum moisture, in thin layers, not dumped dry, and structures on soft black clay may keep settling for years as consolidation proceeds, so wider foundations or ground improvement may be needed.
169: Let us understand earth pressure and plastic equilibrium. Earth pressure is the lateral pressure soil exerts on a retaining structure such as a wall, bund or culvert wing-wall. There are three states: at-rest, K-zero, with no wall movement and intermediate pressure; active, Ka, where the wall moves away from the soil giving minimum pressure; and passive, Kp, where the wall moves into the soil giving maximum pressure. The key formula, Rankine's theory for cohesionless soil, gives the active coefficient Ka equals one minus sine phi over one plus sine phi, and the passive coefficient Kp equals one plus sine phi over one minus sine phi. Note that Kp is the reciprocal of Ka, and Kp is always greater than K-zero which is greater than Ka. For cohesive soils, cohesion reduces active pressure, creating a tension crack near the top, but increases passive pressure. Coulomb's wedge theory is an alternative that accounts for wall friction. Active pressure increases linearly with depth, forming a triangular distribution whose resultant acts at one-third the height from the base. Now we move to slope stability. Slopes are classified as infinite, a long uniform slope with failure parallel to the surface, or finite, failure on a curved, usually circular surface. The factor of safety is resisting forces divided by driving forces; above one means stable. For an agriculture officer, retaining walls of farm terraces and culvert wing-walls resist active pressure, and forward tilting or cracking is the visible warning sign that active pressure has exceeded the wall's resistance.
170: On this page we complete slope stability and then begin surveying. For finite slopes, the friction-circle method and the method of slices, also called the Swedish circle method, trace a trial circular failure surface and balance the driving weight against the resisting shear strength. Taylor's stability number is a dimensionless parameter that lets engineers read the critical height of a slope directly from Taylor's stability charts, given the slope angle and friction angle. Slopes fail most often when saturation after heavy rain raises pore pressure and lowers effective shear strength. A factor of safety greater than one means a stable slope. Now, students, let us begin Block D, Surveying. Surveying is the art of determining the relative positions of points on, above or below the earth's surface by measuring distances, directions and elevations, and representing them on a map. The two fundamental principles are: always work from the whole to the part, fixing a framework of control points first, and always fix a point by at least two independent measurements. Surveys are classified as plane, where the earth's curvature is ignored for small areas, or geodetic, where curvature is considered for large areas. Methods include chain surveying for linear measurement, compass surveying for bearings, plane-table surveying for plotting, levelling for elevations, and theodolite surveying for angles, plus modern total stations and GPS. For officers in watersheds, this explains why bund and embankment failures happen most often during prolonged monsoon saturation.
171: Here we continue chain surveying and move into compass and plane-table methods. The standard Indian metric chain is 20 metres or 30 metres long, with 100 or 150 links. Offsets, perpendicular distances from the chain line to features, locate detail, and a well-conditioned triangle has angles between 30 and 120 degrees. The ranging rod, arrows, cross staff and optical square are basic accessories. Remember the two ruling principles: work from whole to part, and fix every point by at least two measurements. Chain surveying uses triangles because a triangle is the only figure that can be plotted from side lengths alone, which is why it remains the cheapest field method for laying out a field boundary or bund alignment on level ground. Now let us understand compass, plane-table and cross-staff surveying, and their errors. Compass surveying measures the bearings, or directions, of lines with a magnetic compass, and lengths with a chain, useful where there are many details or obstacles. Bearings use the whole-circle system, zero to 360 degrees, or the quadrantal reduced-bearing system. Magnetic bearing differs from true bearing by the magnetic declination, and local attraction from nearby iron is detected when fore and back bearings of a line differ by other than exactly 180 degrees. The prismatic compass measures whole-circle bearings, the cross staff sets out right angles, the plane table plots the survey directly to scale in the field using an alidade, through radiation, intersection, traversing or resection, and the planimeter mechanically measures the area of any plotted irregular figure. Errors are of three kinds: mistakes or gross blunders, which must be eliminated; systematic or cumulative errors, which follow a definite law and can be corrected; and accidental or random errors, which follow the laws of probability and partly cancel out.
172: On this page we study levelling, contouring, and then theodolites and total stations. Levelling determines the relative elevations of points using a level and a graduated staff. A benchmark is a point of known elevation, and the reduced level, RL, of a point is its height above the datum, usually mean sea level. The key formula is height of instrument, HI, equals RL of benchmark plus back sight, and RL of a point equals HI minus fore or intermediate sight. The arithmetic check is: sum of back sights minus sum of fore sights equals last RL minus first RL, which also equals sum of rise minus sum of fall. Contouring connects points of equal elevation with contour lines; the vertical spacing is the contour interval, and closely spaced contours mean a steep slope while widely spaced contours mean a gentle slope. Contours never cross except at an overhanging cliff. Irregular areas are computed by the trapezoidal rule or Simpson's one-third rule, and earthwork volumes by the average-end-area, or trapezoidal, method, or the prismoidal formula. Simpson's rule needs an even number of divisions and is more accurate. For officers, levelling and contouring are the most-used survey skills, because laying out contour bunds and graded bunds exactly on the contour line is the foundation of soil-and-water conservation work. Now, students, let us understand the theodolite, curves, total station and GPS. A theodolite precisely measures horizontal and vertical angles, and theodolite traversing fixes a framework of survey lines by measuring the angles between them and their lengths. Tacheometry uses a theodolite with stadia hairs to measure distances and elevations rapidly without a chain, useful in rough terrain. Curves connecting straight alignments include simple, compound and reverse circular curves and vertical curves, set out by offsets or Rankine's method of deflection angles.
173: Let us finish the surveying instruments and then begin watershed management. GPS, part of the wider Global Navigation Satellite System, GNSS, fixes a point's latitude, longitude and elevation from signals received from at least four satellites, by a method called trilateration, and is now standard for control surveys, mapping and precision agriculture. The electronic theodolite displays angles digitally, and the total station combines an electronic theodolite with an electronic distance-measuring unit, EDM, and a microprocessor, so it reads angles and distances and computes coordinates, areas and levels electronically, storing data for direct transfer to a computer. Remember, a total station measures both angles and distances and computes coordinates, GPS needs a minimum of four satellites for a three-dimensional fix, and Rankine's deflection-angle method is the standard theodolite method for setting out curves. For officers, total stations and GPS now lay out watershed structures, canal alignments and field boundaries far faster and more accurately than chain and compass, and GPS-guided precision farming, meaning variable-rate input application and machine guidance, is an emerging area worth understanding. Now, students, let us begin Block E, Watershed Management. A watershed is the area of land that drains all the rain falling on it to a common outlet, a stream, river or reservoir. It is also called a catchment or drainage basin, and is bounded by a ridge line, the water divide. The watershed, not the individual field, is the natural and most logical unit for planning soil and water conservation, because water and sediment move across field boundaries but stay within the watershed. The guiding principle of watershed development is the ridge-to-valley approach, treating the ridge first and the valley last.
174: On this page we study watershed characteristics and then watershed development, problems, prospects and investigation. Watersheds are classified by size into macro, sub-, milli and micro watersheds; the micro-watershed, commonly 500 to 1000 hectares or less, is the usual planning and treatment unit in India. Physical characteristics such as area, shape, slope and relief, drainage pattern and density, and soil and land use determine how much rain becomes runoff, how fast it leaves, and how much soil it carries. Fan-shaped basins peak in runoff faster than elongated ones, steeper slopes give faster runoff and more erosion, and higher drainage density means quicker runoff. Remember, a watershed is bounded by the ridge line and drains to a single outlet, and treatment always proceeds ridge to valley. Karnataka, being largely semi-arid and rainfed, has adopted the watershed as the core unit of its dryland development, and the Sujala projects and central watershed missions all plan on this ridge-to-valley, micro-watershed basis. Now let us understand watershed development. It is the rational use of land, water and vegetation to conserve soil and water, raise productivity and improve livelihoods sustainably. It addresses problems of soil erosion, runoff and water scarcity, declining groundwater, land degradation and low rainfed yields, with prospects of higher, stable production, recharged wells, reduced erosion and rural employment. Before any treatment, the watershed is investigated: a topographical survey gives the base map of slope and drainage, soil characteristics cover type, depth, texture and erodibility, vegetative cover records existing crops, trees and grass, present land-use practices show current cropping and management, hydrological data covers rainfall, runoff and groundwater, and socio-economic factors cover landholding, livestock, income and willingness to participate.
175: Here we finish watershed investigation and study watershed management planning, land capability and prioritisation. Only after the baseline survey is complete is the treatment plan prepared, because the choice of measures depends entirely on the land's slope, soil, rainfall and the community's needs. An officer is often part of this survey team, mapping soil depth and slope to decide which land can be cropped and which must go under grass or trees, while the socio-economic survey decides whether the community will maintain the structures after the project ends, the real test of success. Now, students, let us understand watershed management, the integrated planning and execution of measures to use and conserve soil, water and vegetation while meeting people's needs. Its objectives are to control runoff and erosion, conserve and harvest water, recharge groundwater, increase and stabilise production, and improve livelihoods. Planning is based on land-capability classification, which groups land into eight classes by capability and limitations. Classes one to four are arable, suited to cultivation, with limitations rising from class one, very good land needing no special practices, to class four, cultivable only with very careful management. Classes five to eight are non-arable, suited only to pasture, forest or wildlife, with class eight being the barest, unfit for cultivation, fit only for recreation or wildlife. Watershed codification is the systematic numbering of watersheds and sub-units for identification, delineation marks the watershed boundary along the ridge line, and prioritisation ranks watersheds for treatment, often using the sediment yield index, so that watersheds losing soil fastest, which threaten downstream reservoirs, are treated first.
176: Let us understand water budgeting and conservation measures. Water budgeting is the accounting of all water entering, leaving and stored in a watershed, a hydrological balance. Rainfall is the input, and runoff, evaporation, transpiration, deep percolation and change in soil and groundwater storage are the components that must balance. The key formula is P equals R plus ET plus delta-S plus D, where P is precipitation, R is runoff, ET is evapotranspiration, delta-S is change in storage, and D is deep percolation. Conservation aims to convert runoff into storage and recharge. Rainwater conservation technologies are of two kinds. In-situ conservation keeps rain where it falls, through contour and graded bunds, contour trenches, terracing, mulching and conservation tillage. Ex-situ conservation collects and stores runoff elsewhere, through farm ponds, percolation tanks, check dams and nala bunds, for recharge and recycling as supplemental or life-saving irrigation. Dry-farming techniques for low-rainfall areas combine moisture conservation, mulching, deep tillage, weed control, with drought-tolerant crops. Remember, in-situ conservation keeps water where it falls, bunds, trenches, terraces, mulching, while ex-situ conservation stores runoff elsewhere, farm ponds, check dams, percolation tanks. Karnataka's Krishi Bhagya scheme promotes farm ponds, called krishi honda, for ex-situ rainwater harvesting and life-saving irrigation in rainfed districts, and an officer promotes contour bunds and farm ponds together, bunds to slow runoff in the field, ponds to store what still escapes. Now, students, let us understand integrated and participatory watershed management. Integrated watershed management treats the whole watershed as one system, combining arable-land development, agriculture and horticulture, non-arable-land development, forestry, fishery and animal husbandry, water-resource development and soil conservation, so every component reinforces the others.
177: This page completes the watershed chapter with participatory watershed management and the project proposal. Execution of a watershed programme follows the plan with works on arable and non-arable land and drainage lines, followed by maintenance, monitoring and evaluation to ensure structures keep working. Participatory watershed management makes the community the driver: a watershed association of all stakeholders, user groups for each set of structures, and self-help groups, especially of women, for thrift and livelihood activities, take ownership, contribute labour or funds, and maintain the assets after the project ends, without which the works decay. Every programme begins with a project proposal setting out the watershed's problems, the planned treatment, the budget, the implementation schedule, and a cost-benefit analysis showing a benefit-to-cost ratio greater than one. Remember, participatory watershed management rests on three community institutions: the watershed association covering the whole community, user groups for each structure or activity, and self-help groups for thrift and livelihoods. The project proposal must include a cost-benefit analysis with a benefit-to-cost ratio above one to be sanctioned. The success of Karnataka's Sujala and integrated watershed management programme, IWMP, watersheds is credited to this participatory model, community watershed committees and self-help groups maintaining the bunds, ponds and plantations long after the engineers leave. An officer's lasting contribution is building this local ownership, not just constructing the structures.
178: This page is a chapter mind map summarising the whole unit on Soil and Water Engineering, so let us do a quick spoken revision tour. The chapter has seven branches. Building materials covers the modular brick at 190 by 90 by 90 millimetres, first-class brick strength of at least 10.5 newtons per square millimetre with under 20 percent water absorption, granite as the strongest common stone, Mangalore interlocking roofing tiles, and timber seasoned to about 12 to 15 percent moisture. Cement and concrete covers clinker formed near 1450 degrees Celsius with 3 to 5 percent gypsum, cement grades 33, 43 and 53 by 28-day strength, Bogue's compounds where C3S gives early strength and C2S gives later strength, M20 concrete meaning 20 newtons per square millimetre with a 1 is to 1.5 is to 3 mix, Abram's law that a lower water-cement ratio gives higher strength, and the Vicat test for initial setting time of at least 30 minutes. Structural analysis covers the elastic curve equation, Euler's buckling formula, effective length rules for different end conditions, simply supported beam deflection under uniform load, the middle-third rule for dams, and indeterminacy degrees for propped cantilever and fixed beams. Soil mechanics covers the plasticity index formula, Terzaghi's effective stress equation, specific gravity of solids around 2.65 to 2.70, the plasticity chart's A-line, and black cotton soil's swell-shrink behaviour. Shear and consolidation covers the Mohr-Coulomb equation, zero cohesion for sand and zero friction angle for undrained clay, the Standard and Modified Proctor tests, and the fact that compaction expels air while consolidation expels water. Surveying covers the levelling formula, the two ruling principles, the standard metric chain, contour spacing and slope, the total station, and GPS needing at least four satellites. Watershed covers the ridge-to-valley definition, the micro-watershed size of 500 to 1000 hectares, land-capability classes one to four as arable and five to eight as non-arable, the sediment yield index for prioritising treatment, in-situ bunds versus ex-situ farm ponds, and the water balance equation.
179: This page is a key-terms-at-a-glance revision table covering the whole unit, so let us go through the important facts quickly, students. The standard modular brick is 190 by 90 by 90 millimetres. A first-class brick needs at least 10.5 newtons per square millimetre strength with water absorption under 20 percent. Mangalore tiles are the interlocking roofing tiles of coastal Karnataka. Ordinary Portland Cement grades are 33, 43 and 53, based on 28-day strength in newtons per square millimetre, and gypsum is added to cement to retard, or slow, the setting time. The main clinker compounds are C3S, C2S, C3A and C4AF, known as Bogue's compounds. Concrete grade M20 means a 28-day characteristic cube strength of 20 newtons per square millimetre, and nominal mixes are M15 as 1 is to 2 is to 4, M20 as 1 is to 1.5 is to 3, and M25 as 1 is to 1 is to 2. In an arch, load acts in compression through the keystone, while a lintel works in bending. The Vicat apparatus tests the initial and final setting time of cement. Euler's buckling load formula is pi-squared EI over effective length squared, with effective length rules for hinged, fixed and free ends. Cantilever tip deflection uses WL cubed over 3EI for a point load, and 5wL to the fourth over 384EI for a uniformly loaded simply supported beam. The middle-third rule keeps the resultant in the middle third of a dam's base to avoid tension. The Hardy Cross method is another name for the moment-distribution method, while the three-moment theorem is Clapeyron's equation for continuous beams. Effective stress equals total stress minus pore pressure, following Terzaghi, and it controls soil strength. The plasticity index is liquid limit minus plastic limit, and the A-line on the plasticity chart separates clay above from silt below.
180: This page finishes the key-terms table and then opens Part B, objective questions covering all five blocks of the unit. From the table, remember that a total station is a theodolite plus EDM giving angles, distances and coordinates together, GPS needs a minimum of four satellites for a three-dimensional position fix, and the watershed unit is the micro-watershed of about 500 to 1000 hectares, treated ridge to valley. Land-capability classes one to four are arable while five to eight are non-arable, eight classes in total, and the sediment yield index is used to prioritise watersheds for treatment. In-situ measures are bunds and trenches, while ex-situ measures are farm ponds and check dams. Participatory institutions are the watershed association, user groups and self-help groups, and Karnataka's flagship programmes are Sujala, aided by the World Bank, and Krishi Bhagya farm ponds. Now the objective questions begin. Question one asks the standard size of a modular brick without mortar joint, and the answer is 190 by 90 by 90 millimetres; the nominal size with a 10 millimetre joint is 200 by 100 by 100, a common trap. Question two asks why gypsum is added to cement clinker, and the answer is to retard, or slow, the setting time, giving working time; accelerating the set is the opposite and a classic wrong option. Question three explains that concrete grade M20 means a 28-day characteristic cube strength of 20 newtons per square millimetre, not a mix ratio or a cement percentage.
181: This page continues the objective questions and answers, testing exam-style traps. Question four confirms the keystone is the central, topmost wedge-shaped unit that locks an arch, while a voussoir is any wedge unit and a springer is where the arch begins. Question five explains a damp-proof course prevents rising ground moisture into walls, not wall strength. Question six defines payback period as the time for savings to recover the initial investment, different from the benefit-to-cost ratio. Question seven gives the effective length for a column fixed at both ends as 0.5 L, while 2L is the fixed-free cantilever case, a common swap. Question eight confirms Euler's critical buckling load formula is Pcr equals pi-squared EI over effective length squared, distinct from the cantilever deflection formula WL cubed over 3EI. Question nine shows that a simply supported beam with a central point load W has maximum deflection WL cubed over 48EI, different from the uniformly distributed load case of 5WL to the fourth over 384EI. Question ten explains the middle-third rule for a masonry gravity dam ensures no tension develops at the base, a separate check from sliding. Question eleven confirms the moment-distribution method for indeterminate beams is also called the Hardy Cross method, while Clapeyron's method is the three-moment equation, a different though related method.
182: This page continues objective questions on structures and soil mechanics. Question twelve shows a propped cantilever beam is statically indeterminate to one degree, while a fixed beam is indeterminate to two degrees, a common point of confusion. Question thirteen confirms Terzaghi's effective stress equation is sigma-prime equals sigma minus u, pore pressure is subtracted, never added. Question fourteen defines the plasticity index as liquid limit minus plastic limit, the difference representing the plastic range, not the sum. Question fifteen clarifies that on the plasticity chart, soils plotting above the A-line are classified as clays, while silts plot below, a position that is often reversed as a trap. Question sixteen identifies the triaxial compression test as the most reliable laboratory shear-strength test for clay because it controls drainage and pore pressure, more reliable than the direct shear test. Question seventeen explains that for a clean sand in the Mohr-Coulomb equation, cohesion c equals zero, while phi equals zero applies instead to undrained clay, a frequently swapped pair. Question eighteen compares Standard and Modified Proctor tests: the Modified Proctor, with greater compactive effort, gives a higher maximum dry density and a lower optimum moisture content, shifting the compaction curve up and to the left. Question nineteen introduces the purpose of Casagrande's and Taylor's methods in a consolidation test.
183: This page continues the objective questions across soil mechanics, earth pressure, slope stability and surveying. Question nineteen's answer confirms both Casagrande's and Taylor's methods find the coefficient of consolidation, cv, while optimum moisture content instead belongs to the compaction test. Question twenty gives Rankine's active earth-pressure coefficient for cohesionless soil as one minus sine phi over one plus sine phi, while the reciprocal expression is the passive coefficient Kp, so active and passive are easily reversed. Question twenty-one confirms earth pressure is minimum in the active state, when the wall moves away from the soil, while passive pressure, when the wall is pushed into the soil, is the maximum. Question twenty-two shows Taylor's stability number is used in slope-stability analysis, a dimensionless parameter distinct from bearing-capacity factors. Question twenty-three restates the two fundamental principles of surveying: fixing a point by two measurements, and always working from the whole to the part, never the reverse. Question twenty-four confirms the height of instrument in levelling equals the reduced level of the benchmark plus the back sight, not minus. Question twenty-five explains that closely spaced contour lines on a map indicate a steep slope, while widely spaced contours indicate a gentle slope, the two being inversely related. Question twenty-six begins describing a total station as a combination of an electronic theodolite and an EDM with a processor.
184: This page finishes the objective questions for the unit, covering surveying, watershed management and building materials, moving into the next chapter. Question twenty-six confirms a total station combines an electronic theodolite, EDM and processor, measuring both angles and distances, unlike a levelling set which measures only height. Question twenty-seven establishes that a minimum of four satellites is required for a three-dimensional GPS position fix, since three satellites give only a two-dimensional fix and the fourth resolves clock error and elevation. Question twenty-eight identifies the watershed, or catchment, as the natural unit for planning soil and water conservation, because water and sediment cross field boundaries but stay within the watershed. Question twenty-nine confirms land-capability classes one to four are arable, suited to cultivation, while classes five to eight are non-arable. Question thirty explains that a farm pond storing harvested runoff for later use is an example of ex-situ rainwater conservation, since it collects and stores water away from where it fell, unlike a contour bund which is in-situ. Question thirty-one confirms watersheds are prioritised for treatment mainly by their sediment yield index, reflecting the rate of soil loss, not population or road connectivity. Question thirty-two identifies Sujala as Karnataka's well-known World Bank-aided watershed development project, distinct from the Krishna Bhagya Jala Nigam, which is an irrigation corporation, not a watershed programme. Question thirty-three then opens a new topic, asking which is the strongest common natural building stone, with granite as the correct answer among laterite, sandstone and limestone, leading into the next chapter's material science content.
185: On this page we finish some general engineering questions and then move into a set of building and civil engineering multiple choice questions with answers. First, granite, an igneous rock, is confirmed as having the highest crushing strength, while laterite is soft when freshly quarried and only hardens on exposure to air. Question 34 asks about the four main compounds of cement clinker, C3S, C2S, C3A and C4AF, which are collectively called Bogue's compounds, named after the chemist; tricalcium silicate, C3S, gives early strength, and dicalcium silicate, C2S, gives later strength. Question 35 covers the instrument for testing the initial and final setting time of cement, which is the Vicat apparatus; remember, the Le-Chatelier apparatus tests soundness, and the Casagrande device tests the liquid limit of soil, so do not confuse these three. Question 36 defines slenderness ratio of a column as effective length divided by least radius of gyration, a high ratio meaning a long column that fails by buckling. Question 37 explains that in a fillet weld, strength is based on throat thickness, about 0.707 times the leg size, not the full leg length. Question 38 gives porosity n related to void ratio e by the formula n equals e divided by 1 plus e. Question 39 says the vane shear test measures undrained strength of soft, saturated clay. Question 40 notes Simpson's one third rule needs an even number of divisions for computing area.
186: This page completes the civil engineering objective questions and then closes the soil and water engineering unit with its reference list. First, we finish question 41 on local attraction in compass surveying, which is suspected when the fore and back bearings of a line differ by other than exactly 180 degrees, indicating nearby iron disturbing the compass needle, so the readings need correction. Question 42 covers treatment of a watershed, which is carried out in the sequence ridge to valley, because this ridge to valley approach treats the upper ridge first so that runoff is slowed before it reaches and erodes the valley below. Question 43 gives the watershed water balance equation, P equals R plus ET plus delta S plus D, where D represents deep percolation, the recharge to groundwater; R is runoff, ET is evapotranspiration, and delta S is the change in storage. After these questions, the page lists the references used for this unit on soil and water engineering, drawn from the Karnataka Public Service Commission syllabus for Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer, Paper 2, Science 15, Agricultural Engineering. Standard textbooks cited include works by Punmia, Jain and Jain on soil mechanics, foundations, strength of materials and surveying; Murthy on geotechnical engineering; Arora on irrigation and water resources; Suresh on soil and water conservation engineering; and Michael and Ojha on principles of agricultural engineering. Relevant Bureau of Indian Standards codes and Karnataka Watershed Development Department reports, including the Sujala Project and Krishi Bhagya scheme guidelines, are also listed.
187: Now, students, we begin Chapter 7, Farm Power and Machinery Engineering, which is Unit 7 of the technical Paper 2, Science 15, combining both theory and objective questions and answers. This chapter covers a very wide range of topics, so let us understand its scope first. It opens with workshop and manufacturing technology, meaning carpentry, smithy and forging, gas and arc welding, casting, and machine tools like the lathe, shaper, drilling machine and milling machine. It then moves into basic electrical engineering, covering magnetic circuits, the single phase transformer, DC machines, single phase induction and shaded pole motors, and AC power. Renewable energy follows, including solar thermal and photovoltaic systems and wind energy. The agricultural machinery core covers farm mechanisation, sources of farm power, field capacity and machinery economics, hitching systems, tillage and tillage implements, and sowing and planting machinery, along with materials and heat treatment for farm machines. The chapter closes with bio energy, meaning biogas, gasification, pyrolysis, biodiesel and bio hydrogen. For a Karnataka Agricultural Officer, this subject is intensely practical, delivered through the Krishi Yantra Dhare custom hire network, the College of Agricultural Engineering at the University of Agricultural Sciences, and renewable schemes like the Pavagada solar park and Surya Raitha solar pumps. A figure shows the five sources of farm power, human, animal, mechanical, electrical and renewable, each with typical examples like manual labour, bullocks, tractors, pump motors, and solar pumps or windmills.
188: Here, we start section 7.1, Carpentry, Wood and Woodworking Operations. Carpentry is defined as the working of wood into useful articles by marking, sawing, planing, chiselling, boring and joining. Wood is broadly classed as softwood, from coniferous trees such as pine and deodar, which is light and easy to work, and hardwood, from broad leaved trees such as teak, rosewood and sal, which is dense, strong and durable. Good timber must be seasoned to remove moisture, which prevents warping, shrinkage and decay, either by natural air drying or artificial kiln drying. The main woodworking operations are marking and measuring, sawing, planing which produces a flat smooth surface, chiselling, boring and finishing. A table lists carpentry tools by function, such as the steel rule and try square for marking and measuring, the carpenter's vice for holding, rip and cross cut saws for cutting, the jack plane for planing, the firmer chisel for chiselling, the bradawl and gimlet for boring, and the mallet for striking. Wood pieces are joined using joints like the lap joint, mortise and tenon joint, dovetail joint, bridle joint and tongue and groove joint, chosen according to the load and how the surfaces meet. For an Agricultural Officer, carpentry skills let officers and farmers fabricate seedling trays, grain storage structures, bullock cart bodies, fencing and tool handles locally, cutting cost and dependence on outside repair shops. Section 7.2 then introduces smithy tools and forging operations, where heated mild steel or wrought iron is hammered on an anvil in its plastic state, using tools like the forge, anvil, swage block, tongs and hammers, refining the grain to give tough, shock resistant parts.
189: On this page we complete a table of basic forging operations, including bending which forms an angle or curve, punching and drifting which makes and enlarges holes, setting down or fullering which forms a step or shoulder, and forge welding which joins two heated pieces by hammering. An important memory point is not to confuse upsetting, which shortens and thickens metal, with drawing down, which lengthens and thins it, since these are opposites and a common exam trap; also, forge welding is done in the solid, plastic state, not by melting the metal. For farmers, village blacksmiths forge and re-sharpen plough shares, sickles, spades, crowbars and tine points, the routine repair that keeps tillage and harvest tools in service through the season. Section 7.3 then covers welding, both gas, using oxyacetylene, and arc welding, defined as joining metals by fusing them together so the joint is as strong as the parent metal. In oxyacetylene gas welding, oxygen and acetylene burn at the torch tip, reaching about 3,200 degrees Celsius, and three flame settings are used based on the oxygen to acetylene ratio, a neutral flame at roughly 1 to 1 for general steel welding, an oxidising flame with excess oxygen for brass and bronze, and a carburising or reducing flame with excess acetylene for hard facing and high carbon steel. In arc welding, an electric arc between an electrode and the workpiece supplies the heat, using equipment like a welding transformer, electrode holder, earth clamp and a flux coated electrode; either AC or DC current may be used, with DC allowing polarity control that governs the depth of penetration. Section 7.4, Casting and Foundry Processes, then begins.
190: Let us understand casting now, defined as pouring molten metal into a mould cavity of the desired shape and letting it solidify, the cheapest route to complex shapes and large components. Sand casting is the most common process, where a pattern, a replica of the part, is packed in moulding sand to form the cavity, a core makes hollow sections, and a gating system of sprue, runner, gate and riser guides the metal in. Casting is classified as expendable mould types, like sand, shell and investment, which are broken to release the casting, or permanent mould types, like die, gravity and centrifugal, which are reused. A table compares sand casting, using cheap versatile sand moulds for engine blocks and pulleys; die casting, using metal moulds and pressure injection for high volume small parts; investment or lost wax casting for precision components; and centrifugal casting, where the mould is spun, for pipes, bushes and rings. Common casting defects include blow holes, shrinkage cavities, cold shuts, misruns and porosity, each traced to a fault in metal temperature, mould venting or gating design. Cast iron and cast steel are used for plough frogs, pump impellers, gear housings, pulleys and engine parts of farm machinery, so understanding casting helps an officer judge component quality and anticipate failure modes. Section 7.5 then introduces the centre lathe, called the mother of machine tools, which holds the workpiece between centres or in a chuck and rotates it while a single point cutting tool removes metal. Its main parts are the bed, headstock, tailstock, carriage and lead screw. A table of main lathe operations lists turning, facing, taper turning, thread cutting, drilling and boring, knurling, and parting.
191: This page finishes the lathe topic and then covers two more machine tools. Lathe accessories include the three jaw self centring chuck, four jaw independent chuck, face plate, centres, mandrel, steady rest and follower rest, chosen according to the shape, accuracy and concentricity required. A key memory point is that a three jaw chuck is self centring, quick to use for round or hexagonal work, while a four jaw chuck holds each jaw independently, useful for irregular or off centre turning with higher accuracy, and reversing these two in an answer is a common trap. For farmers, lathe work turns and threads shafts, bushes, pump spindles and bolts during farm machinery repair, a core skill at agricultural workshops. Section 7.6 then covers the shaper, which machines flat surfaces using a reciprocating single point tool, moving forward on the cutting stroke and back on the faster idle return stroke, driven by a quick return mechanism, usually a crank and slotted lever. A table lists shaper parts, the ram which carries the tool head, the table which holds the work, the standard shaper where the ram moves only horizontally, and the universal shaper whose table can also tilt and swivel. Shapers machine flat, slot and groove surfaces and are simple and cheap for small jobs, though largely superseded by milling machines for production work; in repair shops they cut keyways in pulleys and shafts. Section 7.7 introduces drilling machines and twist drills, where drilling produces or enlarges cylindrical holes using a rotating multi point tool. A table lists machine types from the sensitive bench drill for small holes, to the pillar or upright type, the radial type for large heavy work, the gang type with several spindles, and the multiple spindle type for many holes at once.
192: On this page we learn that the twist drill has a body with two helical flutes for chip removal, a point, a shank and cutting lips, and the standard point angle for general purpose drills is 118 degrees, a favourite direct recall figure. Allied operations include reaming, which finishes and sizes an existing hole rather than creating a new one, boring, counterboring, countersinking and tapping. Drilling is essential to bolt cultivator tynes, mount bearings, fix implement frames and assemble trailers, and accurate hole sizes determine whether a repaired implement runs true. Section 7.8 then covers milling machines, where a rotating multi tooth cutter removes metal while the work is fed past it, producing flat and contoured surfaces, slots, gears and splines at high rates. The two basic methods are up or conventional milling, where the feed opposes cutter rotation, and down or climb milling, where feed and rotation are in the same direction, giving a better finish. Common machine types are the column and knee type, in plain and universal forms, and the bed type. A table explains that in the plain column and knee mill the spindle is horizontal and the table moves in three directions, while the universal mill's table can swivel, enabling helical milling; indexing using a dividing head divides work into equal angular parts for cutting gears and splines. In workshops serving the farm sector, milling produces gear teeth, keyways and flat machined faces in gearboxes and power tiller transmissions. Section 7.9 then begins on magnetic circuits, introducing electromotive force, the voltage induced whenever magnetic flux linking a coil changes, following Faraday's law, and the magnetic circuit as the closed path followed by magnetic flux, driven by magneto motive force and opposed by reluctance.
193: Let us understand the electric versus magnetic circuit analogy on this page. A table compares magneto motive force, MMF, equal to N times I in ampere turns, to EMF in volts, both driving the respective quantity; flux Phi in weber corresponds to current I in amperes; reluctance S corresponds to resistance R; and flux density B in tesla corresponds to current density. In a series magnetic circuit with one flux path, the total MMF is the sum of the MMF for each part, while in a parallel magnetic circuit the flux divides between paths, like current in parallel resistors. Iron core losses are of two kinds, hysteresis loss, the energy lost in repeatedly re-magnetising the core, and eddy current loss, caused by circulating currents induced in the core, reduced by using thin laminations and silicon steel. An important memory point is that hysteresis loss varies with frequency to the first power, while eddy current loss varies with frequency squared; laminating the core cuts eddy losses, while choosing silicon steel cuts hysteresis loss, and examiners often swap these two remedies in questions. These losses explain why a pump set motor or village transformer runs warm, and energy efficient, BEE star rated motors and transformers use better core steel. Section 7.10 then introduces the single phase transformer, a static device with no moving parts that transfers AC power between circuits by electromagnetic induction at constant frequency, stepping voltage up or down, using a laminated silicon steel core with primary and secondary windings. A table of key relations includes the EMF equation, E equals 4.44 times f times N times the maximum flux, the turns to voltage ratio, voltage regulation, and efficiency, which is maximum when copper loss equals iron loss.
194: This page continues the transformer discussion, noting that on load, the secondary current creates a demagnetising MMF balanced by the primary drawing more current, and two standard tests reveal transformer parameters, the open circuit test measuring iron core loss and magnetising current, and the short circuit test measuring copper loss and equivalent impedance; iron loss stays constant at all loads, while copper loss varies with the square of the load current. A key memory point is that the EMF equation's constant, 4.44, comes from 4 times the form factor of 1.11 for a sine wave, and the open circuit test gives iron loss while the short circuit test gives copper loss, a pairing worth memorising. Distribution transformers on rural feeders step 11 kilovolts down to 400 or 230 volts for pump sets and homes, so correct sizing and low no load loss matter greatly during the irrigation season. Section 7.11 then covers DC machines, generator and motor, explaining that a DC machine works as a generator, converting mechanical to electrical energy, or as a motor, converting electrical to mechanical energy, with identical construction for both, comprising the yoke, field poles and windings, armature core and winding, commutator and brushes. A table of core equations gives the generated or back EMF formula, torque formula, motor back EMF as supply voltage minus armature current times armature resistance, and the lap versus wave winding relation. Armature reaction, the distortion of the main field by the armature's own MMF, is countered by interpoles; among motors, the shunt motor runs at nearly constant speed while the series motor gives high starting torque but must never run unloaded since it would race to a dangerous speed, and starters limit the heavy starting current.
195: On this page we finish DC machines with a memory point that one should never start a large DC motor directly on line, since at the instant of starting the back EMF is zero, making the current huge, so a starter resistance limits it; also, a series motor must not run on no load since it over-speeds, while shunt motors give constant speed and series motors give high starting torque. DC and universal motors appear in small farm tools and battery driven equipment, and the same starting current and speed control principles carry over to the AC motors that run irrigation pumps and chaff cutters. Section 7.12 then covers single phase induction and shaded pole motors, explaining that the single phase induction motor is the commonest small motor, but a single winding produces only a pulsating field with no starting torque, explained by the double field revolving theory as two equal, oppositely rotating fields that cancel at standstill, so it needs a starting arrangement. A table of starting methods by phase split lists the split phase type using a resistance start winding for low to moderate torque, the capacitor start type giving high torque, the capacitor start capacitor run type using two capacitors for a high, smooth running torque, and the shaded pole type using a copper shading ring for very low torque but simple, cheap construction. In phase splitting, an auxiliary starting winding is displaced in space with different impedance so its current is out of phase with the main winding, creating a rotating field that starts the rotor, after which a centrifugal switch cuts out the start winding.
196: Let us understand the shaded pole motor further, which uses a short circuited copper ring on part of each pole to delay the flux there, producing a weak sweeping field, used in fans and small appliances where starting torque is unimportant. Speed is controlled by varying applied voltage, tapping windings, or electronically varying supply frequency using a variable frequency drive. A key memory point is that a single phase motor cannot self start because of the double field revolving theory, and the fix is always to create a rotating field, by phase split, capacitor, or shading ring, with the capacitor start motor giving the highest starting torque among common types. These motors run small irrigation pumps, chaff cutters and domestic appliances on single phase feeders in villages, with capacitor start types preferred for loads like centrifugal pumps needing higher starting torque. Section 7.13 then covers AC power, power factor and power measurement, distinguishing real or active power P, which does useful work, reactive power Q, which oscillates with the magnetic field and does no net work, and apparent power S, their vector sum, so that S squared equals P squared plus Q squared; the power factor is the cosine of the angle between voltage and current. A table, the power triangle, lists apparent power as V times I in volt amperes, active power as V I cosine phi in watts, reactive power as V I sine phi in VAR, and power factor as dimensionless. Three phase power is measured by wattmeter methods, the one wattmeter method for balanced loads only, the two wattmeter method, standard for three wire systems whether balanced or not, and the three wattmeter method for unbalanced four wire loads; a low, lagging power factor, common with induction motor loads like pumps, is corrected using capacitor banks.
197: This page finishes the AC power topic and introduces engine and renewable energy content. A key memory point states apparent power S is always the biggest of the three quantities, since power factor cannot exceed 1, and the two wattmeter method needs only two watt meters for a three phase, three wire system; a low power factor means high current for the same useful power. Agricultural pump sets are largely inductive and run at a low power factor, overloading rural feeders, so fitting capacitors on pump sets, often subsidised, improves the power factor and supply reliability, a routine advisory for an Agricultural Officer. A figure then shows the four stroke internal combustion engine cycle, with one power stroke every two crankshaft revolutions across four strokes, suction where the inlet valve opens and the piston moves down drawing in the air fuel charge, compression where both valves are shut and the piston moves up compressing the charge, power where the charge ignites and drives the piston down doing work, and exhaust where the exhaust valve opens and the piston moves up expelling burnt gas. Section 7.14 then introduces renewable energy sources, defined as energy sources naturally replenished within a human timescale, in contrast to finite fossil fuels, though they have limitations of low energy density, intermittency, site dependence and high initial cost. A table lists renewable sources including solar for the sun's radiation, wind for kinetic energy of moving air, biomass or bio energy for chemical energy of organic matter, small hydro for flowing water potential energy, geothermal for the earth's interior heat, and ocean for tidal, wave and thermal energy. Karnataka is noted as a renewable energy leader, with the Pavagada Shakti Sthala solar park in Tumakuru among the world's largest.
198: On this page, Karnataka's leadership in renewable energy continues, noting its solar and wind capacity directly powers solar irrigation pumps for farmers. A classification figure shows renewable energy sources branching into solar, wind, bio energy, small hydro, geothermal and ocean, each with sub types like thermal and photovoltaic for solar, or tidal, wave and OTEC for ocean, summarised as clean, inexhaustible and decentralised but variable and capital intensive, under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy programme. Section 7.15 then covers solar energy, thermal and photovoltaic, explaining that solar radiation just outside the atmosphere, called the solar constant, is about 1,367 watts per square metre. Solar energy is used in two ways, solar thermal conversion, turning radiation into heat using flat plate collectors giving 40 to 80 degrees Celsius for water heating and drying, or concentrating collectors for much higher temperatures, with solar dryers using convection to dry farm produce. A table compares solar thermal, which converts to heat using collectors for water heating and cooking, against solar photovoltaic, which converts to electricity using solar cells for pumps and lighting. In photovoltaics, a solar cell is a semiconductor p n junction where sunlight frees electron hole pairs and the junction field drives a DC current, with cells combining into modules and modules into arrays; PV systems are either stand alone with battery storage for remote pumps, or grid connected, often with net metering. A memory point notes the solar constant is about 1.36 kilowatts per square metre, and the assembly order is cell to module to array.
199: Let us understand how Karnataka's Surya Raitha scheme and the national PM-KUSUM scheme give farmers subsidised solar photovoltaic pump sets, cutting diesel use and grid load, while solar dryers preserve chillies, grapes as raisins, and other Karnataka produce, raising shelf life and price. Section 7.16 then covers wind energy, converting the kinetic energy of moving air into mechanical or electrical power, with the power available in wind proportional to air density, rotor swept area, and the cube of wind speed, making wind speed decisive; the Betz limit caps the fraction of wind power a rotor can extract at 0.593, or 59.3 per cent. A table of terms explains that wind power varies with velocity cubed, the Betz limit is the maximum 59.3 per cent extractable, HAWT means horizontal axis wind turbine, the most common type, VAWT means vertical axis wind turbine like Darrieus or Savonius designs, cut in, rated and cut out are the speeds to start, reach rated output, and shut down, and induction generators are common in grid connected turbines. A memory point stresses that doubling wind speed gives eight times the power, since power varies with velocity cubed, and the Betz limit is a theoretical maximum never exceeded, not the actual turbine efficiency, which is lower. Karnataka is among India's top wind power states, in belts like Chitradurga, Gadag and Davanagere, feeding a grid that also powers irrigation. Section 7.17 then introduces farm mechanisation, field capacity and machinery economics, defining mechanisation as the use of machines and power to raise productivity, timeliness and labour efficiency, with a table beginning on theoretical field capacity, calculated as width in metres times speed in kilometres per hour divided by 10, giving hectares per hour.
200: This page continues field capacity and economics, defining effective field capacity as the actual area covered per hour including losses, field efficiency as effective divided by theoretical capacity times 100 percent, and time losses from turning, filling, adjustment and idle travel. Machinery cost has two parts, fixed costs that occur whether or not the machine works, summarised as the DIRTI five, depreciation, interest, taxes, insurance and housing, and variable or operating costs depending on use, like fuel, lubricants, repairs and labour; comparing owning against hiring decides the break even area, below which hiring is cheaper and above which owning pays, the economic basis of custom hire centres. A worked example shows a tractor drawn implement 2.0 metres wide working at 5 kilometres per hour has a theoretical field capacity of 1.0 hectare per hour, and if it actually covers 0.8 hectares in an hour after turning and filling losses, the field efficiency is 80 percent. The page then covers hitching systems and controls, explaining implements attach to a tractor as trailed, fully supported on its own wheels, semi mounted, partly on the tractor and partly on a wheel, or mounted, fully carried on the tractor's three point linkage, which is sized in categories one, two and three by power. The hydraulic system gives position control, holding a fixed implement height, and draft control, which senses pulling force and automatically adjusts depth to keep draft constant. Karnataka's Krishi Yantra Dhare scheme, launched in 2014, runs custom hire centres at hobli level through trusts such as SKDRDP, putting tractors, rotavators and harvesters within reach of small farmers.
201: On this page, a figure classifies tillage implements into primary tillage, for the deep first cut, including the mould board plough, disc plough and chisel plough or subsoiler, which invert soil except for the chisel type, and secondary tillage, for pulverising and levelling, including the disc or spike harrow, cultivator and rotavator, which refine a ready seedbed. The text then covers land reclamation and earth moving equipment, used for levelling, bunding, removing scrub, and reclaiming saline, waterlogged or ravine land. A table lists the bulldozer, a tractor with a front blade for clearing, pushing and rough levelling, the scraper for cutting, hauling and spreading soil, the motor grader for fine grading and shaping bunds and field channels, the land leveller, including the laser leveller, for precise grading for irrigation efficiency, and the ditcher or ripper for digging drains and breaking hard subsoil. A key memory point clarifies that the mould board plough inverts the soil, burying weeds and residue, while the chisel plough and subsoiler do not invert, they shatter and loosen the soil, so one should choose the chisel or subsoiler for breaking a hardpan or for moisture conservation, not for weed burial, a heavily tested distinction. On Karnataka's red and black soils, an Agricultural Officer advises mould board or disc ploughing for primary tillage and a chisel plough or subsoiler to break the hardpan in long cultivated fields, conserving limited monsoon moisture in rain fed districts. Section 7.19 then begins on sowing, planting and transplanting machinery, where a seed drill drops seed in continuous rows.
202: Here, we continue with sowing and planting machinery, noting a planter places seeds at a precise spacing, for example for maize and cotton, while a transplanter sets out raised seedlings, notably paddy, and no till or strip till drills sow directly into untilled soil, conserving residue and moisture. A table of seed drill components lists the seed and fertiliser hopper for holding material, the metering mechanism, using fluted roller or cup feed types, which meters seed at a set rate, the seed tube conducting seed to the furrow, the furrow opener of shoe, hoe or disc types, the covering device closing the furrow, and the ground or drive wheel driving the metering mechanism. Calibration sets the seed rate before sowing, by jacking up the drill, turning the drive wheel a set number of revolutions equal to a known field distance, collecting and weighing the seed, then adjusting until the rate matches the target in kilograms per hectare. A memory point distinguishes a seed drill, giving continuous rows, from a planter, giving precise individual spacing, and a transplanter, which sets out rice seedlings; calibration by collecting and weighing seed over a measured distance is a near certain descriptive exam question. Karnataka's mechanisation schemes promote seed cum fertiliser drills and mechanical transplanters for paddy, with correct calibration preventing seed wastage. Section 7.20 then covers materials and heat treatment for farm machines, explaining that parts must resist wear, shock and corrosion in abrasive soil, so materials are chosen for strength, hardness, toughness and fatigue resistance, including grey cast iron for frames, mild steel for general structure, and alloy or boron steels for shares, tines and ground engaging edges. A table of heat treatment processes begins with annealing, normalising, hardening, tempering, and case hardening.
203: Let us understand heat treatment further on this page. Critical, ground engaging components like plough shares, cultivator points and disc edges are surface or case hardened, so a hard, wear resistant skin sits over a tough core that resists shock, tailoring the same steel to different needs, hard where it cuts soil and tough where it takes impact. A key memory point pairs hardening, which makes steel hard but brittle, with tempering, which follows to restore toughness; annealing softens through slow cooling, while hardening hardens through rapid quenching, and case hardening gives a hard surface with a tough core, ideal for a plough share. Knowing that a plough share should be hardened, wear resistant steel, re-sharpenable by a smith, helps an officer judge implement quality and advise farmers against cheap, soft steel parts that wear out in a single season.
