Section 7.21 then introduces biogas technology, a combustible gas produced by anaerobic, oxygen free digestion of organic matter, such as cattle dung, crop residue and kitchen or farm waste, by methanogenic bacteria. The gas is roughly 55 to 65 percent methane and 35 to 45 percent carbon dioxide, with traces of hydrogen sulphide, methane being the combustible part; digestion passes through four stages, hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis. A table of common biogas plant designs lists the floating drum or KVIC type, with a steel gas holder floating on slurry giving constant gas pressure, the fixed dome or Deenbandhu and Janata type, a cheaper fixed masonry dome with variable pressure, and the balloon or bag type, a flexible, portable, low cost digester. Gas yield depends on temperature, with an optimum of 30 to 40 degrees Celsius, pH near neutral, and the carbon to nitrogen ratio, with an optimum of about 25 to 30 to 1.
204: On this page we finish biogas and cover gasification and pyrolysis, then begin liquid biofuels. The digested spent slurry is a high quality, nitrogen rich manure returned to the field, so a biogas plant gives both fuel and fertiliser, though it needs daily feeding and is sensitive to temperature; family biogas plants under national programmes like GOBAR-dhan are promoted across rural Karnataka for cattle owning households. Section 7.22 covers biomass gasification and pyrolysis, where pyrolysis is thermal decomposition of biomass without oxygen, yielding char, bio oil and combustible gas, while gasification is partial combustion with limited air, producing producer gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide, hydrogen, methane and nitrogen used to run engines or provide heat. A table of gasifier types lists the updraft gasifier, where air enters the bottom and gas leaves the top with high tar, the downdraft gasifier, where gas is drawn down through the hot zone giving low tar, engine grade gas, and the crossdraft or fluidised bed type; the four reaction zones from top to bottom are drying, pyrolysis, oxidation and reduction. A memory point clarifies pyrolysis uses no oxygen giving char, bio oil and gas, gasification uses limited oxygen giving producer gas, and combustion uses full oxygen giving only heat, with the downdraft gasifier being the one to remember for power generation, useful for irrigation pumps using rice husk, coconut shell or arecanut waste in coastal and Malnad Karnataka. Section 7.23 then introduces biodiesel, bio hydrogen and the bio energy environment, where biodiesel is made by transesterification of vegetable oil or animal fat with an alcohol using an alkali catalyst, producing fatty acid methyl esters plus glycerol, preferably from non edible feedstocks like Jatropha, Pongamia and neem.
205: On this page, let us finish the topic of bio-energy. Bio-hydrogen is produced biologically by three routes, biophotolysis where algae split water, dark fermentation, and photo-fermentation. Improved biomass cook-stoves raise combustion efficiency and cut smoke for rural kitchens, an important rural welfare point. Now, the environmental case for bio-energy. Biomass is said to be carbon-neutral in principle, because the carbon dioxide released on burning was recently absorbed by the plant during its growth. So bio-energy helps mitigate greenhouse-gas emissions, though we must honestly assess the land use, water demand, and emissions involved. There is an Agri Officer Lens box here. Pongamia, also called honge, and other non-edible oilseeds grow well on Karnataka's wastelands and bunds. Promoting these for biodiesel production, alongside improved cook-stoves and ethanol made from sugarcane molasses, fits directly with the state's bio-energy and farmer-income goals. So remember, three hydrogen production routes, biophotolysis, dark fermentation, and photo-fermentation, and the twin benefits of bio-energy, environmental mitigation and farmer income through crops like pongamia and sugarcane.
206: Now, students, this page gives us the Chapter Mind Map for Farm Power and Machinery, a wonderful revision tool. The mind map has seven branches around the central topic. First, Workshop and Welding, covering oxyacetylene flame temperature around 3200 degrees Celsius, arc welding temperature around 6000 degrees, the carburising, neutral and oxidising flames, filler rod and flux removing oxides, and brazing above 450 degrees versus soldering below 450 degrees. Second, Machine Tools, covering the twist drill point angle of 118 degrees, the lathe as the mother of machine tools, cutting speed formula pi D N over 1000, rake and clearance angles, and grinding wheels made of abrasive plus bond. Third, Electrical Machines, covering transformer EMF, induction motors, slip, synchronous speed, and star-delta starters. Fourth, Renewable Energy, covering the solar constant of 1367 watts per square metre, the Betz limit of 59.3 percent, wind power formula, photovoltaic cells, and the Pavagada solar park in Karnataka. Fifth, Farm Machinery, covering field capacity, three-point linkage, PTO standard speed of 540 rpm, and field efficiency. Sixth, Tillage Implements. Seventh, Biogas and Bio-energy. Use this mind map as your quick revision map before the exam.
207: Here, students, is a Key Terms at a Glance table, extremely useful for quick revision. Let us go through the key facts. The twist-drill point angle is 118 degrees for general purpose. Oxyacetylene flame temperature is about 3200 degrees Celsius, with the neutral flame having an oxygen to acetylene ratio of about 1 to 1. The three welding flames are neutral, oxidising, and carburising, which is also called reducing. The lathe is called the mother of machine tools, with a three-jaw self-centring chuck and a four-jaw independent chuck. The shaper works on a crank-and-slotted-lever quick-return mechanism. In up milling, feed is against rotation, while in down or climb milling, feed is with rotation. Faraday's EMF equation is e equals minus N times d phi by dt. Magnetomotive force equals N times I, in ampere-turns. Hysteresis loss is proportional to frequency, while eddy current loss is proportional to frequency squared, which is why cores are laminated. The transformer EMF equation is E equals 4.44 f N phi max. The open-circuit test gives iron loss, the short-circuit test gives copper loss. For DC generators, EMF equals P phi Z N over 60 A. For DC motors, torque equals P phi Z Ia over 2 pi A, and back EMF equals V minus Ia Ra. The series DC motor has high starting torque but must never run on no load. Single-phase induction motors do not self-start, needing phase-splitting, and the capacitor-start motor gives the highest starting torque while the shaded-pole motor gives the lowest. For AC power, apparent power S equals VI, active power P equals VI cos phi, reactive power Q equals VI sin phi. The two-wattmeter method gives P equals W1 plus W2. The solar constant is about 1367 watts per square metre. Wind power varies as velocity cubed, and the Betz limit caps extractable wind power at 59.3 percent.
208: Continuing the Key Terms table, students. The three-point linkage has two lower links plus one top link, giving draft and position control. Earth-moving machines include the bulldozer, scraper, grader, leveller, and ripper. Fixed costs of machine ownership follow the acronym DIRTI, standing for Depreciation, Interest, Repairs and taxes, Taxes, and Insurance and housing. The mould-board plough has four main parts, the share, mould-board, landside, and frog. The mould-board plough and disc plough invert the soil, while the chisel plough and subsoiler do not. Seed-drill metering uses fluted-roller or cup-feed mechanisms, and drills must be calibrated to set the correct seed rate in kilograms per hectare. Heat treatment works as a pair, hardening makes steel brittle, and tempering then restores toughness. Biogas composition is 55 to 65 percent methane plus carbon dioxide, produced by anaerobic digestion. The floating-drum plant is called the KVIC design, and the fixed-dome plant is called the Deenbandhu design. The optimum carbon to nitrogen ratio for biogas feedstock is about 25 to 30 to 1. Producer gas from gasification contains carbon monoxide, hydrogen, methane, and nitrogen. The downdraft gasifier gives low-tar, engine-grade gas. Biodiesel is made by transesterification, giving methyl esters and glycerol. Now Part B begins, a bank of fifty objective questions spanning workshop technology, electrical engineering, renewable energy, farm machinery, and bio-energy. Question one asks the standard point angle of a general-purpose twist drill, and the answer is 118 degrees. Question two asks about the neutral flame used for general steel welding. Question three covers the forging operation called upsetting, which increases cross-section while reducing length.
209: Continuing the objective questions, students. Question four explains that a three-jaw chuck is preferred because it self-centres round or hexagonal work quickly, while a four-jaw chuck holds each jaw independently for off-centre work. Question five confirms the shaper machine uses the quick-return mechanism. Question six clarifies that in down or climb milling, feed direction is the same as cutter rotation, the opposite of up milling. Question seven explains sand casting uses an expendable sand mould, which is broken to remove the casting, unlike permanent metal moulds used in die casting. Question eight confirms the lathe is called the mother of machine tools. Question nine gives the standard gating sequence in sand casting as sprue, then runner, then gate, then riser, with the riser feeding shrinkage as the casting cools. Question ten explains that reaming finishes and sizes an existing hole, it does not create a new hole. Question eleven gives the transformer EMF equation as E equals 4.44 f N phi max, distinguishing it from the DC machine EMF equation which looks different. These questions test your understanding of workshop processes and basic electrical machine formulas, so make sure you can distinguish similar-looking equations for transformers versus DC machines.
210: Continuing the objective questions on electrical machines, students. Question twelve explains the open-circuit or no-load test on a transformer gives mainly the iron or core loss and the magnetising current, while the short-circuit test gives copper loss. Question thirteen explains eddy-current loss is reduced mainly by using thin laminations, since a solid core would increase this loss. Question fourteen clarifies hysteresis loss varies with frequency to the first power, while eddy-current loss varies with frequency squared. Question fifteen explains that in the DC machine EMF equation, for a wave winding, A equals 2, since a wave winding has two parallel paths, while a lap winding has A equal to P. Question sixteen warns that a series DC motor must never be started on no load, because it will race to a dangerously high speed, unlike a shunt motor which runs at nearly constant speed. Question seventeen explains a DC motor needs a starter because at the instant of starting, the back EMF is zero, so the current would be very high without a starter resistance. Question eighteen explains a single-phase induction motor is not self-starting because of the double-field revolving effect, where two equal, opposite rotating fields give zero net starting torque at standstill. Question nineteen tells us that among common single-phase motors, the capacitor-start motor gives the highest starting torque, while the shaded-pole motor gives the lowest.
211: Continuing, students. Question twenty explains the shaded-pole single-phase motor starts by means of a short-circuited copper shading ring on part of each pole, which delays the flux there to create a weak rotating field. Question twenty-one confirms apparent power in an AC circuit is given by S equals VI, in volt-amperes, distinct from active power VI cos phi. Question twenty-two explains that in the two-wattmeter method, total three-phase power equals W1 plus W2, while the difference W1 minus W2 is used to find the power-factor angle. Question twenty-three explains that a low lagging power factor on agricultural pump-sets is corrected by connecting capacitors in parallel, which improves the power factor and cuts losses. Question twenty-four gives the solar constant as approximately 1367 watts per square metre, roughly 1.36 kilowatts per square metre just outside the atmosphere. Question twenty-five confirms a solar photovoltaic cell is essentially a semiconductor p-n junction that converts light directly to DC electricity, unlike a thermal collector which produces heat. Question twenty-six gives the correct assembly order of a photovoltaic system as cell, then module, then array. Question twenty-seven explains wind power varies with the cube of wind speed. Question twenty-eight introduces the Betz limit, the maximum fraction of wind power a rotor can extract.
212: Continuing, students. The answer to question twenty-eight is that the Betz limit equals 0.593, or 59.3 percent, the theoretical maximum extractable wind power. Question twenty-nine explains a Savonius rotor is a vertical-axis wind turbine, a drag-type design, while the Darrieus rotor is a lift-type vertical-axis turbine. Question thirty gives the theoretical field capacity formula for an implement as width in metres times speed in kilometres per hour, divided by 10, giving hectares per hour. Question thirty-one identifies depreciation as a fixed cost of owning a farm machine, since it occurs regardless of use, unlike fuel which is a variable cost. Question thirty-two explains that an implement fully carried on the three-point linkage is classed as mounted, distinct from trailed implements which run on their own wheels, and semi-mounted implements which are partly on a wheel. Question thirty-three confirms the three-point linkage of a tractor consists of two lower links and one top link, forming a triangle, sized in Categories one, two, and three. Question thirty-four explains draft control on a tractor's three-point linkage works by sensing the pulling force and automatically adjusting depth to keep the draft steady, while position control simply fixes the height. Question thirty-five identifies the mould-board as the part of a mould-board plough that turns and inverts the furrow slice, while the share cuts it horizontally. Question thirty-six asks which implement breaks a hardpan without inverting the soil.
213: Continuing, students. The answer to question thirty-six is the chisel plough or subsoiler, which shatters the subsoil without inversion, unlike the mould-board plough which inverts. Question thirty-seven describes the rotavator as a rotary tillage implement that pulverises the soil in a single pass. Question thirty-eight explains that calibration of a seed drill is done to set the correct seed rate in kilograms per hectare. Question thirty-nine identifies the motor grader as the machine used mainly for fine grading and shaping field channels and bunds, while the bulldozer does rough clearing. Question forty explains that hardening of steel is usually followed by tempering, in order to reduce brittleness and restore toughness, since full softening would instead be called annealing. Question forty-one explains that case hardening of a plough share gives it a hard, wear-resistant surface over a tough core, ideal for ground-engaging parts. Question forty-two confirms biogas produced by anaerobic digestion is mainly composed of methane and carbon dioxide, roughly 55 to 65 percent methane, while producer gas from gasification is instead rich in carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Question forty-three identifies the fixed-dome biogas plant as also being called the Deenbandhu plant, while KVIC refers to the floating-drum type. Question forty-four then asks about the optimum carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for biogas feedstock, which we will see answered as about 25 to 30 to 1.
214: Continuing and concluding the objective question bank, students. Question forty-five explains pyrolysis differs from gasification in that pyrolysis occurs in the absence of oxygen entirely, being thermal decomposition, while gasification uses limited oxygen. Question forty-six identifies the downdraft gasifier as giving low-tar, engine-quality producer gas, since it draws gas through the hot zone. Question forty-seven confirms biodiesel is produced from vegetable oils by transesterification with alcohol, yielding methyl esters and glycerol, while fermentation instead gives bioethanol. Question forty-eight identifies densification, meaning briquetting or pelletising, as the process of compacting loose crop residues for better storage and burning. Question forty-nine describes Karnataka's Krishi Yantra Dhare programme as a farm-machinery custom-hire scheme, providing machinery through hobli-level centres, distinct from Surya Raitha which covers solar pumps. Question fifty confirms the Pavagada Shakti Sthala park in Karnataka, located in Tumakuru district, generates solar power and is one of the world's largest solar parks. The chapter then lists its references, including the Karnataka Public Service Commission's Agricultural Officer Paper 2 syllabus for Unit 7 on Farm Power and Machinery Engineering, along with standard textbooks by Hajra Choudhury on workshop technology, Theraja on electrical technology, and Rai on non-conventional energy sources.
215: On this page, we see the remaining references for the Farm Power and Machinery chapter continue briefly, including Jagdishwar Sahay's Elements of Agricultural Engineering, Michael and Ojha's Principles of Agricultural Engineering, Mahesh Varma's work on construction and operation of farm machinery, course material from ICAR-CIAE Bhopal and UAS Bengaluru, and documents from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy covering the Karnataka Krishi Yantra Dhare, Surya Raitha, and Pavagada solar-park programmes. This closes out the reference list for that unit, giving you a full picture of the authoritative sources behind the material you have just studied on farm power, machinery, and bio-energy.
216: Now, students, let us begin Chapter 8, Processing and Food Engineering, part of Paper 2, Technical Paper, Unit 8. This is described as the broadest composite unit in the technical paper. The chapter box tells us it covers the full engineering science behind food processing, the physical or geometric properties of agricultural produce, thermal, frictional and aerodynamic properties, rheological and electrical or dielectric properties of foods, engineering thermodynamics including the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles, refrigeration, psychrometry and air conditioning, cold storage and the cold chain, and the processing of fruits, vegetables, spices and flowers, including peeling, blanching, chilling, freezing, drying, and osmotic dehydration. Part A begins with theory. The unit opens with engineering properties governing how grains and fruits are cleaned, graded, conveyed and stored, then covers thermal properties like specific heat and thermal conductivity, frictional properties like angle of repose, and aerodynamic properties like terminal velocity. It then covers rheological and dielectric properties of foods, engineering thermodynamics, refrigeration, psychrometry, and finally food processing itself. For an Agricultural Officer in Karnataka, this subject is intensely practical, tied to institutions like CFTRI Mysuru, IIHR Hesaraghatta, University of Horticultural Sciences Bagalkot, and agencies KAPPEC and HOPCOMS which run pack-houses and cold chains for the state's grapes, pomegranate, mango, banana and chilli.
217: Here, students, Figure 8.1 classifies the engineering properties of agricultural produce into five branches, physical or geometric, thermal, frictional, aerodynamic, and rheological or electrical. Section 8.1 covers size, shape, sphericity and roundness. Engineering properties are the measurable characteristics describing how a farm product behaves under handling, processing and storage. Size is defined by three principal axial dimensions, length as the longest, width as the intermediate, and thickness as the shortest, measured with a micrometer or image analysis. There are two key shape indices in the table. Sphericity, calculated as the cube root of a times b times c, divided by a, the longest axis, measures how close the shape is to a sphere, with a perfect sphere equal to 1. There is also an area-basis sphericity, the ratio of geometric mean diameter to longest diameter. Roundness equals the projected area divided by the area of the smallest circumscribing circle, measuring sharpness of corners. Roundness ratio is mean radius of corners divided by radius of the maximum inscribed circle. Remember, sphericity is about overall shape, closeness to a ball, while roundness is about corners, sharp versus smooth, and a smooth river pebble can have high roundness but low sphericity. Examiners like to swap these two terms, so be careful.
218: Continuing, students, the Agri Officer Lens box explains that grading machines for Byadagi chilli, arecanut, potato and mango rely on size and shape, so an Agricultural Officer advising a pack-house specifies graders sized to the sphericity and dimensions of the local crop. Section 8.2 covers volume, density, porosity, specific gravity and surface area. These mass-volume properties govern conveying, storage-bin sizing, drying and separation. True or particle density is mass divided by the volume of solid only, excluding air gaps, while bulk density is mass divided by total bin volume, including voids, and is always lower than true density. Porosity equals 1 minus the ratio of bulk to true density, times 100 percent, representing the fraction of bulk volume that is air, and it controls airflow resistance during aeration and drying. Specific gravity is the ratio of a product's density to water's density, forming the basis of flotation grading, where sound grain sinks and chaff or damaged grain floats. The 1000-grain weight is a standard size and quality index. Surface area, often estimated from sphericity, governs drying rate, heat transfer, and coating. The Agri Officer Lens notes that bulk density sets godown or silo capacity, porosity decides fan power for forced-air drying of paddy or maize, and specific-gravity flotation separation is used to clean tamarind seed, paddy and pulses.
219: Now, students, Section 8.3 covers thermal properties of agricultural materials, which decide how fast a product heats or cools, central to drying, blanching, cooking, refrigeration and storage. Specific heat is the heat needed to raise unit mass by one degree, rising with moisture content and often estimated using Siebel's formula for foods. Thermal conductivity is the rate of heat conduction through a material, and foods are generally poor conductors, though conductivity rises when the product freezes, since ice conducts better than water, meaning frozen food actually conducts heat faster than fresh food. Thermal diffusivity combines conductivity, density and specific heat, and governs the rate at which a temperature change penetrates a product, essential for heating, freezing and cooling-time calculations. Heat of respiration is the heat released by living fruits and vegetables in storage, high-respiration produce like leafy greens, peas and broccoli generates a large heat load needing fast cooling, while low-respiration produce like apple, potato and onion stores far longer. The coefficient of thermal expansion describes volume or length change with temperature, relevant to can seams and freezing. Remember the mnemonic, diffusivity tells you how quickly temperature changes, conductivity tells you how much heat flows. The Agri Officer Lens notes that heat of respiration sizes the refrigeration load of a cold store, so an Agricultural Officer must check that plant capacity covers both field heat and respiration heat.
220: Continuing, Section 8.4 covers frictional properties, namely the angle of repose and internal friction, which govern the flow of grains and powders through hoppers, chutes and conveyors. Static friction must be overcome to start motion, kinetic or sliding friction resists motion already underway, and rolling resistance opposes a rolling body. The angle of repose is the angle a free-poured heap makes with the horizontal, used in hopper, bin and conveyor design, and free-flowing grains like wheat and sorghum have a low angle of repose, around 23 to 35 degrees, while sticky or fine materials have a high angle. The angle of internal friction relates shear and normal stresses within the bulk, used for bin-wall pressure and silo design, computed via Janssen or Rankine theory. The coefficient of friction, the tangent of the friction angle, governs chute and conveyor surface design. Remember, angle of repose is about the heap's surface, sizing hoppers and telling you flowability, while angle of internal friction is about stresses inside the mass, sizing silo-wall pressure. The Agri Officer Lens notes that silo and godown design for FCI or Karnataka State Warehousing depots uses the angle of internal friction to set wall thickness, while hopper slopes at rice and dhal mills are set above the grain's angle of repose so it flows freely without bridging. Section 8.5 then introduces aerodynamic properties, drag and terminal velocity, important for pneumatic conveying and air-based cleaning and grading.
221: Continuing, students, terminal velocity is the constant velocity a particle reaches in free fall when drag balances gravity, giving zero net force, and heavier, denser particles have higher terminal velocity. This is the single most useful aerodynamic property, since in an air stream, particles with terminal velocity below the air speed are carried away, such as chaff and light impurities, while heavier grain settles, the working principle of the aspirator, winnower and pneumatic separator. Floating or suspension velocity equals terminal velocity. The Agri Officer Lens notes that aspirators and winnowing on the threshing floor separate grain from chaff using terminal-velocity differences, a principle an Agricultural Officer relies on when promoting improved seed-cleaning units for farmer producer organisations. Section 8.6 then introduces rheological properties, stress, strain and flow behaviour, vital for texture, pumping, mixing and quality of liquid and semi-solid foods. Under load, a body shows stress, force per unit area, and strain, relative deformation. The basic responses are elastic, recovering fully and obeying Hooke's law, plastic, showing permanent deformation beyond a yield point, and viscous, flowing continuously with resistance set by viscosity. Real foods are usually viscoelastic, part solid and part liquid, showing creep and stress relaxation. A table classifies fluid foods, Newtonian fluids like water, milk and clear juice have constant viscosity, pseudoplastic fluids like fruit puree thin as shear rate rises, dilatant fluids like corn-starch suspension thicken as shear rate rises, and Bingham plastics like ketchup need a yield stress before they flow.
222: Continuing, students, the table also lists thixotropic fluids, like stirred yoghurt, whose viscosity falls with time at constant shear and recovers on rest, and rheopectic fluids, a rare type whose viscosity rises with time at constant shear. Figure 8.2 shows the rheological flow curves, plotting shear stress against shear rate, with Newtonian as a straight line through the origin, pseudoplastic and dilatant as curved lines, and Bingham plastic offset by a yield stress before it begins to flow. Time-independent fluids change viscosity with the rate of shear, pseudoplastic fluids thin when stirred or pumped, most purees and concentrates behave this way, while dilatant fluids like concentrated starch thicken under shear. A Bingham plastic behaves like a solid until a yield stress is exceeded, then flows, which is why ketchup will not pour until the bottle is tapped. The power-law model, shear stress equals K times shear rate to the power n, captures pseudoplastic behaviour when n is less than 1, dilatant when n is greater than 1, and Newtonian when n equals 1. Remember the memory hook, pseudoplastic thins with shear rate like puree, dilatant thickens with shear rate like starch, thixotropic thins with time like yoghurt, rheopectic thickens with time, and Bingham plastic needs a yield stress first like ketchup. The Agri Officer Lens notes that designing a tomato-pulp, mango-pulp or jam line, common at Karnataka food parks and CFTRI-incubated units, needs the rheogram to size pumps and pipe diameters correctly.
223: Continuing, students, the Agri Officer Lens on the previous property reminds us that dielectric and microwave drying are used for spices, herbs and high-value produce like Byadagi chilli and cardamom, where colour and aroma must be preserved, and that dry material has a low loss factor, explaining why microwave finishing is gentle on already-dried produce. Section 8.8 now introduces thermodynamic systems, laws, and first-law processes, the science of energy and its transformations, foundational to engines, refrigeration and drying. A thermodynamic system may be closed, where only energy crosses the boundary and mass is fixed, a non-flow system, open, where both mass and energy cross, a flow system like a turbine or compressor, or isolated, where neither crosses. The table gives the four laws of thermodynamics. The zeroth law defines temperature, stating two bodies each in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. The first law defines internal energy and energy balance, stating energy is conserved, non-flow heat Q equals change in internal energy U plus work W. The second law defines entropy and direction, stating heat cannot wholly convert to work and entropy of an isolated system never decreases. The third law defines absolute entropy, stating entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches zero kelvin. The steady-flow energy equation balances enthalpy, kinetic, potential, heat and work terms, and is the working equation for turbines, compressors, nozzles, boilers and heat exchangers.
224: Now, students, Section 8.9 covers entropy, the Carnot cycle, and the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles. Entropy measures the unavailability of energy and disorder of a system, and the Carnot cycle, combining two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, is the ideal reversible cycle setting maximum possible efficiency between two temperatures, eta equals 1 minus T2 over T1, in kelvin. A table compares air-standard power cycles. The Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume, modelling the petrol or spark-ignition engine, with efficiency rising with compression ratio. The Diesel cycle adds heat at constant pressure, modelling the compression-ignition engine. The Dual or mixed cycle adds heat partly at constant volume and partly at constant pressure, modelling modern high-speed compression-ignition engines, with efficiency between Otto and Diesel. For the same compression ratio, the Otto cycle is more efficient than Diesel, but diesel engines use much higher compression ratios in practice, achieving higher real efficiency. The Agri Officer Lens notes that almost all farm power, tractors, power tillers, and pump-set engines, runs on the Diesel cycle, explaining their efficiency and durability under load. Section 8.10 then begins principles of refrigeration, defining the coefficient of performance, COP, as refrigerating effect divided by work input, which unlike efficiency can exceed 1, and introduces the ton of refrigeration, the rate to freeze one ton of water into ice in 24 hours, equal to about 3.5 kilowatts.
225: On this page, let us finish the refrigeration basics table before moving to vapour compression. COP, the coefficient of performance, is refrigerating effect divided by work input, and remember it can be greater than 1, unlike an efficiency. One ton of refrigeration is approximately 3.5 kilowatts, or 3024 kilocalories per hour, defined as the heat needed to freeze one ton of water at 0 degrees Celsius in 24 hours. The Carnot maximum COP for a refrigerator is T2 divided by T1 minus T2, using absolute temperatures in kelvin, and the reversed Carnot cycle is the ideal reference cycle for all refrigerators. Now, an air refrigeration system uses air itself as the refrigerant, working on the reversed Carnot or, more practically, the Bell-Coleman cycle, also called the reversed Brayton or Joule cycle. Air is compressed, cooled at constant pressure, expanded in an expander which sharply drops its temperature, and then it absorbs heat from the cold space at constant pressure. This Bell-Coleman cycle has a low COP and bulky equipment, but needs no special refrigerant and is light, making it the standard system for aircraft air conditioning. A worked example on this page shows a cold store needing to remove 70 kilowatts of heat requires a 20 ton refrigeration plant, since 70 divided by 3.5 equals 20; a 15 ton plant would be undersized and fail in peak season, exactly the check an Agriculture Officer performs on a subsidy proposal for cold stores in places like Kolar, Chikkaballapur or Bagalkot.
226: Let us understand the vapour compression refrigeration system, the VCRS, which is the workhorse of commercial refrigeration and cold storage. A refrigerant circulates through four components. First, the compressor raises the pressure and temperature of the vapour. Second, the condenser rejects heat, and the vapour condenses to liquid. Third, the expansion or throttle valve drops the pressure and temperature. Fourth, the evaporator is where the refrigerant boils, absorbing heat from the cold space, which is the actual refrigerating effect. This cycle is drawn on pressure-volume, temperature-entropy, and especially the pressure-enthalpy or Mollier diagram, where the refrigerating effect and work appear as simple enthalpy differences. Now, on refinements. Dry compression, where the vapour is fully dry or superheated at the compressor inlet, is preferred. Wet compression, where liquid droplets enter the compressor, risks damage and is avoided. Sub-cooling the liquid below the condensing temperature increases the refrigerating effect, giving more cooling per unit of work. Super-heating the vapour ensures the suction gas stays safely dry before compression. On common refrigerants, ammonia, designated R-717, is used in large cold stores and ice plants for its high latent heat, though it is toxic; it is cheap. R-134a, an HFC, is used in domestic fridges and air conditioners, is ozone-safe with no chlorine, though it has a high global warming potential.
227: Now, students, let us continue with refrigerants and move into absorption systems. R-22, an HCFC, was used in older air conditioners but is being phased out for depleting the ozone layer. Carbon dioxide, R-744, is a natural refrigerant used in transport and supermarket systems. R-12, known as Freon, a CFC, is banned entirely under the Montreal Protocol for ozone depletion. Remember, dry compression with dry or superheated vapour going in is good, while wet compression with liquid droplets damages the compressor. Sub-cooling the liquid raises refrigerating effect and COP, while super-heating concerns the vapour side. The throttle or expansion valve drops pressure, it is not the condenser. Ammonia, R-717, is standard for big cold stores, while CFCs like R-12 are banned. Most Karnataka cold stores and ice plants run ammonia vapour compression plants. Now, section 8.12 covers the vapour absorption system and cold storage plants. The vapour absorption refrigeration system replaces the compressor's work input with a heat-driven absorber-generator circuit, so it runs on heat, such as waste heat, steam, gas or solar energy, rather than costly electrical work. The common pairs are ammonia-water, where ammonia is the refrigerant and water the absorbent, or lithium bromide-water, where water is the refrigerant and lithium bromide the absorbent, used for air conditioning. The refrigerant vapour from the evaporator is absorbed in the absorber, pumped to the generator where heat drives it off again, then condensed, with the rest of the circuit matching vapour compression.
228: Here, students, notice that solar or biogas-driven absorption refrigeration suits off-grid rural pack-houses, and an Agriculture Officer can recommend it for Farmer Producer Organisation cold rooms where electric power is unreliable. Karnataka's cold-storage capacity, under schemes like KAPPEC and private chains, is rated and subsidised based on tons of refrigeration of the cooling load. Now, section 8.13 covers psychrometry, the study of moist air. Psychrometry is the study of the properties of moist air, a mixture of dry air and water vapour, and of the processes that heat, cool, humidify and dehumidify it; it forms the basis of drying, air conditioning and storage humidity control. Treating both dry air and water vapour as perfect gases, using Dalton's law of partial pressures, gives simple approximate relations. The key properties are dry-bulb temperature, the ordinary temperature; wet-bulb temperature, read by a thermometer with a wet wick in moving air; dew-point temperature, where the air becomes saturated and condensation starts; relative humidity; humidity ratio, or specific humidity; enthalpy; and specific volume. In the adiabatic saturation process, air passes over water in an insulated duct, picking up moisture while its temperature falls until it leaves saturated. The steady temperature reached practically equals the thermodynamic wet-bulb temperature for air-water vapour. Remember, dry-bulb temperature is the ordinary temperature, wet-bulb is the wet-wick temperature, and dew-point is where condensation starts; at saturation, all three become equal.
229: On this page, we finish psychrometry basics and start air conditioning. The Agriculture Officer Lens note explains grain and produce drying is fundamentally a psychrometric process; an officer sizing a paddy or copra dryer uses the psychrometric chart to find how much moisture a given air temperature and relative humidity can remove. Evaporative, or wet-pad, cooling for low-cost storage works only when the air's wet-bulb depression is large, meaning in dry districts of Karnataka. Now, section 8.14 covers air conditioning, its principles, duct design and cooling load. Air conditioning is the simultaneous control of temperature, humidity, air movement and air purity of an enclosed space, for either human comfort or an industrial process. By function it is comfort air conditioning, for offices, homes and vehicles, based on human comfort physiology, or industrial and process air conditioning, controlling conditions for a product, such as cold storage, food processing rooms or seed stores. A complete system has a cooling or heating coil, a humidifier and dehumidifier, a fan, filters, and the air-distribution duct network with controls. The cooling coil, whether direct expansion or chilled water, provides both sensible and latent cooling, cooling and dehumidifying the air together. A humidifier adds moisture through spray, pad or steam, raising relative humidity, while a dehumidifier removes moisture using a cooling coil or desiccant, lowering relative humidity.
230: Let us understand comfort conditions and cooling load calculation. Physiological principles set the human comfort zone at around 22 to 27 degrees Celsius and 40 to 60 percent relative humidity with gentle air movement, because the body must lose its metabolic heat by convection, radiation and evaporation. Air-distribution ducts route conditioned air to each space, and they are sized by velocity-reduction, equal-friction or static-regain methods to deliver the required airflow at acceptable noise and pressure drop. The cooling load is the total heat to be removed, and it has sensible components, such as solar gain, transmission through walls and roof, lights, equipment, occupants' sensible heat and ventilation, plus latent components, such as occupants' moisture, ventilation moisture and infiltration; these are summed and converted into tons of refrigeration to size the plant. Air conditioners are classified as window, or unitary, split, packaged, and central chilled-water systems, by capacity and layout. Remember, air conditioning controls four things: temperature, humidity, air movement, and air cleanliness, and the cooling load equals sensible plus latent heat gains, summed and converted to tons of refrigeration. Process air conditioning keeps seed stores, mushroom units, food-processing halls and ripening chambers, such as ethylene banana ripening for Nanjangud Cavendish banana, at controlled temperature and humidity; an officer assessing such a proposal checks the cooling-load basis and humidity control specified. Section 8.15 then begins the importance and characteristics of horticultural produce for processing, noting processing converts perishable, seasonal, bulky raw material into stable value-added products, reducing India's 15 to 30 percent post-harvest losses in horticulture.
231: Now, students, let us cover produce quality attributes and processing suitability. Selecting produce for processing depends on characteristics such as maturity and ripeness, size and shape uniformity, colour, flavour, texture and firmness, total soluble solids measured in degrees Brix, acidity or pH, and freedom from blemish and disease. Horticultural crops are living tissues that continue to respire and ripen after harvest. Climacteric fruits, such as mango, banana, papaya and tomato, ripen further off the plant with a respiration and ethylene surge, while non-climacteric fruits, such as grape, citrus and pomegranate, do not ripen further once picked; this distinction governs harvest timing and storage. Processing suitability of a variety, such as Totapuri or Alphonso mango for pulp, or Byadagi chilli for colour and oleoresin, is a key selection criterion. Karnataka is a horticulture powerhouse, leading in coffee, arecanut, and among the top states for mango, grape, pomegranate, banana and chilli. Now, section 8.16 covers peeling, slicing and size-reduction equipment. After cleaning and grading, peeling removes the inedible or tough skin, using four main methods chosen by produce type and scale: manual peeling with knives or peelers, for small scale delicate produce; mechanical peeling using abrasive carborundum rollers, for potato, carrot and root vegetables; chemical or lye peeling, using hot 1 to 2 percent caustic soda to loosen skin, for peach, tomato and root crops; and thermal or flame and steam peeling, which chars or loosens the skin, for tomato, capsicum, onion and garlic.
232: On this page, we finish peeling equipment and cover a full section on blanching. Mechanical or abrasion peeling rubs the skin off against carborundum surfaces; chemical or lye peeling dips produce in hot dilute sodium hydroxide that dissolves the middle lamella so the skin sloughs off, and it must be neutralised and washed afterward; flame and steam, or thermal, peeling chars or loosens the skin by heat, removed by a water spray. After peeling, size reduction by slicing, dicing, shredding, crushing, chopping, pulping or juice extraction prepares the product for the next operation, using rotary and reciprocating slicers, dicers, shredders, pulpers, hammer mills, and screw or basket presses. Remember to match the peeling method to the produce: lye or caustic peeling for tomato and peach, abrasion for potato and root crops, flame or steam for capsicum and onion. Now, section 8.17 covers blanching, its objectives, methods and effects. Blanching is a mild heat treatment, usually 70 to 100 degrees Celsius for a few minutes, given to fruits and especially vegetables before freezing, canning or drying, chiefly to inactivate spoilage enzymes. Its primary objective is to inactivate enzymes such as peroxidase, catalase and polyphenol oxidase that otherwise cause off-flavours, colour loss and nutrient breakdown during storage. Peroxidase, the most heat-stable enzyme, is the standard indicator; if peroxidase is destroyed, blanching is judged adequate. Other objectives include expelling intercellular gas, softening tissue, setting colour, and reducing microbial load.
233: Let us understand blanching methods and then move to chilling and freezing. Hot-water blanching means immersion in 70 to 100 degree Celsius water; it is simple and uniform, but leaches water-soluble vitamins, sugars and minerals into the water, creating effluent. Steam blanching exposes produce to steam, causing less nutrient leaching and less effluent, and is preferred for most vegetables. Microwave and hot-gas blanching are newer, low-leaching methods. Blanching sets and brightens colour, softens texture for packing, removes intercellular air, and lowers surface microbial load, but over-blanching destroys vitamin C and other water-soluble nutrients. Remember, steam blanching beats hot-water blanching on nutrient retention and effluent, and it is always a pre-treatment before freezing, canning or drying, not a cooking step. Now, section 8.18 covers chilling, freezing and cold-preservation microbiology. Refrigeration preserves perishable foods by slowing microbial growth, enzyme action and respiration. Chilling holds food just above freezing, around 0 to 5 degrees Celsius, for short-term storage, while freezing takes it below the freezing point, commercially minus 18 degrees Celsius or lower, so most water turns to ice for long-term preservation. Micro-organisms are classified by growth-temperature range: psychrophilic or psychrotrophic organisms grow around 0 to 7 degrees Celsius and are the main spoilers of chilled food; mesophilic organisms, with an optimum of 20 to 45 degrees Celsius, are most food-poisoning and spoilage organisms including human pathogens; thermophilic organisms, optimum 45 to 70 degrees Celsius, survive heat processing and spoil canned or hot-held food.
234: Now, students, let us cover freezing rate, Plank's equation, and then drying and dehydration. Freezing arrests microbial growth but does not sterilise; microbes revive on thawing. Freezing rate is critical: slow freezing forms large ice crystals that rupture cell walls, causing drip loss and texture damage on thawing, whereas fast or quick freezing forms small crystals that preserve texture. Equipment includes mechanical freezers, such as plate contact, air-blast and fluidised-bed or individual quick freezing systems, and cryogenic freezers using liquid nitrogen at minus 196 degrees Celsius or solid or liquid carbon dioxide, which freeze extremely fast for premium quality. As food is cooled, its temperature first dips slightly below the freezing point without ice forming, a metastable state called supercooling; ice then nucleates, latent heat is released, and temperature jumps back to the freezing point, holding nearly constant during a thermal-arrest period while most water turns to ice, before falling again to storage temperature. Freezing time is estimated by Plank's equation, which shows freezing time rises with product thickness and falls as cooling-medium temperature is lowered and surface heat transfer is improved. Now, section 8.19 begins drying, dehydration and osmotic dehydration. Drying removes water to a level, usually below 10 to 15 percent, at which microbes and enzymes cannot act, giving a light, stable, long-keeping product. Water leaves first as easy-to-remove free moisture at a constant drying rate, then as harder-to-remove bound moisture in falling-rate periods.
235: On this page, let us finish drying methods, minimal processing, and quality control. Dryers for fruits and vegetables include sun or solar dryers, cheap but weather-dependent; cabinet or tray dryers for small-scale batch drying; tunnel dryers with continuous trolleys for medium to large scale; spray dryers, which convert liquids to powders such as milk, instant coffee or fruit powder; drum dryers; fluidised-bed dryers; and freeze dryers, or lyophilisation, giving the best quality at the highest cost through sublimation under vacuum. Osmotic dehydration is a pre-drying step where fruit or vegetable pieces are immersed in a concentrated sugar solution for fruits, or salt solution for vegetables; the osmotic pressure difference draws water out of the tissue while some solute enters, partially dewatering the product at low temperature with better retention of colour, flavour and nutrients before final drying. Remember, free unbound water leaves in the constant-rate period, while bound water leaves in the falling-rate period. Spray dryers convert liquid to powder, freeze dryers use sublimation for the best but costliest quality, and osmotic dehydration means soaking in sugar for fruit or salt for vegetables to pull water out before drying. Solar drying of Byadagi chilli, grapes into raisins, and copra, and spray drying of fruit and vegetable powders, are major Karnataka value-addition routes; an Agriculture Officer promotes improved solar and cabinet dryers, such as CFTRI and IIHR designs, over open-sun drying to cut losses, contamination and weather risk.
236: Let us understand minimal processing, spices, flowers, and quality control systems. Minimal, or fresh-cut, processing gives ready-to-use fresh produce, such as washed, peeled, cut, packed salads and cut fruit and vegetables, using only mild treatments like washing, sanitising, low temperature and modified-atmosphere packaging instead of heat; the product stays fresh-like but is highly perishable and demands an unbroken cold chain and strict hygiene. Post-harvest management of spices covers drying, curing, grading, cleaning, and oleoresin or essential-oil extraction, while cut-flower handling covers grading, bunching, pre-cooling, pulsing with preservative solutions, cold storage and refrigerated transport to extend vase life. Quality control in the fruit and vegetable processing industry covers raw-material grading, in-process checks such as temperature, time, degrees Brix, pH, fill weight and seal integrity, and finished-product standards, governed by FSSAI regulations and systems such as Good Manufacturing Practices, Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points known as HACCP, and traceability. Karnataka's floriculture, including Bengaluru rose, chrysanthemum, and gerbera for domestic and export markets, depends on pre-cooling and cold-chain handling; an Agriculture Officer links flower growers and spice processors of Byadagi chilli and cardamom to FSSAI-compliant grading, pack-house and cold-chain facilities for better returns. Section 8.21 then begins storage methods, cold chain and heat-load design, noting perishables are stored to extend marketable life by slowing respiration, ripening, water loss and microbial growth, ranging from ambient and ventilated storage up to engineered low-temperature and atmosphere-controlled systems.
237: On this page, let us compare controlled atmosphere storage with modified atmosphere packaging, and cover the cold chain. Controlled atmosphere storage, or CAS, actively lowers oxygen and raises carbon dioxide in a gas-tight room, typically to 2 to 5 percent oxygen and 2 to 5 percent carbon dioxide, to slow respiration and ripening, greatly extending storage of apples and other fruit. Modified atmosphere packaging, or MAP, achieves a similar altered gas mix inside a sealed package, either passively through produce respiration and film permeability, or actively through gas flushing, and is widely used for fresh-cut and retail produce. The evaporative cool chamber is a zero-energy double-brick structure with wet sand that cools and humidifies cheaply where the air is dry. The cold chain is the unbroken sequence of refrigerated steps, pre-cooling, cold storage, refrigerated or reefer transport vehicles, and chilled retail, that keeps a perishable within its safe temperature band from farm to consumer; a single break causes large losses. Cold-storage and chamber design rests on the heat, or cooling, load calculation: transmission load through insulated walls, roof and floor, product load meaning field heat plus heat of respiration, air-change or infiltration load, and miscellaneous load from lights, fans and people, all summed and converted to tons of refrigeration. Remember, controlled atmosphere storage is a whole gas-controlled room, such as for apples, while modified atmosphere packaging is inside a pack; both lower oxygen and raise carbon dioxide to slow respiration.
238: This page presents the chapter mind map for Processing and Food Engineering, drawn as a diagram with six branches around the central topic. The branches cover engineering properties, such as sphericity, porosity, roundness, aspect ratio, angle of repose and bulk density; rheology, covering pseudoplastic shear-thinning fluids, dilatant shear-thickening fluids, Bingham plastics with yield stress, Newtonian fluids, thixotropy, and viscosity units in pascal-seconds or poise; thermodynamics, covering the Otto constant-volume cycle, Diesel constant-pressure cycle, Carnot's most efficient cycle, enthalpy, the first law of energy conservation, and the second law on entropy always increasing; refrigeration, covering one ton of refrigeration equal to 3.5 kilowatts, ammonia R-717 and R-134a as refrigerants, COP as refrigerating effect over work input, the four vapour-compression components, and the evaporator absorbing heat from the load; psychrometry, covering the relationship of dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew-point temperatures, relative humidity, sensible and latent heat, and the wet-bulb evaporative cooling limit; and freezing and preservation, covering the latent heat of ice at 334 kilojoules per kilogram, peroxidase as the blanching indicator, slow versus quick freezing and their effect on ice crystals, pasteurisation killing pathogens with mild heat, and water activity controlling spoilage. Use this diagram to revise how all six themes of the chapter connect back to the central subject of processing and food engineering.
239: This page is a key-terms-at-a-glance table, a rapid revision list pairing each concept with its key fact. It reminds you that bulk density is always less than true density because bulk density counts air voids; porosity equals one minus bulk over true density, expressed as a percentage; specific gravity is the ratio of product density to water density, forming the basis of flotation grading; thermal diffusivity, alpha, equals conductivity over density times specific heat, and it governs the rate of temperature change; frozen food has higher thermal conductivity than fresh food because ice conducts heat better than water; heat of respiration is released by living produce in storage and is high in leafy crops; angle of repose is the heap-surface angle, low for free-flowing grain; angle of internal friction relates to stress inside a bulk material, relevant for silo-wall pressure; terminal velocity is the steady fall speed where drag balances gravity, equal to floating velocity; Newtonian fluids like water, milk and clear juice have constant viscosity; pseudoplastic fluids like puree are shear-thinning; dilatant fluids like starch are shear-thickening; thixotropic or rheopectic fluids thin or thicken with time at constant shear; and Bingham plastics like ketchup need a yield stress before they flow. It also notes dielectric constant as stored energy and loss factor as energy converted to heat, with loss tangent equal to loss factor over dielectric constant.
240: This page continues the key-terms table, covering thermodynamics through the cold chain, then opens Part B, the objective questions section. Key reminders include: a closed system is non-flow while an open system involves mass flow; the first law for a non-flow process states heat equals change in internal energy plus work, where work is the integral of pressure times volume change; Carnot efficiency equals 1 minus T2 over T1 in kelvin; entropy change in a reversible process equals heat over temperature; the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles differ by constant-volume, constant-pressure, or both heat-addition; COP equals refrigerating effect over work input and can exceed 1; one ton of refrigeration is about 3.5 kilowatts; air refrigeration uses the Bell-Coleman, or reversed Brayton, cycle for aircraft air conditioning; vapour absorption is heat-driven, using ammonia-water or lithium bromide-water; ammonia, R-717, serves big cold stores, while R-12, a CFC, is banned; at saturation dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew-point temperatures are equal; the comfort zone is about 22 to 27 degrees Celsius and 40 to 60 percent relative humidity; blanching inactivates enzymes with peroxidase as the test enzyme; steam blanching retains more nutrients than water blanching; freezing rate determines ice crystal size, fast being good and slow causing damage; controlled atmosphere storage is a gas-controlled room while modified atmosphere packaging is inside a pack; climacteric fruits like mango, banana, papaya and tomato ripen off the plant; water activity controls microbial growth, not total moisture; and India's horticultural post-harvest loss is roughly 15 to 30 percent. Part B then begins with question one, confirming the sphericity of a perfect sphere equals one.
241: Now, students, let us work through several objective questions on engineering properties and rheology. Question two asks how sphericity of a grain is calculated, and the answer is the geometric mean of the three axes divided by the longest axis, a, in the denominator. Question three defines porosity of a grain bed as one minus the ratio of bulk to true density, times 100 percent, representing the air fraction. Question four confirms that bulk density is always lower than true particle density, since bulk density includes inter-grain air voids. Question five defines thermal diffusivity as conductivity divided by density times specific heat. Question six identifies the heat released by living fruits and vegetables in storage as the heat of respiration, which adds to the cold-store cooling load, not the latent heat of freezing. Question seven describes angle of repose as the angle a free-poured heap makes with the horizontal, distinct from the angle of internal friction which is stress inside the material. Question eight explains terminal velocity is reached when drag equals gravity, giving zero net force. Question nine notes aspirators and winnowers separate grain from chaff using differences in terminal velocity, since light chaff blows away while heavy grain settles. Question ten then begins asking which fluid type describes milk, water and clear fruit juice.
242: Let us continue through the rheology, dielectric and thermodynamics questions. The answer to question ten is Newtonian fluid, since these have constant viscosity, unlike purees which are pseudoplastic. Question eleven confirms a fruit puree whose viscosity falls as shear rate increases is pseudoplastic, or shear-thinning, the opposite of dilatant behaviour where viscosity rises with shear rate. Question twelve identifies tomato ketchup, which needs a yield stress exceeded before it flows, as a Bingham plastic. Question thirteen distinguishes thixotropic fluids, whose viscosity decreases with time at constant shear rate and recovers on standing, like stirred yoghurt, from pseudoplastic fluids which thin with shear rate rather than time. Question fourteen explains that in a food's dielectric behaviour, the energy converted to heat is measured by the dielectric loss factor, which governs microwave heat absorption, while the dielectric constant measures energy stored. Question fifteen gives the loss tangent, tan delta, as the loss factor divided by the dielectric constant. Question sixteen defines a closed thermodynamic system as one where only energy crosses the boundary while mass stays fixed, unlike an open system where mass also crosses. Question seventeen states the first law of thermodynamics for a non-flow process as heat equals the change in internal energy plus work done, noting that heat equals temperature times entropy change applies only to a reversible isothermal step. Question eighteen then begins asking about Carnot efficiency between source and sink temperatures in kelvin.
243: Now, students, let us cover thermodynamic cycles and vapour compression questions. The answer to question eighteen is Carnot efficiency equals 1 minus T2 over T1, with the sink temperature over the source temperature, both in kelvin. Question nineteen confirms that in the Otto cycle, heat is added at constant volume, the petrol or spark-ignition cycle, distinct from the Diesel cycle which adds heat at constant pressure. Question twenty identifies the Dual, or mixed, cycle as the one adding heat partly at constant volume and partly at constant pressure, modelling modern compression-ignition engines. Question twenty-one defines the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator as refrigerating effect divided by work input, and it can exceed 1, unlike an efficiency. Question twenty-two confirms one ton of refrigeration is approximately 3.5 kilowatts, warning that 35 kilowatts would be a factor-of-ten error. Question twenty-three identifies aircraft air-refrigeration systems as working on the Bell-Coleman, or reversed Brayton, cycle, distinct from vapour compression systems which use a refrigerant. Question twenty-four identifies the expansion, or throttle, valve as the component in a vapour compression system that lowers refrigerant pressure and temperature before the evaporator, while the condenser rejects heat at high pressure. Question twenty-five then begins asking about the effect of sub-cooling the liquid refrigerant in a vapour compression cycle.
244: Here, students, let us finish this run of questions on refrigeration, psychrometry and blanching. The answer to question twenty-five confirms sub-cooling raises the refrigerating effect without extra work, improving the coefficient of performance, while compressor damage actually comes from wet compression, not sub-cooling. Question twenty-six identifies ammonia, R-717, as the refrigerant commonly used in large cold-storage and ice plants, since R-12, a CFC, is banned. Question twenty-seven confirms a vapour absorption refrigeration system is driven primarily by heat energy, such as steam, gas or solar, since absorption replaces the compressor that drives vapour compression systems. Question twenty-eight states that at saturation, meaning 100 percent relative humidity, the dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew-point temperatures are all equal, a relationship that only holds at saturation, not for unsaturated air. Question twenty-nine explains that on a psychrometric chart, sensible heating of air is shown as a horizontal line, since sensible heating and cooling keep the humidity ratio constant. Question thirty notes that air conditioning controls temperature, humidity, air movement and cleanliness, but not the colour of the air. Question thirty-one confirms the primary objective of blanching vegetables before freezing or drying is to inactivate enzymes, not to cook them fully or sterilise completely. Question thirty-two identifies peroxidase as the enzyme used as the index to judge whether blanching is adequate, since it is the most heat-stable enzyme. Question thirty-three confirms that compared with hot-water blanching, steam blanching generally gives less nutrient loss and less effluent, since heavy leaching is the drawback of hot-water blanching.
245: On this page we are working through objective questions on food preservation, students. Question 34 asks which micro-organisms grow at refrigeration temperatures and spoil chilled food, and the answer is psychrophilic or psychrotrophic organisms, which are cold-loving, unlike thermophiles which prefer heat. Question 35 tells us quick or fast freezing is preferred over slow freezing because it forms small ice crystals that preserve the food's texture, while slow freezing forms large crystals that damage cells. Question 36 covers cryogenic freezing, which typically uses liquid nitrogen at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, this is the boiling point of liquid nitrogen and gives very fast freezing, note minus 18 degrees is only the storage temperature. Question 37 explains that in osmotic dehydration of fruit, pieces are immersed in a concentrated sugar solution, while vegetables use salt brine instead. Question 38 tells us spray drying is most suitable for converting a liquid into a powder, such as milk, juice or coffee. Question 39 explains Controlled Atmosphere Storage, or CAS, extends fruit life mainly by lowering oxygen and raising carbon dioxide, which slows respiration and ripening. Question 40 draws the key difference between CAS and MAP, CAS controls a whole room's atmosphere for storage, while MAP modifies the atmosphere inside a package. Question 41 asks which property, rather than total moisture content, governs microbial growth in food.
246: Let us continue with the answers, students. The answer to question 41 is water activity, written as aw, which controls whether microbes can grow, while pH also matters but water activity is the specific moisture-related control. Question 42 asks about India's premier food-technology research institute located in Karnataka, and the answer is CFTRI, Mysuru, the Central Food Technological Research Institute, note IARI in Delhi is for agricultural research generally. Question 43 tells us the freezing time of a food product is commonly estimated using Plank's equation, which uses latent heat, thickness, temperature difference and heat-transfer terms, while Siebel's equation gives specific heat instead. Question 44 introduces an important term, during freezing, the brief dip of a food's temperature below its freezing point before ice actually forms is called supercooling, this is the metastable dip before nucleation begins, and it comes before what is called the thermal-arrest plateau. This page closes Unit 8 on Processing and Food Engineering with a references list, citing the KPSC Paper 2 technical syllabus itself, along with textbooks on unit operations of agricultural processing, physical properties of plant and animal materials, engineering thermodynamics, refrigeration and air conditioning, and fruit and vegetable preservation, as well as guidance from CFTRI Mysuru, IIHR Hesaraghatta, ICAR-CIPHET Ludhiana, and FSSAI regulations.
247: Now, students, we begin Chapter 9, Basic Engineering, which is Unit 9 of Paper 2's Specific Paper, and this chapter covers theory plus objective questions and answers. This chapter has two clear halves. The first half is engineering and machine drawing, covering orthographic projection in first-angle and third-angle systems, working drawings, isometric and missing views, systems of dimensioning, sectioning, riveted and leak-proof joints, welded joints and their symbols, screw threads, nuts, bolts, studs, screws and foundation bolts, and computer-aided design, known as CAD. The second half is basic electronics, covering semiconductors and the p-n junction diode, rectifiers and filters, clippers, clampers and voltage multipliers, diode logic, the bipolar junction transistor and its biasing, amplifier classes and coupling, the h-parameter model and the CE amplifier, the RC phase-shift oscillator, the differential amplifier, the operational amplifier and its applications, voltage regulators, Boolean algebra and combinational logic, and measurement of physical quantities. For an Agricultural Officer in Karnataka, this unit is quietly everywhere, engineering drawing and CAD underpin farm implements designed at University of Agricultural Sciences colleges, while electronics powers weather-station sensors, electronic weighbridges, milk analysers, and solar pump controllers. Remember, this chapter rewards recall of conventions and standard formulae.
248: Here, students, we study Section 9.1, Methods of Projection, covering first-angle and third-angle systems. Orthographic projection represents a three-dimensional object using separate two-dimensional views, namely front, top and side, projected onto mutually perpendicular planes. Placing the object in the first quadrant gives first-angle projection, while placing it in the third quadrant gives third-angle projection, the second and fourth angles are not used because the views would overlap. In first-angle projection, which India follows per the Bureau of Indian Standards, the object sits between the observer and the plane, the plane behaves like an opaque screen behind the object, the top view is placed below the front view, and the right-side view is placed on the left of the front view. In third-angle projection, used in the United States and Canada, the plane behaves like transparent glass in front of the object, the top view goes above the front view, and the right-side view goes on the right. The two systems place the same views in mirror-image layout, so a drawing must carry a projection symbol, a truncated cone shown two ways, to declare which system is being used. Remember, India uses first-angle projection as per BIS, and every implement drawing at agricultural engineering colleges follows this standard.
249: Let us understand Section 9.2, Working Drawings, Isometric Views and Missing Views. A working drawing gives all information needed to make a part, namely views, dimensions, material, tolerances and finish, and it is built from orthographic views. A pictorial view shows three faces of the object in one picture, the isometric view is the common type, drawn on axes at 120 degrees to each other, with all three principal directions to the same scale, the isometric scale is approximately 0.82 of true length, though isometric drawings usually use true lengths for convenience. Two reverse skills are tested here. Reading a model or isometric view and drawing its orthographic views, front, top and side, is the forward task. The reverse task is supplying a missing view, given two views, you must deduce and draw the third, this trains spatial visualisation, matching features and curves across views, using a mitre line at 45 degrees to transfer depths between the top and side views. Remember, isometric axes are 120 degrees apart and the isometric scale is about 0.82 of true size. We also begin Section 9.3, Methods of Dimensioning, which states sizes and positions using dimension lines, extension lines, leader lines, arrowheads and figures, with size dimensions and location dimensions being the two main kinds.
250: On this page we complete dimensioning rules, students. General rules are to place dimensions outside the outline, avoid repeating dimensions, avoid dimensioning to hidden lines, and group related dimensions together, diameter is marked with the symbol phi, radius with R, square with a square symbol, and across-flats with A over F. Chain dimensioning lets small errors add up along the chain, while parallel or progressive dimensioning from a single datum avoids this problem, remember, aligned means figures are read along the dimension line, while unidirectional means all figures are read horizontally. Now, students, we move to Section 9.4, Sectioning, covering full, half, offset, revolved and oblique sections. Sectioning shows interior detail by imagining the object cut by a cutting plane with the near part removed, exposing the inside, the cut surface is shown by section lines or hatching at 45 degrees, replacing a confusing mass of hidden dashed lines with a clear solid-line view. The types of sections are full section, where the cutting plane passes fully through the object, half section, where one quarter is removed for symmetric parts, offset section, where the plane is stepped to pass through several features, revolved section, showing a cross-section of a bar or spoke rotated in place, removed section, similar but drawn away from the view, broken-out or local section, and oblique or aligned section, where the cutting plane is inclined. Remember, certain solid parts like shafts, bolts, nuts, rivets, keys, pins, webs and ribs are NOT hatched even when the cutting plane passes along them, to avoid a misleading solid look.
251: Now, students, we study Section 9.5, Riveted Joints, Rivet Heads and Leak-Proof Joints. A rivet is a permanent fastener, a cylindrical shank with a formed head, the second or snap head is formed during driving. Riveted joints are permanent and non-removable, and were standard for boilers, tanks, bridges and ships. Joints are of two basic types, lap joint where plates overlap, and butt joint where plates meet edge-to-edge covered by one or two cover plates or straps, each may be single, double or triple-riveted, arranged in chain or zig-zag diamond pattern. Important terms include rivet head types such as snap, pan, conical, countersunk, flat and round, pitch, which is the distance between centres of adjacent rivets in a row, and margin, the distance from the rivet centre to the plate edge, about 1.5 times the rivet diameter. A riveted joint can fail by three modes, tearing of the plate between holes, shearing of the rivets, or crushing of the plate or rivet, and the joint is designed so these strengths are balanced. For pressure vessels and boilers the joint must be leak-proof, achieved through caulking and fullering, that is burring over the plate edge and rivet heads with a tool to close tiny gaps. Remember, modern practice largely replaces riveting with welding. We then begin Section 9.6, Welded Joints, covering symbols and representation, where welds are shown by standard BIS or ISO symbols on a reference line with an arrow pointing to the joint.
252: Here, students, we continue Section 9.6 on weld symbols. Common weld types include the square butt weld, shown by two parallel lines for thin plates with no edge preparation, the single-V butt, shown with a V symbol where edges are bevelled, the single-U or J butt, used for thick plates, and bead or surfacing welds, used for build-up and hard-facing. The reference line carries the symbol, and a symbol placed below the line means the weld is on the arrow side of the joint, while above the line means the other side. Supplementary symbols show weld-all-around, shown as a circle at the elbow, field or site weld, shown by a flag, and the contour, which may be flat, convex or concave. Welded joints are lighter and more leak-tight than riveted ones, which is why fabrication of farm structures has shifted to welding. Remember, the fillet weld, shown as a triangle, is the most common symbol to recognise first. Now, students, we move to Section 9.7, Screw Threads, covering nomenclature, profiles and representation. A screw thread is a helical ridge cut on a cylinder, forming the basis of bolts, screws and power transmission lead screws. Threads may be external, on a bolt, or internal, in a nut. Key nomenclature includes the crest at the top, root at the bottom, flank at the side, major and minor diameters, pitch diameter, pitch itself, lead, helix angle and thread angle.
253: Let us continue with thread profiles, students. The buttress thread takes load in one direction only, used in vices and presses, while the knuckle thread is rounded for rough use, seen in glass or rail couplings and bottle caps. For a multi-start thread, the lead equals the pitch multiplied by the number of starts, giving fast linear movement, as used in pen caps and camera mounts. A right-hand thread, the normal default, tightens when turned clockwise, while a left-hand thread is used where rotation would otherwise loosen it, such as the left pedal of a bicycle or grinding-wheel nuts on one side. On drawings, threads are shown by a conventional representation as per BIS, the crest shown by a continuous thick line and the root by a thin line, rather than drawing the true helix. Remember, metric V-thread angle is 60 degrees, ACME thread angle is 29 degrees, while square thread has no angle at all, square and ACME threads carry power, while V-threads are used for fastening because they are self-locking. Now, students, we begin Section 9.8, Nuts, Bolts, Lock-Nuts, Studs, Screws and Foundation Bolts. Threaded fasteners are temporary, removable joints. A bolt has a head and threaded shank, used with a nut, a stud is threaded at both ends, and a machine or cap screw screws directly into a tapped hole with the head acting as the clamp. Hexagonal heads are most common because a spanner can re-engage every 60 degrees, while square heads need a 90 degree swing but grip more strongly, used on foundation bolts and coach bolts.
254: On this page we complete Section 9.8, students. A set screw is headless or grub-type, used to locate a pulley or collar on a shaft, while a wood screw is tapered with a gimlet point and coarse thread that bites into wood. Locking devices prevent a nut from loosening under vibration, they are either friction types, such as lock-nut, spring washer and nylon-insert nut, or positive types, such as castle nut with split pin and slotted nut. Foundation bolts anchor heavy machines like engines, pumps and motors to a concrete foundation, common types are the eye foundation bolt, rag foundation bolt with a jagged shank, Lewis foundation bolt which is tapered and removable, cotter foundation bolt, and the simple bent J or L bolt. Remember, a bolt plus nut passes through clearance holes, a stud is threaded at both ends with no head, and a cap or machine screw screws into a tapped hole with its head clamping the part. Now, students, we move to Section 9.9, Design Process and Computer-Aided Design, known as CAD. The design process is the systematic path from a need to a finished, documented product, following six phases, recognition of need, definition of the problem, synthesis of solutions, analysis and optimisation, evaluation by testing the best solution, and presentation through drawings. CAD is the use of computer systems to create, modify, analyse and optimise a design, storing it as an editable digital model that replaces the drawing board.
255: Here, students, we complete Section 9.9 on CAD. The benefits of CAD are higher design productivity, improved accuracy and quality, easy modification, reuse of standard components, automatic documentation, and a design database linking to manufacturing and finite-element analysis. A CAD system has three components, hardware, software and the user. Hardware includes a processor with CPU, GPU and memory, a graphics display, the modern raster-scan display builds the image from a grid of pixels in a frame buffer, while the older vector or random-scan display drew lines directly, input devices such as mouse, keyboard, digitiser and scanner, and output devices such as plotter and printer. Remember, the CAD design process has six steps, need, problem definition, synthesis, analysis and optimisation, evaluation, and presentation, and modern displays are raster-scan using pixels in a frame buffer. Now, students, we begin Section 9.10, Semiconductors and the P-N Junction Diode. A semiconductor such as silicon or germanium has conductivity between a conductor and an insulator. A pure or intrinsic semiconductor has few free carriers, doping makes it extrinsic. Adding a pentavalent impurity like phosphorus, arsenic or antimony gives an n-type material where electrons are the majority carrier, while adding a trivalent impurity like boron, aluminium or gallium gives a p-type material where holes are the majority carrier.
