Joining p-type and n-type materials forms a p-n junction, and its voltage-current characteristic shows a knee at about 0.7 volts for silicon and 0.3 volts for germanium, with breakdown occurring by avalanche or Zener effect on the reverse side.
256: Let us understand the p-n junction more deeply, students. At the junction, diffusion of carriers leaves behind a carrier-free depletion region and sets up a barrier potential. The voltage-current characteristic shows that in forward bias, almost no current flows until the knee or cut-in voltage is reached, about 0.7 volts for silicon and 0.3 volts for germanium, after which current rises steeply. In reverse bias, only a very small reverse saturation current flows until breakdown occurs, either by avalanche or Zener mechanism, at high reverse voltage. The diode therefore conducts in one direction only, acting as a one-way valve for current, this is the basis of rectification. Remember, silicon's cut-in voltage is about 0.7 volts and germanium's is about 0.3 volts, this pair is directly asked in exams, n-type comes from a pentavalent donor giving electrons as majority carriers, while p-type comes from a trivalent acceptor giving holes. Diodes rectify the AC supply inside every solar-pump controller, battery charger and electronic instrument an Agricultural Officer meets in the field. Now, students, we begin Section 9.11, Rectifiers and Filter Circuits. A rectifier converts AC to pulsating DC using diodes. Three standard circuits exist, the half-wave rectifier using one diode and passing one half-cycle, the full-wave centre-tap rectifier using two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer, and the bridge rectifier using four diodes needing no centre tap, full-wave types use both half-cycles, giving smoother, more efficient output.
257: On this page we compare rectifier circuits in detail, students. Looking at figure 9.3, the full-wave bridge rectifier feeds an AC supply through four diodes, then a filter, either capacitor or pi-type, to the DC load, with no centre tap needed. The ripple factor, which measures how un-smooth the output is, is 1.21 for half-wave rectifiers and 0.48 for full-wave rectifiers, lower is better, and rectifier efficiency is a maximum of 40.6 percent for half-wave versus 81.2 percent for full-wave types. The peak inverse voltage per diode is Vm for both half-wave and bridge circuits, but 2Vm for the centre-tap circuit, since each diode there must withstand double the peak voltage. A filter smooths the pulsating DC into steady DC, types include the shunt capacitor filter, the series inductor or choke filter, the LC filter, and the pi or CLC capacitor-input filter, which gives the smoothest output. Remember, the bridge rectifier needs four diodes but its peak inverse voltage is only Vm, while the centre-tap uses just two diodes but each must withstand 2Vm, the bridge needs no centre-tapped transformer, that is its main advantage. This rectifier-plus-filter power supply runs almost every electronic device in agriculture, including weather-station data loggers and electronic weighing scales. Now, students, we begin Section 9.12, Clippers, Clampers and Voltage Multipliers.
258: Here, students, we study diode wave-shaping circuits. A clipper, or limiter, removes part of the waveform above or below a set level, used for wave-shaping and protection, it can be series or shunt, positive or negative, and biased to clip at a chosen level. A clamper, or DC restorer, shifts the whole waveform up or down by adding a DC level without changing its shape, it uses a capacitor and a diode, a positive clamper shifts the wave above zero, a negative clamper below. A voltage multiplier produces a DC output several times the peak AC input using a ladder of diodes and capacitors, the voltage doubler gives about twice the peak input, cascading gives a tripler, quadrupler and so on, called the Cockcroft-Walton circuit, used where high DC voltage at low current is needed. Remember, a clipper changes the shape or amplitude by cutting off a portion, while a clamper shifts the whole wave by a DC level with the shape unchanged, a clamper always needs a capacitor, while a basic clipper needs only a diode and resistor. Now, students, we begin Section 9.13, Diode Logic Gates, covering OR, AND, positive and negative logic. In positive logic the higher voltage represents logic 1, in negative logic this is reversed. A diode OR gate has diodes' anodes at the inputs with cathodes joined to the output, any HIGH input pulls the output HIGH, while a diode AND gate has cathodes at the inputs, giving output HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH.
259: Let us complete Section 9.13, students. An important idea here is that the same physical circuit performs a dual function when the logic convention is switched, a circuit that is an OR gate in positive logic becomes an AND gate in negative logic, and vice versa, this is called the duality principle. Diode logic cannot perform inversion, that is a NOT function, and the signal degrades through stages, so practical gates use transistors, TTL or CMOS, but diode logic shows the basic gate idea simply. Now, students, we begin Section 9.14, BJT, covering Operating Point and Biasing Methods. A bipolar junction transistor, or BJT, is a three-layer, two-junction device, either NPN or PNP, with three terminals, emitter, base and collector. It works in three regions, cut-off where both junctions are reverse-biased and the device is OFF, active region where the emitter junction is forward-biased and collector junction reverse-biased, used for amplification, and saturation where both junctions are forward-biased, fully ON, used for switching. The current gains are alpha, common-base gain, always less than 1, and beta, common-emitter gain, typically 50 to 300. Biasing methods include fixed or base resistor bias, which is simplest but has poorest stability, collector-to-base or self bias, giving moderate stability through negative feedback, voltage-divider bias, which is most stable and widely used in amplifiers, and emitter bias with dual supply, which is very stable. Remember, voltage-divider bias gives the most stable operating point, while fixed bias is the least stable.
260: On this page we study Section 9.15, Amplifier Classes and Coupling Methods, students. Amplifiers are classified by how much of the input cycle the transistor conducts. Class A conducts for the full 360 degrees, giving low distortion but low efficiency, maximum about 50 percent for transformer-coupled types. Class B conducts for 180 degrees, one half-cycle each in a push-pull arrangement, efficiency up to 78.5 percent, but with crossover distortion. Class AB conducts slightly more than 180 degrees, a compromise used in most audio output stages, removing crossover distortion. Class C conducts for less than 180 degrees, giving the highest efficiency above 78.5 percent but very distorted output, used only for tuned radio-frequency amplifiers. Multi-stage amplifiers raise gain by cascading stages joined through coupling. RC or resistance-capacitance coupling is cheapest and gives a flat response over the audio range, transformer coupling matches impedance and is used in power output stages, and direct or DC coupling passes DC and very low frequencies, used in op-amps. Remember, the conduction angle ladder runs Class A at 360 degrees, Class B at 180 degrees, Class AB just over 180 degrees, and Class C under 180 degrees, with efficiency rising and distortion also rising as you go from A to C. Now, students, we begin Section 9.16, the h-Parameter Model and the CE Amplifier, used for small-signal analysis with four parameters, h_i, h_r, h_f and h_o.
261: Here, students, we continue with the CE amplifier. The common-emitter, or CE, amplifier is the workhorse configuration, it gives both voltage and current gain, hence the highest power gain, and it inverts the signal, meaning the output is 180 degrees out of phase with the input. From the h-parameter model, the current gain and other quantities can be derived, and the CE amplifier has medium input and output impedance. In comparison, the common-collector configuration, known as the emitter follower, gives high input and low output impedance acting as a buffer, while the common-base configuration gives low input and high output impedance, useful at high frequency. Remember, the CE amplifier inverts, giving the highest power gain of the three configurations, and h_fe is approximately equal to beta, the forward current gain, do not confuse the emitter follower, which does not invert, with the CE stage, which does. Now, students, we begin Section 9.17, the RC Phase-Shift Oscillator. An oscillator generates an AC waveform with no AC input, it is essentially an amplifier with positive feedback meeting the Barkhausen criterion, where the loop gain equals 1 and the total phase shift around the loop is 0 or 360 degrees. The RC phase-shift oscillator uses a transistor or op-amp amplifier giving 180 degrees phase shift, plus a three-section RC ladder network adding another 180 degrees, each section contributing about 60 degrees, so the total reaches 360 degrees, sustaining oscillation.
262: Let us complete the oscillator topic and move into Section 9.18, the Differential Amplifier, students. For the standard three-section RC phase-shift oscillator, the frequency equals 1 divided by 2 pi RC times the square root of 6, and the amplifier must supply a minimum gain of 29 to overcome losses in the feedback network. Oscillators generate the timing and carrier signals inside radio telemetry systems that send rain-gauge and reservoir-level data to central monitoring servers. Now, a differential amplifier amplifies the difference between two input signals and rejects any signal common to both, it is the input stage of every op-amp, using a matched, emitter-coupled transistor pair, also called a long-tailed pair, sharing a common emitter resistor, ideally a constant-current source. Key terms include differential gain, the gain for the difference signal, common-mode gain, ideally zero, the gain for signals common to both inputs, and common-mode rejection ratio, or CMRR, which is differential gain divided by common-mode gain, often expressed in decibels, higher is better. Replacing the common emitter resistor with a constant-current source greatly raises CMRR. Remember, a differential amplifier amplifies the difference and rejects the common-mode signal, a high CMRR is good, meaning strong rejection of noise common to both inputs. This is why differential amplifiers with high CMRR can extract a strain-gauge weighbridge's tiny signal from electrical noise at a busy market yard.
263: On this page we begin Section 9.19, the Ideal Operational Amplifier, covering linear and non-linear applications, students. An operational amplifier, or op-amp, is a high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with two inputs, inverting and non-inverting, and one output, the 741 IC being a common example. The ideal op-amp has infinite open-loop voltage gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth, infinite CMRR and zero input offset. Two golden rules follow for negative-feedback linear operation, no current flows into the inputs, and the two inputs sit at the same voltage, called a virtual short. Looking at figure 9.4, the inverting amplifier has gain equal to minus Rf over R1, which inverts the signal, while the non-inverting amplifier has gain equal to 1 plus Rf over R1, which does not invert. Other linear applications include the voltage follower or buffer with gain of 1, the summing amplifier giving a weighted sum of inputs, the integrator, whose output is proportional to the integral of the input using a capacitor in the feedback path, the differentiator, whose output is proportional to the rate of change of input using a capacitor at the input, and the instrumentation amplifier, a high-gain, high-CMRR difference amplifier. Non-linear applications include the comparator, whose output swings to positive or negative saturation, the Schmitt trigger, a comparator with hysteresis, and the active or precision rectifier.
264: Let us finish Section 9.19 and move into Section 9.20, Voltage Regulators, students. Remember, the differentiator has a capacitor at the input with a resistor in feedback, recall it as integrate equals capacitor in feedback, and the comparator is a non-linear application because it saturates. Also remember, the non-inverting amplifier gain is 1 plus Rf over R1, not simply Rf over R1, and the instrumentation amplifier is prized for its very high CMRR, turning a load-cell or thermocouple's tiny millivolt output into a clean reading on an electronic farm weighbridge or grain-drier controller. Now, Section 9.20 covers voltage regulators, including Zener, series, current limiting and op-amp types. A voltage regulator keeps the DC output constant despite changes in input voltage or load current. The simplest is the Zener, or shunt, regulator, where a Zener diode in reverse breakdown across the load holds the voltage steady while a series resistor drops the excess, this is cheap but wastes power and suits only small loads. The transistor series or pass regulator places a transistor in series with the load, handling much more current. A series regulator with feedback adds an error amplifier, often an op-amp, comparing output to a reference voltage for precise regulation. Current limiting protects the regulator using a sense resistor, and IC regulators like the 78xx series give fixed positive voltages, for example 7805 gives plus 5 volts, while the 79xx series gives negative voltages. Remember, the Zener regulator is shunt, parallel to the load, while the pass-transistor regulator is series with the load.
265: On this page we begin section 9.21, Boolean algebra and combinational logic circuits. Boolean algebra is the mathematics of two valued, zero or one, logic. Its basic operations are AND, OR and NOT. Remember the key laws: commutative, associative, distributive, identity, complement, and especially De Morgan's theorems, which let you convert any function into NAND or NOR alone, because NAND and NOR are called the universal gates. The page then gives a table of logic gates and building blocks. AND, OR and NOT are the basic gates. NAND and NOR are universal gates, meaning any function can be built from them alone. XOR gives output one when inputs differ, and XNOR when they are equal. SOP and POS are sum of products and product of sums, the standard forms for writing Boolean functions. The Karnaugh map, or K map, is a graphical method to simplify these functions. A half adder gives sum equals A XOR B and carry equals A AND B, using two inputs. A full adder adds two bits plus a carry in. A DAC, or digital to analog converter, converts a digital code into an analog voltage. Combinational circuits have no memory, their output depends only on present inputs, unlike sequential circuits. For exams, remember the DAC gives 2 to the power n output levels for an n bit converter, and that only NAND and NOR are universal, not AND, OR or NOT.
266: Now, students, let us continue with sensors used to measure displacement, temperature, velocity, force and pressure. Displacement is measured by a potentiometer, which is the simplest and cheapest sensor, giving an output voltage proportional to position through a sliding wiper on a resistance track. The LVDT, or linear variable differential transformer, is a more accurate inductive displacement sensor, and capacitive sensors are also used. Temperature is measured by a resistance thermometer, called RTD, or by a thermocouple. The RTD works because a metal's resistance rises with temperature, following R t equals R naught into one plus alpha t. Platinum is the standard, called Pt100, giving 100 ohms at 0 degrees Celsius. The thermocouple uses the Seebeck effect, where two dissimilar metal junctions produce an EMF proportional to temperature difference; common types are K, J, T and E. A thermistor is a semiconductor sensor giving a large but non linear resistance change, usually decreasing with temperature, called NTC. Velocity or rotational speed is measured using a tachometer or electromagnetic pickup, which generates an EMF proportional to speed. Force and weight are measured with a load cell using strain gauges, where strain changes gauge resistance, read by a Wheatstone bridge. Pressure is measured by elastic elements like the Bourdon tube, diaphragm and bellows. Remember, RTD resistance rises with temperature, but most NTC thermistors show the opposite, resistance falling with temperature.
267: Here we have the chapter mind map for Basic Engineering, summarising the whole chapter into eight branches around the central topic. The first branch is engineering drawing, noting India uses first angle projection, third angle is used in USA and Canada, isometric scale is about 0.82, isometric axes are 120 degrees apart, hidden lines are short dashes, and centre lines are long-short chain lines. The second branch is joints and threads, covering metric thread at 60 degree angle, Whitworth thread at 55 degrees, ACME thread at 29 degrees trapezoidal, square thread for power transmission, rivet pitch at least three times rivet diameter, and weld symbols placed on the arrow side of the joint. The third branch is semiconductors and diodes, noting silicon cut in voltage is 0.7 volts, germanium is 0.3 volts, silicon band gap is 1.1 electron volts, germanium 0.7 electron volts, P type uses trivalent impurities giving holes, N type uses pentavalent impurities giving electrons, Zener diodes work in reverse breakdown, and LED is forward biased emitting photons. The fourth branch covers rectifiers and filters with ripple factors and efficiencies. The fifth branch covers transistors and amplifiers. The sixth branch covers op amps and regulators. The seventh branch covers digital logic. The eighth branch covers measurement, including Pt100, Seebeck effect, strain gauges, LVDT, and Wheatstone bridge for small resistances.
268: On this page, students, we have a key terms at a glance table, a quick revision tool listing important concepts alongside the key fact to remember for each one. It begins with engineering drawing basics: India uses first angle projection where the top view is below the front view, while third angle projection, used in USA, places the top view above the front view. Isometric axes are 120 degrees apart with a scale near 0.82. It covers dimensioning systems, which parts are not hatched in section such as shafts, bolts, nuts, keys, rivets and ribs, and that section hatching is drawn at 45 degrees. Rivet failure modes are tearing, shearing and crushing. A leak proof joint uses caulking and fullering. Weld symbols below the reference line mean the arrow side, above means the other side, and a triangle symbol means a fillet weld. It also reviews lead versus pitch, thread angles for metric, ACME and square threads, left hand threads, hex nut dimensions, studs, foundation bolts, the engineering design process from need to presentation, and CAD display types. Moving into electronics, it notes n type and p type semiconductors, diode cut in voltages for silicon and germanium, ripple factors and efficiencies for half wave and full wave rectifiers, peak inverse voltage, the smoothest filter type, and the difference between a clipper and a clamper, plus diode logic duality.
269: Let us continue the key terms table, now covering transistor and amplifier concepts. BJT current gains are defined: alpha equals I C over I E, always less than one, and beta equals I C over I B, related by beta equals alpha over one minus alpha. The most stable biasing method is voltage divider bias. Amplifier classes are distinguished by conduction angle: Class A conducts through the full 360 degrees, Class B through 180 degrees, Class AB more than 180 degrees, and Class C less than 180 degrees. Class B efficiency is 78.5 percent, with Class C being even higher. The common emitter amplifier gives a 180 degree phase shift and the highest power gain. H parameters are listed: h ie, h re, h fe which approximately equals beta, and h oe. For oscillators, the phase shift oscillator frequency formula and the Barkhausen criterion, requiring loop gain of one and phase shift of zero or 360 degrees, are given. Differential amplifiers and CMRR, the ratio of differential gain to common mode gain, are covered, along with the ideal op amp having infinite gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, and infinite CMRR and bandwidth. Op amp gain formulas for inverting and non-inverting configurations, integrator and differentiator circuits, voltage regulators, and IC regulator series are reviewed. The table also revisits universal gates, De Morgan's theorem, the half adder, Karnaugh maps, DAC, RTD, thermocouple, and the sensor map linking each physical quantity to its sensor. The page then begins Part B, objective questions and answers, covering the full chapter.
270: Now let us work through the first several objective questions of Part B, with their answers explained. Question one asks which projection system India follows per BIS standards, and the answer is first angle projection, since third angle is the US and ANSI standard. Question two confirms that in first angle projection, the top view sits below the front view, the exact mirror of the third angle arrangement. Question three establishes that isometric axes are drawn 120 degrees apart from each other, giving an isometric scale of about 0.82. Question four tests which parts are not hatched in sectional views when the cutting plane runs along their length, and the answer is a solid shaft or bolt, along with nuts, keys, rivets and ribs. Question five confirms section hatching lines are conventionally drawn at 45 degrees, with adjacent parts hatched in opposite directions. Question six explains that a leak proof riveted joint for a boiler is made gas or water tight by caulking and fullering, not simply by adding more rivets. Question seven identifies that buckling is not a recognised failure mode of a riveted joint, the three real modes being tearing, shearing and crushing at the bearing. Question eight explains that a weld symbol shown below the reference line means the arrow side, while above the line means the other side. Question nine begins asking about the lead of a double start screw thread.
271: Continuing with the objective questions, question nine confirms that for a double start thread, the lead equals twice the pitch, since lead equals pitch multiplied by the number of starts, and lead equals pitch only for a single start thread. Question ten identifies the square thread, along with ACME, as the profile mainly used for power transmission such as in a screw jack, since V threads are meant for fastening. Question eleven gives the included angle of a metric ISO V thread as 60 degrees, compared to 55 degrees for BSW and 29 degrees for ACME threads. Question twelve defines a stud as a fastener threaded at both ends with no head, distinguishing it from a bolt which has a head. Question thirteen identifies a castle nut with a split pin as a positive locking device against nut loosening, as opposed to friction based devices like spring washers or nylon insert nuts. Question fourteen explains foundation bolts are used to anchor heavy machines, such as engines and pumps, to a concrete foundation. Question fifteen lays out the correct order of the engineering design process: need, then problem definition, then synthesis, then analysis, then evaluation, then presentation. Question sixteen highlights that the benefit of CAD is higher productivity, accuracy and a reusable design database, since it assists rather than replaces the designer. Question seventeen then begins asking what a pentavalent impurity added to silicon produces.
272: We now move into semiconductor and electronics objective questions. Question seventeen confirms that a pentavalent impurity added to silicon produces n type material, where electrons are the majority carriers, while a trivalent acceptor produces p type material with holes as majority carriers. Question eighteen gives the cut in, or knee, voltage of a silicon diode as about 0.7 volts, compared to about 0.3 volts for germanium. Question nineteen states the ripple factor of a half wave rectifier is 1.21, while a full wave rectifier gives a smoother 0.48. Question twenty gives the maximum rectification efficiency of a full wave rectifier as 81.2 percent, compared to 40.6 percent for half wave. Question twenty one explains that in a centre tapped full wave rectifier, each diode experiences a peak inverse voltage of two V m, whereas bridge and half wave rectifiers see only V m. Question twenty two identifies the pi, or C L C, filter as giving the smoothest DC output, better than a simple shunt capacitor. Question twenty three distinguishes a clamper, which shifts a waveform up or down by adding a DC level without changing its shape, from a clipper, which cuts off part of the waveform. Question twenty four covers diode logic gates in positive logic. Question twenty five then introduces the relation between alpha and beta in a bipolar junction transistor, a bipolar junction transistor being commonly called a BJT.
273: Continuing with transistor and amplifier objective questions. Question twenty five confirms beta equals alpha over one minus alpha, and since alpha is always less than one, beta becomes a large number. Question twenty six identifies voltage divider, or potential divider, bias as the BJT biasing method giving the most stable operating point, since fixed bias is the least stable. Question twenty seven explains a Class B amplifier conducts for 180 degrees of the input cycle, meaning one half cycle, while Class A conducts the full 360 degrees and Class C conducts less than 180 degrees. Question twenty eight gives the maximum theoretical efficiency of a Class B push pull amplifier as 78.5 percent, compared to just 50 percent for a transformer coupled Class A amplifier. Question twenty nine explains the common emitter amplifier produces a 180 degree phase shift between input and output, since it inverts the signal, while the emitter follower gives zero degrees. Question thirty identifies h fe in the h parameter model as representing forward current gain, approximately equal to beta, while h ie represents input impedance. Question thirty one gives the frequency formula for a three section RC phase shift oscillator as one over two pi RC root six, distinguishing it from the LC tank circuit oscillator formula. Question thirty two states the Barkhausen criterion requires loop gain equal to one and a total phase shift of zero or 360 degrees for sustained oscillation. Question thirty three then asks what a high CMRR in a differential amplifier means.
274: We continue with op amp and digital logic objective questions. Question thirty three confirms a high CMRR means the amplifier strongly rejects signals common to both inputs, that is, common mode noise. Question thirty four explains an ideal operational amplifier has infinite input impedance and infinite open loop gain, while its output impedance is zero. Question thirty five gives the voltage gain of an inverting op amp amplifier as negative R f over R one, distinguishing it from the non-inverting gain formula of one plus R f over R one. Question thirty six explains an op amp integrator is built by placing the capacitor in the feedback path with the resistor at the input, the reverse arrangement being a differentiator. Question thirty seven describes a Zener voltage regulator, where the Zener diode is connected in parallel, or shunt, with the load and operated in reverse breakdown. Question thirty eight identifies NAND and NOR as the universal gates, since any logic function can be built from them alone, unlike AND and OR. Question thirty nine gives the half adder outputs as sum equals A XOR B and carry equals A AND B. Question forty explains a resistance thermometer such as Pt100 measures temperature because metal resistance rises as temperature rises, a positive coefficient, following R t equals R naught into one plus alpha t, with Pt100 reading 100 ohms at 0 degrees Celsius; falling resistance instead describes an NTC thermistor. Question forty one then asks what effect lets a thermocouple measure temperature.
275: We now finish the objective question bank for this chapter. Question forty one confirms a thermocouple measures temperature using the Seebeck effect, where two dissimilar metals produce an EMF proportional to the temperature difference at their junction. Question forty two identifies the load cell, using strain gauges, as the sensor used to measure force or weight, while the Bourdon tube measures pressure and the tachometer measures speed. Question forty three confirms pressure is most commonly measured by a Bourdon tube, a curved tube that straightens under pressure, forming the common dial gauge. Question forty four identifies the 78xx series as the IC voltage regulator supplying a fixed positive output, such as plus 5 volts, while the 79xx series gives negative outputs. Question forty five explains a right hand screw thread tightens when turned clockwise, the normal default, while a left hand thread tightens anticlockwise for special anti-loosening applications. The chapter then closes with its references section, listing sources including the KPSC AO and AAO Paper 2 syllabus for Unit 9, Basic Engineering, textbooks on engineering and machine drawing by Bhatt and Gopalakrishna, the BIS SP-46 drawing practice standard, CAD/CAM references by Ibrahim Zeid and Groover and Zimmers, electronics textbooks by Boylestad and Nashelsky, Millman and Halkias, Sedra and Smith, and Gayakwad, Morris Mano's Digital Design text, Sawhney's Electrical and Electronic Measurements book, and UAS and ICAR course material along with KSNDMC telemetric weather network documentation.
276: Now, students, we begin Chapter 10, Food Science and Nutrition, a technical paper unit combining theory with objective questions and answers. This chapter covers the three functions of food, methods of cooking, the major food groups such as cereals and millets, legumes, nuts and oilseeds, fruits and vegetables, egg, meat, poultry and fish, sugars, honey and royal jelly, fats and oils, beverages, condiments and spices, and processed and convenience foods. It also covers food spoilage and preservation principles, preservation by salt and sugar, heat, low temperature, drying and dehydration, irradiation, chemicals and fermentation, non thermal processing and quality testing, and food additives including colours, preservatives, stabilisers, sweeteners and emulsifiers. Part A theory opens with real world scenarios: a self help group in Mandya preserving mango pulp, a millet entrepreneur near Bengaluru managing ragi malt, a Nandini dairy supervisor explaining pasteurisation at 72 degrees for fifteen seconds, and a honey collector failing a purity test due to high HMF. This unit is where chemistry meets the kitchen and processing shed, covering what food does in the body, what happens to nutrients on heating, freezing, drying or fermenting, why food spoils, and how preservation methods work. An Agricultural Officer uses this knowledge to advise farmer groups on value addition, judge processing subsidy proposals, and promote millet and horticulture processing across Karnataka.
277: Continuing the chapter introduction, the text notes that the Defence Food Research Laboratory in Mysuru develops preserved rations, the Karnataka Milk Federation runs the state's dairy under the Nandini brand, and the state's millet, horticulture, coffee, spice and honey value chains all depend on this science. We then reach Block A, Functions of Food and Methods of Cooking, and section 10.1, the three functions of food: energy giving, body building, and protective. The energy giving function is met mainly by carbohydrates and fats, which supply calories. The body building function, meaning growth and repair, is met chiefly by proteins along with minerals like calcium and phosphorus. The protective and regulatory function is met by vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre. A table gives the exact energy values: one gram of carbohydrate equals 4 kilocalories, one gram of fat equals 9 kilocalories, and one gram of protein equals 4 kilocalories, making fat the most concentrated energy source. Nutrients are classified as macronutrients, needed in large amounts, and micronutrients, needed in small but essential amounts. Vitamins are either fat soluble, meaning A, D, E and K which get stored in the body, or water soluble, meaning B complex and C which are not stored. Deficiency diseases mentioned include protein energy malnutrition, anaemia from iron deficiency, goitre from iodine deficiency, night blindness from vitamin A deficiency, rickets from vitamin D deficiency, scurvy from vitamin C deficiency, and beriberi from thiamine deficiency.
278: This page shows three important diagrams. Figure 10.1 classifies nutrients into a tree: nutrients divide into macronutrients, which are carbohydrate at 4 kilocalories per gram, protein at 4 kilocalories per gram, and fat at 9 kilocalories per gram; micronutrients, which are vitamins and minerals; and water, which serves a regulatory and solvent role. It reminds us that energy giving nutrients are carbohydrate and fat, body building nutrients are protein and minerals, and protective nutrients are vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Figure 10.2 classifies vitamins into fat soluble vitamins, which are stored in the body, namely A linked to night blindness, D linked to rickets, E as an antioxidant, and K linked to blood clotting; and water soluble vitamins, which are not stored and must be taken daily, namely B complex linked to beriberi and C linked to scurvy. Figure 10.3, shown as a pyramid, illustrates the balanced diet food group pyramid: fats, oils and sugars at the narrow top to be used sparingly; pulses, milk, egg, meat and fish next for building the body; vegetables and fruits below that for their protective role; and cereals and millets forming the wide base, the energy foods to be eaten the most. The rule shown is that the base of the pyramid should be eaten most, and the apex eaten least.
279: On this page, we study section 10.2, methods of cooking, their types, merits and demerits. Cooking improves digestibility, palatability and safety by destroying microbes and toxins, but it also causes nutrient losses. Methods are grouped by how heat reaches the food. Moist heat methods, such as boiling, simmering, poaching, stewing, steaming, pressure cooking and blanching, use water or steam, and cause water soluble vitamins B and C to leach into the cooking water, though steaming and pressure cooking conserve more nutrients. Dry heat methods, such as roasting, grilling, baking and toasting, use hot air or radiation, developing colour and flavour through the Maillard browning reaction, but causing surface vitamin loss and possible charring. Frying, whether shallow or deep, is fast and tasty but raises calories, and repeated heating degrades the oil. Microwave cooking heats food by internal friction of water molecules at 2450 megahertz, giving fast cooking with good nutrient retention but uneven heating. The general rule for conserving nutrients is to cook for the shortest time, in the least water, with the lid on, and to avoid adding cooking soda, which destroys thiamine and vitamin C even though it keeps green vegetables looking bright. This is a favourite exam point. The page then begins Block B, covering cereals, millets, legumes, nuts and oilseeds, starting with section 10.3 on the structure and composition of cereals and millets and the functions of starch.
280: Now let us understand grain structure and composition, and the chemistry of starch. A cereal grain has three parts: the outer bran, rich in fibre, B vitamins and minerals, which is removed on polishing; the endosperm, which is about 70 to 80 percent starch with some protein and forms the bulk of the grain remaining after milling; and the germ, rich in fat, protein and vitamin E, which is removed to prevent rancidity in stored flour. Wheat protein forms gluten, giving dough its elasticity, a feature unique to wheat. Ragi, or finger millet, is notable for having the highest calcium content among cereals and millets, about 344 milligrams per 100 grams. Starch, made of amylose and amylopectin molecules, behaves in three important ways during cooking. Gelatinisation happens when starch is heated in water, causing granules to swell and thicken the mixture, as in custards and sauces. Dextrinisation happens on dry heating, where starch breaks down into dextrins and browns, as in toast or roti crust. Retrogradation happens on cooling, where a gelatinised starch paste re-associates and firms or stales, as in bread going stale. Remember, gelatinisation needs starch, water and heat, while dextrinisation needs dry heat, and examiners often test students by swapping these two. Karnataka is India's millet hub under the Siri Dhanya program, supplying about 40 percent of the country's millet output.
281: We now move to section 10.4, legumes, nuts and oilseeds, their composition and anti-nutritional factors. Legumes, or pulses, such as redgram, bengalgram, greengram, blackgram, cowpea and soybean, are the cheapest protein source and complement cereals, since cereals lack the amino acid lysine while pulses lack methionine, so a cereal-pulse mix gives complete protein through mutual supplementation. Nuts and oilseeds, including groundnut, coconut, sesame, sunflower, mustard and soybean, are rich in fat and protein, with soybean being the richest plant protein at about 40 percent protein and 20 percent oil. However, these foods contain anti-nutritional and toxic constituents. The trypsin inhibitor in soybean and raw pulses blocks protein digestion but is destroyed by cooking heat. Phytic acid in cereal bran and pulses binds iron, zinc and calcium, but is reduced by soaking, germination and fermentation. Tannins in coloured pulses and sorghum reduce protein digestibility and are removed by dehulling. BOAA, or beta-ODAP, found in khesari dal, causes lathyrism, a form of paralysis, and its sale is banned or restricted. Aflatoxin, a carcinogen produced by Aspergillus mould on damp-stored groundnut and maize, is prevented by proper drying and storage rather than by cooking, since it is heat stable. The chapter then turns to Block D, fruits, vegetables and their pigments, in section 10.5.
282: Continuing section 10.5, fruits and vegetables are classified by the plant part used, such as root, tuber, bulb, stem, leaf, flower or fruit, and their colour comes from four pigment groups that behave differently with heat, acid and alkali, a favourite exam theme. Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leafy vegetables, turns dull olive-green in acid, forming pheophytin, and stays bright green in alkali, though cooking soda used for greening destroys vitamins and softens texture. Carotenoids, the yellow-orange-red pigments in carrot, tomato and mango, are fat soluble and remain stable to heat and pH, serving as the provitamin A source. Anthocyanins, the red-purple-blue pigments in jamun, red cabbage and beet skin, turn red in acid and blue-green in alkali, and are very water soluble, leaching out easily. Anthoxanthins, or flavonoids, the white-cream pigments in cauliflower and onion, stay white in acid but turn yellow in alkali. Two further changes matter: enzymatic browning, where cut apple, banana, potato and brinjal darken due to the enzyme polyphenol oxidase acting on phenols in air, prevented by blanching or acid dipping; and the loss of vitamin C, the most easily destroyed nutrient by heat, air and alkali. The page then moves into Block D, covering egg, meat, poultry and fish, beginning with section 10.6 on egg structure, grading and functions in cookery, describing the shell, membranes, air cell, albumen and yolk.
283: We continue with egg quality and cookery functions. Eggs are graded by candling, spinning the egg before a light to judge the air cell size and yolk position, and by breaking out the egg to measure the Haugh unit, a quality index based on albumen height and egg weight, where a higher Haugh unit means a fresher egg. A simple freshness test is that a fresh egg sinks in water, while a stale egg floats because its air cell has enlarged over time. In cookery, egg white coagulates, or sets, around 60 to 65 degrees Celsius, and yolk around 65 to 70 degrees, useful for custards and puddings. Egg white also foams, trapping air for meringue and sponge cake, while the yolk's lecithin acts as an emulsifier, stabilising mayonnaise and salad dressing. Eggs also bind, thicken, clarify and glaze in various recipes. Overcooking forms a harmless green ring of ferrous sulphide at the yolk-white boundary, which cooling the egg quickly can prevent. Remember, the Haugh unit measures freshness from albumen height and egg weight, a fresh egg sinks while a stale one floats, and the yolk, not the white, is the emulsifier. The page then begins section 10.7, meat, poultry and fish, covering their structure, tenderness and postmortem changes, noting that muscle consists of actin and myosin fibres, and that the red colour comes from the pigment myoglobin, not haemoglobin.
284: Continuing section 10.7, we study tenderness and postmortem changes in meat in more detail. Tenderness depends on the animal's age, with young animals being more tender, the muscle's workload, the amount of connective tissue and marbling fat, and post-slaughter handling. After death, muscle passes through rigor mortis, a temporary stiffening as glycogen and ATP are exhausted and actin and myosin lock together as actomyosin, making the meat tough; it tenderises again as the stiffness resolves during chilled ageing, or conditioning, which also develops flavour. Tough cuts, having high collagen, are best cooked slowly using moist heat, which converts collagen into soluble gelatin, while tender cuts suit fast dry heat cooking. Enzyme tenderisers include papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, and ficin from fig. Because fish and meat spoil quickly, an unbroken cold chain is essential. Remember, the red colour of meat is myoglobin, a muscle pigment, not blood haemoglobin, changing from purple myoglobin to bright red oxymyoglobin on fresh cutting, and to brown metmyoglobin on ageing; rigor mortis makes meat tough, while ageing makes it tender again. The page then opens Block E, sugars, honey and royal jelly, with section 10.8 on sugars, their types, manufacture and functions in cookery, covering monosaccharides, disaccharides, sucrose manufacture from sugarcane, and the sweetness scale where fructose is the sweetest natural sugar, along with sugar chemistry reactions like caramelisation and Maillard browning.
285: On this page we look at sugar cookery chemistry and the start of honey. Sugar does more than sweeten. Inversion is when sucrose, under acid, heat, or the enzyme invertase, splits into glucose and fructose, giving invert sugar, which resists crystallisation and keeps jams and syrups smooth. Crystallisation happens when a concentrated syrup is cooled and forms sugar crystals, something you control for fudge but prevent for clear candy. Hygroscopicity means sugar binds water and lowers water activity, which is why high sugar jam and candied fruit preserve well. Remember the two key browning reactions. Caramelisation is sugar alone under dry heat, browning at around 160 degrees Celsius. Maillard browning needs sugar plus protein or amino acids, as in a bread crust. Sugarcane and jaggery are central to the Mandya Mysuru belt, and Karnataka is a leading sugar state, so an agriculture officer advising a jaggery or candy self-help group applies inversion to stop graining, boiling stages for texture, and the sugar acid pectin balance for jam set. The page then introduces honey, the natural sweet substance made by honey bees from floral nectar or honeydew. Honey is classified by source, such as mustard, eucalyptus, or litchi honey, and by processing method, including comb, extracted, strained, or creamed honey.
286: Now, students, let us continue with honey's composition and quality. Honey is dominated by sugars, about 80 percent, chiefly fructose and glucose, with fructose usually exceeding glucose. It contains about 17 to 18 percent water, plus small amounts of acids, enzymes like invertase, diastase, and glucose oxidase, minerals, vitamins, pollen, and aroma compounds. Because fructose predominates, honey is sweeter than table sugar and tends to stay liquid, while honey with more glucose tends to granulate. On properties, purity, and storage, honey is viscous, hygroscopic, has high density, low water activity, and rotates the plane of polarised light to the left, called laevorotatory. Granulation is simply glucose crystallising and is reversed by gentle warming, so it is not spoilage. Purity and quality are judged using indices such as moisture, which should be no more than about 20 to 25 percent, the HMF or hydroxymethylfurfural value which is low in fresh honey and rises with overheating and ageing, diastase activity, the fructose to glucose ratio, sucrose content, and fibre or pollen content. Fermentation, on the other hand, is true spoilage, caused by osmophilic yeasts when moisture rises above roughly 19 to 20 percent. Honey must be stored cool, dry, airtight, and away from light, and must never be overheated, since heat raises HMF and destroys the beneficial enzymes.
287: Here we complete honey and preservation topics, then move into fats and oils. Honey is regulated in India under Agmark grading and by FSSAI, with adulteration checked through moisture, HMF, diastase, and sugar ratio tests. Karnataka's Western Ghats and apiculture sector, supported by KVIC and the state horticulture department, produce multifloral and eucalyptus honey, and an agriculture officer supporting a beekeeping farmer producer organisation uses these quality indices to certify honey and command a premium price. Royal jelly is next, the milky secretion of the hypopharyngeal and mandibular glands of young worker or nurse bees, fed to all larvae briefly but to the queen larva throughout her development, which is why the queen develops as she does. Royal jelly is about two thirds water, with proteins including royalactin, sugars, lipids such as the marker compound 10 hydroxy 2 decenoic acid, B vitamins rich in pantothenic acid, and minerals. It is sold as a nutritional and health supplement and used in cosmetics, though it is a minor, low yield bee product and lightly examined. Royal jelly, bee pollen, and propolis are valuable diversification products for beekeeping groups. The page then opens fats and oils, describing them as triglycerides, glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, with fats solid and oils liquid at room temperature, and fatty acids classed as saturated, monounsaturated, or polyunsaturated depending on double bonds.
288: Let us understand the cookery functions and spoilage of fats and oils today. Fat is the most concentrated energy source at 9 kilocalories per gram, carries the fat soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, and gives food flavour, satiety, and texture. In cookery, fat acts as a heat transfer medium in frying, a shortening agent that gives baked goods a tender, flaky texture, an emulsifier or emulsion component, and a carrier of flavour and aeration. The smoke point is the temperature at which heated fat begins to smoke and break down, releasing acrolein, and it falls with repeated frying, making over-used frying oil unsafe. Refining, through degumming, neutralising, bleaching, and deodorising, makes crude oil edible, while hydrogenation adds hydrogen to unsaturated oil to make it semisolid, as in vanaspati, but this process also creates trans fatty acids linked to heart disease. Rancidity is fat spoilage of two kinds. Hydrolytic rancidity happens when lipase or moisture splits fat into free fatty acids, producing a soapy smell, as in stale butter with butyric acid. Oxidative rancidity happens when atmospheric oxygen attacks unsaturated double bonds, forming peroxides, and this is the more common type, sped up by light, heat, and metals, and slowed by antioxidants and airtight, cool, dark storage. Groundnut, sunflower, safflower, sesame, and coconut are key Karnataka oilseed crops, and an agriculture officer advising an oil expeller unit stresses good drying to prevent rancidity and aflatoxin, along with nitrogen flushing and opaque packing.
289: On this page the chapter shifts into convenience foods and then into food spoilage. Processed foods rely on preservation and processing principles like freezing, dehydration, retort sterilisation for ready to eat pouches, packaging, and additives, and they cut household drudgery, reduce post-harvest losses, and add value for the processor, though they can be costlier and less nutritious than fresh food. The Defence Food Research Laboratory, or DFRL, at Mysuru is India's lead developer of ready to eat and convenience rations for the armed forces, and CFTRI Mysuru has incubated many instant mix and ready to eat technologies. Instant millet mixes, ready to eat millet meals, and dehydrated horticulture products are exactly the value added lines Karnataka's millet mission and food parks promote. Now, students, we move to Block G, food spoilage and the principles of preservation. Foods differ in how fast they spoil. Perishable foods like milk, meat, fish, and most fruits and vegetables spoil within days, semi-perishable foods like potato, onion, and hard cheese last weeks to months, and non-perishable or shelf-stable foods like cereals, pulses, sugar, and oil last long if kept dry. Spoilage causes are microbial, which is the chief cause, enzymatic and chemical, physical such as moisture or light damage, and biological such as insects and rodents.
290: Let us understand preservation science today. Preservation prevents or slows spoilage so food keeps its safety, nutritive value, and acceptability for longer. It works on core principles, remember the acronym FATTOM, which stands for Food, Acidity or pH, Time, Temperature, Oxygen, and Moisture, since every preservation method removes one or more of these hurdles that microbes need to grow. Water activity, not total moisture, actually governs microbial growth, with most bacteria stopping below a water activity of 0.90 and most moulds below 0.80. India loses a large share of its fruits and vegetables to spoilage, so an agriculture officer who can match each cause of spoilage to the right preservation principle helps farmer groups choose low-cost methods like solar drying, brining, jam-making, or cold storage. Block H then begins with preservation by salt and sugar, which work by raising osmotic pressure and lowering the water activity of food, causing microbes to lose water through plasmolysis and stop growing. Salting or curing is used for fish, meat, and vegetables, applied as dry salt or brine, forming the basis of pickles, salted fish, and cured meat, often combined with smoking, acid, or spices. Sugar preserves at high concentration, about 65 to 70 percent soluble solids, in jam, jelly, marmalade, murabba, and candied or crystallised fruit, since the high sugar level binds water so tightly that microbes are inhibited.
291: Now, students, we look closely at salt and sugar products and then heat preservation. A stable fruit jam or jelly needs the correct balance of sugar, about 65 to 68 percent total soluble solids, acid at around pH 3.0 to 3.4, and pectin, which together set the gel. Too little acid or pectin gives a runny product, while too much acid causes the gel to weep, called syneresis. Jam, squash, pickle, and murabba from mango, amla, lime, and mixed vegetables are classic Karnataka self-help group products, and an agriculture officer trains groups on this sugar acid pectin balance and safe salt levels so products are stable and meet FSSAI standards. Section 10.17 then covers preservation by heat, through blanching, pasteurisation, sterilisation, and canning. Heat preserves food by destroying spoilage and pathogenic microbes and inactivating enzymes, with intensity ranging from mild to severe. Blanching is a brief mild heat, around 85 to 100 degrees Celsius for a few minutes, given before freezing, drying, or canning, mainly to inactivate enzymes, judged by the peroxidase test, and to set colour and expel air. It is a pre-treatment, not preservation on its own. Pasteurisation is a mild heat that kills pathogens and most spoilage microbes but not spores, extending shelf life under refrigeration, used for milk, juice, and beer. Sterilisation, or commercial sterilisation, is a severe heat that destroys all microbes including spores, giving a long, shelf-stable product like canned and retort-pouch foods and UHT milk.
292: Here we finish heat preservation and begin low temperature methods. Milk pasteurisation uses either the low-temperature long-time method, 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, or the high-temperature short-time method, 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, which is the standard milk process, while ultra-high-temperature treatment at 135 to 150 degrees Celsius for a few seconds with aseptic packing gives long-life milk. Canning, devised by Nicolas Appert, seals food in a container and heat-processes it to commercial sterility, with the benchmark being the 12-D process for low-acid foods, a heat treatment reducing the heat-resistant pathogen Clostridium botulinum, which causes deadly botulism, by twelve logarithmic cycles. Low-acid foods with pH above 4.6, such as vegetables, meat, and fish, must be processed at 121 degrees Celsius under pressure in a retort, while high-acid foods with pH below 4.6, such as most fruits and pickles, need only a gentler boiling-water process because acid prevents botulinum growth. KMF Nandini dairies pasteurise milk by the HTST method and sell UHT tetra-pack toned milk, and Karnataka fruit canneries run retort sterilisation, so an agriculture officer assessing a dairy or cannery proposal checks these temperature-time combinations for safety. Section 10.18 then opens preservation by low temperature, chilling and freezing, noting that low temperature only slows microbial growth, it does not kill microbes, so food spoils again once it warms up. Chilling holds food at about 0 to 5 degrees Celsius for short-term storage.
293: On this page we cover freezing methods and begin food irradiation. The rate of freezing matters greatly. Fast or quick freezing forms many small ice crystals that do little damage to cell structure, preserving texture on thawing, whereas slow freezing forms large crystals that rupture cells and cause drip loss. Freezing storage is kept at about minus 18 degrees Celsius for long-term preservation, while cryogenic freezing using liquid nitrogen at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, or carbon dioxide, is very fast and used for premium products. Individual quick freezing equipment includes plate freezers, air-blast freezers, and fluidised-bed units, commonly used for peas and prawns. Vegetables are blanched before freezing to inactivate enzymes that would otherwise cause off-flavours during storage. IQF peas, sweet corn, vegetables, and marine prawns are major Karnataka cold-chain products, especially from coastal seafood exports and Bengaluru area vegetable freezing, and an agriculture officer evaluating a cold-storage proposal checks the freezing rate, the minus 18 degree storage, and an unbroken cold chain. Section 10.20 then introduces food irradiation, which preserves food using controlled doses of ionising radiation, gamma rays from cobalt-60 or caesium-137, electron beams, or X-rays, which kill or inactivate microbes, insects, and sprouting tissue without appreciably raising the food's temperature, making it a cold process. Importantly, irradiation does not make food radioactive, and dose is measured in gray or kilogray.
294: Let us continue with irradiation levels and then chemical preservation. At low doses, below 1 kilogray, irradiation inhibits sprouting of onions, potatoes, and garlic, and disinfests stored grain and pulses, a process called radurisation or disinfestation. At medium doses, 1 to 10 kilogray, called radicidation, it reduces spoilage organisms and pathogens, extending the life of spices, meat, and seafood, and at high doses above 10 kilogray, called radappertisation, it achieves commercial sterility for products like sterile rations. In India irradiation is regulated, irradiated food must carry the green Radura logo, and the technology is delivered through Department of Atomic Energy facilities. Onion and potato are major Karnataka crops with heavy sprouting and storage losses, so an agriculture officer aware of low-dose irradiation can flag it as a residue-free way to extend storage. Section 10.21 then covers preservation by chemicals, substances added to food to prevent or delay microbial and oxidative spoilage. Indian regulation under FSSAI divides chemical preservatives into Class I, natural preservatives usable without a specific limit such as common salt, sugar, vinegar or acetic acid, spices, honey, and edible oils, and Class II, permitted chemical preservatives used within prescribed limits, including benzoic acid and benzoates, sorbic acid and sorbates, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, nitrites and nitrates, and propionates. The common acid-food preservatives are benzoic acid and sodium benzoate, effective in acidic products such as squash and jam.
295: Now, students, we finish chemical preservatives and move to fermentation. Sorbic acid and potassium sorbate are chiefly antifungal, used in cheese, baked goods, and beverages. Sulphur dioxide and its salts, especially potassium metabisulphite or KMS, act against microbes and also prevent browning and oxidation, so they are used in dried fruit, fruit pulp, and squash. Nitrites and nitrates are used in cured meats to inhibit Clostridium botulinum and to fix the pink cured colour, though their use is limited due to nitrosamine concerns. Antioxidants such as BHA, BHT, TBHQ, and natural tocopherols are not antimicrobials but delay oxidative rancidity of fats. Every Class II preservative has a legal maximum, and exceeding that limit is an offence. Squash, pickle, and dried-fruit self-help groups in Karnataka routinely use KMS and sodium benzoate, and an agriculture officer must teach the correct legal dose so the product both keeps well and passes FSSAI inspection. Section 10.22 then covers preservation by fermentation, which uses the controlled action of desirable microorganisms to produce acids, alcohol, or other metabolites that inhibit spoilage organisms and develop flavour and texture. The main types are lactic acid fermentation, where lactic-acid bacteria lower the pH, as in curd, yoghurt, idli, dosa, and sauerkraut, alcoholic fermentation, where yeast turns sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide, as in wine, beer, toddy, and bread leavening, and acetic acid fermentation, where acetic-acid bacteria turn alcohol into vinegar.
296: On this page we cover novel, non-thermal preservation processes. Non-thermal or novel processes preserve food while keeping it close to fresh, because they inactivate microbes with little or no heat, protecting colour, flavour, vitamins, and texture better than conventional thermal processing, making them a favourite of exam question-setters since each has a one-line principle. High-pressure processing, or HPP, subjects packaged food to very high pressure, around 100 to 1000 megapascals, which inactivates microbes at or near room temperature, acting as a cold pasteurisation for juices and ready-to-eat meats. Pulsed electric field processing applies short bursts of high voltage that rupture microbial membranes through electroporation, suited to liquid foods like juice and milk with minimal heat. Pulsed intense light uses brief, powerful broad-spectrum flashes to decontaminate surfaces and packaging. Ultrasound or sonication uses high-frequency sound whose cavitation bubbles disrupt cells, often combined with mild heat. Dielectric or microwave heating, ohmic heating, and infrared heating are rapid heating methods used for cooking, drying, tempering, and pasteurising. Remember that the first four methods are largely non-thermal, while the last three are rapid heating methods. HPP and pulsed electric field technology are emerging in Indian premium juice and ready-to-eat product lines and could suit Karnataka's high-value fruit and coffee products, and an agriculture officer can use this knowledge when evaluating modern food-park proposals incubated through CFTRI.
297: Let us understand quality testing, shelf life, and food additives now. The shelf life of a preserved food is the period it stays safe and acceptable under stated storage conditions, verified through several quality tests. Microbiological tests count total plate count, yeasts and moulds, coliforms, and specific pathogens to confirm safety. Chemical tests check moisture, water activity, pH or acidity, peroxide value and free fatty acid for rancidity, HMF for honey and heated products, preservative levels, and nutrient retention. Physical and sensory tests judge colour, texture, viscosity, and overall acceptability through a taste panel. Shelf life is estimated through real-time storage studies and accelerated shelf-life testing at higher temperature and humidity, and shown on the label as a best-before or use-by date. Before a farmer producer organisation's jam, squash, or dried product can be sold under FSSAI, it must meet these microbiological and chemical limits and carry a shelf-life date, so an agriculture officer links the producer to CFTRI, DFRL, or a state food-testing laboratory. Block J then opens with food additives, defined as any substance not normally consumed as a food in itself but added intentionally for a technological purpose, to preserve food, improve colour, flavour, texture, or nutrition, or to aid processing. Additives are intentional, deliberately added like preservatives and colours, or incidental, entering accidentally like pesticide residues or packaging migrants.
298: Here we cover additive safety and food colours. Safety of additives is evaluated through toxicological study, feeding trials in animals to find the no-observed-adverse-effect level, or NOAEL, from which a safety factor, usually 100, gives the Acceptable Daily Intake, or ADI, the amount a person can consume daily for life without appreciable risk. Substances with a long history of safe use may be listed as GRAS, Generally Recognised As Safe. An agriculture officer advising food-processing entrepreneurs must know that only FSSAI-permitted additives, within limits, may be used, and adding one to hide spoilage fails inspection. Section 10.26 covers food colours and dyes. Colour is the first quality cue a consumer judges, so colouring is added to restore colour lost in processing or to make food attractive. Colours are natural, from plant, animal, or mineral sources, such as turmeric or curcumin yellow, annatto orange, beta-carotene, anthocyanins, chlorophyll, caramel, beetroot, and cochineal or carmine red, or synthetic coal-tar or azo dyes. India permits exactly eight synthetic food colours, the reds Ponceau 4R, Carmoisine, and Erythrosine, the yellows Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow FCF, the blues Indigo Carmine and Brilliant Blue FCF, and the green Fast Green FCF, each usable only up to a prescribed maximum, commonly 100 parts per million, and only in specified foods. Non-permitted colours like metanil yellow and lead chromate are dangerous, illegal adulterants. Turmeric and Byadagi chilli are natural colourants Karnataka exports.
299: Now, students, we move into texture additives and functional additive groups. Section 10.27 covers stabilisers, thickeners, chelating agents, and salts. Thickeners increase viscosity, and stabilisers keep emulsions, foams, and suspensions from separating, including natural gums and polysaccharides such as pectin, agar, alginate, carrageenan, guar gum, gum arabic, xanthan gum, gelatin, and modified starches. Chelating or sequestering agents bind trace metal ions like iron and copper that catalyse oxidation and discolouration, examples being EDTA, citric acid, and polyphosphates, which protect colour and flavour and improve the action of antioxidants. Pectin is the gelling agent of fruit jams and jellies, gelatin, an animal protein, sets desserts, and agar and carrageenan come from seaweed. Pectin recovery from fruit waste such as citrus peel and apple pomace, and seaweed hydrocolloids, are value-addition opportunities, and an agriculture officer advising a jam or dairy self-help group explains how a little pectin or stabiliser gum within FSSAI limits gives the set and smoothness buyers expect. Section 10.28 then covers humectants, anti-caking, firming, bleaching, antioxidant, and sweetener additives. Humectants, polyhydric alcohols like glycerol, sorbitol, and propylene glycol, hold moisture and keep foods soft. Anti-caking agents, like silicates and calcium phosphate, keep powders free-flowing. Firming agents, like calcium chloride, keep canned and pickled fruits and vegetables crisp by strengthening cell-wall pectin, while flour bleaching and maturing agents whiten flour and develop dough strength.
300: Let us understand sweeteners and the final additive groups today. Sweeteners are nutritive or caloric, the sugars and sugar alcohols such as sucrose, glucose, fructose, sorbitol, and mannitol, which also provide bulk and texture, or non-nutritive, high-intensity sweeteners such as saccharin, aspartame, acesulfame-potassium, sucralose, and the natural steviol glycosides from stevia, which sweeten with negligible calories and are used in diabetic and diet products. Saccharin is about 300 to 400 times as sweet as sucrose and heat-stable, the oldest artificial sweetener. Aspartame is about 200 times as sweet as sucrose but not heat-stable, and must carry a warning for people with phenylketonuria. Stevia, or steviol glycoside, is about 200 to 300 times as sweet, natural and plant-derived, with zero calories. Stevia is grown as a niche crop in parts of Karnataka, and an agriculture officer can flag stevia cultivation and permitted sweeteners as value-addition routes for farmer groups targeting health-conscious and diabetic consumers. Section 10.29 then covers enzymes, leavening agents, fat substitutes, flavour enhancers, acidity regulators, and emulsifiers. Enzymes are biological catalysts used as processing aids, such as amylases and proteases in baking and brewing, rennet or chymosin to coagulate milk for cheese, and pectinase to clarify fruit juice. Leavening agents make baked goods rise, either biologically through yeast producing carbon dioxide, or chemically through baking soda or baking powder.
301: On this final page of the chapter's teaching content, we complete the additive groups. Fat substitutes mimic the mouthfeel of fat with fewer calories and are carbohydrate-based, protein-based, or fat-based like olestra. Flavour and taste enhancers do not add a flavour of their own but intensify what is present, monosodium glutamate, or MSG, supplies the savoury umami taste, and the 5 prime nucleotides, disodium inosinate and guanylate, act with it synergistically. Acidity regulators, including citric, acetic, lactic, tartaric, and malic acids, and phosphate or citrate salts, adjust and stabilise pH, contribute tartness, and aid preservation. Emulsifiers allow oil and water to mix and stay mixed by reducing interfacial tension, lecithin from soybean and egg yolk, mono- and di-glycerides, DATEM, and polysorbates stabilise mayonnaise, ice cream, chocolate, bakery products, and dairy analogues. Together these additive classes, within FSSAI limits, give modern processed foods their consistency, rise, flavour, and stability. Remember that leavening compares yeast, which is biological and produces carbon dioxide by fermentation, against baking soda or baking powder, which are chemical, with baking powder being soda plus an acid salt. An emulsifier joins oil and water, lecithin coming from egg yolk or soy, while MSG is a flavour enhancer, not a flavour itself, and acidity regulators like citric acid control pH. Lecithin from soybean, enzymes, and acidulants like citric acid are inputs an agriculture officer may encounter when advising bakery, dairy-analogue, juice, or confectionery farmer producer organisations, checking that a processor's formulation is both functional and FSSAI-compliant.
302: This page presents a chapter mind map summarising Food Science and Nutrition as a revision tool. The central topic branches into Animal Foods, covering fish and poultry tenderness, meat myoglobin and rigor mortis, and egg Haugh unit and candling, into Fruits and Vegetables, covering pigments like chlorophyll and carotenoid, anthocyanin and anthoxanthin, and acid or alkali effects on enzymatic browning, into Plant Foods, covering cereals with bran, endosperm, and germ, starch gelatinisation and retrogradation, and legumes and oilseeds with anti-nutritional factors, into Functions and Cooking, covering energy, body-building, and protective functions, and moist, dry, and frying or microwave cooking methods, into Sweeteners, covering caramelisation, Maillard reaction, inversion, honey and HMF, and royal jelly, into Fats, Beverages, and Spices, covering hydrolytic and oxidative rancidity, hydrogenation and smoke point, and tea, coffee, and convenience foods, into Preservation, covering the FATTOM spoilage principle, heat methods like pasteurisation and 12-D canning, low temperature, drying, irradiation, fermentation, and novel processing like HPP and PEF, into Food Additives, covering ADI, NOAEL, and GRAS, the 8 permitted colours, Class I and II preservatives, and sweeteners, emulsifiers, and leavening, and into Karnataka, covering Byadagi chilli and Kodagu coffee, KMF-Nandini and the millet mission, and CFTRI and DFRL Mysuru. Use this map to see how all the chapter's topics connect before moving into the revision tables that follow.
303: This page opens the Key Terms at a Glance revision table, described as the single most exam-dense table in the chapter, covering dates, full forms, values, formulae, institutions, and confused pairs that question-setters favour. It begins with the three functions of food, energy-giving from carbohydrate and fat, body-building from protein, and protective or regulatory from vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water, and the energy values, carbohydrate and protein at 4 kilocalories per gram, fat at 9, and alcohol at 7. It distinguishes gelatinisation, where starch, water, and heat cause thickening, from dextrinisation, dry heat browning of starch, and covers retrogradation, where cooked starch cools and firms or stales, as in bread staling. It notes the cereal-pulse complement, where cereal lacks lysine and pulse lacks methionine so combining them gives mutual nutritional benefit. It covers aflatoxin, produced by Aspergillus flavus on damp groundnut or maize, a heat-stable carcinogen, and lathyrism, caused by BOAA or beta-ODAP in khesari or Lathyrus dal, causing paralysis. It lists food pigments, chlorophyll as green, carotenoid as yellow-orange and stable, anthocyanin as red in acid and blue in alkali, and anthoxanthin as white turning yellow in alkali, and enzymatic browning, caused by polyphenol oxidase plus oxygen, stopped by blanching, acid, or salt. It also covers egg quality through candling and the Haugh unit, and meat pigment changing from myoglobin to bright red oxymyoglobin to brown metmyoglobin.
304: This page continues the Key Terms revision table, covering rigor mortis as postmortem stiffening as ATP falls, with ageing tenderising meat, and tenderising enzymes papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, and ficin from fig. It lists the sweetness order, fructose at 173, sucrose at 100, glucose at 74, then maltose and lactose, and distinguishes caramelisation, sugar alone, from Maillard browning, sugar plus amino acid or protein, and inversion, sucrose splitting into glucose and fructose by acid or invertase, stopping crystallisation. It recaps honey, about 80 percent sugar with fructose exceeding glucose, about 18 percent water, HMF as the freshness marker, and laevorotatory behaviour, and royal jelly, the nurse-bee secretion that determines the queen, marked by 10-HDA and rich in pantothenic acid. It covers rancidity types, hydrolytic and oxidative, hydrogenation creating trans fats, and pasteurisation and canning benchmarks including the 12-D process against Clostridium botulinum, and D-value and Z-value definitions, freezing methods, drying methods, irradiation using cobalt-60 with the Radura logo, Class I versus Class II preservatives, KMS, fermentation types, novel processing methods, the 8 permitted synthetic colours versus illegal adulterants like metanil yellow, ADI, NOAEL, and GRAS, emulsifiers and MSG, and key Karnataka institutions including CSIR-CFTRI Mysuru established in 1950, DRDO-DFRL Mysuru, KMF-Nandini, HOPCOMS, and IIHR. The page then begins Part B, Objective Questions and Answers, spanning the whole unit, starting with a question on the body-building function of food, answered as proteins, and a question on the energy value of fat, answered as 9 kilocalories per gram.
305: On this page we continue with objective questions on food science. Fat gives about 9 kilocalories per gram, making it the most concentrated energy source, roughly twice as energy-dense as carbohydrate or protein at 4 kilocalories per gram. Adding cooking soda, that is alkali, to green vegetables while boiling destroys thiamine and vitamin C, even though it keeps the vegetable looking green. Now, students, on starch chemistry, gelatinisation is the thickening of a starch paste when heated in water, as starch granules absorb water and swell. This is different from dextrinisation, which is dry-heat browning of starch. The staling of cooked starch, for example bread going hard on cooling, is called retrogradation, where the gelatinised starch re-associates and firms up. In cereal grains, the germ, or embryo, is richest in fat and is removed during milling to prevent rancidity in stored flour, unlike the bran which is the fibre and vitamin layer. Karnataka contributes roughly 40 percent of India's millet production, making it the country's millet hub, linked to the Siri Dhanya initiative. In soybean, the anti-nutritional factor called trypsin inhibitor blocks protein digestion but is destroyed by proper cooking, unlike aflatoxin which is heat-stable. Lathyrism, a paralytic disease, is caused by excessive consumption of khesari, that is Lathyrus, dal.
306: Let us understand more objective questions here. The neurotoxin BOAA present in khesari dal is what causes lathyrism, not groundnut, which is instead linked to aflatoxin contamination. Aflatoxin in stored groundnut and maize is produced by Aspergillus mould, specifically species like Aspergillus flavus and parasiticus, not by bacteria or yeast. Green leafy vegetables turn a dull olive colour during acidic cooking because the chlorophyll converts to pheophytin. In an alkaline medium, anthocyanin pigments turn blue or purple, whereas in acid they are red. Enzymatic browning of cut apple, potato and brinjal is caused by the enzyme polyphenol oxidase acting in the presence of oxygen, which is different from amylase that acts on starch. Egg freshness is commonly assessed by candling and by the Haugh unit, which scores albumen height against egg weight, with a higher value meaning a fresher egg. Here is a simple field test, students, a fresh egg placed in water sinks and lies flat, while a stale egg floats because its air cell has enlarged over time. Finally, the red colour of fresh meat comes from the pigment myoglobin, the muscle's oxygen-storing protein, not haemoglobin which is the blood pigment.
307: Now, students, we move into meat and sugar chemistry. The temporary postmortem stiffening of muscle is called rigor mortis, occurring as ATP falls and actomyosin forms; ageing or conditioning happens afterward and actually tenderises the meat. Natural enzymes used to tenderise meat include papain from papaya, along with bromelain from pineapple and ficin from fig, unlike amylase which only digests starch. Among common natural sugars, fructose is the sweetest, with a relative sweetness around 173, while lactose is the least sweet. Browning of sugar by dry heat alone, without any protein, is called caramelisation, distinct from the Maillard reaction which needs both sugar and protein. Adding acid or invertase to sucrose produces invert sugar, a mix of glucose and fructose, which mainly helps prevent crystallisation, or graining, in syrups and jams. In honey, a rising HMF value, that is hydroxymethylfurfural, indicates old or overheated honey, since fresh unheated honey has a low HMF reading. On this page, also note that granulation, or crystallisation, of honey is a natural and reversible change, not a sign of spoilage, and it reverses on gentle warming; this is different from fermentation caused by yeast, which is genuine spoilage. Royal jelly is the secretion that determines the development of the queen bee, since continuous feeding on royal jelly, rather than brief feeding, produces the queen.
308: Here, students, more useful facts for the exam. Continuing the previous point, larvae fed royal jelly throughout their development become the queen bee, while worker bees receive it only briefly. The soapy off-odour of stale butter results from hydrolytic rancidity, where lipase releases free fatty acids like butyric acid, which is different from oxidative rancidity where oxygen attacks fat double bonds. Hydrogenation of vegetable oil to make vanaspati also produces trans fatty acids as a by-product, now restricted for health reasons, while essential fatty acids are actually lost in this process. Karnataka is India's largest producer of coffee, a beverage crop grown mainly in Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru and Hassan districts, whereas tea production in India is centred in Assam and West Bengal. Byadagi, a GI-tagged Karnataka chilli, is prized mainly for its deep red colour and relatively low pungency, valued for colour extraction rather than heat. Ready-to-eat retort-pouch military rations in India are developed chiefly by DFRL Mysuru, the Defence Food Research Laboratory, which is distinct from the broader CFTRI food-technology institute also based in Mysuru. Let us understand, the chief cause of food spoilage overall is micro-organisms, that is bacteria, yeasts and moulds, more so than sunlight, packaging or cooking.
309: On this page, salt and sugar preserve food mainly by lowering water activity through an osmotic effect, drawing water out of microbial cells so they cannot grow; this is not a toxic action, nor is it about raising pH. Standard HTST pasteurisation of milk, that is High Temperature Short Time, is carried out at 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, while the older LTLT method, Low Temperature Long Time, uses 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes. The 12-D process in canning is designed to destroy Clostridium botulinum spores by reducing them across twelve log cycles, ensuring safety against this deadly spore-forming organism.
