Low-acid canned foods, those with pH above 4.6, must be processed at about 121 degrees Celsius under pressure, since boiling water at 100 degrees Celsius is only sufficient for high-acid foods. The D-value of a microbial population is defined as the time at a given temperature needed to kill 90 percent, that is one log cycle, of the population; no single time treatment achieves 100 percent kill. Quick freezing is preferred over slow freezing because it forms small ice crystals that preserve texture, whereas slow freezing forms large crystals that rupture cells and damage quality. Now, students, spray drying is most suitable for converting a liquid into a powder, commonly used for milk, coffee and egg products.
310: Here we continue with preservation and additive rules important for the exam. Low-dose food irradiation is used mainly to inhibit sprouting, for example in onion and potato, and to disinfest grain, and importantly it does not make the food radioactive. Among Class II preservatives, potassium metabisulphite, known as KMS, releases sulphur dioxide, which acts against microbes and also prevents browning and oxidation, unlike sodium benzoate which does not prevent browning. Curd, idli and dosa are products of lactic-acid fermentation, where lactic-acid bacteria lower the pH, distinct from alcoholic fermentation by yeast which gives wine and bread. High-pressure processing, known as HPP, preserves food using very high pressure at near-ambient temperature, making it a specifically non-thermal method, sometimes called cold pasteurisation. Under FSSAI regulations in India, exactly eight synthetic food colours are permitted, each within legal limits. Metanil yellow and lead chromate, sometimes found illegally in dals, sweets and turmeric, are illegal toxic adulterant colours, not permitted pigments. The Acceptable Daily Intake, or ADI, of a food additive is obtained by dividing the NOAEL, the no-observed-adverse-effect-level, by a safety factor, commonly 100, giving a safe intake value in milligrams per kilogram body weight per day. Lecithin, from egg yolk and soybean, is used in foods as an emulsifier.
311: Let us understand this concluding point and then a useful revision table. Lecithin is an emulsifier that lets oil and water mix and stay mixed, unlike leavening agents such as yeast or baking powder which produce gas. Monosodium glutamate, known as MSG, is added to food as a flavour, or taste, enhancer that gives the umami sensation, rather than functioning as a preservative or colour. This page then presents a rapid revision table of high-yield facts for this unit. It reminds us of the three functions of food: energy from carbohydrate and fat, body-building from protein, and protective functions from vitamins, minerals and fibre. In starch cookery, remember gelatinisation is the wet thickening process while dextrinisation is dry browning. For food pigments, chlorophyll dulls in acid, anthocyanin turns red in acid and blue in alkali, while carotenoids remain stable. For meat, myoglobin changes from oxymyoglobin, which is red, to metmyoglobin, which is brown, and rigor mortis is followed by ageing. For sugar reactions, caramelisation needs sugar alone while the Maillard reaction needs sugar plus protein, and inversion stops sugar graining. Rancidity has two types, hydrolytic, producing free fatty acids, and oxidative, involving oxygen attacking double bonds. Pasteurisation and canning values to remember are HTST at 72 degrees for 15 seconds, LTLT at 63 degrees for 30 minutes, and canning using the 12-D process against Clostridium botulinum. For freezing and drying, quick freezing gives small crystals and spray drying handles liquids. Remember exactly 8 permitted synthetic colours under FSSAI, and the ADI formula as NOAEL divided by the safety factor of 100.
312: This page lists the references used for this unit on food science and nutrition, drawn from the Karnataka Public Service Commission's Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer Paper 2 syllabus, Unit 10. The sources include standard textbooks such as Food Science by Srilakshmi, Foods: Facts and Principles by Manay and Shadaksharaswamy, Food Science by Potter and Hotchkiss, and Food Processing Technology by Fellows, covering topics like the functions of food, food groups, cookery, composition, processing and preservation. Also referenced are works by Girdharilal, Siddappa and Tandon on preservation of fruits and vegetables published by ICAR, Frazier and Westhoff's Food Microbiology covering spoilage and fermentation, and Branen, Davidson and Salminen on food additives, alongside FSSAI's Food Safety and Standards regulations. Additional practical resources cited are technology bulletins from CSIR-CFTRI Mysuru and DRDO-DFRL Mysuru, as well as materials from KMF-Nandini and the Karnataka Department of Agriculture's millet mission, and HOPCOMS resources. This is simply an orientation page listing source material, without new exam content.
313: Now, students, we begin a brand new chapter, Chapter 11, titled Food Processing Technology, forming Unit 11 of Paper 2's Specific Paper, combining theory with objective questions and answers. This chapter covers two broad halves. First, dairy and milk technology, including the history of dairying in India and the White Revolution, milk production and use, its composition and physico-chemical properties, collection, preservation, processing, packaging and storage, plant equipment such as the bulk milk cooler, clarifier, separator, pasteuriser and homogeniser, hygienic design, adulteration detection, quality defects, market milk types, cream, and fermented milks. Second, food packaging, covering the need and functions of packaging, the four material families of paper, glass, metal and plastic, package classification, lamination and coating, moulding processes, aseptic packaging, permeability and barrier theory, and functional tests, followed by an objective question bank. Part A on theory begins with Figure 11.1, classifying food preservation methods into four families: by low temperature such as chilling and freezing, by high temperature such as pasteurisation, sterilisation and canning, by moisture removal such as drying and concentration, and by chemicals or biological methods such as salting, pickling and fermentation, all sharing the principle of controlling microbial and enzymatic activity to extend shelf life. Block A then opens with section 11.1 on the historical development of dairying in India, noting that organised scientific dairying is recent, with the turning point being the co-operative movement at Anand in Gujarat, where the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers Union, the Amul brand, was founded in 1946, pioneering farmer ownership through a three-tier structure of village society, district union and state federation.
314: On this page, we learn that the National Dairy Development Board, NDDB, was set up in 1965 at Anand to replicate the Amul model nationwide. Under its first chairman, Dr Verghese Kurien, called the Father of the White Revolution and the Milkman of India, the NDDB ran Operation Flood from 1970 to 1996, the world's largest dairy-development programme, in three phases. It built a national milk grid and made India the world's largest milk producer, overtaking the United States in 1998, a transformation called the White Revolution. Karnataka's own federation, KMF, was created in 1974 as the Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation and restructured under its present name with the Nandini brand in 1984. A milestone table reinforces these dates, and an exam pointer highlights anchoring four names: Amul in 1946 as the model, NDDB in 1965 as the spread, Operation Flood from 1970 to 1996 as the programme, and Kurien as the man, with India being the world's number one milk producer since 1998, holding about 24 percent of world milk, and KMF being the second largest co-operative federation after Amul. An Agri Officer Lens box notes KMF procures milk from over 2.7 million farmer-members through more than 15,000 village dairy co-operative societies into 16 district unions, the Anand three-tier pattern in living Karnataka form. Section 11.2 then covers production and utilisation of milk, noting India produces the most milk of any country, mostly from buffaloes and crossbred cows, with the unorganised sector still handling a large share, and lists major dairy products including liquid milk, ghee, curd and buttermilk, khoa and paneer, butter and cream, milk powder, and cheese and ice cream.
315: Let us understand milk composition now. Per-capita milk availability in India has risen steadily and now exceeds the world average, reflecting both rising production and the milk grid built by Operation Flood, with buffalo milk, richer in fat and solids, dominating by volume while crossbred-cow milk increases. Section 11.3 explains milk is an oil-in-water emulsion of fat globules with a colloidal suspension of protein in a solution of lactose and minerals. Average cow milk is about 87 percent water and 13 percent total solids, of which fat is roughly 3.5 to 4 percent and solids-not-fat, called SNF, is about 8.5 to 9 percent; buffalo milk is richer, with about 7 percent fat and 9 to 10 percent SNF. A composition table lists water at 87 percent, fat at 3.5 to 4.0 percent as triglycerides carrying vitamins A, D, E and K, protein at 3.2 to 3.5 percent split into about 80 percent casein and 20 percent whey, lactose at 4.6 to 5.0 percent, and minerals at 0.7 percent rich in calcium. Milk protein casein exists as calcium-phosphate micelles and precipitates at its iso-electric point of pH 4.6, which is the basis of curd, paneer and cheese formation, while whey proteins stay in solution at that pH but are denatured by heat. Milk is a good source of calcium, phosphorus and riboflavin, vitamin B2, but is low in iron and vitamin C. Remember, SNF equals protein plus lactose plus minerals and does not include fat, and casein's iso-electric point of pH 4.6 is the single number behind curd, paneer and cheese formation.
316: On this page, note that casein precipitates while whey proteins do not, and whey proteins are heat-labile while casein is heat-stable. An Agri Officer Lens notes Nandini dairies pay farmers on a two-axis, fat plus SNF, basis, so understanding why watered or skimmed milk reads low on both axes helps explain fair pricing at the society level. Section 11.4 covers physico-chemical properties of milk, which are exploited both for processing and for detecting adulteration. Fresh milk is slightly acidic, with pH about 6.6, ranging from 6.5 to 6.7, and a natural titratable acidity of 0.14 to 0.16 percent lactic acid, which is apparent acidity from proteins, phosphates and carbon dioxide, not real sourness. Density is about 1.030 grams per cc, measured with a lactometer; adding water lowers density while removing fat raises it, so density alone cannot prove purity. A standard constants table lists pH at 6.6, titratable acidity at 0.14 to 0.16 percent, density at 1.028 to 1.032, freezing point at negative 0.512 to negative 0.55 degrees Celsius as the most constant property for detecting added water, boiling point at about 100.17 degrees Celsius, specific heat at about 0.93 calories per gram per degree, and colour as white to yellowish from casein-calcium-phosphate scattering and carotene. The freezing point is the most constant property and the standard test for added water, since water pushes the freezing point toward zero in proportion to dilution. Milk's white colour comes from light scattering by casein micelles and fat globules, with the yellow tinge in cow milk coming from carotene, since buffalo milk lacks carotene and is whiter. An Agri Officer Lens notes that electronic ultrasonic milk analysers now read fat, SNF, density and added water in seconds at collection points, replacing the older lactometer-and-Gerber method.
317: Now, students, Block B covers collection, processing and plant equipment, beginning with section 11.5 on collection, preservation, packaging and storage of liquid milk. Because milk spoils fast in warm temperatures, the governing rule is chill early and keep cold; the single most important preservation method is refrigeration, cooling milk to 4 degrees Celsius or below within hours of milking, and the cold chain, from bulk milk cooler at the village through insulated tanker to refrigerated silo at the dairy, must stay unbroken from producer to consumer. A table of preservation methods lists refrigeration as the primary method, pasteurisation as the main commercial method using mild heat, sterilisation or UHT for severe heat and long ambient shelf life, activation of the lactoperoxidase system for cold-chain-free short-term rural preservation, concentration or drying to remove water, and notes that adding chemical preservatives is generally not permitted in market milk. Processed liquid milk is packaged mostly in heat-sealed polyethylene pouches, the dominant Indian format, and also in laminate cartons and bottles; pasteurised pouch milk must be stored cold and consumed within a day or two, while UHT or aseptic milk keeps for months at room temperature until opened. An exam pointer summarises the whole liquid-milk system as one idea, the cold chain: chill to 4 degrees at the village bulk milk cooler, then insulated tanker, chilled silo, pasteurise, pouch, and sell cold, noting chemical preservatives in market milk are illegal. Section 11.6 then begins on pasteurisation, sterilisation and UHT processing, alongside Figure 11.2 showing the canning or thermal processing flow: raw material, blanch, fill can, exhaust air, seal, retort to sterilise at 115 to 121 degrees Celsius under steam pressure targeting Clostridium botulinum, then cool.
318: Let us understand pasteurisation and sterilisation in detail here. Pasteurisation is a mild heat treatment destroying all pathogenic and most spoilage micro-organisms without seriously altering the milk; it is not sterilisation, since some harmless bacteria survive, so the milk must still be chilled. The benchmark organism historically was Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and now Coxiella burnetii. Two standard methods exist: the batch or holder method, LTLT, Low Temperature Long Time, at 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, and the continuous method, HTST, High Temperature Short Time, at 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, done in a plate heat exchanger with regeneration. The phosphatase test confirms adequate pasteurisation, since the enzyme alkaline phosphatase is destroyed at pasteurisation conditions, so a negative test means success. A heat-treatment table adds higher-heat-shorter-time, HHST, at 89 to 100 degrees for about 0.01 to 1 second for extended shelf life, UHT, ultra-high temperature, at 135 to 140 degrees for 2 to 4 seconds giving commercially sterile ambient milk, and in-bottle sterilisation at 108 to 115 degrees for 20 to 30 minutes. Sterilisation destroys all micro-organisms and spores, giving a commercially sterile product that keeps for months without refrigeration, done either in-container or, more commonly today, by UHT followed by aseptic filling into sterile laminate cartons; UHT keeps the cooked flavour low because the treatment time is so short. Remember these exact pairs: LTLT is 63 degrees for 30 minutes, HTST is 72 degrees for 15 seconds, and UHT is 135 to 140 degrees for 2 to 4 seconds, and note that pasteurisation is not sterilisation, only sterilised or UHT milk is shelf-stable without refrigeration. Section 11.7 then opens on reception, chilling, clarification and centrifugal separation.
319: On this page, Figure 11.3 shows the fluid milk processing flow: reception and weighing, chilling to 4 degrees at the bulk milk cooler, clarification to remove dirt, separation into cream and skim, then standardising fat, pasteurising at 72 degrees for 15 seconds HTST, homogenising at about 170 bar, and finally filling and packing into pouches, with the cold chain maintained throughout and the phosphatase test confirming pasteurisation. At the dairy, milk passes through a sequence of unit operations, each with its own equipment. Reception equipment weighs and grades incoming milk using a weigh tank or electronic flow meter, with samples tested for fat, SNF and adulteration. Chilling equipment lowers temperature using a surface cooler or, more usually, a plate chiller, bringing milk to 4 degrees, while at the village level the bulk milk cooler, or BMC, is an insulated refrigerated stainless-steel tank that both cools and stores. A table lists key equipment: the reception unit for receiving, weighing and sampling; the bulk milk cooler for village-level chilling and storage; the plate or surface chiller for rapid cooling at the dairy; the clarifier, a centrifuge removing dirt, sediment and somatic cells; the cream separator, a centrifuge splitting milk into cream and skim by density; the storage silo, an insulated stainless-steel tank; the homogeniser, which reduces fat-globule size; the pasteuriser, a plate heat exchanger; and the filling machine, which forms, fills and seals pouches or cartons. A clarifier spins milk to remove heavier dirt, sediment and cells without separating cream, while a cream separator, the classic De Laval design, spins faster using conical discs to split milk into cream and skim-milk streams by density, with the cream's fat content set by a throttling screw; both are centrifuges but perform different jobs.
320: Now, students, remember the clarifier has one outlet while the separator has two, cream and skim, a distinction examiners love. An Agri Officer Lens notes cream separators at Nandini chilling centres divert surplus fat to butter and ghee, while the skim stream is dried into skim-milk powder used to make toned milk in the lean season, following Operation Flood's recombination logic still running in Karnataka today. Section 11.8 covers homogenisation, which forces hot milk under very high pressure, about 170 bar or roughly 2500 psi, through a narrow valve, breaking fat globules from an average of 3 to 4 micrometres down to under 2 micrometres. The huge increase in fat-surface area, recoated by casein, keeps fat permanently dispersed so cream no longer rises, and homogenisation is usually done just before or after pasteurisation at about 60 to 65 degrees. A table lists the purpose as preventing creaming for uniform milk, the mechanism as high-pressure shear, pressure at about 170 bar, globule size reduction from 3 to 4 micrometres to under 2, effects including whiter colour and richer mouthfeel, and the process temperature at 60 to 65 degrees, near pasteurisation. Homogenised milk looks whiter and tastes fuller, and it must be paired with pasteurisation because disrupted fat globules expose fat to native lipase, so heat-inactivating the lipase prevents rancidity; it changes only the physical state, not the nutritional value, of the fat. Section 11.9 then opens on filling and packaging machines and Clean-In-Place, or CIP, noting the dominant Indian format is the form-fill-seal, FFS, pouch machine that makes a tube from a roll of polyethylene film, fills a measured volume, and heat-seals each pouch automatically at high speed.
321: Let us understand Clean-In-Place, or CIP, which is the cleaning of tanks, pipes, pumps and heat exchangers without dismantling them, by circulating cleaning solutions through the closed system. The standard CIP cycle has six steps: first, pre-rinse with water to flush residues; second, hot alkaline wash using caustic soda at about 0.5 to 1.5 percent at 70 to 80 degrees Celsius to remove fat and protein; third, an intermediate water rinse; fourth, an acid wash using nitric or phosphoric acid to remove mineral, or milk-stone, deposits; fifth, a final rinse; and sixth, sanitising with hot water or chemical before use. CIP is essential in modern dairies because it gives reliable, repeatable hygiene with low labour and no dismantling required. Remember the CIP order: rinse, then alkali for organic soil, then rinse, then acid for mineral scale, then rinse, then sanitise; and remember the form-fill-seal machine is the standard milk-pouch equipment. An Agri Officer Lens notes CIP systems let a Nandini dairy clean kilometres of pipework and dozens of tanks overnight to food-grade hygiene without opening a single joint. Block C then opens on hygienic design, adulteration and quality defects, with section 11.10 covering hygienic design, sanitary pipes and fittings, corrosion and its control. Hygienic design means building equipment so it can be completely cleaned and leaves nowhere for microbes to hide, following principles codified in the 3-A Sanitary Standards: food-grade corrosion-resistant material, stainless steel 304 or, for harsher duty, 316; smooth crevice-free surfaces with roughness below about 0.8 micrometre; no dead-legs or sharp internal corners; self-draining slopes; and easily dismantled or CIP-cleanable joints.
322: On this page, note that corrosion types include uniform, pitting, crevice, galvanic, intergranular and stress corrosion, and control measures include stainless-steel selection, passivation, coatings or lining, cathodic protection, and avoiding chloride and acid stagnation. Stainless steel resists corrosion because chromium, at least about 11 percent, forms a thin self-healing passive chromium-oxide film. Corrosion is deterioration of metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment; its main forms are uniform or general attack, pitting caused by chlorides, the worst enemy in dairies, crevice corrosion in gaps under deposits, galvanic corrosion between two dissimilar metals in contact, intergranular corrosion at grain boundaries, sometimes called weld decay, and stress-corrosion cracking. Control measures include choosing the right stainless-steel grade, passivation to restore the oxide film, protective coatings and linings, cathodic protection using sacrificial anodes, good design avoiding crevices and stagnant chloride-rich solutions, and proper welding to avoid sensitisation. Remember pitting corrosion, caused by chlorides, is the dairy's main corrosion problem, and don't confuse passivation, which restores the protective film, with cathodic protection, which uses a sacrificial anode. Section 11.11 then covers adulteration of milk and its detection, defining adulteration as adding a foreign substance or removing a natural one to lower quality or value; milk is one of the most adulterated foods, and adulterants fall into three groups: those adding bulk or masking watering, such as water, starch, glucose and skim-milk powder; preservatives added illegally, such as formalin and boric acid; and neutralisers added to hide developed acidity, such as sodium carbonate or caustic soda. A table begins listing detection tests: added water via the lactometer plus freezing-point test, starch or flour via the iodine test turning blue-black, cane sugar via the resorcinol or Seliwanoff test turning red, glucose via Barfoed's test, urea via the DMAB test turning yellow, and detergent via a bromocresol-green or methylene-blue colour change.
323: Continuing the adulterant detection table, sodium carbonate, a neutraliser, is detected using rosolic acid in alcohol turning rose-pink or red, formalin as a preservative is detected by Hehner's test using concentrated sulphuric acid and ferric chloride giving a violet ring, hydrogen peroxide is detected using para-phenylenediamine turning blue, and skim-milk powder or synthetic milk is detected through off-taste, nitrate testing, and chemical profiling. Two quality, rather than adulteration, tests are also standard here. The Methylene Blue Reduction Test, or MBRT, grades bacterial load, since the dye decolourises faster when bacteria are abundant, so a longer reduction time actually means cleaner milk. The Clot-On-Boiling, or COB, test screens for high acidity or the presence of colostrum, since such milk clots when boiled and is rejected; the alcohol test similarly checks heat stability before processing. For detecting added water specifically, the freezing-point depression test is the most reliable, because milk's freezing point is its most constant property and water pushes it toward zero. Remember these matches: starch with iodine gives blue; cane sugar with resorcinol gives red; urea with DMAB gives yellow; sodium carbonate with rosolic acid gives rose-red; formalin with Hehner's test gives a violet ring; and added water is best confirmed by the freezing point or lactometer, not density alone. Section 11.12 then covers quality defects in milk, their causes and prevention, explaining defects are unwanted changes in flavour, colour, body or appearance, mostly traceable to microbial growth, enzyme action, feed, or contamination, graded by sense and prevented chiefly through hygiene and an unbroken cold chain. The major flavour defects include sour or acid from lactic-acid bacteria, rancid from lipase splitting fat into free fatty acids, oxidised or tallowy from fat oxidation catalysed by copper, iron and light, bitter from proteolytic bacteria or certain weeds, and feed or cowy flavours from the animal's diet.
324: Here, students, we complete the quality defects table, noting colour defects such as red or blue tints are caused by pigmented bacteria or by blood from mastitis, prevented through sanitation and udder health. Body and texture defects include ropiness or sliminess, caused by Alcaligenes and other gum-producing bacteria, and bitterness; colour defects arise from pigmented bacteria, red from Serratia and blue from Pseudomonas, or from blood and mastitis. The common thread in prevention is hygiene at milking, rapid chilling, clean stainless-steel, non-copper, equipment, protection from light, and prompt processing, since light and metal, especially copper, are the two classic catalysts of oxidised off-flavour, which is exactly why dairy equipment is made of stainless steel and milk is packed in opaque or pigmented material. Remember, rancid defects trace to lipase and free fatty acids, oxidised or tallowy defects trace to fat oxidation catalysed by copper, iron and light, and sour defects trace to lactic-acid bacteria, with hygiene and rapid chilling curing nearly all of them. An Agri Officer Lens notes off-flavours are the commonest reason a society's milk is downgraded or rejected at the chilling centre, so an Agricultural Officer advising farmers on clean milk production, wiping the udder, using stainless-steel cans, and chilling promptly, directly prevents these defects. Block D then begins, covering types of milk, cream and fermented milks, opening with section 11.13 on types of milk including reconstituted, recombined, standardised, skim, sterilised and flavoured milk. Reconstituted milk is made by adding water back to milk powder, while recombined milk goes further, blending milk fat, skim-milk powder and water to resemble whole milk, the technology that let Operation Flood supply cities from buffer stocks. A table then gives FSSAI's minimum fat and SNF standards: full-cream milk at 6.0 percent fat and 9.0 percent SNF, standardised milk at 4.5 and 8.5, toned milk at 3.0 and 8.5, double-toned milk at 1.5 and 9.0, and skim milk at a maximum of 0.5 percent fat with 8.7 percent SNF, noting toned milk is buffalo milk diluted with skim-milk powder and water to bring fat down while keeping SNF up, the central product of Operation Flood.
325: On this page we continue milk types and move into cream. First, remember the market milk varieties. Reconstituted milk is simply water added back to milk powder to rebuild the original milk. Recombined milk is different, it is fat plus skim milk powder plus water, built up from separate parts, and note that recombined milk adds fat while reconstituted milk does not. Toned milk, at 3 percent fat, is the flagship product of Operation Flood. Skim milk has a maximum fat of 0.5 percent. Learn the FSSAI fat and SNF pairs by heart, full cream is 6.0 fat and 9.0 SNF, toned is 3.0 and 8.5, double toned is 1.5 and 9.0. Ordering by fat, it goes full cream at 6 percent, standardised at 4.5 percent, toned at 3 percent, double toned at 1.5 percent, then skim below 0.5 percent. Flavoured milk is toned milk with sugar, flavour and colour, sterilised. Now, students, section 11.14 introduces cream. FSSAI defines cream as containing not less than 25 percent milk fat. It is made by centrifugal separation into a light cream stream and a heavy skim stream, then standardised to the target fat, pasteurised, cooled and aged. Cream types by fat percentage include table cream at 20 to 25 percent for coffee, whipping cream at 30 to 40 percent, heavy or double cream above 48 percent, and plastic cream at 65 to 85 percent, which is butter-like and used for spreading. Cream is pasteurised at a higher temperature than milk, around 75 to 80 degrees Celsius, because its fat protects the bacteria inside it.
326: Let us understand fermented milk products now, covered under section 11.15. These include dahi, cultured buttermilk, acidophilus milk and yoghurt. Fermented or cultured milks are made by inoculating heat treated milk with a starter culture of lactic acid bacteria. These bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid, and the falling pH brings the milk down to casein's iso electric point of 4.6, which coagulates the protein into a set or thick body, giving the tangy flavour and better keeping quality. The process, shown in figure 11.4, is pasteurised milk, heated to 85 to 90 degrees Celsius to denature whey proteins, cooled to incubation temperature, starter culture added, incubated to set, then cooled and stored at 4 degrees Celsius. Each product has its own starter culture and incubation temperature. Dahi, the Indian curd, uses Lactococcus lactis plus Streptococcus thermophilus, sometimes with Leuconostoc for aroma, set at 22 to 30 degrees Celsius or 37 to 42 degrees Celsius. Yoghurt is defined by its specific thermophilic pair, Lactobacillus delbrueckii subspecies bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, in roughly equal numbers, incubated at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius for 3 to 4 hours, the two organisms actually help each other, called protocooperation. Cultured buttermilk uses Lactococcus with Leuconostoc, fermenting citrate into diacetyl, the buttery aroma, incubated at 20 to 22 degrees Celsius. Acidophilus milk uses Lactobacillus acidophilus, a probiotic with therapeutic gut health benefits, incubated at 37 degrees Celsius.
327: Here, remember the fixed culture pair for yoghurt, Lactobacillus bulgaricus plus Streptococcus thermophilus at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius. Do not confuse this with dahi's mesophilic Lactococcus lactis culture, and do not swap yoghurt's thermophilic pair with dahi's mesophilic one, that is a classic exam trap. In one line, yoghurt equals bulgaricus plus thermophilus at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius. Buttermilk's buttery aroma comes from diacetyl, made from citrate by Leuconostoc, while yoghurt's green apple aroma comes from acetaldehyde. Acidophilus milk is the probiotic, therapeutic one. All of these set because the falling acid hits casein's iso electric pH of 4.6. Now section 11.16 covers the biochemical changes in fermented milks. The central change is the conversion of lactose to lactic acid by starter bacteria, homofermentative cultures mainly make lactic acid through glycolysis, while heterofermentative ones also make carbon dioxide, ethanol and acetic acid. The falling pH, from 6.6 toward 4.6, does three things, it coagulates casein to form the gel, it inhibits spoilage and pathogenic bacteria for preservation, and it gives the sour taste. Alongside acid production, proteolysis breaks down protein into peptides and amino acids, contributing flavour but causing bitterness in excess, and aroma compounds form, chiefly diacetyl, which is buttery, from citrate, and acetaldehyde, the typical yoghurt aroma. Factors affecting fermentation include the type and ratio of starter culture, the inoculum percentage and activity, incubation temperature, incubation time, milk solids content, heat treatment, and contamination by phages or yeasts. Wrong incubation temperature gives a weak set or over acid product, and too long incubation causes whey separation, known as syneresis.
328: On this page, remember that the driver behind fermentation is lactose converting to lactic acid, dropping the pH to 4.6 to coagulate casein. Over incubation causes over acid product plus whey separation, called syneresis. The aroma compounds are diacetyl, which is buttery, for buttermilk, versus acetaldehyde for yoghurt. Higher milk solids and pre heating give a firmer gel, and prompt cooling stops fermentation at the right acidity level. Now, students, we begin Block E, Food Packaging, covering need, functions and materials. Section 11.17 explains packaging in India and the world. Packaging is the science and art of enclosing a product to protect, contain, transport and present it. Food packaging has grown rapidly in India with urbanisation, organised retail, exports and processed food demand, though per capita use is still far below developed countries. The need for packaging is to deliver food safely and wholesomely with adequate shelf life, reducing post-harvest and handling losses. A package performs four classic functions, known as the 4 Cs of packaging. Protection is a barrier against moisture, gases, light, microbes, pests and physical damage. Containment holds the product in a defined quantity and prevents leakage. Convenience means it is easy to handle, store, open, dispense and reseal. Communication covers the label, brand, ingredients, date, instructions and barcode. A good food package must be non-toxic, an effective barrier matched to the food's needs, mechanically strong, tamper evident, economical, and increasingly, environmentally responsible.
329: Now let us look at paper and paperboard packaging under section 11.18. Paper is made from cellulose fibres, mostly wood pulp produced by the kraft, or sulphate, chemical process, which gives strong brown kraft paper. Paper and board are cheap, light, printable, rigid in the case of board, recyclable and biodegradable, but on their own they are poor moisture and gas barriers, so they are usually waxed, coated or laminated for food use. Common paper types include kraft, which is strong, used for sacks and wraps, greaseproof and glassine, which are dense and grease resistant for fats and bakery items, vegetable parchment, which is acid treated and wet strong for butter, and waxed or coated papers with an added moisture barrier. Paperboard is thicker paper used for folding cartons. The corrugated fibreboard box, the common cardboard shipping carton, is the workhorse of transport packaging, it has a fluted middle layer glued between flat liners, and the flutes act like columns, giving high stacking strength and shock absorption at low weight and cost. This is why corrugated boxes carry almost everything from fruit to bottles. Their main limitation is loss of strength when wet, which is addressed by wax or plastic coating. Now, students, section 11.19 introduces glass packaging. Glass is made by melting silica sand with soda ash and limestone at about 1500 degrees Celsius, formed by blow and blow or press and blow moulding, then annealed to relieve stress. Glass is chemically inert, a total barrier to gases and moisture, transparent, odourless, rigid and reusable, ideal for liquids, sauces, jams and beverages.
330: Let us understand the advantages and disadvantages of glass packaging. Advantages include being inert with no reaction with food, a total barrier to gas and moisture, transparent so it shows the product, reusable and recyclable, and rigid enough to withstand internal pressure, which suits carbonated drinks. Disadvantages include being heavy, which raises transport cost, fragile and brittle, breaking under impact or thermal shock, transmitting light which can be a problem unless amber or green glass is used to protect light sensitive contents, high energy needed to make and melt it, and the risk of glass splinters as a hazard. Remember, glass equals inert plus total barrier plus transparent, but heavy, fragile and light transmitting. It is made from silica sand, soda ash and limestone, formed by blow moulding, then annealed to relieve stress. Amber or green glass protects light sensitive products like beer and some milks. Glass is the only common material that is a 100 percent gas and moisture barrier yet still transparent. Now, students, section 11.20 covers metal packaging, tinplate, tin free steel and aluminium. Metal containers give the highest protection of all, they are a total barrier to gases, moisture, light and microbes, mechanically strong, hermetically sealable through the double seam of a can, and can withstand the heat of retort sterilisation, making them ideal for canned foods. The three main metals are tinplate, tin free steel and aluminium. Tinplate is mild steel sheet coated on both sides with a thin layer of tin, which resists corrosion and is non-toxic, it is the classic tin can. Tin free steel, also called TFS or electrolytically chromium coated steel, replaces the tin with a chromium coating, is cheaper, but must be lacquered.
331: On this page, aluminium is described as light, naturally corrosion resistant thanks to a passive oxide film, and used as rigid cans especially for beverages, collapsible tubes, foil, and as a barrier layer in laminates. Aluminium foil is an outstanding barrier to gas, moisture and light when free of pinholes, but it is weak and tears easily, so it is laminated with paper and plastic, as in the aseptic carton. Interior lacquers, or enamels, line metal cans to stop the metal reacting with acidic, sulphur containing or pigmented foods, which would cause corrosion, discolouration and metallic taint. Metal's drawbacks are the weight of steel, the cost of aluminium, and the need for lacquering with reactive foods, but for long life thermally processed foods it remains unmatched. Stainless steel, an iron chromium nickel alloy, is a packaging material in its own right where reuse and total inertness matter, milk cans, bulk transport tanks, drums, kegs and reusable bins are made of stainless steel because it is strong, completely non-reactive, and survives repeated cleaning and sterilisation, though its high cost rules it out for single use consumer packs. Remember, tinplate is steel plus tin coating, the tin can, while TFS or ECCS is steel plus chromium coating that must be lacquered and cannot be soldered. Cans are lacquered inside to stop reaction with acidic or sulphur containing foods. Metal is the only fully retortable, hermetic, total barrier pack. Now, section 11.21 introduces plastic packaging, covering classification, properties and uses. Plastics are synthetic polymers, now the most widely used flexible packaging material because they are light, cheap, mouldable, heat sealable, and available with a wide range of barrier, strength and clarity properties. They divide into thermoplastics, which soften on heating and can be re-melted repeatedly, and thermosets, which set permanently on first moulding.
332: Let us understand the common packaging plastics and their uses. Each plastic offers a different balance of properties. Polyethylene, in its low density and high density forms, is the cheap, heat sealable moisture barrier used for milk pouches and films, but it is a poor gas barrier. Polypropylene is clearer and more heat resistant, used for retort pouches. PET, or polyethylene terephthalate, is strong, glossy and a good gas barrier, used for beverage bottles. PVDC and EVOH are outstanding gas and odour barriers, used as thin inner layers in laminates. Nylon resists puncture well. Because no single plastic is good at everything, films are often laminated or co-extruded to combine, for example, the moisture barrier of polyethylene, the gas barrier of EVOH, and the strength of PET. Plastics' main drawbacks are limited heat resistance, except for polypropylene and PET, possible additive migration, and environmental persistence. Remember, thermoplastics, such as PE, PP, PVC, PET and PS, re-melt and are used for films and packaging, while thermosets like melamine and phenolics set permanently and are never used for films. Split the plastics by barrier type, moisture barrier belongs to the polyethylene family, while gas or oxygen barrier belongs to PET, PVDC, EVOH and nylon. The milk pouch is low density polyethylene, the beverage bottle is PET, and the retort pouch is polypropylene or PET foil laminate. Now, students, we begin Block F, covering classification of packages, lamination, coating, moulding and aseptic packaging, starting with section 11.22. Packages are classified in several overlapping ways. By level, primary packaging directly contacts the food, such as the pouch, can or bottle, secondary packaging groups primaries together, like the carton or corrugated box, and tertiary packaging is for bulk handling and transport, like the pallet.
333: Continuing section 11.22, packages are also classified by rigidity, rigid, semi rigid, and flexible, and by use, consumer retail packs versus distribution transport packs. Lamination is the bonding together of two or more layers of material, papers, foils, films, into a single multilayer structure, so that the strengths of each are combined and the weaknesses cancelled, for example paper for stiffness and printability, aluminium foil for total barrier, and polyethylene for heat sealing and moisture protection, the classic aseptic carton laminate. Lamination is done by adhesive lamination, where an adhesive bonds pre-made films, extrusion lamination, where a molten plastic is extruded between two webs acting as both glue and a layer, or co-extrusion, where layers are extruded together. Coating is the application of a thin surface layer, such as wax, lacquer, polyethylene or PVDC, onto paper or film to add a property it lacks, such as moisture barrier, grease resistance, heat sealability or gloss, without adding a full extra ply. Remember, the levels are primary which touches food, then secondary which groups them into a carton, then tertiary for transport on a pallet. Lamination bonds several full layers together to combine properties, while coating is just a thin surface film added for one property. Now, section 11.23 covers moulding processes, injection, blow and extrusion. Plastic packaging is shaped by three principal processes. In injection moulding, molten plastic is injected under pressure into a closed mould cavity, making solid precise items such as caps, closures, tubs, crates and preforms. In blow moulding, a hot tube or preform, called a parison, is placed in a mould and inflated with compressed air against the mould walls to make hollow containers, chiefly bottles. Extrusion forces molten plastic continuously through a shaped die to make products of constant cross section, films, sheets, pipes, tubes and filaments.
334: On this page we learn that blow moulding has two main variants, extrusion blow moulding, where an extruded parison is clamped in the mould and blown, used for high density polyethylene bottles and jerry cans, and injection or stretch blow moulding, where an injection moulded preform is reheated, stretched and blown, giving the strong, clear PET beverage bottle. Extrusion is also the first stage of film and sheet making, and of co-extrusion for multilayer films, so the three processes are linked, extrusion makes profiles and films, injection makes solid parts and preforms, and blow moulding makes hollow bottles. Remember, match the process to the product, injection makes solid items like caps, tubs and crates, blow moulding makes hollow bottles, and extrusion makes continuous profiles like film, sheet and pipe. A PET bottle is injection stretch blow moulded, first the preform, then the blow, while a high density polyethylene bottle is extrusion blow moulded. Now, students, section 11.24 introduces aseptic packaging. In aseptic packaging, the product and the package are sterilised separately, and then the sterile product is filled into the sterile package in a sterile environment, and hermetically sealed. This differs fundamentally from conventional canning, where the food is filled into the container first and then the sealed container is heat sterilised, called retorting. The need for aseptic packaging is to give a long ambient shelf life without refrigeration, while keeping much higher product quality than canning, because the product is sterilised by a brief ultra high temperature flash at 135 to 140 degrees Celsius for just a few seconds, rather than a long retort cook. Comparing the two, aseptic packaging uses a lightweight laminate carton or pouch, while conventional canning uses a rigid metal can or glass jar, and aseptic retains taste and vitamins better because of the shorter heat exposure.
335: Here, remember that aseptic packaging means you sterilise the product and the pack separately, then fill in a sterile zone, unlike canning, which sterilises after filling and sealing. The pack sterilant is usually hydrogen peroxide plus heat. The ultra high temperature product treatment at 135 to 140 degrees Celsius for just seconds keeps quality far better than the long retort cook. The typical Tetra Pak laminate structure is paper, polyethylene, aluminium foil, then polyethylene again. In one line, aseptic equals sterile product plus sterile pack, joined in a sterile room, giving ambient, long life, high quality milk or juice in a laminate carton, which tastes better than canned food because the heat exposure is so brief. Now, students, we move to Block G, covering permeability, transport, simulation and package tests, starting with section 11.25. Permeability is the rate at which a gas or vapour passes through a packaging material, the key property that decides how long an oxygen or moisture sensitive food keeps. Permeation happens in three steps, the gas or vapour dissolves into the material on the high concentration side, diffuses through the thickness, and desorbs on the low side. The theory combines Fick's law of diffusion and Henry's law of solubility, giving the permeability coefficient as the product P equals D times S, diffusivity times solubility. The transmission rate through a film is proportional to P and the area and pressure difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness. Key terms include the water vapour transmission rate, measured in grams per square metre per day, and the oxygen or gas transmission rate, measured in cubic centimetres per square metre per day. For a multilayer material, the layers act like resistances in series, so total resistance is the sum of thickness divided by P for each layer.
336: On this page, remember the favourite formula, permeability P equals D times S, the diffusion coefficient times the solubility coefficient. The steps are sorption, then diffusion, then desorption. For a multilayer pack, resistances add in series, one over P total equals the sum of thickness over P for each layer, so the best barrier layer dominates the calculation. Water vapour transmission rate relates to moisture, and oxygen transmission rate relates to oxygen, and low values of either mean a good barrier. Fresh produce needs a film that breathes, enabling a modified atmosphere, while dry or fatty foods need a film that blocks, meaning low water vapour and oxygen transmission rates. Now, students, section 11.26 covers barrier transport properties, product package simulation, specific foods and package tests. Transport properties of a barrier material are the rates at which gases, vapours and light move through it, along with related sorption, how much it absorbs, and migration, the transfer of package substances into food. These determine whether a film protects a given food. Engineers use product package environment simulation, shelf life prediction models, sorption isotherms and accelerated storage tests at raised temperature and humidity, to predict before launch how a product will deteriorate in a chosen package, so the package can be designed to give the wanted shelf life without over or under packaging. Packaging is then matched to specific foods, milk and dairy need a light and oxygen barrier in a pouch or aseptic carton, fresh fruit and vegetables need a breathable film with modified atmosphere and ventilation, fats, oils and nuts need a low oxygen barrier, often opaque with nitrogen flushing, and dehydrated powders need a very low water vapour transmission rate using foil laminate.
337: Here, students, we complete the specific food packaging rule, frozen foods need low temperature tough, moisture proof film, and carbonated drinks need a pressure resistant pack such as PET, glass or a can. Finally, packages are checked by mechanical and functional tests. Mechanical tests include tensile strength, tear and bursting strength of paper and film, the box compression test for the stacking strength of corrugated boxes, and drop, impact and puncture tests. Functional tests include seal strength testing, leak or integrity testing, the water vapour and oxygen transmission rate barrier tests already described, grease resistance, and the Cobb test for water absorption of paper. Together these confirm that the package will protect the product through filling, transport, storage and use. Remember the specific food rule, dairy needs a light and oxygen barrier, produce needs to breathe, fats and nuts need an oxygen barrier with nitrogen flushing, powders need a moisture barrier using foil, and fizzy drinks need a pressure resistant pack. Tests split into mechanical tests, covering tensile, tear, burst, box compression and drop, and functional tests, covering seal strength, water vapour transmission rate, oxygen transmission rate and the Cobb water absorption test. Box compression and drop tests decide whether a mango or grape carton survives a long truck journey stacked six high, while water vapour transmission rate and seal tests decide whether dried chilli or millet powder stays crisp, these tests justify the packaging specifications that buyers demand from exporters and food processing units.
338: This page presents the chapter mind map for Food Processing Technology, summarising the whole chapter visually under seven branches. These are milk composition, covering water content, lactose, fat, protein, casein, whey proteins and pH, heat treatment, covering LTLT and HTST pasteurisation, UHT sterilisation, homogenisation pressure, and the phosphatase test, milk products, covering casein's iso electric point, butter, ghee, cheese, khoa and skim milk powder, fermented milks, covering yoghurt and dahi cultures, lactose converting to lactic acid, and probiotic acidophilus, packaging materials, covering low density polyethylene pouches, Tetra Pak laminate, glass, tinplate cans, PET bottles and aluminium foil, packaging science, covering aseptic packaging, modified atmosphere packaging, vacuum packing, shelf life and FSSAI labelling rules, and dairy in India, covering Amul's founding, Operation Flood, Dr Verghese Kurien, the White Revolution and the National Dairy Development Board. This map is meant as a quick revision tool tying together every topic covered across the chapter.
339: Now, students, this page begins the Key Terms at a Glance section, described as the densest source of marks in the chapter. You are told to memorise the temperature time pairs, the FSSAI fat and SNF figures, the starter cultures, the adulteration tests, and the packaging material properties, since most objective questions are lifted straight from these tables. Table 3.1 lists dairy temperatures, standards and constants. LTLT or batch pasteurisation is 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, HTST pasteurisation is 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, UHT processing is 135 to 140 degrees Celsius for 2 to 4 seconds, and in bottle sterilisation is 108 to 115 degrees Celsius for 20 to 30 minutes. Pasteurisation is verified by the alkaline phosphatase test, which must be negative. Milk is chilled to 4 degrees Celsius for the cold chain. Homogenisation pressure is about 170 bar, reducing fat globules to under 2 micrometres. Milk pH is 6.6, in a range of 6.5 to 6.7. Milk titratable acidity is 0.14 to 0.16 percent lactic acid. Milk density is 1.028 to 1.032, roughly 1.030. Milk freezing point is minus 0.512 to minus 0.55 degrees Celsius, used to detect added water. Casein's iso electric point is pH 4.6, and casein makes up about 80 percent of milk protein, with whey at about 20 percent. Yoghurt incubation is 40 to 45 degrees Celsius. Table 3.2 then lists milk grades by FSSAI fat and SNF, full cream milk is 6.0 percent fat and 9.0 percent SNF, standardised is 4.5 and 8.5, toned is 3.0 and 8.5, double toned is 1.5 and 9.0, and skim milk has a maximum of 0.5 percent fat and 8.7 percent SNF. Cream must have not less than 25 percent milk fat by FSSAI rule, and dahi's culture is Lactococcus lactis plus Streptococcus thermophilus.
340: This page continues the key terms tables. Yoghurt's culture is Lactobacillus bulgaricus plus Streptococcus thermophilus, and acidophilus milk uses Lactobacillus acidophilus, the probiotic. Buttermilk's aroma compound is diacetyl, from citrate by Leuconostoc, while yoghurt's aroma compound is acetaldehyde. The starch adulteration test uses iodine, giving a blue black colour, the sodium carbonate or neutraliser test is the rosolic acid test, giving a rose red colour, and bacterial quality is assessed by the Methylene Blue Reduction Test, where a longer reduction time means better quality. Section 3.3 covers history and Karnataka dairy facts. The Amul or Anand pattern was founded in 1946 in Kaira district, Gujarat. The National Dairy Development Board was founded in 1965 at Anand. Operation Flood ran from 1970 to 1996 in three phases, and is the world's largest dairy programme. Dr Verghese Kurien is called the Father of the White Revolution. India has been the world's top milk producer since 1998, when it overtook the USA. The Karnataka Milk Federation was founded in 1974 as the Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation, and was renamed KMF with the Nandini brand in 1984. KMF ranks as the second largest dairy cooperative in India, after Amul. The Anand pattern has three tiers, village society, then district union, then state federation. Section 3.4 begins packaging facts, the four functions of a package are protection, containment, convenience and communication, package levels are primary which touches food, secondary which is the carton, and tertiary for transport, kraft paper uses the sulphate or kraft pulping process, corrugated box strength comes from the fluted core giving cushioning and stacking strength, glass raw materials are silica sand, soda ash and limestone, tinplate is steel with a tin coating, the tin can, and TFS or ECCS is steel with a chromium coating that must be lacquered.
341: On this page, the packaging facts table concludes, the milk pouch plastic is low density polyethylene for its moisture barrier, good gas barrier plastics are PET, PVDC, EVOH and nylon, injection moulding makes solid items like caps, tubs and preforms, blow moulding makes hollow bottles, extrusion makes film, sheet and pipe as continuous profiles, the aseptic pack sterilant is hydrogen peroxide plus heat, and the permeability coefficient formula is P equals D times S, with the multilayer formula being one over P total equals the sum of thickness over P. A second table then presents these as term, attribute and value or year or formula triples for quick revision, covering HTST pasteurisation at 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, LTLT pasteurisation at 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, UHT processing at 135 to 140 degrees Celsius for 2 to 4 seconds, casein's iso electric point at pH 4.6, milk's freezing point range for the added water test, toned milk's FSSAI fat and SNF figures, yoghurt culture organisms and temperature, Operation Flood's period and leader, the permeability coefficient formula, and the KMF brand and its rank as Nandini, second largest cooperative after Amul. A reminder box advises drilling these ten facts until automatic, since in a 12 to 18 question unit, these alone typically secure 6 to 8 marks, with the rest following from the section 3 reference tables. Part B then begins, a bank of objective questions and answers covering the full chapter, dairy temperatures and standards, milk composition and properties, plant equipment, adulteration and quality, types of milk, cream and fermented milks, and the whole of food packaging. Question 1 asks about the HTST pasteurisation temperature and time.
342: This page works through a practical question and answer set. Question 1's answer is 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, noting that 63 degrees for 30 minutes is the LTLT batch method, not HTST, a common point of confusion candidates should watch for. Question 2 asks which physical property is most constant and used to detect added water in milk, the answer is freezing point, since density is tempting but changes with both watering and skimming, making it ambiguous, whereas freezing point, in the range minus 0.512 to minus 0.55 degrees Celsius, is the true added water test. Question 3 asks the pH at which casein precipitates, the answer is 4.6, noting 6.6 is the pH of fresh milk, not the iso electric point. Question 4 covers UHT processing temperature, the answer is 135 to 140 degrees Celsius for 2 to 4 seconds, noting 115 degrees for 20 minutes is in bottle sterilisation, not UHT. Question 5 asks which enzyme test confirms adequate pasteurisation, the answer is the alkaline phosphatase test, noting the peroxidase or Storch test checks for over heating instead, and a negative phosphatase result means pasteurisation succeeded. Question 6 asks the main purpose of homogenisation, the answer is preventing creaming by reducing fat globule size, not killing pathogens, which is pasteurisation's job, and it does not change fat content. Question 7 asks which equipment removes dirt, sediment and somatic cells without separating cream, the answer is the clarifier, distinguished from the cream separator, which splits cream from skim with two outlets, while the clarifier has only one outlet. Question 8 asks what the acid wash in a standard CIP cycle removes, using nitric or phosphoric acid.
343: Continuing the question bank, question 8's answer is mineral or milk stone deposits, noting fat and protein are removed by the alkali or caustic wash instead, and candidates often reverse these two roles. Question 9 asks the FSSAI minimum fat of toned milk, the flagship product of Operation Flood, the answer is 3.0 percent, noting 1.5 percent is double toned milk, and toned milk is made by diluting high fat buffalo milk with skim milk powder and water. Question 10 asks the maximum fat content of skim milk under FSSAI, the answer is 0.5 percent, noting 0 percent is unrealistic since a trace of fat always remains. Question 11 asks how reconstituted milk differs from recombined milk, the answer is that reconstituted milk is made by adding only water to milk powder, while recombined milk blends fat, skim milk powder and water, and the two are routinely confused. Question 12 asks yoghurt's starter culture characteristic, the answer is Lactobacillus bulgaricus plus Streptococcus thermophilus, noting Lactococcus lactis is the mesophilic dahi culture instead, and yoghurt's specific thermophilic pair works at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius. Question 13 asks the cause of cultured buttermilk's buttery aroma, the answer is diacetyl, made from citrate by Leuconostoc, noting acetaldehyde is the yoghurt aroma instead, a classic aroma compound swap. Question 14 asks what ferments acidophilus milk, the answer is Lactobacillus acidophilus, the probiotic valued for gut health, noting candidates often mistakenly pick more common dairy organisms. Question 15 asks the FSSAI minimum milk fat required in cream.
344: This page concludes the question bank shown so far. Question 15's answer is 25 percent, noting that 18 to 20 percent is table or single cream's typical fat, but the legal regulatory minimum for the term cream is 25 percent, so do not confuse a product's typical fat with its regulatory floor. Question 16 asks what colour the iodine test gives when starch is added to milk, the answer is blue black, noting red is the resorcinol or cane sugar test and a violet ring is Hehner's formalin test. Question 17 asks how sodium carbonate, used as a neutraliser, is detected in milk, the answer is the rosolic acid test, noting the Methylene Blue Reduction Test is a bacterial quality test, not an adulteration test, while the rosolic acid or soda test turns rose red when a carbonate or bicarbonate neutraliser is present. Question 18 asks what the Methylene Blue Reduction Test assesses, the answer is bacterial quality, since the dye decolourises faster with more bacteria, so a longer reduction time indicates cleaner, better quality milk. Question 19 asks why stainless steel resists corrosion, the answer is that chromium forms a thin, self healing layer of chromium oxide, noting iron oxide is rust, the very failure being prevented. Question 20 asks about the localised corrosion caused mainly by chlorides, the chief corrosion problem in dairies, the answer is pitting corrosion, noting galvanic corrosion needs two dissimilar metals and intergranular corrosion follows bad welding, while pitting, driven by chlorides, is what most troubles dairy stainless steel equipment. Question 21 asks the fourth basic function of a food package, alongside protection, containment and convenience, the answer is communication, covering the label, brand, date and instructions, together known as the 4 Cs. Question 22 asks about the corrugated shipping box that groups several retail packs, the answer is the secondary package.
345: On this page we continue the objective questions on food packaging materials. Secondary package is the correct answer when a question asks which pack groups primary packs together, since the carton or corrugated box is the secondary layer, while the pallet load is tertiary and the wrapper touching the food is primary. Glass containers are made from silica sand together with soda ash and limestone, melted and blow moulded. Tinplate used for cans is essentially steel coated with a thin layer of tin, not solid tin, because solid tin would be far too costly, and not aluminium either. The plastic used for the common Indian milk pouch is LDPE, low density polyethylene, chosen for its heat sealability and moisture barrier, while PET is used for beverage bottles because of its good gas barrier. Hollow plastic bottles are produced mainly by blow moulding, since injection moulding makes solid items like caps and preforms, and extrusion makes continuous film or pipe. In aseptic packaging, the packaging material is most commonly sterilised using hot hydrogen peroxide and heat, which is different from retorting at 121 degrees Celsius, that being conventional canning where the sealed can itself is heat processed after filling. The permeability coefficient P of a film equals the diffusion coefficient D multiplied by the solubility coefficient S, so P equals D times S, and thickness, area and pressure only scale the transmission rate rather than being part of P itself.
346: Now, students, this page explains how multilayer laminated films behave for permeability, plus a set of dairy science questions. For a laminated film, the layers act like resistances in series, so permeabilities do not simply add up. Instead, the reciprocals combine, meaning 1 over P total equals the sum of x sub i over P sub i, so the best barrier layer dominates the overall performance. The Karnataka Cooperative Milk Producers Federation markets its products under the brand name Nandini, which is India's second largest dairy cooperative brand after Amul, while Aavin is the Tamil Nadu brand. In bottle or in container sterilisation of milk is typically carried out at 108 to 115 degrees Celsius for 20 to 30 minutes, giving a long shelf life at ambient temperature, unlike pasteurisation which uses 63 degrees for 30 minutes or 72 degrees for 15 seconds. The test used to verify that milk has been correctly pasteurised is the alkaline phosphatase test, where the enzyme is destroyed by correct pasteurisation, so a negative result confirms success. Casein makes up approximately 80 percent of total milk protein, with the remaining 20 percent being whey or serum protein. Buffalo milk compared with cow milk is generally richer in fat and total solids, having about 7 percent fat and 9 to 10 percent solids not fat. The aroma compound that gives cultured buttermilk its characteristic flavour is diacetyl, formed from citrate by Leuconostoc, while acetaldehyde is the typical yoghurt aroma compound. The yoghurt starter culture is a pairing of Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus.
347: Here, this page continues with more dairy and packaging exam questions and their explanations. The yoghurt starter is confirmed as Lactobacillus bulgaricus plus Streptococcus thermophilus, incubated at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius. Milk pouch film, chosen mainly for its moisture barrier and heat sealability, is usually LDPE, low density polyethylene. Hollow containers such as bottles are formed by blow moulding, while injection moulding makes solid items and extrusion makes continuous film, sheet or pipe. The sterilant most commonly used in aseptic packaging of the package surface is hydrogen peroxide with heat, as used in systems like Tetra Pak, which sterilise the carton separately before filling in a sterile zone. The three basic raw materials of glass are silica sand, soda ash and limestone, melted together to make glass. Tin free steel, also called TFS or ECCS, differs from tinplate in that it is coated with chromium or chromium oxide instead of tin, and because this coating is less corrosion resistant than tin, tin free steel must be lacquered. Per the FSSAI standard, double toned milk must have 1.5 percent fat and 9.0 percent SNF, solids not fat, whereas full cream milk is 6.0 percent fat and 9.0 percent SNF, and skim milk is 0.5 percent fat and 8.7 percent SNF. The kraft paper used for strong sacks and corrugated board is made by the sulphate or kraft pulping process, which gives long, strong fibres, hence the name kraft meaning strength. Plastics valued specifically as good gas or oxygen barriers include PET, PVDC, EVOH and nylon.
348: On this page, the objective question bank on Unit 11 concludes, followed by a full reference list. PET, PVDC, EVOH and nylon are confirmed as plastics that provide good gas barrier performance for oxygen sensitive foods. Milk is best described physico chemically as an oil in water emulsion plus a protein colloid in a lactose mineral solution, since the fat is emulsified, the protein exists as a colloid, and the lactose and minerals are present in true solution. The starter organism of acidophilus, a probiotic milk, is Lactobacillus acidophilus itself. After these questions, the chapter lists its references, which anchor the material to authoritative sources. These include the Karnataka Public Service Commission syllabus for Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer, Paper 2, Unit 11 on Food Processing Technology, along with standard textbooks such as Outlines of Dairy Technology by De Sukumar, Dairy Plant Engineering and Management by Tufail Ahmad, Dairy Science and Technology by Walstra, Wouters and Geurts, Modern Dairy Technology by Robinson, and Food Packaging: Principles and Practice by Robertson. Also referenced are FSSAI food product standards for milk and milk products, BIS and 3 A sanitary standards for hygienic dairy equipment design, and official publications of the National Dairy Development Board and the Karnataka Milk Federation, which is the Nandini brand, describing the structure of dairy cooperatives and Operation Flood.
349: Let us understand a new chapter now, Chapter 12, titled Food Safety and Quality, which is Unit 12 of Paper 2. This chapter covers food safety, food quality, the farm to fork chain, food hazards of biological, chemical and physical types, food contamination and spoilage, foodborne diseases, food adulteration and its detection, food additives and preservatives, the microbiology behind food safety, food laws and standards including the FSS Act 2006, FSSAI, Codex Alimentarius, ISO 22000, AGMARK and BIS, quality control versus quality assurance, HACCP and its seven principles, GMP, GHP and prerequisite programmes, sensory evaluation, food packaging and labelling, water quality, and risk analysis, followed by objective questions. Food safety is defined as the assurance that food will not cause harm to the consumer when prepared and eaten according to its intended use, an absolute, non negotiable attribute concerned with the absence of hazards. Food quality is the sum of all characteristics of a food that bear on its acceptability, such as appearance, colour, flavour, texture, nutritional value and freedom from defects, graded along a scale rather than being pass or fail. The modern approach treats safety along the whole supply chain, summed up as farm to fork, meaning hazards can enter at the farm, during harvest, in transport, at processing, in storage, at retail and in the kitchen, so safety is the shared duty of every actor in the chain. Food quality has several dimensions: sensory quality covering appearance, colour, aroma, taste and texture; nutritional quality covering proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals; hygienic or safety quality covering freedom from hazards; and functional quality covering shelf life and suitability for processing.
350: Now, students, an Agricultural Officer must keep food safety and food quality separate on paper. A sample that fails a coliform or pesticide residue limit is a safety failure and is rejected outright, while a sample that merely loses colour or grade is a quality matter that may still be sold at a lower price. Confusing the two leads to wrong enforcement decisions in the field. Moving to section 12.2, a food hazard is defined as any biological, chemical or physical agent in food, or a condition of food, with the potential to cause an adverse health effect, and it becomes a risk only when there is a real chance of exposure and harm. Food hazards fall into three classes, biological, chemical and physical, and this classification is the foundation of every food safety system because each class is controlled by different measures, and identifying the hazard class is the first step in hazard analysis under HACCP. Biological hazards are living agents or their products, including bacteria such as Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, Staphylococcus, Clostridium and Campylobacter, viruses such as Hepatitis A and Norovirus, fungi and their mycotoxins such as aflatoxin from Aspergillus flavus, and parasites such as Taenia, Ascaris and Entamoeba, and they cause the largest share of foodborne illness worldwide. Bacteria are the most important biological hazard because many multiply rapidly in the danger zone of temperature, between about 5 and 60 degrees Celsius, and spore forming bacteria such as Clostridium botulinum and Bacillus cereus survive ordinary cooking and resist heat, which is why low acid canned foods receive a severe botulinum cook rather than mere pasteurisation. Chemical hazards are harmful substances in food, which may be natural, such as toxins in some mushrooms, or added, such as pesticide residues, veterinary drug residues, and heavy metals like lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium.
351: On this page we cover physical hazards and the beginning of food contamination and spoilage. Allergens such as peanut, milk, egg and gluten are also treated as chemical hazards because they harm sensitive consumers, and mycotoxins straddle the biological and chemical classes, being chemical poisons of fungal origin. Physical hazards are hard or sharp foreign objects that can injure the consumer, common examples being fragments of glass, metal, stone, wood, bone, plastic, and pests such as insects and rodent hairs, entering from raw materials, machinery, packaging or careless handling, and controlled by sieving, magnets, metal detectors, X ray inspection and strict housekeeping. To remember the three classes, biological hazards are killed by heat and held back by cold, chemical hazards are kept out at source by approved inputs and legal limits, and physical hazards are screened out by detectors and good housekeeping. In Karnataka, Aspergillus flavus producing aflatoxin in poorly dried groundnut and maize is a leading cause of consignment rejection, so an Agricultural Officer who insists on rapid drying to safe moisture and on aflatoxin testing before sale is controlling the single most important biological chemical hazard of the state's dryland produce. Moving to section 12.3, food contamination is the presence in food of any unwanted matter, microbes, chemicals or foreign bodies, that makes it unsafe or unfit, and cross contamination is the transfer of contaminants from one food, surface or person to another. Food spoilage is the deterioration of food to a point where it becomes unacceptable in appearance, smell, taste or texture, usually through microbes, enzymes or chemical change, and spoiled food is unfit though not always dangerous. Contamination is classed by source: primary contamination occurs in the living animal or growing plant, secondary contamination occurs after harvest during handling, processing or storage, and cross contamination, a special case of secondary contamination, is the carry over of pathogens from raw to cooked food through hands, boards, knives or cloths, the leading cause of kitchen level food poisoning.
352: Here we look at factors affecting microbial growth in food and the start of foodborne diseases. Spoilage has microbial, enzymatic, chemical and physical causes: microbial spoilage, the commonest, is driven by bacteria, yeasts and moulds; enzymatic spoilage is caused by the food's own enzymes, as in the browning of cut fruit; chemical spoilage includes rancidity of fats by oxidation; and physical spoilage covers bruising, drying and freezer burn. The rate of spoilage and safety of food depend on intrinsic factors belonging to the food itself, such as water activity, pH, nutrient content, redox potential and natural antimicrobials, and extrinsic factors belonging to the surroundings, such as temperature, humidity and gas atmosphere. Water activity, written as aw, is the most important intrinsic factor, measuring the free water available to microbes on a scale up to 1.0; most bacteria need an aw above about 0.90, yeasts above 0.88, and moulds above 0.80, so drying, salting and adding sugar all lower aw and preserve food. The pH matters too, since most bacteria prefer near neutral pH, so acid foods below pH 4.6 resist bacterial growth and need only a milder heat process. The danger zone of temperature is roughly 5 to 60 degrees Celsius, where pathogens multiply fastest, so keeping cold food below 5 and hot food above 60 is the simplest rule of food safety, and these two limits are worth memorising. Karnataka's mango and lime pickle industry preserves produce by combining low pH from vinegar and fermentation, low water activity from salt, and a layer of oil that excludes oxygen, so an Agricultural Officer licensing a pickle unit is, in effect, checking that these intrinsic hurdles are correctly set against spoilage microbes. Section 12.4 then defines foodborne disease as any illness resulting from eating food contaminated with pathogenic microbes, their toxins, or harmful chemicals, with food poisoning being the common term for the acute illness that follows such a meal.
353: Now, students, foodborne diseases are divided by mechanism into three groups. Food infection follows the eating of live pathogens that grow in the gut, as with Salmonella and Listeria. Food intoxication follows the eating of a pre formed toxin, where the microbe itself may already be dead, as with Staphylococcus aureus and Clostridium botulinum. Food toxico infection is a mixed case where ingested microbes produce toxin in the gut, as with Clostridium perfringens, and this distinction decides incubation time and treatment. Botulism is the most feared foodborne intoxication: Clostridium botulinum, an anaerobic spore former, produces a potent neurotoxin in under processed canned and bottled foods, causing paralysis, which is why low acid canned foods receive a severe heat process. Staphylococcal poisoning, from a heat stable enterotoxin, has a short incubation of one to six hours and follows handling by an infected food worker. Mycotoxins are toxins of fungal origin that cause chronic foodborne disease; aflatoxin from Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, found in damp groundnut, maize and chillies, is a potent liver carcinogen and a leading cause of consignment rejection, with ochratoxin, patulin and fumonisins being other important mycotoxins, prevented by rapid drying, safe storage and strict testing limits. Endospore knowledge is why an Agricultural Officer insists on retort sterilisation, not mere pasteurisation, for low acid canned vegetables processed by Karnataka Farmer Producer Organisations, and the same officer flags aflatoxin in poorly dried groundnut, tracing the chronic disease risk back to harvest time moisture management. Section 12.5 then introduces food adulteration, the act of debasing a food by adding an inferior, cheaper or harmful substance, by removing a valuable constituent, or by selling a damaged or substandard food as genuine; adulteration may be intentional, incidental or natural, with intentional adulteration, done deliberately to raise profit such as water in milk, brick powder in chilli, or argemone oil in mustard oil, being the most dangerous and the chief target of food law.
354: On this page we finish the food adulteration detection table and move into food additives and preservation methods. Detection tests include the lactometer and iodine test for milk, sediment and colour bleed tests for chilli powder, the nitric acid test turning red for argemone oil in mustard oil, thread or flame tests for honey adulterated with sugar syrup, the hydrochloric acid test turning pink for metanil yellow in turmeric, and wet filter paper colour tests for tea leaves. Detection of adulteration ranges from simple home tests to laboratory analysis; for legal action, samples are sealed and sent to a notified food laboratory for confirmatory chemical analysis, and FSSAI publishes a manual of simple tests known by the brand DART to help citizens screen common foods at home. An Agricultural Officer is often the first responder to an adulteration complaint at a santhe or fair price shop, so knowing these field tests lets the officer make a rapid preliminary judgement before drawing a legal sample for the laboratory. Section 12.6 then defines a food additive as any substance not normally consumed as food in itself, added intentionally for a technological purpose such as preservation, colour, flavour, texture or nutrition, and additives must be approved and used within prescribed limits.
