Additives are grouped by function: preservatives delay spoilage, examples being sodium benzoate, sorbic acid and nisin; antioxidants such as BHA, BHT and ascorbic acid prevent rancidity; colours such as beta carotene and tartrazine improve appearance; emulsifiers and stabilisers such as lecithin, pectin and guar gum control texture; sweeteners such as aspartame, saccharin and sucralose replace sugar; and acidity regulators such as citric and acetic acid control pH. Each approved additive carries an international numbering system code, the INS number, used on labels worldwide. Preservation methods include high temperature methods like pasteurisation, sterilisation, canning and retorting, low temperature methods like refrigeration and freezing, water removal methods like drying and dehydration, pH lowering methods like fermentation and pickling, plus chemical preservatives, irradiation and modified atmosphere packaging.
355: Let us understand two classes of chemical preservative recognised in Indian law. Class I preservatives are natural and generally unrestricted, such as common salt, sugar, vinegar, honey, spices and edible oils, while Class II preservatives are chemical and permitted only within limits, such as benzoates, sorbates, sulphur dioxide and nitrites. A natural bacteriocin, nisin from Lactococcus lactis, coded E234, preserves cheese and canned foods against Gram positive spore formers and is generally recognised as safe. Remember that Class I preservatives, salt, sugar, vinegar and oil, are natural and unrestricted, while Class II preservatives, benzoate, sorbate, sulphur dioxide and nitrite, are chemical and limited by law, since examiners test which class a named preservative belongs to. Section 12.7 then turns to the microbiology behind food safety, noting that food safety rests on applied microbiology, and the officer who can read a lab report, judge a heat process and harness useful microbes controls both the enemy and the workforce of the food chain. On the founders and scope of microbiology, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed bacteria in 1676 and is the Father of Microbiology; Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, developed pasteurisation and vaccines, and is the Father of Modern Microbiology; Robert Koch gave the pure culture technique and Koch's postulates linking a microbe to a disease, and is the Father of Bacteriology; and Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928. On classification and naming of bacteria, Carl Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature, a two word italic Latin name with a capitalised genus, as in Escherichia coli, while Carl Woese in 1977 used 16S ribosomal RNA to propose the three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, with Bergey's Manual as the standard reference for bacterial identification. Bacteria are classed by shape, coccus, bacillus, spirillum and vibrio, and by their Gram reaction. A bacterium is a prokaryote with no membrane bound nucleus, its cell wall is peptidoglycan, thick in Gram positive cells and thin with an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane in Gram negative cells, its genetic material is a single circular chromosome with extra genes on plasmids, and its ribosomes are 70S.
356: On this page, remember the recurring one mark question on cell wall composition: bacteria use peptidoglycan or murein, which is the target of penicillin and lysozyme; fungi use chitin, which distinguishes fungi from bacteria; and algae and plants use cellulose, being photoautotrophs. Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, made of 30S and 50S subunits, and are an antibiotic target, while the bacterial marker for identification is 16S ribosomal RNA, with 18S rRNA used for fungi instead. On growth, the growth curve and metabolites, bacterial growth means an increase in cell number, mostly by binary fission, and the generation or doubling time of Escherichia coli is about 20 minutes under ideal conditions. In a closed culture, growth passes through four phases, lag, log, stationary and death; antibiotics and disinfectants strike hardest in the log phase, while antibiotics themselves, as secondary metabolites, are produced in the stationary phase, also called the idiophase. In the lag phase cells adapt and make enzymes with no division; in the log or exponential phase there is constant maximum division rate, where antibiotics are most effective; in the stationary phase births equal deaths as nutrients limit growth, and secondary metabolites are made; and in the death or decline phase, deaths exceed births and cells lyse. Remember that secondary metabolites such as antibiotics are made in the stationary phase, not the log phase, since this pairing, log phase kills cells, stationary phase makes antibiotics, is a favourite exam trap. Starter culture timing for Nandini curd is set by the log phase, since inoculating active log phase Lactobacillus gives fast, reliable setting in dairy plants, while the same growth curve explains why antibiotic residues, themselves stationary phase products, must never enter the milk. Section 12.8 then covers control and destruction of microorganisms: sterilisation kills all microbes including spores, disinfection kills vegetative pathogens on non living surfaces, antisepsis does the same on living tissue, sanitisation lowers microbial numbers to a safe level, and the suffix cidal means killing, as in bactericidal, while static means inhibiting, as in bacteriostatic.
357: Now, students, let us look at physical and chemical methods of microbial control. Physical control uses heat, radiation and filtration. Moist heat in an autoclave at 121 degrees Celsius, 15 pounds per square inch, for 15 to 20 minutes is the most reliable method and kills spores by protein coagulation. Dry heat in a hot air oven uses 160 to 180 degrees Celsius. Pasteurisation uses mild heat for milk, either LTLT at 63 degrees for 30 minutes or HTST at 72 degrees for 15 seconds, and radiation, filtration and tyndallisation complete the physical toolkit. Membrane filtration uses a 0.22 micrometre pore for heat labile liquids and antibiotics, UV radiation at 254 nanometres works on surfaces only, for air, water and surfaces, and gamma or ionising radiation using cobalt 60 is used for spices and single use packaging. Remember that autoclave numbers are a permanent fixture, 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, 15 to 20 minutes, killing spores, while HTST pasteurisation is 72 degrees for 15 seconds and does not sterilise, so do not let the two fifteens collide in your memory. Chemical disinfectants and antiseptics include phenolics, against which others are rated by the phenol coefficient, alcohols at 60 to 70 percent, halogens such as chlorine and iodine, hydrogen peroxide, aldehydes, ethylene oxide gas, and quaternary ammonium compounds. Antibiotics are antimicrobials made by microbes that kill or inhibit other microbes with selective toxicity: penicillin targets the cell wall, while streptomycin and tetracycline target the ribosome. By mode of action, cell wall synthesis inhibitors targeting peptidoglycan include penicillin and cephalosporin; protein synthesis inhibitors targeting the 30S or 50S ribosome include streptomycin and tetracycline; nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors targeting DNA gyrase or RNA polymerase include quinolones and rifampicin; and cell membrane disruptors include polymyxin.
358: Here we cover thermal death values and the start of beneficial microbes and fermentation. Heat processing is quantified by thermal death values: thermal death time is the time to kill a population at a set temperature; the decimal reduction time, or D value, is the time to kill 90 percent, one log cycle, at a set temperature; and the Z value is the temperature rise needed to cut the D value ten fold. These values govern the design of canning, retorting and pasteurisation, and decide whether a heat process is adequate. The F value is the equivalent kill time at a reference temperature of 121 degrees Celsius. Remember that the D value is a time, killing 90 percent at a fixed temperature, while the Z value is a temperature interval needed to change D ten fold, and mixing up the units of D and Z is the standard trap. These exact conditions sit behind an officer's plant inspections, verifying that a dairy's HTST holding tube reaches 72 degrees, that a fruit pulp unit's retort meets its target F value, or that a spice exporter's gamma irradiation dose is within the approved limit for FSSAI compliance. Section 12.9 then introduces beneficial microbes: fermentation is a process in which microbes act on a food substrate to produce desirable changes, acids, alcohol, flavour and texture, that preserve the food and improve its value, essentially microbial control turned to advantage. Fermentation preserves food by lowering pH and producing alcohol or acids that inhibit spoilage microbes, while also improving flavour and texture, raising nutrition by adding vitamins and predigesting protein, and removing antinutrients. Food fermentations are lactic acid, as in curd, idli and pickles, alcoholic, as in bread, beer and wine, acetic acid, as in vinegar, and alkaline, as in some legume ferments. Industrial microbiology grows microbes on a large scale to make commercial products in a vessel called a fermentor or bioreactor, the commonest type being the stirred tank reactor, whose core parts are the jacketed vessel, the impeller for mixing, baffles to prevent a vortex, the sparger to supply sterile air, and probes for pH, temperature and dissolved oxygen.
359: On this page we cover fermentation types, product organism pairs and probiotics. Fermentation is run either as submerged liquid fermentation, where microbes grow in a liquid medium and which suits bacteria and yeast, or as solid state fermentation, where microbes grow on a moist solid substrate with little free water and which is dominated by fungi, yielding products such as tempeh, koji and some enzymes. Each product is linked to a characteristic organism: ethanol comes from Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a primary product; lactic acid comes from Lactobacillus, also primary; citric acid comes from Aspergillus niger, primary; glutamic acid, that is MSG, comes from Corynebacterium glutamicum, an amino acid product; penicillin comes from Penicillium chrysogenum, a secondary metabolite; and streptomycin comes from Streptomyces griseus, also secondary. Remember three product organism pairs first, as they appear most often: citric acid equals Aspergillus niger, glutamic acid or MSG equals Corynebacterium glutamicum, and penicillin equals Penicillium, since the species name often carries the answer. Idli dosa batter and Nandini curd are everyday Karnataka lactic acid fermentations, while CFTRI Mysuru anchors the state's food microbiology research, with citric acid, ethanol and food grade enzymes underpinning its processed food sector. Section 12.10 covers probiotics, bacteriocins, enzymes and downstream processing: a probiotic is a live microorganism that, taken in adequate amounts, benefits the health of the host, chiefly lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, plus the yeast Saccharomyces boulardii. Probiotics in fermented foods such as curd, yoghurt and kefir improve gut flora, aid digestion, boost immunity and antagonise pathogens; prebiotics are non digestible fibres such as inulin that feed probiotics, and synbiotics combine both. Bacteriocins are antimicrobial peptides made by bacteria that kill closely related strains, and nisin, from Lactococcus lactis, coded E234, is the best known bacteriocin and a natural preservative against Gram positive spore formers. Microbial enzymes are preferred industrially because microbes grow fast on cheap media, and important food enzymes include amylase for starch and protease for protein.
360: Now, students, we finish the enzyme table and move to downstream processing and food law. Pectinase, from Aspergillus niger, is used for fruit juice clarification; rennet or chymosin, from Mucor or recombinant sources, is used for cheese making; and invertase, from Saccharomyces, is used in confectionery. Downstream processing is everything after fermentation, recovering and purifying the product from the broth, and it often accounts for the major share of production cost; the sequence is solid liquid separation, cell disruption if the product is intracellular, extraction, purification, concentration and final recovery, with cell disruption needed only for intracellular products, while secreted products go straight to separation. Remember that cell disruption in downstream processing is required only for intracellular products, while extracellular, secreted products skip disruption and go straight to separation, a frequent trap in process sequencing questions. Spray drying and ultrafiltration in downstream processing are the same unit operations behind Nandini's milk powder and whey protein lines, while pectinase and amylase serve Karnataka's fruit pulp, juice and brewing units, connecting microbiology directly to the state's dairy and processing economy. Section 12.11 then covers food laws and standards: food law gives safety its legal force, and India once had many overlapping food laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act of 1954, which were consolidated into a single statute, the Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006, creating one integrated regulator and one set of standards, operating alongside voluntary quality marks and international standards. Figure 12.4 shows the food law structure under FSSAI: the FSS Act 2006 sits at the top as the single integrated food law, below it is FSSAI as the apex regulator under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and below that sit State Food Safety Commissioners, Designated Officers at district level, Food Safety Officers who inspect, and Notified Food Laboratories that test samples, with standards set through the FSS Regulations 2011 aligned with Codex Alimentarius global food standards. The FSS Act, 2006, is the single integrated food law of India, which repealed and replaced eight earlier laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act of 1954, and set up one apex regulator with uniform standards from farm to fork.
361: Here we cover FSSAI's structure and international and voluntary food standards. FSSAI, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, is the apex regulator created under the FSS Act 2006, working under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, setting food standards and licensing and inspecting food businesses. FSSAI sets standards through the Food Safety and Standards Regulations of 2011, covering licensing and registration, food additives, contaminants, packaging, labelling and hygiene; enforcement runs through State Food Safety Commissioners, district Designated Officers, Food Safety Officers who inspect and draw samples, and notified food laboratories that test them, and every food business must register or take a licence according to its scale of operation. On international and voluntary standards, Codex Alimentarius is the collection of international food standards, guidelines and codes of practice set jointly by the FAO and WHO, serving as the global reference for food safety and the benchmark for world trade under the WTO. ISO 22000 is the international standard for a food safety management system, combining HACCP principles with prerequisite programmes and management system requirements, and it can be certified by a third party for any organisation in the food chain. Several voluntary marks signal quality in India: AGMARK, run under the Agricultural Produce Grading and Marking Act of 1937 by the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, grades agricultural produce such as ghee, honey, spices and oils; the BIS, the Bureau of Indian Standards, runs the ISI mark for manufactured goods and it is mandatory for packaged drinking water and some food products; these marks add a quality assurance layer above the legal safety floor. Remember to pin the authorities: Codex equals FAO and WHO, ISO 22000 is the international certifiable system, AGMARK is agricultural produce grading under the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, and BIS is the ISI mark and packaged water standard.
362: On this page we finish the standards table and move into quality control versus quality assurance. FSSAI is confirmed as the single Indian food regulator under the FSS Act 2006. An Agricultural Officer issues and verifies AGMARK grading for ghee, honey and spices, and checks FSSAI registration at the farm gate and santhe level, and knowing that the FSS Act 2006 replaced the old PFA Act of 1954 lets the officer cite the correct, current law when prosecuting an adulteration case. Section 12.12 then defines quality control as the operational techniques and activities used to check and fulfil quality requirements, chiefly inspection, testing and measurement of the product to detect defects, being product oriented and detective, while quality assurance is the planned and systematic activities built into the whole system to give confidence that a product will meet quality requirements, being process oriented and preventive. Quality control and quality assurance are complementary: quality control detects defects by examining the finished product, sorting good from bad after the event, while quality assurance prevents defects by designing quality into the process, so that fewer defects arise in the first place; modern food management leans towards assurance and prevention, with HACCP as its leading tool, and total quality management extends this idea to every person in the organisation. Figure 12.3 shows the food safety management system hierarchy as a pyramid: at the base sit prerequisite programmes and SSOP, standard sanitation operating procedures; above that sits GMP plus GHP, good manufacturing and hygienic practice; above that sits HACCP, with its seven principles of hazard analysis and critical control points; and at the apex sits ISO 22000 or FSSC 22000, the certifiable food safety management system, with each layer building on the one below it.
363: Let us understand quality control versus quality assurance clearly before moving to HACCP. Quality control is detective and product based, it finds defects, while quality assurance is preventive and process based, it stops defects arising, and HACCP belongs firmly to assurance, not control. Section 12.13 introduces HACCP, Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points, a systematic, preventive food safety system that identifies, evaluates and controls hazards significant to food safety, shifting the focus from end product testing to control at the points that matter. HACCP was developed in the 1960s for the United States space programme, to guarantee safe food for astronauts, and it is now the world's standard food safety system and the core of ISO 22000. HACCP is built on seven principles, applied after five preliminary tasks, forming the team, describing the product, identifying intended use, drawing a flow diagram, and confirming it on site. Figure 12.2 shows the seven principles of HACCP in sequence: Principle 1, conduct a hazard analysis; Principle 2, determine the critical control points, or CCPs; Principle 3, establish critical limits for each CCP; Principle 4, establish a monitoring system; Principle 5, establish corrective actions; Principle 6, establish verification procedures; and Principle 7, establish record keeping and documentation. The seven principles run in strict order: first, conduct a hazard analysis to list significant hazards; second, determine the critical control points, the steps where control is essential; third, establish critical limits, the measurable boundaries that separate safe from unsafe; and fourth, establish monitoring to watch each critical control point.
364: Now, students, we complete the seven principles of HACCP and move into GMP and GHP. Fifth, establish corrective actions for when a critical limit is breached; sixth, establish verification to confirm the system works; and seventh, establish record keeping and documentation. A critical control point, or CCP, is a step in the process at which control can be applied and is essential to prevent, eliminate or reduce a food safety hazard to an acceptable level, and missing a CCP allows an unsafe product to reach the consumer. Remember the order of the seven principles: the first two define where control is needed, hazard analysis then critical control points; the next three define how it is controlled, limits, monitoring, corrective action; and the last two prove it works, verification and records. When an Agricultural Officer audits a Nandini milk plant, the pasteuriser is a classic critical control point, its critical limit is 72 degrees for 15 seconds, monitoring is the continuous chart recorder, and the corrective action is automatic flow diversion if the temperature falls, and reading a plant this way is HACCP in practice. Section 12.14 then introduces GMP, Good Manufacturing Practices, the basic conditions and activities necessary to produce food in a hygienic environment, covering premises, equipment, layout, maintenance and process control, so that food is consistently produced to the required quality and safety, and GHP, Good Hygiene Practices, the hygiene measures and conditions applied at every step of the food chain to ensure food safety and suitability, covering personal hygiene, cleaning, sanitation, waste disposal and pest control. GMP and GHP are the foundation on which HACCP is built, called prerequisite programmes because HACCP cannot work unless they are already in place; a HACCP plan controls a few critical control points, while the prerequisite programmes control the general hygienic environment around them, and without clean premises, trained staff and pest control, even a well written HACCP plan will fail. The main prerequisite programmes cover premises and layout design that prevents cross contamination, safe water supply, cleaning and sanitation through SSOPs, pest control, waste management, and personal hygiene and training of food handlers.
365: On this page we finish the food safety programmes and move into sensory evaluation. First, a quick note on prerequisite programmes. Training controls the competence of food handlers, and maintenance keeps equipment in working, hygienic order. Then we meet Good Agricultural Practices, or GAP. GAP covers practices on the farm that address environmental, economic and social sustainability, and that result in safe, quality produce. It covers safe use of agro-chemicals, water, soil and harvest hygiene, before the food even enters the processing chain. Remember the layered picture. GAP is on the farm, GMP and GHP are the foundation inside the plant, HACCP sits on top and controls the critical points, and ISO 22000 wraps the whole system together. HACCP fails if GMP and GHP underneath it are weak. Now, section 12.15, sensory evaluation of food. This is the scientific discipline used to measure, analyse and interpret human responses of sight, smell, taste, touch and hearing to food, under controlled conditions to reduce bias. There are three families of sensory tests. Discrimination or difference tests, like the triangle test, ask whether two samples differ. Descriptive tests use trained panels to score intensity. Affective or acceptance tests ask ordinary consumers how much they like a product, often on a nine-point hedonic scale.
366: Now, students, let us look at section 12.16, food packaging and labelling. Food packaging is the science and technology of enclosing food to protect it from physical, chemical and biological damage, to preserve quality and extend shelf life, and to carry information to the consumer. Packaging performs four functions, protection, containment of the right quantity, convenience in handling, and communication through the label. Active packaging adds substances like oxygen scavengers, modified-atmosphere packaging changes the internal gas mix, and aseptic packaging fills sterile food into sterile containers, as in tetra-pack milk. Labelling is the legal voice of the package. Under FSSAI labelling regulations, a label must declare the food name, ingredient list in descending order, net quantity, manufacturer details, the FSSAI licence number, manufacture and best-before or use-by dates, maximum retail price, batch number, nutritional information, and the veg or non-veg symbol, a green dot for vegetarian and a brown dot for non-vegetarian. Two points are favourite exam questions, every package must carry the FSSAI licence number, and ingredients are listed in descending order of weight. Section 12.17 begins, water quality in food safety. Potable water must be free from harmful microorganisms and chemical contaminants.
367: Here, we continue with water quality parameters. Coliforms and E. coli are indicator organisms, their absence shows freedom from faecal contamination. pH affects corrosion and cleaning, total dissolved solids affect taste, hardness affects scaling of equipment, and heavy metals, nitrate and fluoride above limits are chemically toxic. In India, packaged drinking water must carry the mandatory BIS or ISI mark. Remember, the key microbial test for water safety is the absence of coliforms and E. coli, these are indicator organisms for faecal pollution. Now section 12.18, risk analysis and traceability. Risk analysis is the structured framework used to manage food-safety risk, made of three linked components. Risk assessment is the scientific step, it identifies the hazard, characterises it, and assesses exposure and risk. Risk management is the policy step, weighing options and setting limits and standards. Risk communication is the interactive exchange of information among assessors, managers, consumers and industry. Keeping assessment separate from management keeps the science honest. Traceability is the ability to track and trace a food, its ingredients and its history through all stages, one step back to the supplier and one step forward to the customer. Traceability lets an unsafe product be located and recalled quickly, and good records, batch numbers, supplier details, make this possible.
368: On this short page, let us consolidate risk analysis and traceability. Remember, risk analysis equals assessment plus management plus communication. Assessment is the science, management is the policy, and communication is the exchange of information among all parties. Traceability means one step back and one step forward, and this is exactly what makes a recall possible. Think of the Agri Officer's role here. After a contamination scare, the Agricultural Officer relies on traceability, using batch numbers and supplier records, to trace the source one step back and to recall the affected stock one step forward. This limits the harm reaching consumers. This closes out the theory on risk analysis and traceability, which, together with sensory evaluation, packaging and labelling, and water quality, completes the food safety and quality toolkit for this unit. Keep these definitions crisp for the exam, risk assessment is scientific, risk management is policy-based, and risk communication is about exchanging information, while traceability and recall work together to protect consumers when something goes wrong in the food chain.
369: Now, students, here is the chapter mind map for food safety and quality, a single picture tying together everything we have studied. At the centre is food safety and quality, branching into eight areas. Food hazards are divided into biological, chemical and physical types, with the danger zone of 5 to 60 degrees Celsius where microbes multiply fastest. Foodborne pathogens include Clostridium botulinum, a neurotoxin from canned food, Salmonella from eggs and poultry, Staphylococcus aureus with heat-stable toxin, E. coli O157:H7 from undercooked beef, Listeria which grows even at fridge temperature, and Vibrio cholerae from contaminated water. Adulteration examples include argemone oil in mustard causing epidemic dropsy, metanil yellow as a banned dye, melamine as fake protein in milk, and kesari dal causing lathyrism. Additives and preservatives include nisin, class one natural preservatives like salt, and class two chemical preservatives like benzoate. HACCP has seven principles built around critical control points, originating from Pillsbury and NASA space food. Food laws include the FSS Act 2006, FSSAI as India's apex regulator, and Codex by FAO and WHO. GMP, GHP and ISO 22000 cover quality management, and water quality covers coliforms, MPN test, chlorination and BIS standards.
370: On this page we have a key terms glossary, useful for quick revision before moving to objective questions. Food safety is the assurance that food will not cause harm when prepared and eaten as intended. Food quality is the sum of attributes making food acceptable, sensory, nutritional and hygienic. A food hazard is any biological, chemical or physical agent that can cause harm. Contamination is the entry of an unwanted agent, while spoilage is deterioration making food unfit. Foodborne infection comes from live pathogens like Salmonella, while foodborne intoxication comes from a pre-formed toxin like botulism. Adulteration means adding, removing or substituting to debase food quality. A food additive is added intentionally for a technical function. HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points, with seven principles. GMP and GHP are prerequisite hygiene programmes underpinning HACCP. Quality control is detective and product-based, while quality assurance is preventive and process-based. The FSS Act 2006 created FSSAI, India's apex food regulator under the Ministry of Health. Codex Alimentarius sets global food standards through FAO and WHO. ISO 22000 is a certifiable food-safety management system. Sensory evaluation measures food through human senses, risk analysis combines assessment, management and communication, and traceability enables recall by tracking one step back and one step forward.
371: Now, students, we begin Part B, objective questions and answers for this chapter. Work through these after reading the theory. Question one asks how food safety is best defined, and the answer is that food will not cause harm when prepared and eaten as intended. Question two asks about the movement of food from production to consumer viewed for safety, and the answer is the farm-to-fork chain. Question three asks which option is a biological food hazard, and the answer is Salmonella bacteria, since glass is physical and pesticide or heavy metal are chemical hazards. Question four asks about pieces of glass, metal or stone in food, and these are classified as physical hazards. Question five covers pesticide residues, heavy metals and allergens, which are chemical hazards. Question six asks what metal detectors and magnets in a food plant control, and the answer is physical hazards, since they remove metal fragments. Question seven asks about deterioration making food unfit to eat, and the answer is spoilage. Question eight asks about the minimum water activity below which most bacteria cannot grow, with the answer being around 0.91, an important number to remember for exam purposes regarding food preservation and microbial growth control.
372: Here we continue with more objective questions. Question nine covers the temperature range where foodborne pathogenic bacteria grow best, and the answer is 20 to 45 degrees Celsius, part of the broader danger zone of 5 to 60 degrees. Question ten distinguishes foodborne infection, caused by live pathogens like Salmonella, from intoxication. Question eleven confirms botulism is an intoxication, since the toxin is pre-formed in the food by Clostridium botulinum. Question twelve identifies adding water to milk or chicory to coffee powder as adulteration. Question thirteen defines a food additive as a substance added intentionally for a technical function such as colour or preservation. Question fourteen notes that pasteurisation, canning and retorting preserve food using high temperature. Question fifteen explains that pickling and fermentation preserve food mainly by lowering the pH, making the food too acidic for spoilage microbes. Question sixteen asks how drying and dehydration preserve food, with the answer being removal of available water, which lowers water activity and stops microbial growth. These questions reinforce the preservation principles taught throughout the chapter, especially the role of temperature, acidity and moisture control in keeping food safe.
373: Let us understand more questions here. Question seventeen names Antonie van Leeuwenhoek as the scientist often called the father of microbiology, for first observing microbes, with Pasteur and Koch coming later. Question eighteen explains binomial nomenclature, in Escherichia coli, Escherichia is the genus and coli is the species. Question nineteen identifies pasteurisation at 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds as the HTST method, meaning High-Temperature Short-Time. Question twenty defines the D-value as the time required to destroy 90 percent, or one log cycle, of a microbial population at a given temperature. Question twenty-one notes that lactic acid bacteria carry out the fermentation of milk into curd. Question twenty-two defines probiotics as live microorganisms that, given in adequate amounts, benefit host health. Question twenty-three identifies bacteriocins, like nisin, as antimicrobial proteins produced by bacteria that inhibit closely related bacteria, and these are used as natural preservatives. Question twenty-four names the FSS Act 2006 as the single integrated food law of India that replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. These are all high-yield definitional questions worth memorising precisely for the exam.
374: Now, students, more important questions on food regulation. Question twenty-five names FSSAI, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, as the apex food regulator set up under the FSS Act 2006. Question twenty-six confirms FSSAI functions under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Question twenty-seven identifies Codex Alimentarius as the collection of international food standards set jointly by FAO and WHO. Question twenty-eight names ISO 22000 as the certifiable international standard for a food-safety management system. 375: Here we continue, question thirty-three confirms HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. Question thirty-four notes HACCP was originally developed for the United States space programme in the 1960s, to ensure safe food for astronauts. Question thirty-five confirms HACCP has seven principles, applied after five preliminary tasks. Question thirty-six identifies the first principle of HACCP as conducting a hazard analysis. Question thirty-seven defines a critical control point, or CCP, as a step where control is essential to prevent or eliminate a food-safety hazard. Question forty-three confirms the nine-point hedonic scale measures consumer liking, an acceptance test. 377: Here we finish the objective questions. Question forty-nine confirms risk analysis equals assessment plus management plus communication. The page then lists the references used to prepare this chapter, including the Karnataka Public Service Commission syllabus for Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer, Paper 2, Unit 12 on Food Safety and Quality, the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 and its 2011 regulations from FSSAI, the Codex Alimentarius Commission's international standards, ISO 22000 food safety management systems, textbooks by Frazier and Westhoff on Food Microbiology, Pelczar, Chan and Krieg on Microbiology, Srilakshmi on Food Science, and the Bureau of Indian Standards together with the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection for ISI mark and AGMARK grading standards.
378: Now, students, we begin Chapter 13, Food Process Engineering, under Paper 2's technical paper, Unit 13. This chapter covers the full theory of food process engineering, engineering thermodynamics including systems, properties, the Zeroth, First and Second Laws, entropy and availability, properties of pure substances and steam, thermodynamic and power cycles such as Carnot, Rankine, reheat, Otto, Diesel and Brayton, psychrometry of moist air, principles of refrigeration, air, vapour-compression and vapour-absorption refrigeration, refrigerants and azeotropes, ice manufacture, food freezing and Plank's equation, freeze concentration and freeze drying, cold storage and the refrigerated cold chain, and air-conditioning with sensible heat factor and cooling-load calculations. Section 13.1 covers the scope and field relevance. Figure 13.1 shows food process engineering branching into five concept areas, thermodynamics, steam and pure substances, psychrometry, refrigeration, and freezing and storage. This is the most quantitative unit of the technical paper, opening with basic thermodynamic concepts of systems, properties, state and process, the fundamental laws, entropy and availability, properties of steam, and standard thermodynamic cycles used in engines, gas turbines and refrigeration.
379: Here, the text explains why this subject matters intensely for an Agricultural Officer in Karnataka. The Karnataka Milk Federation, brand Nandini, runs the state's dairy cold chain of bulk-milk coolers and chilling centres. CFTRI and DFRL at Mysuru work on freezing and freeze drying. HOPCOMS, the APMC mandis and horticulture missions run cold stores and pre-cooling for fruit, vegetables and flowers. Reefer vans move mango, grape, pomegranate and cut flowers, and the sugar mills of the Mandya-Belagavi belt run on steam and cogeneration. The Agricultural Officer does not design a compressor, but appraises cold-store and reefer-van subsidy proposals, advises farmer producer organisations and dairy societies on chilling and the cold chain, judges whether a refrigeration or freeze-drying plant is correctly sized, and explains why post-harvest losses fall when the cold chain holds. Section 13.2 introduces systems, properties, state and process. Thermodynamics is the science of energy and its transformations. A thermodynamic system is the matter or region chosen for study, everything outside is the surroundings, and the boundary separates them. A closed system lets only energy cross, an open system, or control volume, lets both mass and energy cross, and an isolated system lets neither cross.
380: On this page, we finish the types of thermodynamic processes. A process may be isothermal at constant temperature, isobaric at constant pressure, isochoric at constant volume, adiabatic with no heat transfer, isentropic at constant entropy, or polytropic following pV to the power n equals constant. A quasi-static process passes through a succession of equilibrium states slowly enough to be treated as reversible. Remember, closed versus open, a closed system lets energy cross but not mass, an open system lets both cross, and an isolated system lets neither cross. Properties are point functions, path-independent, while heat and work are path functions. Section 13.3 introduces the Zeroth Law, temperature, heat and work. The Zeroth Law states that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with one another. This is the basis of temperature measurement, the third body is the thermometer. Temperature scales include Celsius, Kelvin as the absolute SI scale, and Fahrenheit, with Kelvin equals Celsius plus 273.15. Heat is energy in transit due to temperature difference, positive when added to the system, and work is energy in transit by a force acting through a distance, positive when done by the system.
381: Now, students, let us understand section 13.4, the First Law of Thermodynamics, covering energy, internal energy, enthalpy and specific heats. The First Law is the law of conservation of energy, energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another. For a closed system, heat supplied equals the increase in internal energy plus the work done, written as Q equals dU plus W. For a cycle, net heat transfer equals net work transfer, and the First Law denies a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind. Internal energy is the energy stored in molecules, and for an ideal gas depends only on temperature. Enthalpy, H, equals U plus pV, and is the useful property for flow, or open, systems and constant-pressure heating. Specific heat at constant volume, Cv, is the heat needed to raise unit mass by one degree at constant volume, while specific heat at constant pressure, Cp, does the same at constant pressure. Cp is always greater than Cv because at constant pressure some heat also does expansion work, their difference equals the gas constant R, and their ratio gamma equals Cp over Cv, about 1.4 for air. The steady-flow energy equation applies the First Law to open systems like turbines, compressors, boilers and nozzles.
382: Here, we move into section 13.5, the Second Law of Thermodynamics, covering the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, entropy and availability. The Second Law gives heat transfer a direction and limits how much heat can become work. The Kelvin-Planck statement says it is impossible to build a heat engine that converts all the heat it receives from a single reservoir into work in a cycle, some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir. The Clausius statement says heat cannot, of itself, flow from a colder to a hotter body without external work, this is the basis of refrigeration. The Second Law denies a perpetual-motion machine of the second kind. A reversible process is ideal, frictionless and quasi-static, and gives the maximum possible work, while an irreversible process has friction and finite temperature drops, generating entropy. Entropy is the property measuring the unavailable energy or molecular disorder of a system, with dS equals dQ over T for a reversible process. The Clausius inequality states the cyclic integral of dQ over T is less than or equal to zero. The Second Law also gives the thermodynamic, or Kelvin, absolute temperature scale, defined from a reversible Carnot engine, independent of any working substance. Availability, or exergy, is the maximum useful work obtainable relative to the surroundings.
383: On this page, remember, Kelvin-Planck is the engine statement, Clausius is the refrigerator statement, and they are equivalent. Entropy always increases for an isolated or real process, and dS equals dQ over T only for a reversible process. Think about it this way, the Clausius statement is exactly why every cold store and milk chiller needs a compressor drawing power, heat will not leave the cold milk and enter the warmer surroundings by itself. Section 13.6 introduces properties of pure substances, P-V-T behaviour and the phase rule. A pure substance has a fixed and uniform chemical composition throughout, like water, ammonia or nitrogen, and can exist in solid, liquid and vapour phases while remaining pure. The triple point is the unique pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist, for water this is 0.01 degrees Celsius and 0.6113 kilopascals. The critical point is where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable, for water this is 374.15 degrees Celsius and 221.2 bar. Sublimation, solid changing directly to vapour, is the basis of freeze drying. The Gibbs phase rule states F equals C minus P plus 2, where F is degrees of freedom, C is components and P is phases. At water's triple point, F equals zero, an invariant fixed point.
384: Here, we finish the phase rule discussion, noting that sublimation is the key to freeze drying, and that water's fusion line slopes backward because ice floats, meaning ice is less dense than water. Freeze drying of tender-coconut water, instant coffee and biologicals at CFTRI Mysuru exploits sublimation below water's triple point, the frozen water leaves as vapour without melting. Section 13.7 covers properties of steam, wet, dry saturated, superheated, and steam tables. Steam is the vapour of water and the most important working and heating fluid in food processing. When water is heated at constant pressure, it first becomes saturated liquid at its boiling point, then wet steam, a mixture of boiling water and vapour, then dry saturated steam when all liquid has evaporated, and on further heating, superheated steam, hotter than its saturation temperature. The dryness fraction, x, is the fraction of dry vapour in wet steam, ranging from zero for saturated water to one for dry saturated steam. The enthalpy of wet steam equals hf, the sensible heat, plus x times hfg, the latent heat of evaporation. For dry saturated steam, x equals one, so enthalpy equals hg. Steam tables tabulate these properties so an engineer can read off steam's state at any pressure rather than calculate it. Dry steam carries the most usable latent heat per kilogram.
385: On this page we look at Carnot, Rankine and reheat cycles for vapour power. A thermodynamic cycle returns the working fluid to its starting state while producing work or moving heat. The Carnot cycle is the ideal, most efficient cycle between two temperatures, made of two reversible isothermal processes and two reversible adiabatic, or isentropic, processes. Its efficiency depends only on the two absolute temperatures, given by 1 minus T low over T high, and no real engine can beat this between the same two temperatures. The Rankine cycle is the practical steam power cycle all power plants use, with four steps, boiler for heat addition, turbine for work output, condenser for heat rejection, and feed pump. Rankine is preferred over a steam Carnot cycle because the fluid condenses fully to liquid before pumping, which keeps the pump small and practical. The reheat cycle expands steam partway, sends it back to the boiler for reheating, then expands it again, raising efficiency and keeping the turbine exit steam dry, which avoids blade erosion. The regenerative cycle uses bled steam to preheat feed water, raising the mean temperature of heat addition. Remember, Carnot efficiency equals 1 minus T low over T high in Kelvin, and Rankine is boiler, turbine, condenser, pump.
386: Continuing with power cycles, remember that to raise Rankine cycle efficiency you increase boiler temperature and pressure, lower condenser pressure, and add reheat and regeneration. Karnataka's sugar mills use Rankine cycle cogeneration burning bagasse, exporting surplus power to the grid. Now we move to air standard cycles, Otto, Diesel and Brayton, which model internal combustion and gas turbine engines used in farm machinery, pumpsets and generators. The Otto cycle is the ideal petrol or spark ignition engine cycle, with heat added at constant volume, and its efficiency depends only on compression ratio, higher ratio giving higher efficiency. The Diesel cycle is the ideal compression ignition engine cycle, with heat added at constant pressure, and its efficiency depends on both compression ratio and cutoff ratio. The dual, or mixed, cycle used in modern diesels adds heat partly at constant volume and partly at constant pressure, giving efficiency between Otto and Diesel. The Brayton, or Joule, cycle is the ideal gas turbine cycle, with heat added at constant pressure in steady flow, and when reversed it becomes the basis of air refrigeration. For the same compression ratio, Otto beats Diesel in efficiency, but real diesel engines run at much higher compression ratios, so they achieve better real world efficiency and fuel economy.
387: This page compares Otto and Diesel cycles in practice, noting diesel engines run tractors, pumpsets, threshers and gensets across Karnataka's farms, while Otto cycle engines run petrol start engines and small sprayers. Then we begin section thirteen point ten on moist air properties, dry bulb temperature, wet bulb temperature, dew point temperature and humidity, the foundation of psychrometry, the study of moist air. Moist air is a mixture of dry air and water vapour, each exerting its own partial pressure under Dalton's law. The amount of water vapour air holds, and how close it is to saturation, is described by psychrometric properties read from a psychrometric chart. In unsaturated air, dew point temperature is less than or equal to wet bulb temperature, which is less than or equal to dry bulb temperature, and at full saturation, one hundred percent relative humidity, all three become equal and wet bulb depression is zero. Dry bulb temperature is what an ordinary thermometer reads. Wet bulb temperature is read by a thermometer with a wet wick in moving air, reflecting evaporative cooling. Dew point temperature is the temperature at which moist air, cooled at constant pressure, just begins to condense. Absolute or specific humidity is the mass of water vapour per kilogram of dry air, while relative humidity is the ratio of actual vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure.
388: Continuing psychrometric definitions, humid volume is the volume of moist air per kilogram of dry air, humid heat is the heat needed to raise one kilogram of dry air plus its moisture by one degree, and wet bulb depression is dry bulb minus wet bulb temperature, becoming zero at saturation. Remember the order, dew point is less than or equal to wet bulb, which is less than or equal to dry bulb, always, and at saturation all three are equal. The larger the wet bulb depression, the drier the air. Grain and chilli drying, cold store humidity control and mushroom house climate all depend on these properties. Section thirteen eleven covers psychrometric processes, sorption isotherms and humidity measurement. Sensible heating or cooling changes dry bulb temperature at constant humidity ratio. Humidification adds moisture, dehumidification removes it. Cooling below the dew point condenses moisture out, which is how an air conditioner's cooling coil dehumidifies air. Adiabatic saturation, or evaporative cooling, cools air by evaporating water into it without external heat, the principle behind the desert cooler and the wet bulb thermometer. A sorption isotherm is a curve, at fixed temperature, linking a food's equilibrium moisture content to the surrounding relative humidity, central to drying, packaging and shelf life design.
389: This page stresses that cooling air only dehumidifies it when cooled below the dew point, where moisture condenses on the coil, while evaporative or adiabatic cooling follows the wet bulb line and adds moisture while lowering dry bulb temperature. A sorption isotherm links a food's equilibrium moisture to relative humidity at constant temperature, the basis of safe drying and packaging. Desert evaporative coolers work well in dry interior Karnataka but poorly on the humid coast. Section thirteen twelve introduces refrigeration principles, unit of capacity and coefficient of performance, COP. Refrigeration removes heat from a body or space, keeping it below surrounding temperature. By the Clausius statement of the second law, heat will not flow from cold to hot by itself, so a refrigerator needs work or heat input to pump heat uphill. A refrigerator and heat pump are the same machine, just different purposes, cooling effect versus heating effect. One ton of refrigeration, one TR, is the rate of heat removal to freeze one short ton, two thousand pounds, of water at zero Celsius into ice in twenty four hours, equal to about three point five kilowatts, three thousand and twenty four kilocalories per hour, or twelve thousand British thermal units per hour. COP of a refrigerator equals refrigerating effect divided by work input, and COP of a heat pump equals COP of refrigerator plus one. The Carnot maximum COP for a refrigerator is T low over T high minus T low, in Kelvin.
390: Continuing on refrigeration performance, remember one ton of refrigeration equals three point five kilowatts, three thousand and twenty four kilocalories per hour, or twelve thousand British thermal units per hour. COP equals useful effect over work input, and Carnot refrigerator COP equals T low over T high minus T low in Kelvin. When a dairy plans a cold store or bulk milk cooler, the engineer sizes it in tons of refrigeration based on the heat to be removed. Section thirteen thirteen covers methods of producing low temperatures. Throttling, or expansion, of a compressed liquid through a valve makes part of it flash to vapour, and the heat for this evaporation is drawn from the rest, cooling it, the core effect in every vapour compression system. Expanding a high pressure gas does work and cools it, reversible adiabatic, or isentropic, expansion through an expander gives the most cooling, while irreversible expansion through a throttle valve gives the Joule Thomson cooling used in gas liquefaction. Thermoelectric, or Peltier, cooling passes direct current through a junction of two dissimilar conductors, one junction absorbing heat and the other releasing it, with no moving parts. Adiabatic demagnetisation magnetises then demagnetises a paramagnetic salt, reaching temperatures within a fraction of a degree of absolute zero, used in cryogenics.
391: Section thirteen fourteen explains the reversed Carnot cycle and how operating temperatures are chosen. An air refrigeration system uses air as refrigerant without phase change, and the reversed Carnot cycle, run backwards so work is put in and heat pumped from cold to hot, is the ideal benchmark. It has isentropic compression, isothermal heat rejection, isentropic expansion, and isothermal heat absorption, giving the maximum possible COP between two temperatures. Because COP depends only on the two absolute temperatures, operating temperatures are chosen to keep the cold space only as cold as needed and reject heat as low as the surroundings allow. The smaller the temperature lift, the gap between cold space and heat rejection temperature, the better the performance, which is why over cooling a store wastes energy and good condenser ventilation matters. An AO advising a cold store should set the holding temperature no lower than the produce needs, for example potatoes near four degrees Celsius rather than zero, and insist on good condenser ventilation. Section thirteen fifteen introduces the Bell Coleman, or reversed Brayton or Joule, air refrigerator, the practical air refrigeration cycle. Air is compressed isentropically, cooled at constant pressure, expanded in an expander where it does work and cools sharply, then passed through the cold space absorbing heat at constant pressure before returning to the compressor. Unlike a throttle valve, the expander recovers work and produces a much greater temperature drop.
392: Continuing on the Bell Coleman cycle, because air has low specific heat and carries little heat per kilogram, the system has a low COP and needs large air flows, making it bulky compared to a vapour compression plant of the same capacity. Multistage compression with intercooling is used for high pressure ratios. Its merits are that air is free, non toxic, non flammable and leak proof, making the Bell Coleman, or open air, cycle the standard for aircraft air conditioning, where weight and safety outweigh efficiency. For ground based food refrigeration, vapour compression systems are far more efficient and have displaced it. Bell Coleman uses air as refrigerant with an expander, not a throttle valve, doing work and cooling the air, giving low COP but the main use is aircraft air conditioning, not food cold stores. Section thirteen sixteen discusses using a vapour, instead of air, as refrigerant, transforming refrigeration because a vapour absorbs and rejects large amounts of latent heat at constant temperature, giving high COP from a compact machine. The ideal would be a reversed Carnot cycle run with a wet vapour, but it has two practical limitations that the actual vapour compression cycle must correct, wet compression harming the compressor through slugging and wear, and isentropic expansion in an expander being costly and impractical for the small liquid work involved.
393: This page confirms the two fixes turning the reversed Carnot vapour cycle into the real vapour compression cycle, dry compression instead of wet, keeping liquid out of the compressor, and a simple throttle valve instead of an expander, cheap and reliable even though throttling is irreversible. Every domestic fridge, milk chiller, ice plant and cold store an AO inspects is a vapour compression machine using dry compression and a throttle or capillary valve. Section thirteen seventeen covers the vapour compression cycle, the pressure enthalpy, or p h, diagram, superheating and subcooling. The cycle has four components in a loop, the evaporator where liquid refrigerant boils, absorbing heat from the cold space, the refrigerating effect, the compressor which compresses low pressure vapour to high pressure, raising its temperature and consuming work, the condenser where high pressure vapour rejects heat to the surroundings and condenses to liquid, and the expansion or throttle valve which drops the liquid to low pressure, partly flashing and cooling it before it re enters the evaporator. The cycle is best drawn on the pressure enthalpy diagram, where the four processes form a simple loop and enthalpy differences directly give the refrigerating effect and the work.
394: Continuing on vapour compression cycle enhancements, two improvements matter. Superheating the suction vapour, heating it a little above saturation temperature before compression, guarantees no liquid enters the compressor and slightly raises the refrigerating effect. Subcooling the liquid leaving the condenser, cooling it below condensing temperature, increases the refrigerating effect for the same compressor work, improving COP. A liquid vapour, or regenerative, heat exchanger achieves both at once, letting cold suction vapour subcool the warm condenser liquid while the vapour is superheated in the same device. The actual vapour compression cycle differs from the ideal due to pressure drops in pipes and valves, heat gains and losses, and non isentropic, inefficient, compression. Subcooling clearly improves COP at the same work, while superheating mainly protects the compressor and raises refrigerating effect, though it also raises compressor work, so its net COP gain depends on the refrigerant. Field service engineers tune the expansion valve so suction vapour is slightly superheated and the liquid line is subcooled for more cooling per rupee of power. Section thirteen eighteen introduces the vapour absorption refrigeration system, which replaces the energy hungry compressor with a heat driven absorber generator unit, running mainly on heat such as steam, gas flame, solar or waste heat, plus a tiny pump power. In the ammonia water system, ammonia is refrigerant and water the absorber.
395: This page details absorption system essentials. Working pairs are ammonia water, with ammonia as refrigerant and water as absorbent, and lithium bromide water, with water as refrigerant and lithium bromide as absorbent. Energy input is mainly heat, steam, gas, solar or waste heat, plus small pump work, replacing the compressor with an absorber, pump and generator. Key components are evaporator, absorber, pump, generator, condenser, and sometimes an analyser and rectifier. The lithium bromide water system cannot cool below zero degrees Celsius since water is the refrigerant, limiting it to air conditioning duty. Maximum COP of a heat operated machine is set by an ideal three temperature arrangement, the product of a Carnot engine efficiency between heat source and surroundings, and a Carnot refrigerator COP between surroundings and cold space, and in practice absorption COP is well below compression systems, chosen not for efficiency but because it uses heat instead of expensive shaft power. Ammonia water can reach sub zero temperatures, suiting cold storage and ice making, but needs an analyser and rectifier to keep water vapour out of the ammonia. Absorption chillers driven by sugar mill or biomass waste heat fit Karnataka's agro industries well. Section thirteen nineteen begins refrigerant classification, nomenclature and azeotropes, covering desirable properties of a good refrigerant, thermodynamic, physical, chemical, safety and economic.
396: This page classifies refrigerants. Halocarbons, CFC, HCFC, HFC, include R twelve and R twenty two and R one thirty four A, numbered by a scheme where digits give carbon atoms minus one, hydrogen atoms plus one, and fluorine atoms. Inorganic refrigerants include ammonia, R seven seventeen, water, R seven eighteen, and carbon dioxide, R seven forty four, in the seven hundred series with molecular weight added. Hydrocarbons like propane, R two ninety, and isobutane, R six hundred A, are natural but flammable. Azeotropes, the R five hundred series, are mixtures that boil at constant composition like a single fluid, for example R five oh two. Zeotropes, or blends, the R four hundred series, change composition on boiling, showing temperature glide. Chlorofluorocarbons such as R twelve are banned under the Montreal Protocol for damaging the ozone layer, while hydrofluorocarbons that replaced them are potent greenhouse gases being phased down under the Kigali Amendment, so natural refrigerants, ammonia, carbon dioxide and hydrocarbons, are returning to favour. Most Karnataka cold stores and ice plants run on ammonia, R seven seventeen, a cheap, efficient natural refrigerant, which is why ammonia leak safety training matters at every plant. Section thirteen twenty covers ice manufacture, principles, systems and quality, made by removing heat from water using a refrigeration plant, usually ammonia vapour compression, in the can, or block, ice system using galvanised steel cans in circulating brine.
397: This page details ice making essentials. The primary refrigerant is ammonia, with brine, a sodium chloride or calcium chloride solution, as secondary coolant. Block, or can, ice is water in cans frozen in a brine tank, slow, clear and easy to store and transport. Water treatment includes softening, filtration and sometimes distillation for clear, hard ice. Air agitation bubbles air through the freezing can water to expel dissolved gas and impurities. Core sucking removes the last unfrozen, impurity rich core and refills it for clear ice. Other ice types, flake, tube, plate and slice ice, are made continuously on cold surfaces. Good ice quality means clear, hard, free of air bubbles and impurities, from treated water. Dissolved minerals and gases make ice cloudy, brittle and quick melting, so air agitation drives off dissolved gases and pushes impurities toward the still liquid core, which is sucked out and replaced with fresh water. Brine, chilled by the ammonia evaporator, circulates around the cans, letting one central plant freeze many cans uniformly. Ice is the backbone of Karnataka's coastal fisheries cold chain in places like Mangaluru, Malpe and Karwar, and of fish and meat markets inland. Section thirteen twenty one covers food freezing, Plank's equation and freezing systems, preserving food by lowering temperature below freezing so water turns to ice, stopping microbial growth and slowing enzyme reactions, with storage at minus eighteen degrees Celsius or below.
398: This page covers freezing time and freezing systems in detail. Plank's equation estimates freezing time from latent heat, density, surface and internal resistance, with two resistance terms, a surface term and an internal conduction term, using shape factors P and R for slab, cylinder or sphere. Freezing time rises with larger size, lower surface heat transfer coefficient, higher freezing point load, and warmer medium. Air blast freezing uses cold fast moving air over food in tunnels or fluidised beds. Plate, or contact, freezing presses food between refrigerated plates for fast freezing of regular shapes. Immersion, or direct contact, freezing dips food in cold brine or sprays it with a cryogen like liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide. Individually quick frozen, IQF, products are loose pieces frozen separately by fluidised bed air blast. Quick freezing gives small ice crystals and better texture, while slow freezing gives large crystals that rupture cells and cause drip loss on thawing. Thawing is actually slower than freezing of the same product, because thawed surface water conducts heat far less well than ice and insulates the still frozen core, which is why careless thawing causes drip and microbial risk. IQF lines for green peas, sweet corn, prawns and mango cubes operate in Karnataka's frozen food and seafood units.
399: This page covers frozen storage, freeze concentration and freeze drying. Even in continuous cold storage at minus eighteen degrees Celsius or below, slow quality changes occur, moisture migrates and sublimes causing freezer burn, dry discoloured patches, ice crystals grow during temperature fluctuations called recrystallisation, fats oxidise, and colour and texture slowly deteriorate, so fluctuating storage temperature is the chief enemy of frozen quality. Freeze concentration partly freezes a liquid so nearly pure ice crystals form and are separated, concentrating the rest, preserving aroma, colour and heat sensitive nutrients far better than evaporation, used for premium fruit juices, coffee extract and milk. Freeze drying, or lyophilisation, first freezes the food solid, then removes the ice by sublimation under high vacuum, solid turning directly to vapour without melting, leaving a dry, porous, lightweight product. It proceeds in three stages, freezing, primary drying by sublimation of free ice, and secondary drying to remove bound moisture, needing heat input for sublimation and a vacuum and condenser system, making it slow and expensive, reserved for high value products like instant coffee, soups, biologicals and tender coconut powder. CFTRI and DFRL at Mysuru pioneered freeze drying in India for instant coffee, soups and defence rations. Section thirteen twenty three begins cold storage design, insulation and construction.
400: This page details cold store design elements. A cold store is an insulated, refrigerated building holding perishable produce at controlled low temperature and humidity, with design depending on produce type, since potatoes, onions, apples, fruit, vegetables, meat, fish and flowers each need particular temperature and relative humidity, and some need controlled or modified atmosphere conditions adjusting oxygen and carbon dioxide to slow respiration. Insulation, using polyurethane foam, expanded polystyrene or cork, minimises heat gain, with higher R value giving lower running cost. A vapour barrier must be placed on the warm, outer, side of insulation, since warm air holds more moisture that would otherwise seep in and condense or freeze within the insulation. The floor needs insulation and sometimes gentle heating to prevent ground freezing and heaving, called frost heave, beneath a freezer store. A compact shape reduces surface area and heat gain, doors and air curtains limit air exchange, and modern automated cold stores use mechanised racking for high storage density and low labour. The refrigeration plant is sized in tons of refrigeration from the peak cooling load. Karnataka's cold store network, backed by NHB, NHM and APMC, serves potato, onion, apple, grape, pomegranate and flowers, with controlled atmosphere stores for apples in cooler belts. Section thirteen twenty four begins refrigerated transport and the cold chain.
401: This page introduces the cold chain from farm to consumer. Refrigeration is useless if the cold breaks during transport, so refrigerated transport and the cold chain carry low temperature from farm to consumer through an unbroken sequence, pre cooling at the farm, cold storage, refrigerated vehicles such as reefer vans, insulated trucks, rail and containers, cold rooms at markets, and refrigerated display at retail, keeping produce within its safe temperature band at every step. A break of even a few hours can spoil produce or restart microbial growth, so monitoring and handling discipline are as important as the equipment. Pre cooling rapidly removes field heat right after harvest using forced air, hydro, or vacuum cooling, and is the crucial first link since produce loaded warm into a reefer van overwhelms its refrigeration and arrives spoiled. Refrigerated vehicles are insulated trucks, vans, rail wagons or sea containers each carrying their own refrigeration unit. Refrigerated display cabinets are the final chilled link at the retailer. End to end temperature monitoring with data loggers proves the chain held, and disciplined handling, hygiene, fast loading, minimal door open time, protects it. Because the chain is only as strong as its weakest link, a single warm gap can undo all the upstream cooling.
402: This page emphasises that the cold chain removes field heat right after harvest as the make or break first link, and is only as strong as its weakest link, since one warm gap restarts spoilage. Reducing India's huge post harvest losses is a core AO mission, and the cold chain is the lever, with an AO promoting pre cooling units, reefer vans and pack houses for Karnataka's mango, grape, pomegranate, flower and vegetable exporters building exactly this farm to fork cold chain. Section thirteen twenty five begins air conditioning, comfort, classification and sensible heat factor. Air conditioning is simultaneous control of temperature, humidity, air movement and cleanliness of air in an enclosed space, for human comfort or an industrial process. Comfort air conditioning aims at conditions where people feel comfortable, depending on dry bulb temperature, relative humidity, air movement and the body's heat and moisture balance, while industrial, or process, air conditioning controls air for a product or process like textiles, printing, pharmaceuticals or food storage rather than for people. Summer air conditioning cools and dehumidifies air, winter air conditioning heats and humidifies it, and year round systems do both, switching with season. Unitary systems, like window and split units, serve a single space, while central systems condition air at one plant and distribute it by ducts to many spaces. The sensible heat factor, SHF, is sensible heat load divided by total, sensible plus latent, heat load.
403: This page confirms unitary systems are self contained, window or split units, while central systems use one plant plus ducts. Controlled atmosphere stores, mushroom houses, seed stores and food processing clean rooms in Karnataka are industrial air conditioning, where humidity control matters as much as temperature. Section thirteen twenty six begins cooling load calculations and load sources. Sizing any refrigeration or air conditioning plant means estimating the cooling load, the total rate of heat that must be removed to hold the space at its design temperature, and adding the sources together. For a cold store, the load is dominated by the produce itself, the field heat removed to pull produce down to storage temperature, called the product cooling load, and for living produce like fruit and vegetables, the continuing heat of respiration given off throughout storage. Added to these are heat conducted in through walls, floor and roof, heat brought in by warm infiltrating and ventilation air, and internal heat from people, lights, fans, motors and forklifts. The product cooling load is the sensible heat removed to bring produce from arrival temperature down to storage temperature, calculated from mass, specific heat and temperature drop, plus latent heat of fusion if freezing is involved. The heat of respiration is unique to living produce, a load that a frozen meat store does not carry. The plant must be sized for the peak load, the largest simultaneous sum, usually with a safety margin.
404: This final page on the topic gives a worked example, a mango cold store receiving twenty tonnes of fruit at thirty two degrees Celsius to be held at thirteen degrees Celsius. The product cooling load is mass times the specific heat of mango, about three point seven kilojoules per kilogram per degree Celsius, times the nineteen degree drop, all removed within the desired pull down time. On top of this comes the mango's heat of respiration, the heat conducted through the insulated walls, the infiltration through doors, and the internal heat from lights and forklifts. Summing these and sizing for the peak gives the tons of refrigeration the plant must provide. To remember, cooling load equals product cooling, field heat, plus heat of respiration for living produce only, plus conducted heat through walls, plus convected or infiltration heat from warm air coming in, plus internal heat from people, lights and motors, plus any freezing latent load, and the plant must be sized for the peak, simultaneous maximum, load. Heat of respiration is the load that fruit and vegetable stores have but meat stores do not. When an AO appraises a mango or grape cold store proposal, the heat of respiration and the field heat, product, load are the items most often underestimated, leading to undersized plants that never reach temperature. Knowing every load source lets an AO sanity check the tonnage and reject a plant that will fail in the field.
405: On this page we have a chapter mind map for Food Process Engineering, tying together eight sub-topics around one central idea. Branch one, thermodynamic laws, covers the zeroth law defining thermal equilibrium, the first law Q equals dU plus W meaning energy is conserved, the second law saying heat will not flow from cold to hot by itself, entropy dS equals dQ over T which never decreases in an isolated system, enthalpy H equals U plus pV, and Cp minus Cv equals R with gamma, the ratio Cp over Cv, about 1.4 for air. Branch two, power cycles, gives Carnot efficiency as 1 minus Tlow over Thigh, the maximum possible, the Otto cycle for petrol engines at constant volume, Diesel cycle at constant pressure, Brayton cycle for gas turbines at constant pressure, and Rankine cycle for steam power plants. Branch three covers steam and pure substances, including the triple point of water at 0.01 degrees Celsius and 0.6113 kilopascals, the critical point at 374.15 degrees Celsius and 221.2 bar, latent heat of water as 2257 kilojoules per kilogram at 100 degrees, dryness fraction, and the Gibbs phase rule F equals C minus P plus 2. The remaining branches, which we will explore next, cover psychrometry, refrigeration, refrigerants, freezing, and the cold chain.
406: Now, students, this page gives you a key terms table, a quick memorization list of the most frequently asked facts in this chapter. The zeroth law establishes temperature by saying two bodies in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. The first law for a closed system is Q equals dU plus W, meaning energy is conserved and no perpetual motion machine exists. Enthalpy is H equals U plus pV. Cp minus Cv equals R, with gamma about 1.4 for air, and Cp is always greater than Cv. The Kelvin-Planck statement says no engine converts all heat from one reservoir into work, while the Clausius statement says heat will not flow cold to hot by itself without work input. Entropy change is dS equals dQ over T for reversible processes, and it never decreases in an isolated system. The Gibbs phase rule is F equals C minus P plus 2, giving zero degrees of freedom at water's triple point. Water's triple point is 0.01 degrees Celsius and 0.6113 kilopascals, and its critical point is 374.15 degrees Celsius and 221.2 bar. Dryness fraction x equals 0 for saturated water and 1 for dry saturated steam. Carnot efficiency is 1 minus Tlow over Thigh in Kelvin, the maximum for any engine. Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles add heat at constant volume, constant pressure, and constant pressure steady flow respectively. The psychrometric order is dew point temperature less than or equal to wet-bulb temperature less than or equal to dry-bulb temperature. One ton of refrigeration equals 3.5 kilowatts, 3024 kilocalories per hour, or 12000 British thermal units per hour. And the Bell-Coleman cycle is the reversed Brayton or Joule cycle using air as refrigerant.
407: Here, we continue the key terms table with more must-know facts. Subcooling raises the coefficient of performance at the same compressor work, while superheating mainly protects the compressor by ensuring dry vapour enters it. In absorption refrigeration, the ammonia-water pair uses ammonia as refrigerant and can go below zero degrees, while the lithium bromide-water pair uses water as refrigerant and works only above zero degrees Celsius. Refrigerant numbers to remember are R-12, a banned chlorofluorocarbon, R-22, R-134a, ammonia as R-717, carbon dioxide as R-744, and water as R-718. An azeotrope, like the R-500 series, boils at constant composition like a pure fluid, while a zeotrope, like R-400, has a temperature glide. Plank's equation calculates freezing time using latent heat, a surface term, and a conduction term. Quick freezing produces small ice crystals with low drip loss, while slow freezing produces large crystals and cell damage, and frozen storage is kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius. Freeze drying removes ice by sublimation under vacuum, giving the best quality but being slow and costly. In cold store construction, the vapour barrier must be placed on the warm side of the insulation. The cold chain runs from pre-cooling to cold store to reefer transport to display, and is only as strong as its weakest link. The sensible heat factor is sensible load divided by sensible plus latent load, and cooling load sources include product heat, respiration heat, conduction, infiltration and internal loads, with the plant sized for the peak. After this table, Part B begins, a bank of objective questions covering every topic in the chapter, starting with question one on the Zeroth Law being the basis of measuring temperature, and question two confirming the first law for a closed system is Q equals dU plus W.
408: Let us understand these objective questions and answers one by one. Question three asks the relation between specific heats of a perfect gas, and the answer is Cp minus Cv equals R, with Cp always greater than Cv because constant-pressure heating also does expansion work. Question four identifies the Kelvin-Planck statement as concerning a heat engine, since no engine can convert all heat from a single reservoir into work, while the equivalent Clausius statement concerns refrigerators. Question five gives the entropy change for a reversible process as dS equals dQ over T. Question six confirms the Gibbs phase rule is F equals C minus P plus 2, and for water at its triple point this gives F equals zero, since one component minus three phases plus two equals zero. Question seven establishes that dry saturated steam has a dryness fraction of exactly 1, since all liquid has evaporated. Question eight gives the enthalpy of one kilogram of wet steam with dryness fraction x as h equals hf plus x times hfg, sensible heat plus the fraction of latent heat supplied. Question nine states that Carnot engine efficiency depends only on the two absolute temperatures, the source and sink, and is famously independent of the working fluid.
