The bacteriophage lambda can carry inserts of about 15 to 23 kilobases, a cosmid, which is a plasmid combined with a phage cos site, carries about 35 to 45 kilobases, and BAC and YAC artificial chromosomes carry very large inserts from 100 kilobases to over 1 megabase, used in genome projects. For plants, the most important vector is the Ti, or tumour inducing, plasmid of the soil bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. In nature this plasmid transfers a piece of its DNA, the T-DNA, into the plant genome, causing crown gall tumours. Genetic engineers disarm the plasmid by removing the tumour genes and insert the gene of interest into the T-DNA, turning Agrobacterium into nature's own plant genetic engineer, making the Ti plasmid the workhorse of dicot transformation. Most genetically engineered crops are made using this Agrobacterium mediated transformation. Now, restriction endonucleases are the molecular scissors of genetic engineering, bacterial enzymes that recognise a specific short DNA sequence, usually a 4 to 8 base pair palindrome, and cut the DNA there, acting as the bacterium's natural defence against phage DNA. The first to be characterised, EcoRI, from Escherichia coli, recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts to leave single stranded sticky, or cohesive, ends, while other enzymes leave blunt ends. Sticky ends are valuable because the same enzyme leaves complementary overhangs on both the gene and the vector, so they pair up and can be joined. Other enzymes include DNA ligase which joins fragments, DNA polymerase which synthesises new strands, reverse transcriptase which makes DNA from RNA, and alkaline phosphatase which prevents self ligation.
463: On this page we finish the enzyme toolkit and begin gene cloning. Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, is heat stable and is used in PCR. DNA ligase seals the gene into the vector, acting as molecular glue. DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA, and heat stable Taq polymerase makes PCR possible. Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA, or cDNA, from messenger RNA, essential for cloning eukaryotic genes without introns. Alkaline phosphatase, exonucleases, kinases and methylases each carry out a specific modification. Restriction enzymes are named for the bacterium they come from, written in italics with a roman numeral, such as EcoRI, HindIII and BamHI, a detail examiners often test. Restriction enzymes are also the basis of RFLP markers and DNA fingerprinting used to certify crop variety identity and purity in Karnataka's seed certification system. Now, gene cloning means making many identical copies of a gene. After the recombinant DNA is built, it is introduced into a host cell, usually the bacterium Escherichia coli, or yeast, or a plant or animal cell, by transformation, often after making the cells competent with calcium chloride and a heat shock, or by electroporation. The host then multiplies, copying the foreign gene along with its own DNA, so a single recombinant molecule becomes millions of copies. The challenge is identifying the few cells that actually took up the recombinant DNA, done using selectable markers and screening, for example antibiotic resistance, or blue white selection using the lacZ gene, where recombinant colonies appear white and non recombinant ones appear blue. This gene cloning principle powers mass production of the Bt gene and recombinant Rhizobium and bio pesticide strains.
464: Now, students, we look at genomics, proteomics and DNA sequencing. Genomics is the study of the entire genome, the complete set of an organism's DNA, including its sequence, structure and function. Structural genomics maps and sequences the genome, while functional genomics studies what the genes do. Proteomics is the large scale study of the proteome, the entire set of proteins an organism makes, and transcriptomics is the study of all RNA transcripts. Reading the genome depends on DNA sequencing, the classic method being Sanger sequencing, also called the chain termination or dideoxy method, developed in 1977, which uses dideoxynucleotides to stop the growing DNA chain at known bases. Modern next generation sequencing, or NGS, reads millions of fragments at once, massively parallel, fast and cheap, and has made whole genome projects routine. Genomics underpins modern crop improvement, once a crop genome is sequenced, breeders can locate genes and markers for yield, quality, drought tolerance and disease resistance, and select for them directly. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, was the landmark achievement, and rice was the first crop genome sequenced, in 2002. Proteomics and metabolomics extend the picture to proteins and metabolites, and these omics sciences feed bioinformatics, which stores and analyses the vast data they produce. Genomics led breeding is shortening the time to release improved varieties of Karnataka's key crops, ragi and other millets, pigeonpea, sugarcane and rice, work done at UAS Dharwad, UAS Bangalore and national genomics centres. Then we begin molecular markers, DNA pieces used as signposts to track genes, identify varieties and map genomes, of two families, hybridization based like RFLP, and PCR based like RAPD, AFLP, SSR and SNP, the backbone of marker assisted selection.
465: On this page, we continue the table of DNA markers, finishing with SNP, the single nucleotide polymorphism, which is a single base change and today the most abundant marker type used. Let us understand how the markers compare. RFLP was the very first DNA marker, and it works by cutting DNA with restriction enzymes and detecting fragment size differences after hybridization with a probe. RAPD uses random short primers in PCR and is quick, but less reproducible. AFLP combines restriction digestion with selective PCR to give many reliable bands. SSRs, also called microsatellites, are short repeated sequences, co-dominant and highly polymorphic, making them the marker of choice for variety identification and genetic mapping. SNPs are now the most used markers in high-throughput genotyping. All of these markers support marker-assisted selection, letting a plant breeder pick out a plant carrying a desired gene just by testing for the marker, without waiting to see the trait itself, which greatly speeds up developing resistant and quality varieties. Remember, sort these by basis, RFLP is hybridization-based, the rest are PCR-based, SSR is co-dominant and most informative, SNP is most abundant. Then we move to section 15.19, genetic transformation and transgenic organisms. Genetic transformation means introducing foreign DNA into a cell so it becomes stably integrated and expressed, and an organism carrying such a gene is called transgenic, or genetically modified. In plants this is delivered mainly by two methods, the natural Agrobacterium tumefaciens system using its Ti plasmid, which works best for dicots, and the direct biolistic gene gun method, which fires DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles into cells, used mainly for cereals and other monocots.
466: Now, students, we look at landmark transgenic crops that examiners love to ask about. Bt cotton uses the Cry gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis to give resistance against the bollworm insect, and it was India's first genetically modified crop, released in 2002. Bt brinjal uses the Cry1Ac gene for resistance against fruit and shoot borer, and though it has been approved, it remains under a moratorium in India and has not been commercially released. Golden Rice is engineered to produce beta-carotene, which is provitamin A, to fight vitamin A deficiency, using genes from daffodil and maize along with bacterial genes. The Flavr Savr tomato, developed in 1994 in the USA, was the world's first commercial genetically modified food, engineered for delayed ripening using an antisense gene. Herbicide-tolerant crops, like Roundup Ready soybean and maize, carry glyphosate tolerance genes such as EPSPS. Transgenic technology raises pest resistance, herbicide tolerance, stress tolerance and nutritional quality, but it also raises debate over biosafety, environmental effects and farmer dependence, which is exactly why it is tightly regulated. Remember, Agrobacterium with its Ti plasmid works for dicots, while the gene gun or biolistics method works for monocots like cereals. Bt cotton is India's first GM crop from 2002, Golden Rice targets vitamin A, and Flavr Savr tomato is the first GM food from 1994. Here, we move to section 15.20, bioinformatics, which is the application of computers, statistics and information technology to store, retrieve and analyse biological data, especially the huge sequences of DNA, RNA and protein generated by genomics and proteomics work. The major public databases students should know are GenBank from NCBI in the USA, EMBL in Europe, and DDBJ in Japan for sequences, plus the Protein Data Bank, or PDB, for protein structures, and BLAST is the standard tool for comparing a sequence against a database. Then in section 15.21, we begin biosafety guidelines, the set of measures ensuring genetically modified organisms are safe for human health and the environment, regulated in India under the Environment Protection Act of 1986.
467: On this page, we complete the picture of India's biosafety regulatory bodies through a tiered system of committees. At the base is the Institutional Biosafety Committee, or IBSC, which oversees rDNA work at each institution. Above it sits the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation, or RCGM, under the Department of Biotechnology, which monitors ongoing research. At the very top is the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, or GEAC, under the Ministry of Environment, which gives the final approval for environmental release and commercial cultivation of genetically modified crops. Laboratory biosafety itself is graded into containment levels from BSL-1 to BSL-4 depending on the risk posed by the organisms being handled. Internationally, the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, from the year 2000, governs the trans-boundary movement of living modified organisms between countries. Biosafety review covers food safety, meaning allergenicity and toxicity testing, environmental safety, meaning gene flow to wild relatives and effects on non-target organisms, and also ethical concerns. It was on GEAC's advice, followed by a government moratorium, that Bt brinjal was held back from commercial release in India. Remember the three Indian tiers from bottom to top, IBSC at the institution, RCGM under the Department of Biotechnology, and GEAC at the apex under the Ministry of Environment giving final approval. Now, students, we begin an entirely new block, Block G, on molecular biology, covering the central dogma, nucleic acids, replication and transcription. Section 15.22 opens with the history of molecular biology and the central dogma. Molecular biology studies life at the molecular level of genetic information. Its landmark discoveries include Griffith's transforming principle from 1928, the Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment of 1944 proving DNA is the genetic material, the Hershey-Chase phage experiment of 1952, and above all, the Watson and Crick double helix model of DNA from 1953. The central dogma, stated by Francis Crick, describes the one-way flow of genetic information, DNA is copied into DNA through replication, DNA is transcribed into RNA through transcription, and RNA is translated into protein through translation, with reverse transcription by retroviruses being the recognised exception.
468: Let us understand the central dogma table in full. Replication copies DNA into DNA, and this happens before cell division. Transcription copies DNA into RNA, producing messenger RNA, transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA. Translation converts RNA into protein, as the ribosome reads messenger RNA into amino acids. Reverse transcription is the exception, converting RNA into DNA, used by retroviruses through the enzyme reverse transcriptase, and this reverse step is also the basis of making complementary DNA, or cDNA, used for cloning genes from eukaryotes. Watson and Crick, along with Wilkins, won the Nobel Prize in 1962, and Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction data were crucial evidence behind their model. These names, dates and the direction of information flow are dependable one-mark exam questions. Remember the central dogma sequence attributed to Crick, DNA to DNA by replication, DNA to RNA by transcription, RNA to protein by translation, with reverse transcription as the RNA to DNA exception carried out by retroviruses. DNA structure itself was solved by Watson and Crick in 1953, aided by Franklin's X-ray data, and DNA being the genetic material was proven earlier by Avery in 1944 and confirmed by Hershey and Chase in 1952. Now, students, we move to section 15.23, the structure of DNA and RNA and gene structure. DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, is a double helix of two antiparallel strands, each a chain of nucleotides made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogen base. The bases are the purines adenine and guanine, and the pyrimidines cytosine and thymine, held together by hydrogen-bonded base pairs, adenine with thymine through two bonds, and guanine with cytosine through three bonds, which is the basis of complementarity. This gives Chargaff's rule, where the amount of adenine equals thymine, and guanine equals cytosine. The helix itself is right-handed, in the B-form, with about ten base pairs per turn. RNA differs in three ways, it is usually single-stranded, it uses ribose sugar instead of deoxyribose, and it uses uracil in place of thymine.
469: On this page, we complete the DNA versus RNA comparison, then move into DNA structure and gene organisation in eukaryotes. In eukaryotes, a gene has coding stretches called exons interrupted by non-coding stretches called introns, which are spliced out of the transcript, plus regulatory regions such as a promoter, where transcription begins, and terminator and enhancer sequences. Prokaryotic genes generally lack introns altogether. Remember the classic DNA versus RNA traps, DNA has deoxyribose sugar and thymine and is double stranded, while RNA has ribose sugar and uracil and is single stranded. In base pairing, adenine pairs with thymine in DNA, or with uracil in RNA, through two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, meaning DNA rich in guanine and cytosine is more stable. By Chargaff's rule, adenine equals thymine, and guanine equals cytosine. Exons are the coding regions that are kept in the final message, while introns are non-coding and are spliced out. Now, students, section 15.24 introduces DNA replication, the copying of DNA before a cell divides. Replication is semi-conservative, meaning each old strand acts as a template for a new one, so every daughter molecule ends up with one old strand and one new strand. This was elegantly proved by the Meselson-Stahl experiment in 1958 using heavy-nitrogen labelling. Replication begins at an origin point, the two strands are unwound by the enzyme helicase, and DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides only in the five prime to three prime direction, starting from an RNA primer laid down by the enzyme primase. Because the two DNA strands run antiparallel to each other, one strand, called the leading strand, is made continuously, while the other, called the lagging strand, is made in short pieces known as Okazaki fragments, which are later joined together by the enzyme DNA ligase.
470: Here, we finish the replication topic and open transcription and the genetic code. Let us understand the key players in replication together. Helicase unwinds the double helix at the replication fork. Primase lays down the short RNA primer needed to start synthesis. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the five prime to three prime direction and also proofreads its work as it goes, which makes replication highly accurate. The leading strand is made continuously, while the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, and DNA ligase joins those fragments together. Because replication is semi-conservative, each daughter DNA molecule consists of one old strand plus one new strand, as proven by Meselson and Stahl in 1958. Replication is also fast and bidirectional, starting from each origin point, and it is the defining molecular event of the S phase of the cell cycle. Now, students, section 15.25 covers transcription, the synthesis of RNA from a DNA template, which is the very first step of gene expression. The enzyme RNA polymerase binds at the promoter, unwinds the DNA, and reads the template strand in the three prime to five prime direction, while building the new RNA strand in the five prime to three prime direction using the bases adenine, uracil, guanine and cytosine, and notably, no primer is needed for this process. Only one of the two DNA strands is copied, and the resulting RNA sequence matches the coding, or sense, strand except that uracil replaces thymine. Transcription proceeds through three stages, initiation at the promoter, elongation, and termination. Prokaryotes have just one type of RNA polymerase, while eukaryotes have three, called Pol I, Pol II and Pol III, with Pol II being the one responsible for making messenger RNA.
471: On this page, we learn how eukaryotic messenger RNA is processed before it can be used, and then we begin the genetic code and translation. In eukaryotes, the primary transcript, called pre-messenger RNA, is processed before it leaves the nucleus. A five prime cap and a three prime poly-A tail are added for stability, and the introns are removed through splicing, so that only the exons remain in the mature messenger RNA. Prokaryotes, lacking a nucleus, transcribe and translate at the same time and do very little processing of their RNA. This distinction, capping, tailing and splicing occurring only in eukaryotes, alongside the coupled transcription and translation of prokaryotes, is a very common comparison question in exams. Remember that transcription converts DNA into RNA using RNA polymerase, needs no primer, reads the template in the three prime to five prime direction, builds RNA in the five prime to three prime direction, and uses uracil instead of thymine. Eukaryotic messenger RNA processing means a five prime cap, a poly-A tail, and splicing to remove introns, while prokaryotes have just one RNA polymerase and couple transcription with translation directly. Now, students, we move to an entirely new block, Block H, covering translation, the genetic code, gene regulation, genomes and nucleotides. Section 15.26 introduces the genetic code and translation. Translation is the synthesis of protein from the messenger RNA message, carried out by the ribosome. The message is read in groups of three bases called codons, and the rules matching codons to amino acids form the genetic code. There are 64 possible codons in total, of which 61 specify amino acids and three are stop codons. The code is described as a triplet code, it is non-overlapping, it has no gaps between codons, it is nearly universal across all life, and it is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. The start codon is AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine, and the three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. Transfer RNA brings each amino acid to the ribosome, matching its own anticodon to the codon on the messenger RNA.
472: Let us understand how translation actually proceeds and why the universality of the genetic code matters so much. Translation happens in three stages, initiation, where the ribosome assembles at the start codon, elongation, where transfer RNAs add amino acids one by one as the ribosome moves along, forming peptide bonds, and termination, at a stop codon, which releases the finished protein chain. Prokaryotes use 70S ribosomes and begin protein synthesis with a modified methionine called formyl-methionine, while eukaryotes use 80S ribosomes, begin with ordinary methionine, and only translate after the messenger RNA has left the nucleus. The near-universality of the genetic code is precisely what allows a bacterial gene, such as the Bt gene, to be read correctly inside a plant cell, and this is the foundation of all genetic engineering. Remember the key numbers, 64 codons in total, made up of 61 that code for amino acids plus 3 stop codons, UAA, UAG and UGA. The start codon is AUG, which also codes for methionine. The code is degenerate, meaning many codons per amino acid, but it is never ambiguous. It is universal, meaning nearly all life uses the same code, which is exactly why a bacterial gene can work inside a plant. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, while eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S. Now, students, section 15.27 covers the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes. A genome is the complete genetic content of a cell. The prokaryotic genome is a single, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule lying free in a region called the nucleoid, with very little associated protein, usually just one chromosome plus small extra pieces of DNA called plasmids, and very few non-coding sequences. The eukaryotic genome, by contrast, is much larger, divided into several linear chromosomes housed inside a nucleus, packaged together with histone proteins into a material called chromatin, and it is rich in non-coding DNA, introns and repetitive sequences.
473: On this page, we complete the genome comparison and step into gene regulation. Beyond the main nuclear genome, eukaryotes also carry small organelle genomes, the circular DNA found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts, a relic of their ancient bacterial ancestry. In agriculture, organelle genomes matter greatly, because chloroplast and mitochondrial DNA are usually inherited only from the mother, called maternal or cytoplasmic inheritance, and this is the very basis of cytoplasmic male sterility, a tool used to produce hybrid seed without the need for costly hand-emasculation. Remember that the prokaryotic genome is one circular, naked DNA molecule sitting in the nucleoid, plus plasmids, while the eukaryotic genome consists of several linear chromosomes wrapped in histone proteins as chromatin, plus circular mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA, and this organelle DNA is inherited maternally, which is exactly the basis of cytoplasmic male sterility used for hybrid seed production of crops like sunflower, maize and pigeonpea in Karnataka. Now, students, section 15.28 introduces gene regulation in prokaryotes through the lac and trp operons. Cells switch genes on and off so that proteins are made only when they are actually needed. In bacteria this is achieved through the operon, a cluster of genes controlled together by one shared promoter and operator, a model proposed by Jacob and Monod in 1961 based on the lac operon. The lac operon controls the enzymes needed to break down lactose, and it is an inducible system, meaning it is normally switched off, and is switched on only when lactose, acting as the inducer, is present. Lactose inactivates the repressor protein, freeing the operator so that RNA polymerase can transcribe the genes, and when lactose runs out, the repressor binds again and the genes switch back off.
474: Let us understand the trp operon, which is the mirror image of the lac operon. The trp operon controls the enzymes that build the amino acid tryptophan, and it is a repressible system, meaning it is normally switched on, and is switched off only when tryptophan becomes plentiful. Here, tryptophan itself acts as a co-repressor, activating the repressor protein so it blocks transcription, meaning the cell stops making something it already has enough of. The classic contrast tested in exams is that the lac operon is inducible and catabolic, meaning it breaks lactose down, while the trp operon is repressible and anabolic, meaning it builds tryptophan up. Together these two systems show how a bacterial cell economises by producing enzymes only when they are actually required. Remember, the lac operon is inducible, normally off, and switched on by lactose, while the trp operon is repressible, normally on, and switched off by tryptophan, which acts as a co-repressor. This operon concept was proposed by Jacob and Monod in 1961. Now, students, section 15.29 briefly covers the biosynthesis of purines and pyrimidines and their regulation. Nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA and RNA, are made by cells in two ways, de novo synthesis from simple precursors, and salvage pathways that recycle bases from broken-down nucleic acids. Purines, adenine and guanine, are built up on a ribose-phosphate framework using atoms from amino acids, carbon dioxide and folate-carried one-carbon units, first forming inosine monophosphate and then AMP and GMP. Pyrimidines, cytosine, thymine and uracil, are made differently, with the ring built first as orotate and then attached to ribose-phosphate to give UMP, from which CTP and TMP follow. Both pathways are controlled by feedback inhibition, where the end product switches off its own first enzyme. This is a biochemistry-heavy but low-frequency topic for this particular exam, so it is only summarised rather than detailed here.
475: On this page, we open an entirely new block, Block I, on microbial genetics and the tools of molecular biology. Section 15.30 covers microbial genetics, specifically conjugation, transformation and transduction. Bacteria exchange genes not through sexual reproduction but through three mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer, and the syllabus names all three. Conjugation is the direct transfer of DNA, often a plasmid, from a donor cell to a recipient cell through a tube-like structure called a pilus, essentially bacterial mating, requiring direct cell-to-cell contact, and it was discovered by Lederberg and Tatum in 1946. Transformation is the uptake of naked DNA from the surroundings by a competent cell, the very phenomenon that Griffith first observed back in 1928. Transduction is the transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another carried by a bacteriophage, which is a type of virus, acting as the courier. These mechanisms matter for two important reasons. First, they spread antibiotic-resistance genes, often carried on plasmids, among bacterial populations, which is a serious public-health issue. Second, transformation is exactly the process genetic engineers use to insert recombinant DNA into bacterial hosts, and conjugation, through the Ti plasmid system, underlies Agrobacterium-mediated plant transformation. Remember the three bacterial gene-transfer routes, conjugation happens through a pilus and needs direct contact, discovered by Lederberg and Tatum, transformation is the uptake of naked DNA, as Griffith observed, requiring competent cells, and transduction is carried by a bacteriophage virus. A simple memory hook is that conjugation is like touch, transformation is like swallowing, and transduction is virus delivery. Now, students, section 15.31 introduces the tools in molecular biology, focusing on the role of enzymes. Modern molecular biology rests on a small toolkit of enzymes that act with precision on DNA and RNA, including restriction endonucleases that cut DNA at specific sites, acting like molecular scissors, and DNA ligase, which joins fragments together like glue.
476: Let us continue with the enzyme toolkit before moving into PCR. Besides restriction enzymes and ligase, the toolkit includes DNA polymerases, including the heat-stable Taq polymerase, which synthesise new DNA, reverse transcriptase, which makes complementary DNA from RNA, nucleases that trim DNA or RNA, alkaline phosphatase and polynucleotide kinase, which add or remove terminal phosphate groups, and methylases and topoisomerases, which modify and relax DNA structure. Every genetic-engineering procedure, whether it is cloning, PCR, sequencing or labelling, is really just a particular combination of these enzymes, and they are the reason DNA can be manipulated as readily as it is today. Now, students, section 15.32 introduces the Polymerase Chain Reaction, or PCR, a technique used to make millions of copies of a specific segment of DNA inside a test tube. This DNA amplification method was invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, who won the Nobel Prize for it in 1993. PCR needs a DNA template, two short primers that flank the target region, the four nucleotide building blocks called dNTPs, a heat-stable DNA polymerase called Taq, sourced from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, and a buffer solution containing magnesium. The reaction runs through repeating cycles made of three temperature steps, denaturation at about 94 degrees Celsius, where the strands separate, annealing at about 50 to 60 degrees, where the primers bind, and extension at about 72 degrees, where Taq polymerase builds new strands. Each cycle doubles the amount of DNA, so around 30 cycles can give roughly a billion-fold amplification of the target sequence. PCR is one of the most important inventions in modern biology, with uses spanning disease diagnosis by detecting pathogen DNA, DNA fingerprinting, molecular marker analysis, cloning, and detecting genetically modified material, and the heat-stable Taq polymerase is precisely what allows the reaction to survive being repeatedly heated to 94 degrees.
477: On this page, we finish PCR and begin electrophoresis and marker-detection techniques. Variants of the basic PCR method include reverse-transcription PCR, or RT-PCR, which starts from RNA, and real-time or quantitative PCR, known as qPCR. The three temperature steps of each cycle, their correct order, and Taq polymerase's bacterial source and heat-stable role remain the most frequently tested points on this topic. Remember, PCR means making millions of copies of DNA, a method invented by Kary Mullis in 1983. Each cycle has three steps, denaturation at about 94 degrees where strands split, annealing at about 55 degrees where primers bind, and extension at about 72 degrees where Taq builds new DNA, and every cycle doubles the DNA amount. Taq polymerase comes from Thermus aquaticus, and its heat-stability is exactly why it survives the repeated 94-degree denaturation step, while RT-PCR is the variant that starts from RNA instead of DNA. Now, students, section 15.33 covers gel electrophoresis and marker-detection techniques. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA or protein fragments by size using an electric field. The sample is loaded into a gel, agarose for DNA or polyacrylamide for finer separation and for proteins, and a current is applied. Because DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate backbone, the fragments move towards the positive electrode, called the anode, with smaller fragments travelling faster and farther than larger ones. After staining with ethidium bromide or a safer dye and viewing under ultraviolet light, the fragments appear as bands, which are sized against a known reference ladder. Electrophoresis is the essential visualisation step behind nearly every molecular technique, including checking PCR products, and viewing RFLP and AFLP fragment patterns and overall DNA quality.
478: Let us understand blotting and hybridization techniques, which follow electrophoresis. After fragments are separated on a gel, they can be transferred onto a membrane and identified through hybridization with a labelled probe, a family of methods known as blotting. Southern blotting detects a specific DNA sequence using a labelled DNA probe, Northern blotting detects RNA using a labelled DNA or RNA probe, and Western blotting detects a protein using an antibody as the probe. These techniques underlie the two broad families of molecular markers in the syllabus, hybridization-based markers such as RFLP, which use restriction digestion, blotting and a probe, and PCR-based markers such as RAPD, SSR, AFLP and SNP, which use amplification with primers instead. Electrophoresis remains the common readout that makes all of these techniques visible as bands on a gel. Remember, in electrophoresis, DNA carries a negative charge, so it runs towards the positive electrode, the anode, and smaller fragments always move faster. A simple memory hook for the blotting techniques is 'snow drop', Southern equals DNA, Northern equals RNA, and Western equals protein, since W stands for antibody detection of protein. Molecular markers split neatly into hybridization-based ones like RFLP, and PCR-based ones like RAPD, SSR, AFLP and SNP. Agarose gel is used for DNA, and ethidium bromide stain is viewed under ultraviolet light. Now, students, we begin an entirely new block, Block J, on plant tissue culture, covering totipotency, asepsis and culture media. Section 15.34 introduces plant tissue culture and the concept of totipotency. Plant tissue culture is the growing of plant cells, tissues or organs on a sterile, nutrient-rich medium under controlled conditions, known as in vitro growth.
479: On this page, we learn the foundational vocabulary of tissue culture. Plant tissue culture rests on the concept of totipotency, the ability of a single plant cell to divide and develop into a complete plant, because every plant cell carries the full genome. This idea was predicted by Haberlandt in 1902, who is regarded as the father of plant tissue culture, and it was later proved when whole plants and embryos were successfully regenerated from cultured cells, with F. C. Steward famously raising entire carrot plants starting from single cells. The explant, meaning the piece of plant tissue taken to start a culture, is placed onto a nutrient medium, where it may form an unorganised mass of dividing cells called callus, from which shoots, roots or entire embryos can later be induced. Totipotency is the single most important concept in this whole unit, because it means that even a tiny piece of tissue can be multiplied into thousands of genetically identical plants. The general workflow is to take an explant, sterilise it, culture it on a suitable medium to form callus or directly induce organs, regenerate small plantlets, root them, and then harden or acclimatise them before they are finally planted out in soil. The entire process must remain aseptic throughout, because the rich nutrient medium would otherwise quickly be overrun by contaminating bacteria and fungi. Remember, totipotency means one single plant cell can regenerate a whole plant because it carries the full genome, and this is the founding principle of the whole field of tissue culture. Haberlandt, in 1902, predicted totipotency and is called the father of plant tissue culture, while Steward successfully regenerated whole carrot plants starting from single cells. An explant is simply the starting piece of plant tissue used, and callus is the unorganised mass of dividing cells that often forms first, and everything in this process must be kept strictly aseptic, meaning completely sterile.
480: Now, students, section 15.35 covers aseptic practices and sterilization techniques. Because culture media are rich in sugar and nutrients, the greatest enemy of tissue culture is microbial contamination, so asepsis must be absolute throughout the process. Sterilization is applied at three different levels. The culture medium, glassware and instruments are sterilised by autoclaving, which uses moist heat at 121 degrees Celsius under 15 pounds per square inch of pressure for about 15 to 20 minutes, a process that kills all microbes and even their spores. Heat-sensitive substances, such as certain vitamins and growth regulators, are instead sterilised by passing them through a fine membrane filter with pores of about 0.22 micrometres. The surface of the explant itself is sterilised chemically, by dipping it in agents such as sodium hypochlorite, which is common bleach, mercuric chloride, or ethanol, followed by rinsing in sterile water. All transfers and cutting work are carried out inside a laminar air-flow cabinet, which blows HEPA-filtered sterile air across the work surface to keep airborne contaminants away, and the cabinet is typically wiped with alcohol and often treated with ultraviolet light before use, with instruments flamed between operations. Getting the surface sterilisation of the explant exactly right, strong enough to kill microbes but mild enough to avoid damaging the tissue, is the most common practical challenge in this work. Remember the key autoclave settings to memorise, 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi of pressure, for 15 to 20 minutes, using moist heat that kills even spores. Heat-sensitive additives go through a 0.22 micrometre membrane filter instead of the autoclave. The explant surface is sterilised using sodium hypochlorite, mercuric chloride, or ethanol, and all transfers happen inside a laminar air-flow cabinet with HEPA-filtered air.
481: On this page, we learn about culture media, nutrients and growth regulators, then step into microbial biology's plant equivalent, morphogenesis. The culture medium supplies everything an explant would normally receive from soil and photosynthesis. Its components include inorganic macronutrients, namely nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur, and micronutrients such as iron, manganese, zinc, boron, copper and molybdenum, plus a carbon and energy source, usually sucrose, since cultured tissues photosynthesise very poorly, vitamins, notably thiamine along with nicotinic acid, pyridoxine and myo-inositol, amino acids, a gelling agent called agar for solid medium, and crucially, plant growth regulators. The Murashige and Skoog medium, known as MS medium, developed in 1962, is the most widely used formulation and is well known for its unusually high salt content. Plant growth regulators steer development, and the single most important rule in tissue culture is the ratio between auxin and cytokinin, discovered by Skoog and Miller. A high ratio of auxin to cytokinin induces root formation, a low ratio, meaning high cytokinin, induces shoot formation, and a roughly balanced ratio keeps the tissue growing simply as callus. The chief auxins used are IAA, IBA, NAA and the potent 2,4-D, which is much used to induce callus formation, while the chief cytokinins are kinetin, BAP and zeatin. Remember the exam's favourite rule, the auxin to cytokinin ratio decides organ formation, high auxin produces roots, high cytokinin with low auxin produces shoots, and a balanced ratio produces callus. A helpful memory hook is that cytokinin helps shoots come up. The MS medium was developed by Murashige and Skoog in 1962 and is known for its high salt content, and 2,4-D is a strong auxin used specifically to induce callus formation.
482: Let us understand somaclonal variation, which appears among plants regenerated from tissue culture even though they all descend from a single identical parent. Somaclonal variation is genetic variation that arises among these somaclones due to mutations and chromosomal changes induced during the culturing process itself, and it becomes more common with a prolonged callus phase and with the use of strong growth regulators such as 2,4-D. Although this variation is a nuisance for clonal micropropagation, where the entire goal is producing identical uniform plants, it also serves as a genuinely useful source of new variation for crop improvement, since breeders can screen these somaclones for desirable changes such as disease resistance, stress tolerance, or improved quality, and then select stable new lines from among them. The practical lesson is to keep the callus phase short and avoid harsh growth regulators whenever uniformity is the goal, but to deliberately exploit this same variation when searching for useful new traits. The equivalent term for variation arising specifically from gamete or anther culture is called gametoclonal variation. Remember, somaclonal variation means genetic variation among plants regenerated through tissue culture, caused by culture-induced mutation, and it becomes worse with a longer callus phase and with 2,4-D use. It is a problem for clonal micropropagation because it breaks uniformity, but it is also a genuinely useful source of new variation for plant breeding, and variation coming specifically from gamete or anther culture is called gametoclonal variation. When a tissue-culture nursery reports off-type banana or sugarcane plants unexpectedly appearing, somaclonal variation is usually the underlying cause, and the same phenomenon, when used deliberately, has actually produced improved, disease-tolerant sugarcane lines and other useful new varieties in the past.
483: This page presents the chapter mind map for Plant Biotechnology, organised as a visual diagram rather than running text, so it is best studied on screen rather than read aloud in full. It branches from the central topic into eight groups, cell biology, molecular biology, replication and the genetic code, recombinant DNA tools, gene transfer methods, transgenic crops, PCR, and tissue culture, each with short memory-cue phrases such as the central dogma flowing from DNA to RNA to protein, Watson and Crick's double helix from 1953, EcoRI cutting the sequence GAATTC, Bt cotton being India's first GM crop from 2002, and micropropagation producing clonal plants. Use this map as a quick revision tool to see how all of this unit's topics connect to one another around the shared idea of plant biotechnology.
484: On this page, we open a key terms at a glance table, a rapid-revision list of the facts most likely to be tested directly, since they reward memory rather than reasoning and should be revised until they become automatic. Cell theory is credited to Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow, who established that cells arise only from pre-existing cells, and the endosymbiotic theory, from Lynn Margulis, explains that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from bacteria. Light microscopes resolve down to about 200 nanometres, while electron microscopes resolve to about 0.2 nanometres, a thousand times finer, and while a transmission electron microscope reveals internal detail, a scanning electron microscope reveals surface, three-dimensional detail. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S while eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, though organelles inside eukaryotic cells still carry 70S ribosomes. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, while bacterial walls are peptidoglycan and fungal walls are chitin. The fluid-mosaic model of the cell membrane was proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are called semi-autonomous because they carry their own DNA and their own 70S ribosomes, and plasmodesmata are the plant equivalent of gap junctions linking adjacent cells. The cell cycle proceeds through G1, then S where DNA is synthesised, then G2, then M for mitosis, driven by cyclins and CDKs, and mitosis produces two identical diploid cells while meiosis produces four genetically varied haploid cells. Modern biotechnology is dated to Cohen and Boyer's recombinant DNA work of 1973, and the first recombinant DNA product was human insulin, called Humulin, in 1982. EcoRI is the classic restriction enzyme example, cutting the sequence GAATTC and leaving sticky ends, DNA ligase is the joining enzyme, the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the main plant transformation vector, and the gene gun, or biolistics, is used for monocots and cereals. India's first GM crop was Bt cotton in 2002, carrying the Cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis, while the world's first GM food was the Flavr Savr tomato in 1994. DNA sequencing uses Sanger's chain-termination, or dideoxy, method from 1977, the first DNA marker developed was the hybridization-based RFLP, while SNP is the most abundant marker and SSR is the most informative co-dominant marker. India's apex GM regulator is GEAC under the Ministry of Environment and Forests, supported by RCGM and IBSC, and DNA structure itself was solved by Watson and Crick in 1953, with adenine pairing to thymine through two bonds and guanine pairing to cytosine through three bonds.
485: On this page we have a rapid-revision table for the Plant Biotechnology chapter, listing key facts and values side by side. Chargaff's rule tells us that A equals T and G equals C in a DNA molecule. Replication is semi-conservative, proved by Meselson and Stahl in 1958. The genetic code has 64 codons, with AUG as the start codon and UAA, UAG, UGA as stop codons. Comparing operons, the lac operon is inducible by lactose, while the trp operon is repressible by tryptophan, and this operon model was given by Jacob and Monod in 1961. Gene transfer in bacteria happens by conjugation through a pilus, transformation, or transduction through a phage. PCR was invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, using Taq polymerase, with steps of denature, anneal and extend. In electrophoresis, DNA, being negatively charged, moves to the anode, and smaller fragments move faster. Blots are named by molecule: Southern for DNA, Northern for RNA, Western for protein. Totipotency means one cell can regenerate a whole plant, a concept from Haberlandt in 1902. The most used culture medium is Murashige and Skoog, or MS medium, from 1962, known for its high salt content. A high auxin to cytokinin ratio favours root formation, while high cytokinin favours shoots. Autoclaving sterilises at 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, for 15 to 20 minutes. Meristem culture produces virus-free plants, anther culture produces haploids leading to doubled haploids, and protoplast fusion creates somatic hybrids such as pomato.
486: Continuing the high-yield revision table, we complete the ten most important concepts for this chapter. The rDNA toolkit includes restriction enzymes like EcoRI that cut DNA, DNA ligase that joins fragments, and the Ti plasmid that carries genes into plants. Transgenic crops covered are Bt cotton, India's first genetically modified crop, approved in 2002, carrying the Cry gene, and Golden Rice, engineered for vitamin A. PCR is again highlighted with Mullis in 1983, Taq polymerase, and the three temperature steps of denaturing at 94 degrees, annealing at 55 degrees, and extending at 72 degrees. Totipotency and MS medium are recalled together, showing one cell becoming a whole plant, and the auxin to cytokinin balance controlling roots versus shoots. Culture techniques are summarised as meristem culture giving virus-free plants, anther culture giving haploids, and protoplast fusion giving somatic hybrids. Students, this page reminds you to master these ten points and the commonly confused pairs, such as mitochondrion versus chloroplast, DNA versus RNA, lac versus trp operon, and auxin versus cytokinin, since together they secure a large share of marks in this chapter. Then Part B begins, a bank of objective questions and answers. Question 1 asks who proposed the endosymbiotic theory explaining the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts, and the answer is Lynn Margulis. Question 2 asks what truly measures microscope quality, and the answer is resolving power, not magnification. Question 3 asks which ribosome type is found in prokaryotic cells, and the answer is 70S, which is also found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts.
487: Here we continue with more objective questions and answers on cell biology and plant biotechnology. Question 4 asks who proposed the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane, and the answer is Singer and Nicolson in 1972, not Watson and Crick, who instead gave the DNA double helix. Question 5 asks what mainly makes up a plant cell wall, and the answer is cellulose, along with hemicellulose, pectin and lignin in woody tissue. Question 6 asks which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell, and that is the mitochondrion, the site of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis. Question 7 asks which plant cell structure is functionally equivalent to the animal gap junction, and the answer is the plasmodesma, a cytoplasmic channel linking adjacent plant cells. Question 8 asks who proved that DNA replication is semi-conservative, and that was Meselson and Stahl in 1958, using heavy nitrogen labelling. Question 9 tests a commonly reversed fact, that a high auxin to cytokinin ratio in tissue culture induces root formation, not shoot formation. Question 10 confirms that Murashige and Skoog, known as MS medium from 1962, is the most widely used plant tissue culture medium, noted for its high salt content. The page ends by introducing question 11, about how tissue-cultured, disease-free banana plants, widely grown in Karnataka's banana belt, are produced.
488: This page continues the objective question bank. We learn that tissue-cultured, disease-free banana plants in Karnataka are produced mainly through meristem-tip culture, since anther culture instead gives haploids. India's first and so far only commercially cultivated genetically modified crop is Bt cotton, approved in 2002; Bt brinjal is approved but under moratorium, and GM mustard is still pending. The Cry gene that gives insect resistance in Bt cotton comes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, while Agrobacterium tumefaciens merely supplies the Ti plasmid vector. That Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the natural vector used for genetic transformation of dicot plants. Cereals and other monocots, which resist Agrobacterium, are instead transformed using the gene gun, also called the biolistic method, which fires DNA-coated microparticles into cells. The start codon that signals the beginning of translation is AUG, which also codes for methionine, while UAA, UAG and UGA are the three stop codons. The lac operon of E. coli is best described as inducible and catabolic, switched on by lactose, in contrast to the trp operon which is repressible and anabolic. Finally, the page asks about the heat-stable DNA polymerase that makes PCR possible, leading into the next page's answer.
489: Continuing the question bank, we learn that the heat-stable DNA polymerase used in PCR, called Taq polymerase, is obtained from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, since ordinary E. coli polymerase cannot survive the high heat of PCR. In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate towards the positive electrode, the anode, because DNA carries a negative charge and opposite charges attract. The transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another by a bacteriophage is called transduction, distinct from transformation, which is uptake of naked DNA. The ability of a single plant cell to regenerate into a complete plant is called totipotency, the founding principle of tissue culture, and different from the animal term pluripotency. A somatic hybrid such as the famous pomato is produced by protoplast fusion of potato and tomato cells, bypassing sexual crossing altogether. Among DNA markers, RFLP is the one based on hybridization, using restriction digestion and a labelled probe, while RAPD, SSR and SNP are all PCR-based markers. In the autoclave, culture media and glassware are sterilised at 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, for 15 to 20 minutes using moist heat, different from dry heat ovens at 160 degrees. Finally, anther or pollen culture is used in plant breeding chiefly to produce haploid, and later doubled-haploid, plants.
490: This page continues with more answers and questions. Haploid plants from anther culture, when their chromosomes are doubled, give instantly homozygous lines, useful in plant breeding, while virus-free plants instead come from meristem culture. The apex regulatory body that approves the commercial release of genetically modified crops in India is the GEAC, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, under the Ministry of Environment, distinct from IBSC, RCGM and FSSAI which handle other stages or standards. According to Chargaff's rule, in a DNA molecule, A equals T and G equals C, since pairing is always purine to pyrimidine. Somaclonal variation in tissue culture is best described as genetic variation among plants regenerated from tissue culture itself, a culture-induced phenomenon worsened by a long callus phase and the hormone 2,4-D. Bengaluru is often called India's biotechnology capital partly because it hosts institutions such as Biocon, C-CAMP and IBAB. In eukaryotic messenger RNA processing, the non-coding regions removed by splicing are called introns, while exons are the coding parts that are kept. The first recombinant DNA product to be commercially produced was human insulin, known as Humulin, launched in 1982, well before Bt cotton or Golden Rice. The page ends introducing programmed, orderly cell death, as seen in xylem formation and the plant's hypersensitive defence response.
491: Continuing the question bank, programmed, orderly cell death is called apoptosis, a genetically controlled process, unlike necrosis, which is accidental and messy death with inflammation. Virus-free citrus plants can be raised in vitro by the technique of in vitro micrografting, where a virus-free shoot tip is grafted onto a seedling rootstock, different from protoplast fusion which makes somatic hybrids. The enzyme that synthesises a DNA copy, called cDNA, from an RNA template is reverse transcriptase, the key exception to the usual flow of genetic information. The middle lamella that cements adjacent plant cells together is composed mainly of pectin, specifically calcium pectate, while cellulose forms the wall proper. The principle that a single plant cell can regenerate into a whole plant is totipotency, since every cell carries the full genome. The most widely used plant tissue culture medium, noted for its high salt content, was formulated in 1962 by Murashige and Skoog. The Ti plasmid used for plant genetic transformation comes from Agrobacterium tumefaciens, whose disarmed plasmid carries the gene into the dicot genome. Bt cotton, India's first commercial genetically modified crop, was approved for cultivation in 2002, and it remains the only commercially cultivated GM crop in India. The page ends by asking what Golden Rice was chiefly engineered to enhance.
492: This page confirms that Golden Rice was engineered chiefly to enhance its content of provitamin A, or beta-carotene, to combat vitamin A deficiency. The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises and cuts the palindromic sequence GAATTC, leaving single-stranded sticky ends. The enzyme that seals a gene into a vector by joining DNA fragments is DNA ligase, acting as the molecular glue in recombinant DNA technology. The semi-conservative nature of DNA replication was demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl in 1958, using heavy nitrogen, written as 15N, labelling. Correctly pairing the two classic bacterial operons, the lac operon is inducible while the trp operon is repressible. The ribosome found in the eukaryotic cytoplasm is of the 80S type, though 70S ribosomes persist inside mitochondria and chloroplasts, an important endosymbiont clue. Anther or pollen culture is used in breeding mainly to obtain haploid and doubled-haploid lines, since with colchicine these become instantly homozygous. To raise virus-free planting material, the technique of choice is meristem-tip culture, because the tiny apical dome outruns the virus infection. The page ends asking which apex committee clears the commercial environmental release of genetically modified crops in India.
493: This page confirms once more that GEAC, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee under the Ministry of Environment, is the apex body that clears commercial environmental release of genetically modified crops in India. Somaclonal variation refers to genetic variation arising specifically among tissue-culture-regenerated plants, and it worsens with a long callus phase and use of the hormone 2,4-D. This closes the objective question bank for the plant biotechnology chapter. The page then lists the References used for this chapter, including the Karnataka Public Service Commission's Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer Paper 2 technical syllabus, Unit 15 on Plant Biotechnology. Other cited sources include Gupta's Cell and Molecular Biology and Biotechnology from Rastogi Publications, Bhojwani and Razdan's Plant Tissue Culture: Theory and Practice from Elsevier, Razdan's Introduction to Plant Tissue Culture, Lewin's Genes and Lodish's Molecular Cell Biology for fundamentals, Primrose and Twyman's Principles of Gene Manipulation and Genomics for recombinant DNA, vectors and markers, and Singh's Biotechnology: Expanding Horizons. Also cited are the Department of Biotechnology and GEAC biosafety guidelines from the Government of India, ICAR e-course material, TNAU and UAS Agritech portals, and resources from the University of Agricultural Sciences at Bangalore and Dharwad, and IIHR Hesaraghatta, covering tissue culture and crop biotechnology.
494: Now, students, we begin Chapter 16, Microbial and Environmental Biotechnology, Unit 16 of Paper 2. This chapter covers the scope of microbial biotechnology, microbial diversity and classification, microbial nutrition and the growth curve, batch versus continuous culture, industrial microbiology and fermentation technology including bioreactors and downstream processing, microbial products such as antibiotics, enzymes, organic acids, amino acids, vitamins and single-cell protein, biofertilizers, biopesticides, bioremediation and phytoremediation, biodegradation of xenobiotics, sewage and wastewater treatment, solid waste management and composting, biofuels, biosensors, and biosafety regulation of genetically modified organisms, followed by objective questions. Part A begins with Section 16.1, Introduction and Scope. Biotechnology is defined as the application of biological systems, living organisms, or their derivatives to make or modify products and processes for a specific use. Microbial biotechnology specifically exploits micro-organisms, including bacteria, fungi, yeasts, algae and viruses, for the benefit of agriculture, industry, medicine and the environment. Microbes are humanity's oldest biotechnology tools, used for beer, bread and curd long before cells were understood; modern microbial biotechnology adds genetics and engineering to scale these processes industrially. Its scope spans agriculture through biofertilizers and biopesticides, industry through antibiotics, enzymes and alcohols, medicine through vaccines and therapeutic proteins, and the environment through pollution clean-up. An important note for the Agricultural Officer is that Bengaluru hosts Biocon, India's largest biotechnology firm, while CFTRI Mysuru pioneered industrial enzyme technology.
495: Here we learn how microbial biotechnology developed through distinct historical stages. The ancient, empirical era, before 1850, used fermentation by tradition, without knowing the cause, for beer, bread, curd and vinegar. The Pasteur-Koch era, from 1850 to 1900, proved scientifically that specific microbes cause fermentation and disease. The antibiotic era began in 1928 with Fleming's discovery of penicillin, followed by its mass production in the 1940s. The recombinant DNA era, from the 1970s onward, allowed engineered microbes to make human proteins such as insulin and vaccines. Each stage widened the toolkit, moving from selecting natural strains to mutation and screening, and finally to precise genetic engineering, supported by modern bioprocess engineering that scales production in large sterile reactors, making India a major low-cost producer. Section 16.2 then introduces Microbial Diversity and Classification. The most fundamental division in the microbial world is between prokaryotes, organisms with no membrane-bound nucleus, such as bacteria and archaea, and eukaryotes, organisms with a true nucleus and organelles like mitochondria, such as fungi, algae and protozoa. Carl Woese divided all life into three domains using ribosomal RNA: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, with archaea being prokaryotes of extreme habitats like hot springs and salt lakes. Viruses are acellular and lie outside this scheme entirely. A table then lists defining features and examples: bacteria have a peptidoglycan cell wall and reproduce by binary fission, with examples like Rhizobium and Bacillus; archaea live in extreme habitats with unusual lipids, such as methanogens and Halobacterium; fungi have a chitin wall and are heterotrophic, forming spores, like Aspergillus and yeast; and algae are photosynthetic aquatic organisms, such as Chlorella and Spirulina.
496: Continuing the classification table, protozoa are eukaryotic, animal-like, motile organisms with no cell wall, such as Amoeba and Paramecium, while viruses are acellular obligate parasites made of nucleic acid and a protein coat, with examples like NPV and bacteriophage. Bacteria are further grouped by shape into cocci, spherical; bacilli, rods; spirilla, spiral; and vibrios, comma-shaped. The Gram stain divides them into Gram-positive bacteria, which retain a violet stain due to a thick peptidoglycan wall, and Gram-negative bacteria, which lose it and counter-stain pink due to a thin wall plus an outer membrane. By oxygen requirement, bacteria are classified as obligate aerobes needing oxygen, obligate anaerobes killed by oxygen, facultative anaerobes that grow either way, and microaerophiles needing only a little oxygen; this classification matters directly in fermentation and waste treatment. Remember, students, archaea are prokaryotes of extreme habitats, a common trap is to mistakenly call them bacteria. Fungi, algae and viruses each play distinct roles in biotechnology. Fungi like Aspergillus and Penicillium make antibiotics, organic acids and enzymes, while yeasts like Saccharomyces drive baking, brewing and bioethanol. Algae are photosynthetic eukaryotes, though cyanobacteria, called blue-green algae, are actually photosynthetic prokaryotes; microalgae like Chlorella and Spirulina are grown for food, feed, pigments and biofuel, and cyanobacteria also fix nitrogen, making them valuable paddy biofertilizers. A heterocyst is a specialised, thick-walled cell of certain cyanobacteria, such as Anabaena and Nostoc, where nitrogen fixation occurs in an oxygen-free environment. Section 16.3 then begins, Microbial Nutrition and Growth, explaining that microbes need carbon, energy, nitrogen, minerals and water, classified by their nutritional type.
497: This page completes the nutritional classification table: chemoautotrophs use carbon dioxide as carbon source and inorganic chemicals as energy source, like nitrifying bacteria, while chemoheterotrophs use organic carbon and organic chemicals, covering most bacteria and fungi. Next we study the microbial growth curve, shown in Figure 16.1, which follows a characteristic four-phase pattern when cells are inoculated into fresh liquid medium in a closed flask. The lag phase is a period of adjustment where cells do not divide but synthesise enzymes to adapt, so the population stays flat. The log, or exponential, phase follows, where cells divide at a constant maximum rate, giving the fastest, most balanced growth. In the stationary phase, new cell formation equals cell death, so the viable number stays constant, nutrients become scarce, wastes accumulate, and many secondary products such as antibiotics are made during this phase. Finally, in the death or decline phase, cells die faster than they form and the population falls. Generation, or doubling, time is defined as the time required for a microbial population to double during the exponential phase; for E. coli in rich medium this is about twenty minutes. A worked example shows that 1,000 bacteria with a 30-minute generation time, growing for 3 hours, double six times, giving a final count of 1,000 multiplied by 2 to the power 6, which equals 64,000 cells. The page then introduces batch versus continuous culture: batch culture uses a fixed volume run until nutrients are exhausted, while continuous culture continuously adds fresh medium and removes an equal volume, holding cells in exponential phase indefinitely in a chemostat.
498: This page presents a comparison table between batch and continuous culture. In batch culture, medium is added once at the start in a fixed, closed system, passing through all four growth phases, and suits secondary products like antibiotics, with lower contamination risk due to a short run. In continuous culture, medium is added and removed continuously in a constant, open system, held in a steady exponential phase, suiting primary products and biomass production, though with higher contamination risk over a long run. Remember, students, a chemostat keeps cells in the log phase forever, which is the defining purpose of continuous culture. The page then discusses physical factors affecting microbial growth. Temperature defines four groups: psychrophiles favour cold, mesophiles favour moderate warmth near body heat, thermophiles favour hot conditions, and hyperthermophiles favour near-boiling habitats, with most industrial and pathogenic microbes being mesophiles, growing best between twenty-five and forty degrees Celsius. Most bacteria prefer near-neutral pH, while many fungi tolerate acid; oxygen need ranges from obligate aerobes to obligate anaerobes; and microbes need available water, so high salt or sugar preserves food by withdrawing it. Specific growth rate is defined as the rate of increase of biomass per unit biomass during exponential growth, a constant for a given organism and medium, symbolised by mu. Finally, in a fed-batch culture, fresh medium is added in stages without removing the broth, keeping substrate at a low, controlled level; this is the standard mode for antibiotic and recombinant protein production, since it avoids substrate inhibition. Section 16.4 then begins, Industrial Microbiology and Fermentation Technology, defining industrial microbiology as the use of micro-organisms in large, controlled processes to produce useful goods on a commercial scale.
499: This page explains that an industrial fermentation has three stages, shown in Figure 16.2: upstream processing, the fermentation itself, and downstream processing, each carried out under strict control to keep the culture pure and productive. Upstream processing prepares everything before fermentation, covering strain selection and improvement, medium formulation and sterilisation, and build-up of a healthy inoculum; a poor inoculum or contaminated medium ruins the whole batch. In the fermentation stage, the inoculum grows in the bioreactor under controlled temperature, pH, aeration and stirring until the product accumulates. Downstream processing then recovers and purifies the product through separation, extraction and polishing, and this stage is often the largest part of total cost, especially for a pure pharmaceutical. A bioreactor, or fermenter, is defined as a closed vessel in which micro-organisms or their enzymes are grown under controlled conditions to carry out a desired biochemical conversion, with the stirred-tank reactor being the most common industrial design. A typical stirred-tank bioreactor is a sealed stainless-steel vessel with an impeller to mix the broth, a sparger to supply sterile air, a jacket or coil to control temperature, and probes to monitor pH, dissolved oxygen and temperature. Other designs include the airlift reactor, which mixes using rising air bubbles alone, avoiding moving parts, and the packed-bed and fluidised-bed reactors, which hold immobilised cells or enzymes on a support. Fermentations are also classified by medium, as submerged, in a liquid broth, or solid-state, on a moist solid like bran, and by feeding mode as batch, fed-batch or continuous. Downstream processing then begins by separating cells from broth using filtration or centrifugation, followed by extraction through precipitation, solvent extraction, or chromatography, then concentration, and finally polishing and drying.
500: A worked example on this page describes penicillin manufacture: Penicillium is first grown in a stirred-tank fed-batch fermenter for the upstream and fermentation stages, then the broth is filtered to remove the mould, the penicillin is extracted into a solvent at low pH, back-extracted, crystallised and dried during the downstream stage. Naming the correct stage for each step is the key marks-earning skill here. The page then covers sterilisation, aeration and agitation. Sterilisation destroys all unwanted microbes from the medium, usually by heat under pressure, the air supply by fine membrane filters, and the vessel by steam, since a single contaminant can outgrow the production strain and ruin the batch. Aeration and agitation supply oxygen and mix the broth; since oxygen dissolves poorly in water, sterile air is sparged in as fine bubbles while an impeller stirs to spread it and keep cells, heat and nutrients uniform, together setting the oxygen transfer rate that often limits productivity. An inoculum is defined as the starter culture of active, healthy micro-organisms added to begin a fermentation, usually built up in stages from a stock culture. A table compares bioreactor types: stirred-tank uses a mechanical impeller and suits most aerobic fermentations; airlift uses rising air bubbles only, suited to shear-sensitive cells; packed-bed uses a fixed bed of support for immobilised cells or enzymes; and fluidised-bed uses an up-flow to suspend particles, suited for immobilised biocatalysts and waste treatment. Strain improvement uses classical mutation and screening, or modern genetic engineering, and has raised penicillin yields thousands of times above Fleming's original mould. Immobilisation is defined as fixing whole cells or enzymes onto or within an inert carrier so the biocatalyst can be retained, reused and easily separated from the product. Section 16.5 then begins, Microbial Products, dividing them into primary metabolites, made during active growth and essential to the cell, and secondary metabolites, made in the stationary phase and not essential to growth.
501: A secondary metabolite is defined as a product formed mainly in the stationary phase, not essential for growth, such as antibiotics, often having ecological or defensive value to the producing microbe. An antibiotic is a chemical produced by a micro-organism that, in low concentration, kills or inhibits the growth of other micro-organisms. Antibiotics are the most valuable microbial products; penicillin, the first, was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the mould Penicillium notatum, while most antibiotics today come from the filamentous bacteria Streptomyces, including streptomycin, tetracycline and erythromycin, produced by submerged fed-batch fermentation. A table lists antibiotics and their producing organisms: penicillin from Penicillium chrysogenum, streptomycin from Streptomyces griseus, tetracycline from Streptomyces aureofaciens, erythromycin from Saccharopolyspora erythraea, and cephalosporin from Acremonium mould. Industrial enzymes are widely used because they work at mild conditions, are highly specific and biodegradable: amylases convert starch to sugars for baking and brewing, proteases are used in detergents and to tenderise meat, lipases split fats, pectinases clarify fruit juice, and cellulase breaks cellulose for textile, biofuel and juice applications; many are produced by Aspergillus and Bacillus species. Organic acids made by fermentation include citric acid from Aspergillus niger, used in foods and beverages, lactic acid from Lactobacillus, used as an acidulant and in bioplastics, and acetic acid, the basis of vinegar, from Acetobacter. Amino acids are primary metabolites made in bulk by fermentation: glutamic acid, sold as monosodium glutamate, and lysine, an animal-feed supplement, are both produced by Corynebacterium glutamicum. Among vitamins, vitamin B12 comes from Pseudomonas and Propionibacterium, and riboflavin, or B2, from the fungus Ashbya gossypii.
502: This page summarises key microbial products in a table: citric acid, an organic acid, from Aspergillus niger; lactic acid from Lactobacillus; acetic acid, or vinegar, from Acetobacter aceti; glutamic acid, or MSG, and lysine, both amino acids, from Corynebacterium glutamicum; vitamin B12 from Pseudomonas and Propionibacterium; riboflavin, or B2, from Ashbya gossypii; and ethanol, an alcohol, from Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Single-cell protein, or SCP, is defined as protein-rich microbial biomass, from algae, bacteria, yeast or fungi, grown on cheap substrates and used as food or animal feed. Spirulina, a cyanobacterium, is grown in ponds as a health food, yeasts are grown on molasses, and the fungus Fusarium gives the meat-substitute mycoprotein sold as Quorn; SCP grows far faster than crops or livestock but must be tested for safety and nucleic-acid content. An important note for the Agricultural Officer is that Spirulina cultivation is promoted in Karnataka as a nutritional supplement and income source for self-help groups, and it doubles as a biofertilizer through nitrogen fixation. Remember, students, antibiotics are secondary metabolites, while amino acids, organic acids and vitamins are primary metabolites; citric acid pairs with Aspergillus niger, MSG and lysine with Corynebacterium glutamicum, and vinegar with Acetobacter, and these pairings are repeatedly tested. Ethanol is the largest-volume microbial product, made when yeast ferments sugars anaerobically, serving as a beverage, industrial solvent and petrol-blending biofuel. Vaccines are grown in microbial or cell cultures, and recombinant microbes now make human insulin, growth hormone and clotting factors. Human insulin, the first such recombinant product, is made by Escherichia coli or yeast carrying the human insulin gene, ending dependence on animal pancreas; the same approach makes hepatitis-B vaccine, interferons and clot-dissolving enzymes, with India, especially Bengaluru, a leading low-cost manufacturer.
503: Following on, Biocon of Bengaluru began with enzyme manufacture and grew into India's largest biopharmaceutical company, producing recombinant insulin and other proteins, while CFTRI Mysuru pioneered Indian industrial enzymes from fungi, linking Karnataka institutions directly to microbial product technology. Section 16.6 then begins, Biofertilizers. A biofertilizer is defined as a preparation containing living micro-organisms that, when applied to seed, soil or root, colonises the rhizosphere and increases the supply of nutrients, chiefly nitrogen and phosphorus, to the plant. Biofertilizers are eco-friendly, cheap and renewable, fixing atmospheric nitrogen, solubilising fixed phosphorus, secreting growth-promoting substances and improving soil health, grouped by the nutrient they supply as shown in Figure 16.3, into nitrogen fixers, phosphate mobilisers, and others. Rhizobium is the most important symbiotic nitrogen-fixer, living in root nodules of leguminous plants such as pulses and groundnut, fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia by the enzyme nitrogenase, and can add fifty to a hundred and fifty kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. Azolla is a water fern harbouring the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena in its leaf cavities, and the Azolla-Anabaena symbiosis is grown in paddy fields as green manure. Among free-living and associative nitrogen fixers, Azotobacter is free-living in soil, helping cereals and vegetables, while Azospirillum is associative, living close to roots of cereals like maize, sorghum and millets. Blue-green algae such as Nostoc, Anabaena and Aulosira fix nitrogen freely in waterlogged paddy soil using heterocysts, a practice called algalisation. Phosphate-solubilising bacteria, or PSB, such as Bacillus and Pseudomonas, secrete organic acids that dissolve fixed soil phosphorus, applied with rock phosphate or phosphatic fertilizer to raise its efficiency.
504: This page defines mycorrhiza as a symbiotic association between a fungus and plant roots, where the fungus extends fine threads into the soil to supply phosphorus and water, receiving carbon in return; vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza, or VAM, now called arbuscular mycorrhiza, is the most useful type, also improving drought tolerance and root health. A summary table lists biofertilizers and their suited crops: Rhizobium, a symbiotic nitrogen-fixer, for legumes like pulses, groundnut and soybean; Azotobacter, free-living, for cereals and vegetables; Azospirillum, associative, for maize, sorghum, millets and rice; blue-green algae, free-living, for paddy through algalisation; Azolla, symbiotic with Anabaena, as paddy green manure; PSB, a phosphate solubiliser, for all crops with rock phosphate; and mycorrhiza, a phosphorus and water mobiliser, for horticulture and forestry. A worked example describes a pulse grower treating green-gram seed with Rhizobium culture before sowing, so the bacterium forms nodules, fixes nitrogen, and reduces urea need, but the same farmer must use Azospirillum or Azotobacter on adjoining maize, since Rhizobium nodulates only legumes. For the Agricultural Officer, Karnataka's Department of Agriculture and state agricultural universities produce and distribute Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, PSB and Azolla cultures, and the officer must match the right inoculant to the crop. Remember, students, Rhizobium works only with legumes symbiotically, Azotobacter is free-living, Azospirillum is associative for non-legumes, Azolla carries Anabaena as paddy green manure, and PSB with mycorrhiza handle phosphorus, not nitrogen. The page ends introducing production, carriers and application of biofertilizers, explaining that a biofertilizer is made by growing the chosen microbe in a fermenter, mixing the broth with a carrier such as sterilised peat or lignite, and applying it by seed treatment, seedling-root dipping, or soil application.
505: On this page we look at biofertilizer application and biopesticides. A carrier is an inert, moisture-holding material such as peat or lignite that keeps biofertilizer microbes alive and viable until use. Soil application, where the biofertilizer is mixed with compost and broadcast, suits standing or perennial crops. Remember, biofertilizers have limits, they only supplement, never fully replace, chemical fertilizer, they act slowly, their living cells have a short shelf life, and the right strain must match the crop and soil. Even so, they cut fertilizer cost and improve soil structure and biology, which is why the State actively promotes them. Now, students, section 16.7 introduces biopesticides, pesticides derived from a living organism, a bacterium, fungus, virus or plant, used to control insect pests, weeds or plant diseases. They are target-specific, biodegradable and safe to non-target life, and are classified as microbial pesticides, bio-derived chemicals like neem, and plant-incorporated protectants. Bacillus thuringiensis, or Bt, is the most widely used microbial insecticide. During sporulation this soil bacterium makes a crystal protein, the Cry or delta-endotoxin, which dissolves in the alkaline gut of an insect larva, binds to gut-wall receptors, and punches pores in the cells, so the larva stops feeding and dies. Bt cotton is the only Bt crop approved for commercial cultivation in India.
506: Let us understand more biopesticides on this page. Neem, a plant product, yields azadirachtin, which controls many sucking and chewing pests.
