In Karnataka, Trichoderma and Bt are central to integrated pest management advice for crops such as cotton, pigeonpea and chilli, remember that Bt cotton is India's only commercially approved transgenic crop, and NPV is the host-specific virus used against Helicoverpa on pigeonpea. Beauveria and Metarhizium are entomopathogenic fungi, meaning they infect and kill insects directly by penetrating the body surface, without needing to be eaten. Beauveria bassiana causes white muscardine disease, its spores germinating on the insect cuticle and growing inside to kill the host, while Metarhizium anisopliae acts similarly against white grubs, hoppers and termites. Pheromone traps use insect scent chemicals to monitor and trap pests, and predators and parasitoids such as Trichogramma wasps are released as living biocontrol agents. Biopesticides are specific, biodegradable, safe to natural enemies, and slow resistance build-up, but they act slowly, are sensitive to sunlight and storage, and have a narrow host range, so they suit integrated use rather than standing alone. Section 16.8 then opens environmental biotechnology, defined as the use of living organisms, mainly microorganisms and plants, to treat pollution, manage waste and restore a damaged environment sustainably.
507: Here we study bioremediation and phytoremediation in detail. Bioremediation is the use of microorganisms or their enzymes to break down or detoxify pollutants in soil, water or air, converting harmful compounds into harmless products such as carbon dioxide and water. It is cheaper and gentler than digging out and burning polluted soil, and is used for oil spills, pesticide residues, heavy-metal sites and industrial effluents. There are two settings, in-situ bioremediation treats the pollutant where it lies, using bioventing, where air is pumped into soil to feed aerobic microbes, and biostimulation, where nutrients are added to boost native microbes. Ex-situ bioremediation removes contaminated material to a treatment site, giving more control but at higher cost. Bioaugmentation means adding selected or engineered microorganisms to speed up breakdown of a pollutant native microbes cannot handle efficiently. A famous case is the oil-eating bacterium engineered by Ananda Chakrabarty, who combined plasmids from several Pseudomonas strains into one bacterium able to degrade many components of crude oil, becoming the first genetically engineered organism granted a patent, in 1980. Phytoremediation uses green plants and their associated microbes to remove, contain or detoxify pollutants, especially heavy metals, through phytoextraction, phytostabilisation, rhizofiltration and phytodegradation. A xenobiotic is a man-made chemical foreign to nature, such as DDT, plastics or dyes, that resists microbial breakdown and persists in the environment.
508: Now, students, this page continues with the mechanisms and limits of bioremediation. Aerobic microbes oxidise hydrocarbons and many organics fully to carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobes can reduce chlorinated solvents that resist aerobic attack. Some microbes do not destroy a metal but change its form, making it less mobile or toxic. Bioremediation works only within limits, the microbes need the right temperature, moisture, pH and nutrients, and cannot survive very high concentrations of toxic waste, and heavy metals cannot be destroyed, only moved or immobilised. A table summarises techniques, bioventing pumps air to feed aerobes for fuel-contaminated soil, biostimulation adds nutrients for oil-spill clean-up, bioaugmentation adds selected or engineered microbes for hard-to-degrade waste, phytoextraction lets plants take up and store metals from metal-polluted farmland, and rhizofiltration uses roots to absorb pollutants from contaminated water. Phytoremediation is cheap, solar-powered and improves the soil, but it is slow and reaches only as deep as the roots. Section 16.9 then opens wastewater and sewage treatment, defining sewage as waste water from homes, institutions and industry carrying organic matter, suspended solids, microorganisms and dissolved chemicals that must be treated before discharge. The page introduces the activated-sludge process shown in Figure 16.4, moving through screening, primary sedimentation, an aeration tank of activated sludge and aerobic microbes, a secondary clarifier, and disinfection to effluent, with excess sludge sent to an anaerobic digester for biogas. Biochemical oxygen demand, or BOD, is the oxygen microorganisms need to break down organic matter in a water sample, and a high BOD signals heavy organic pollution.
509: On this page we cover the stages and treatment types of sewage. Preliminary and primary treatment are physical, screening removes large objects and grit, and primary sedimentation lets heavy solids settle out as primary sludge, but this does not yet treat the dissolved organic matter. Secondary treatment is the biological heart of the process, aerobic microorganisms oxidise the dissolved and colloidal organic matter to carbon dioxide, water and more microbial cells, using either the activated-sludge process or the trickling filter, where sewage trickles over a bed of stones coated with a microbial film. In the activated-sludge process, air is blown into an aeration tank and the settled sludge is partly returned to keep the microbe population high. Anaerobic treatment handles strong organic wastes and collected sludge without oxygen, methanogenic archaea break down the organic matter in an anaerobic digester, producing biogas, a mixture of methane and carbon dioxide, and a stabilised slurry. Remember, activated sludge and the trickling filter are aerobic, while the digester is anaerobic and makes biogas through methanogens. In Karnataka, sewage treatment plants run under the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board, and treated water is increasingly reused for irrigation around Bengaluru. A high BOD means heavy organic pollution, and good treatment lowers the BOD. The page ends by introducing the UASB reactor, the up-flow anaerobic sludge blanket, which passes waste water upward through a dense blanket of granular anaerobic sludge, needs little energy, produces useful gas, and suits warm climates, alongside oxidation ponds and septic tanks for smaller or rural settings.
510: Let us understand tertiary treatment and composting on this page. Tertiary treatment is the final polishing stage of sewage treatment, removing residual nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus and disinfecting the water before discharge or reuse. Excess nutrients in treated water cause eutrophication, the over-enrichment of a water body that triggers algal blooms and then oxygen loss as the algae decay, so tertiary treatment prevents this. Section 16.10 introduces solid waste management and composting, composting being the controlled aerobic, microbial decomposition of organic solid waste into a dark, stable, humus-like material used as an organic soil amendment. In aerobic composting, bacteria, actinomycetes and fungi decompose organic matter, passing through a hot thermophilic phase that kills weed seeds and pathogens, and then a cooler maturing phase, with success depending on a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about thirty to one and regular turning. Vermicomposting is the conversion of organic waste into nutrient-rich compost using earthworms, chiefly Eisenia fetida, which fragment the waste and enrich it as it passes through their gut, giving a finer, more nutrient-rich product than ordinary composting. In Karnataka, vermicomposting is heavily promoted under organic-farming and watershed programmes as an income source and soil-health tool. Remember, composting is aerobic and microbial, while vermicomposting uses earthworms and gives a richer product, the thermophilic hot phase kills pathogens and weed seeds, and the ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is about thirty to one.
511: Here, students, we look at landfilling and biofuels. Landfilling is the last resort for solid waste, in a sanitary landfill the waste is sealed under a liner and cover, where anaerobic microbes slowly digest the organics and release landfill gas rich in methane, which can be tapped as fuel, while poorly run dumps instead leak methane and a toxic liquid called leachate, the polluted liquid draining from decomposing waste that can contaminate soil and groundwater. Composting and digestion are preferred because they recover nutrients and energy and cut landfill volume. Section 16.11 then introduces biofuels, fuels produced from recent biological material, or biomass, rather than fossil deposits, which are renewable and release less net carbon dioxide. The three biofuels in the syllabus are bioethanol, biogas and biohydrogen. Bioethanol is ethyl alcohol made by fermentation of sugars using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, first-generation bioethanol uses sugar or starch crops like sugarcane molasses, maize and broken rice, while second-generation bioethanol uses lignocellulosic waste like straw and bagasse. Biogas is a mixture of about sixty per cent methane and forty per cent carbon dioxide produced by anaerobic digestion of organic matter such as cattle dung and crop residue by methanogenic archaea, through three microbial steps, hydrolysis, acid formation, and methane formation, using floating-drum or fixed-dome plant designs common in India. Biohydrogen is hydrogen gas produced biologically, a clean fuel yielding only water on burning, made by dark fermentation or photo-fermentation, though still mainly at the research stage.
512: On this page we finish biofuels and begin biosensors. A village biogas plant fed daily with cattle dung shows the idea clearly, methanogens act in the sealed digester without air to release biogas for cooking, while the outflowing slurry is used as manure. Karnataka has installed lakhs of family biogas plants under the national biogas programme, cutting firewood use and giving farmers both cooking gas and enriched slurry, using the fixed-dome and floating-drum designs. Remember, bioethanol comes from yeast fermentation of sugars for petrol blending, biogas comes from anaerobic digestion via methanogens giving about sixty per cent methane, and biohydrogen is the cleanest, burning to water, but still mostly experimental. Biodiesel is a renewable diesel substitute made by trans-esterification of vegetable oils or animal fats with an alcohol, giving fatty-acid esters, in India made from non-edible oils such as jatropha and pongamia and from used cooking oil. Biofuels are grouped by generation, first-generation fuels come from food crops raising a food-versus-fuel concern, second-generation fuels use non-food biomass such as straw, bagasse and non-edible oilseeds, and third-generation fuels use algae, which give high oil yields on non-farm land. Trans-esterification is the chemical reaction of a vegetable oil or fat with an alcohol to make fatty-acid esters, or biodiesel, and glycerol as a by-product. Section 16.12 then opens biosensors, an analytical device coupling a biological sensing element, such as an enzyme, antibody, microbe or nucleic acid, with a physical transducer that converts the biological response into a measurable electrical signal.
513: Let us understand biosensors and biosafety regulation on this page. A biosensor has three parts, the bio-recognition element binds the target molecule specifically, the transducer converts that binding event into an electrical, optical or thermal signal, and the signal processor amplifies and displays the reading. Biosensors are fast, specific and portable, needing little sample preparation. The blood-glucose meter, based on the enzyme glucose oxidase, is the best-known example guiding diabetes care, and in agriculture and the environment biosensors detect pesticide residues, heavy metals and pathogens in soil, water and food. Biosensors are grouped by their sensing element, enzyme-based, antibody-based or immunosensors, microbial or DNA-based, and by their transducer, electrochemical, optical, thermal or mass-based, the blood-glucose meter being an enzyme-based electrochemical biosensor while a pregnancy-test strip is an antibody-based optical device. Section 16.13 then introduces biosafety and regulation of genetically modified organisms. Biosafety is the set of measures, practices and regulations adopted to prevent harm to human health and the environment from biotechnology, especially from genetically modified organisms. A genetically modified organism, or GMO, is an organism whose genetic material has been deliberately altered by recombinant DNA technology to introduce a new, useful trait. In India, GMOs are regulated under the Environment Protection Act, 1986, through the 1989 Rules on hazardous microorganisms and genetically engineered organisms, with the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, or GEAC, under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change as the apex approval body.
514: Now, students, this page details India's GMO regulatory bodies and the Bt crop story. GEAC is the apex body approving environmental release and commercial use of GMOs, the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation, or RCGM, monitors ongoing research and small-scale field trials, and institutional biosafety committees, or IBSC, operate at the laboratory level, while the Cartagena Protocol is the international treaty on safe transboundary movement of GMOs. Bt cotton was approved by GEAC in 2002 and is the only genetically modified crop cleared for commercial cultivation in India, while Bt brinjal cleared the scientific committees but was placed under an indefinite moratorium in 2010 after public and State objections, including protests in Karnataka. Food safety for GM foods is regulated by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, or FSSAI, under the Food Safety and Standards Genetically Modified Foods Regulations notified in 2022, a packaged food with more than one per cent genetically modified ingredients must declare it on the label, more lenient than the European Union's 0.9 per cent threshold. A Karnataka Agricultural Officer should remember GEAC as the apex GMO approval body, Bt cotton, 2002, as India's only approved GM crop, and the Bt brinjal moratorium since 2010 amid Dharwad-area protests. The debated benefits of genetic modification include higher yield, pest tolerance and better nutrition such as vitamin-A rich golden rice, while feared risks include gene flow to wild relatives, harm to non-target species, and resistant pests, all governed internationally by the precautionary-principle-based Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety.
515: This page closes the chapter's core theory with a short table and containment levels. Society gains lower cost and food security from genetic modification but faces risks of seed dependence and ethical questions. Biosafety practice also classifies laboratory work by risk, containment levels range from BSL-1 for harmless microbes to BSL-4 for the most dangerous pathogens, and these levels set the equipment and procedures required, enforced by institutional biosafety committees in research. For the exam candidate, the key chain to remember is the Environment Act as the legal basis, GEAC as the apex body, Bt cotton as the lone approved crop, and the Bt brinjal moratorium as the well-known case of biosafety being scientific, social and political all at once.
516: On this page you will see the Chapter Mind Map for Microbial and Environmental Biotechnology, a visual summary linking nine branches around the central topic. These branches are microbial growth, covering the growth curve and generation time, fermentation, covering bioreactors and batch versus continuous types, microbial products such as penicillin from Penicillium chrysogenum and citric acid from Aspergillus niger, biofertilizers such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter, biopesticides such as Bt and NPV, bioremediation including Chakrabarty's patented oil-eating bacterium, wastewater treatment covering activated sludge and BOD, biofuels such as biogas and biodiesel, and biosafety covering GEAC, RCGM and the Cartagena Protocol. Students should use this map as a quick revision tool to recall how all the chapter's microbes, processes and regulatory bodies connect to one another before moving into the objective-question practice that follows.
517: Here we begin the exam-focused revision material. First is a Key Terms at a Glance table giving one-line meanings for the chapter's core vocabulary, including microbial biotechnology, growth curve phases of lag, log, stationary and death, generation time, chemostat, bioreactor, downstream processing, secondary metabolite, the nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers Rhizobium, Azotobacter and Azospirillum, the biopesticides Bt, Trichoderma and NPV, bioremediation, phytoremediation, BOD, activated sludge, anaerobic digestion, vermicomposting, the biofuels bioethanol, biogas and biohydrogen, biosensors, and GEAC as the apex body approving GMOs in India. Part B then begins objective questions and answers, to be worked through after reading the theory, with each question's answer given directly below it and explanations naming the common mistake. Question one asks which group of organisms microbial biotechnology chiefly exploits, and the answer is micro-organisms and their products, since the field uses bacteria, fungi, yeasts, algae and viruses and their products for human benefit.
518: Now, students, this page works through questions two to ten on microbial growth and fermentation basics. A cell lacking a true membrane-bound nucleus is a prokaryote, covering both bacteria and archaea. Archaea are prokaryotes best described as being found in extreme habitats, such as hot springs and salt lakes, and methanogens are archaea. Gram-positive bacteria retain the violet stain because they have a thick peptidoglycan wall, unlike Gram-negative bacteria with a thin wall that stains pink. Most bacteria and fungi are chemoheterotrophs, taking both carbon and energy from organic compounds. In a batch culture, the log or exponential phase is when cells divide at the fastest, most balanced rate, while antibiotics and other secondary metabolites are produced mainly in the stationary phase, when nutrients are scarce and growth has slowed. Generation, or doubling, time is the time taken for a microbial population to double during exponential growth, about twenty minutes for E. coli in rich medium. A chemostat is used to keep cells continuously in the log, or exponential, phase, since continuous culture adds and removes medium to hold steady exponential growth, unlike batch culture, which is a closed system passing through all four phases.
519: Let us continue with questions eleven to eighteen on fermentation technology and microbial products. The three stages of industrial fermentation, in order, are upstream preparation, fermentation in the bioreactor, then downstream recovery and purification, this recovery and purification step being called downstream processing, often the costliest stage for a pure pharmaceutical. The most common and versatile industrial bioreactor design is the stirred-tank reactor, using a mechanical impeller for mixing and aeration, while growth of microbes on a moist solid substrate with little free water is called solid-state fermentation. Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming from the mould Penicillium notatum. Most clinically used antibiotics, such as streptomycin, are obtained from Streptomyces, filamentous bacteria that also yield tetracycline and erythromycin. Citric acid is produced industrially by fermentation using Aspergillus niger, the standard producer of citric acid, and monosodium glutamate and lysine are produced by Corynebacterium glutamicum, which makes both glutamic acid and lysine.
520: On this page, questions nineteen to twenty-six cover fermentation products and nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers. Vinegar, or acetic acid, is produced by fermentation using Acetobacter, which oxidises ethanol to acetic acid. Single-cell protein, or SCP, refers to protein-rich microbial biomass used for food or feed, with Spirulina, yeast and Fusarium mycoprotein as examples, and Spirulina itself is a cyanobacterium that also fixes nitrogen. Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants such as pulses, groundnut and soybean, nodulating only legumes. Azotobacter, by contrast, is a free-living aerobic nitrogen fixer used on non-legumes such as cereals and vegetables, while Azospirillum is an associative nitrogen fixer for cereals such as maize and sorghum. The water fern Azolla fixes nitrogen in paddy because it harbours the cyanobacterium Anabaena in its leaf cavities, and blue-green algae used as a biofertilizer in flooded rice fields fix nitrogen using heterocysts, specialised cells within cyanobacteria.
521: Here, students, questions twenty-seven to thirty-five cover biofertilizers, biopesticides and bioremediation basics. Phosphate-solubilising bacteria, or PSB, help the crop by dissolving fixed soil phosphorus through secreted organic acids, while a mycorrhiza is a symbiosis between plant roots and a fungus, its threads mobilising phosphorus, zinc and water for the plant. Bacillus thuringiensis controls insects through a Cry, or delta-endotoxin, acting in an alkaline gut, and Bt cotton, approved by GEAC in 2002, is the only Bt transgenic crop approved for commercial cultivation in India, while Bt brinjal remains under a moratorium. Trichoderma is used as a biopesticide mainly against soil-borne fungal diseases such as wilt and root rot, and the nuclear polyhedrosis virus, a baculovirus, is used against caterpillars such as Helicoverpa and Spodoptera, being host-specific. Bioremediation is the use of organisms to break down or detoxify pollutants, and treating a pollutant where it lies without excavation is called in-situ bioremediation, for example through bioventing and biostimulation.
522: Let us understand questions thirty-five to forty-three on bioremediation, phytoremediation and sewage treatment. Adding nutrients to boost the activity of native microbes at a polluted site is biostimulation, while bioaugmentation instead adds selected microbes. The use of green plants to remove heavy metals from soil is phytoremediation, using plants such as mustard and water hyacinth. The first genetically engineered organism to be granted a patent, in 1980, an oil-degrading bacterium, was developed by Ananda Chakrabarty, who engineered an oil-eating Pseudomonas for bioremediation of spills. A man-made chemical foreign to nature and resistant to microbial breakdown is a xenobiotic, such as DDT, plastic or a synthetic dye. A high biochemical oxygen demand in water indicates heavy organic pollution, since good treatment lowers the BOD. The activated-sludge process of sewage treatment is essentially an aerobic biological process, where microbes in an aerated tank digest the organic matter, and in an anaerobic digester treating sludge, the biogas produced is rich in methane, made by methanogenic archaea. Among sewage-treatment units, the trickling filter is aerobic, along with the activated-sludge tank, while digesters are anaerobic.
523: On this page, questions forty-three to fifty-one cover composting, biofuels and biosensors. Composting of organic solid waste is essentially aerobic and microbial, breaking material down into stable, humus-like compost, while vermicomposting converts organic waste into manure using earthworms, chiefly Eisenia fetida, which give a finer, nutrient-rich compost. The ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for good composting is about thirty to one, since too little nitrogen slows the process and too much causes ammonia loss. Bioethanol is produced by fermentation of sugars using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae for petrol blending, while biogas is produced by the anaerobic digestion of organic matter by methanogenic archaea, which form methane in the absence of oxygen. Among biofuels, biohydrogen burns to yield only water and is considered the cleanest, though still mainly experimental. Common Indian biogas plant designs include the floating-drum and the fixed-dome, also called Deenbandhu or Janata designs. A biosensor consists of a biological recognition element coupled to a transducer that converts the biological response into a measurable electrical signal, and the most familiar commercial biosensor, the blood-glucose meter, uses the enzyme glucose oxidase.
524: Now, students, this final page in our range covers questions fifty-two to fifty-nine on biosafety, GMOs and fermentation techniques. The apex body that approves the commercial release of GMOs in India is GEAC, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, under the Environment Ministry, and GMOs in India are regulated under the parent Environment Protection Act, 1986, along with its 1989 Rules on genetically engineered organisms. Bt brinjal in India is best described as being under an indefinite moratorium since 2010, having cleared scientific committees but faced objections. Under FSSAI's GM Foods Regulations of 2022, GM labelling on packaged food is mandatory above a GM-ingredient threshold of one per cent, slightly more lenient than the European Union's 0.9 per cent. Recombinant human insulin is produced industrially using Escherichia coli or yeast carrying the human insulin gene, and Aspergillus niger is the standard fungal producer of industrial citric acid and many enzymes. Fed-batch fermentation, used for antibiotics, differs from batch fermentation in that fresh medium is fed in stages without withdrawing broth, avoiding substrate inhibition, and fixing whole cells or enzymes onto an inert support for reuse is called immobilisation.
525: On this page we continue the objective questions on microbial and environmental biotechnology, moving through questions 60 to 67. Question 60 tells us the usual carrier material used to keep biofertilizer microbes alive is sterilised peat or lignite, because it holds moisture and protects the living cells until use. Question 61 explains that the fungi Beauveria bassiana and Metarhizium control insects by penetrating and infecting the insect body, since these entomopathogenic fungi infect through the insect's body surface and kill it. Question 62 covers the UASB reactor, or up-flow anaerobic sludge-blanket reactor, used in wastewater treatment, which is a high-rate anaerobic reactor that digests waste anaerobically and yields biogas. Question 63 defines eutrophication as the over-enrichment of a water body with nutrients causing algal blooms, and notes tertiary treatment removes nitrogen and phosphorus to prevent it. Question 64 explains biodiesel is produced from vegetable oils or fats by trans-esterification, a reaction with alcohol yielding fatty-acid esters, which is biodiesel, and glycerol. Question 65 classifies algae-based biofuels as third generation, since they use algae which give high oil yield on non-farm land. Question 66 identifies a pregnancy-test strip as an immunosensor, an antibody-based biosensor giving an optical readout. Question 67 introduces the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, the international treaty governing safe transboundary movement of genetically modified organisms.
526: Now, students, this page finishes the objective question bank for the microbial and environmental biotechnology unit and closes with the reference list. The answer to question 67 explains that the Cartagena Protocol, under the Convention on Biological Diversity, is based on the precautionary principle. Question 68 asks which committee monitors ongoing genetically modified organism research and field trials in India, and the answer is the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation, known as RCGM, which oversees research and small trials, while the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, or GEAC, gives final release approval. Question 69 explains that Spirulina is valued both as single-cell protein and as a biofertilizer because, being a cyanobacterium, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, so it doubles as food and biofertilizer. After the questions, the References section lists the sources used for this unit, unit 16 of the KPSC Agricultural Officer and Assistant Agricultural Officer Paper 2 syllabus, covering microbial and environmental biotechnology. The references include standard textbooks such as Glazer and Nikaido's Microbial Biotechnology, Pelczar's Microbiology, Subba Rao's Soil Microorganisms and Plant Growth, and Rangaswami and Bagyaraj's Agricultural Microbiology, along with guidelines from the Central Pollution Control Board, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, FSSAI regulations of 2022, and ICAR e-course material from the University of Agricultural Sciences at Bangalore and Dharwad.
527: Here, students, we begin a brand new chapter, chapter 17, on Biochemistry, which is unit 17 of the specific paper. This page opens with a summary box describing what the whole chapter will cover, including the four classes of biomolecules, enzymes and their classification, vitamins as coenzyme precursors, bioenergetics and ATP, the central metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, gluconeogenesis, glycogen metabolism and the pentose phosphate pathway, lipid metabolism, amino-acid metabolism, photosynthesis and carbon fixation, plant hormones, and secondary metabolites. Section 17.1 introduces the scope and importance of biochemistry, defined as the branch of science studying the chemical substances and processes occurring within living organisms, explaining life at the molecular level. It sits at the meeting point of biology and chemistry, explaining how a cell builds itself, captures and spends energy, and copies genetic instructions. For agriculture, biochemistry explains enzyme catalysis in fermentation and food processing, lipid roles in cell membranes, metabolic pathways driving plant growth, and analytical methods used in food quality laboratories across Karnataka. The page also lists branches such as plant biochemistry, nutritional biochemistry, enzymology, clinical biochemistry and molecular biology. An Agri Officer Lens box notes that biochemistry explains why pulses fix nitrogen, why oilseeds store fat, and why neem-based azadirachtin works as a biopesticide, with Karnataka anchor points including CFTRI Mysuru, turmeric curcumin from Bidar and Haveri, and Coorg coffee's chlorogenic acids.
528: Let us understand the cell and biomolecules on this page, continuing from the Karnataka anchor points about amino acids in pulses and fatty acids in oilseeds grown around Bengaluru. Section 17.2 explains that the cell is the basic unit of life. A prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium, has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, while a eukaryotic cell, found in plants, animals and fungi, has a true nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts, the endoplasmic reticulum and lysosomes. Plant cells additionally have a cellulose cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts. Each organelle acts as a biochemical workshop: the nucleus stores DNA and directs protein synthesis, mitochondria run the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation as the cell's power plant, chloroplasts capture light for photosynthesis, ribosomes build proteins, and lysosomes digest waste. The page then introduces the four classes of biomolecules built from repeating units. Carbohydrates, made of monosaccharide units like glucose, store and supply energy and build structures such as cellulose. Proteins, made of amino acids, build tissue and act as enzymes. Lipids, made of fatty acids and glycerol, store energy and form membranes. Nucleic acids, made of nucleotides, store and transmit genetic information. A diagram, figure 17.1, classifies biomolecules into these four branches with their sub-types. A remember box states the useful rule that large biomolecules are built by condensation, which removes water, and broken down by hydrolysis, which adds water, in all four classes.
529: On this page we study carbohydrates in section 17.3. Carbohydrates are defined as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances yielding them on hydrolysis, following the general formula CH2O subscript n, and they are the most abundant biomolecules and the primary fuel of the cell. They are classified by the number of sugar units: monosaccharides are single sugars, disaccharides have two, oligosaccharides have three to ten, and polysaccharides are long chains of many units. Under monosaccharides, we learn a triose has three carbons, a pentose five, and a hexose six; an aldose carries an aldehyde group and a ketose a ketone group. Glucose is an aldohexose existing as an open chain and two ring forms, alpha and beta D-glucopyranose. Fructose, the sweetest natural sugar, is a ketohexose. Galactose is an aldohexose and an epimer of glucose at carbon four, found in lactose. Ribose and deoxyribose form the backbones of RNA and DNA. Under disaccharides, a table shows sucrose is glucose plus fructose joined by an alpha-1, beta-2 bond and is non-reducing; lactose is galactose plus glucose joined by a beta-1,4 bond and is reducing; maltose is glucose plus glucose joined by an alpha-1,4 bond and is reducing. Sucrose is table sugar, lactose is milk sugar linked to lactose intolerance, and maltose comes from starch hydrolysis by amylase. The page then begins polysaccharides, long polymers serving as energy stores like starch and glycogen, or structural materials like cellulose in plant walls, with a table beginning to compare amylose, amylopectin, glycogen and cellulose by their linkage and role.
530: Now, students, we finish the polysaccharide table from the previous page: cellulose is a linear beta-1,4 glucose chain, hydrogen-bonded into fibrils, giving plant structure that is not digestible by mammals. Starch, a mixture of helical amylose and branched amylopectin, is the chief storage carbohydrate of plants and the staple energy source of human diets. Glycogen is the animal equivalent, stored in liver and muscle and mobilised rapidly. Cellulose, the most abundant organic molecule on Earth, resists mammalian digestion because mammals lack the enzyme beta-glucosidase; only rumen microbes can break it down. A remember box gives the classic iodine test: amylose with iodine gives blue-black because the helix traps iodine, amylopectin gives purple-red, glycogen gives brown-red, and cellulose gives no colour, a frequent examination question. An Agri Officer Lens notes that Karnataka's maize, ragi and paddy are all starch crops, and the amylose-to-amylopectin ratio decides cooking quality and glycaemic index, with UAS breeders adjusting this ratio for consumer preference and food processing. Section 17.4 then introduces proteins and amino acids. Amino acids are the monomers of proteins, each having a central alpha-carbon bearing an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain called the R-group that defines its identity. At physiological pH near 7.4, the molecule carries both a positive and negative charge, called a zwitterion. Amino acids are classified by side chain into non-polar, polar uncharged, positively charged and negatively charged groups, and by dietary need into nine essential amino acids that must come from the diet, and non-essential ones the body can make. A remember box notes lysine and tryptophan are limiting in cereals, while pulses are rich in lysine, the biochemical basis for combining cereals with pulses. The page ends by introducing the peptide bond, an amide linkage formed by condensation between amino acids with loss of water, which is planar and usually trans, restricting rotation.
531: Here, students, we study the levels of protein structure. Protein structure is described at four levels, each building on the one before. The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids fixed by the gene. The secondary structure is local regular folding, the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional fold of one chain. The quaternary structure is the assembly of several folded chains into one functional protein. A table shows what stabilises each level: primary by peptide covalent bonds, secondary by hydrogen bonds in the backbone, tertiary by disulphide, hydrophobic, ionic and hydrogen bonds, and quaternary by the same non-covalent forces between chains. Figure 17.2 illustrates these four levels visually, from amino-acid sequence through local folding and whole-chain shape to multi-subunit assembly. The alpha-helix is a right-handed coil with about 3.6 residues per turn, and the beta-pleated sheet forms through hydrogen bonds between neighbouring strands. Tertiary structure determines function because the precise fold creates an enzyme's active site, and haemoglobin, with two alpha and two beta subunits, is the classic example of quaternary structure. A watch-out box warns not to confuse denaturation, the loss of three-dimensional structure without breaking peptide bonds, usually caused by heat, acid or detergents and often irreversible, with hydrolysis, which actually breaks the peptide bonds and splits the chain into pieces. Section 17.5 then introduces lipids, a chemically diverse group of hydrophobic biological molecules soluble in organic solvents, grouped into simple lipids like fats and oils, compound lipids like phospholipids and glycolipids, and derived lipids including sterols, fat-soluble vitamins, terpenes and prostaglandins.
532: On this page we look closely at fatty acids. Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains ending in a carboxyl group. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bond, such as palmitic acid and stearic acid, and are solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds; oleic acid is monounsaturated, while linoleic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid, and alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid, are polyunsaturated. Natural unsaturated fatty acids have the cis form, which kinks the chain and keeps oils liquid, while industrial hydrogenation creates the trans form linked to heart disease. Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential fatty acids that must come from the diet. An Agri Officer Lens notes Karnataka groundnut and sunflower oils are rich in linoleic acid, and GKVK Bengaluru has developed high-oleic sunflower varieties whose oil resists rancidity. The page then covers phospholipids and membranes: a phospholipid has a glycerol backbone, two fatty acids and a phosphate group joined to a polar head, making it amphipathic, so such molecules line up tail-to-tail in water to form the bilayer basis of every cell membrane. Sterols, derived lipids with a four-ring steroid skeleton, include cholesterol in animals, which stiffens membranes and is a precursor of steroid hormones, bile salts and vitamin D, while plants contain phytosterols and fungi contain ergosterol. Section 17.6 then introduces nucleic acids, polymers of nucleotides that store and transmit genetic information, existing as DNA and RNA. Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and phosphate groups. Nitrogenous bases are purines, adenine and guanine, with a double-ring structure, or pyrimidines, cytosine, thymine and uracil, with a single ring; thymine occurs only in DNA while uracil replaces it in RNA. A table begins comparing DNA and RNA by sugar, bases, strands, pairing and function.
533: Now, students, we complete the DNA versus RNA comparison and move into enzymes. DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands, the common B-form, paired by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine through two bonds, guanine with cytosine through three. RNA is usually single-stranded and uses ribose, with three types: messenger RNA, transfer RNA carrying amino acids, and ribosomal RNA forming part of the protein-making machinery. A watch-out box flags two classic traps: uracil is present in RNA but not DNA, while thymine is in DNA but not standard RNA, and guanine-cytosine pairs, held by three hydrogen bonds, make DNA rich in G-C more thermally stable than one held by only two bonds for adenine-thymine. Section 17.7 introduces enzymes as biological catalysts that speed up life's chemical reactions without being consumed; most are proteins, though some RNA molecules called ribozymes also act as catalysts. An enzyme works by lowering the activation energy of a reaction through its active site, a pocket whose shape, charge and polarity match the substrate. Two models describe this fit: the lock-and-key model of Emil Fischer pictured a rigid active site matching the substrate exactly, while the more accurate induced-fit model of Daniel Koshland shows the active site changing shape slightly as substrate binds. The page then introduces the six IUBMB classes of enzymes, each given a four-part Enzyme Commission number: EC1 oxidoreductases catalyse oxidation-reduction, like lactate dehydrogenase; EC2 transferases transfer functional groups, like hexokinase; EC3 hydrolases catalyse hydrolysis, like amylase and lipase; EC4 lyases handle addition or removal without hydrolysis, like aldolase; EC5 isomerases interconvert isomers, like phosphoglucose isomerase; and EC6 ligases form bonds using ATP hydrolysis, like DNA ligase.
534: Let us understand the six enzyme classes visually and then move into enzyme kinetics. Figure 17.3 diagrams the six IUBMB enzyme classes with their reaction types: redox for oxidoreductases, group transfer for transferases, hydrolysis for hydrolases, addition or removal for lyases, isomer interconversion for isomerases, and bond formation with ATP for ligases. A remember box gives the mnemonic 'Over The Hill Lies Indian Land' for oxidoreductase, transferase, hydrolase, lyase, isomerase, ligase in order, noting only ligases need ATP to form a new bond. The page then explains Michaelis-Menten kinetics, which describes how reaction rate depends on substrate concentration. The Michaelis-Menten equation states velocity equals Vmax times substrate concentration divided by the sum of Km and that concentration; as substrate rises, velocity climbs and then levels off as the enzyme becomes saturated. Vmax is the maximum velocity when every active site is occupied, and Km, the Michaelis constant, is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax; a low Km means high affinity. The Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot turns the curve into a straight line to read Km and Vmax. Figure 17.4 plots the classic Michaelis-Menten curve, showing reaction velocity rising steeply at low substrate concentration, the first-order region, and flattening near Vmax at high substrate, the zero-order or saturation region, with Km marked at the substrate concentration reaching half of Vmax. A worked example box notes that at low substrate the reaction is first-order, rising nearly in proportion to substrate, while at high substrate it becomes zero-order, flat at Vmax because all active sites are full.
535: On this page we finish Michaelis-Menten kinetics and study the factors that affect enzyme activity, along with inhibition. The crossover point where velocity is exactly half of Vmax marks the substrate concentration equal to Km. Temperature raises enzyme activity up to an optimum, about 37 degrees Celsius for mammalian enzymes and far higher for thermophilic microbes, beyond which the enzyme denatures. Each enzyme also has an optimum pH; pepsin works near pH 2, salivary amylase near pH 7, and trypsin near pH 8. The page then covers enzyme inhibition, vital in medicine and pest control. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, raising apparent Km while Vmax stays unchanged; a non-competitive inhibitor binds a separate allosteric site, lowering Vmax while Km stays the same; an irreversible inhibitor binds covalently and permanently, as organophosphate pesticides do to acetylcholinesterase. A table compares competitive, non-competitive, uncompetitive and irreversible inhibition by binding site and effect on Km and Vmax. An Agri Officer Lens explains that irreversible inhibition is the mechanism behind organophosphate and carbamate insecticides used in Karnataka, which permanently block acetylcholinesterase in the insect nervous system, the same mechanism making them toxic to humans, requiring Agricultural Officers to enforce safe-use and pre-harvest interval rules. The page then introduces cofactors: a cofactor may be a metal ion, a coenzyme is an organic helper often derived from a vitamin, and enzyme immobilisation, the attachment of an enzyme to an insoluble support for reuse, uses three methods, entrapment, covalent binding, and cross-linking. Another Agri Officer Lens notes CFTRI Mysuru uses immobilised enzyme systems for glucose isomerase, lactase and pectinases in food and spice processing, including curcumin extraction from Karnataka turmeric.
536: Here, students, we study vitamins and coenzymes in section 17.8, then begin bioenergetics. Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts that the body cannot synthesise sufficiently, and many act as precursors of coenzymes. They fall into two groups: water-soluble vitamins, the B-complex and vitamin C, which are not stored and must be supplied regularly and mostly become coenzymes, and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, which are stored in fat. A detailed table links each B-vitamin to its coenzyme and metabolic role: B1 thiamine becomes TPP for decarboxylation reactions; B2 riboflavin becomes FAD or FMN for redox reactions; B3 niacin becomes NAD-plus or NADP-plus as a hydrogen and electron carrier; B5 pantothenate becomes coenzyme A, an acyl-group carrier; B6 pyridoxine becomes PLP for transamination; B7 biotin assists carboxylation; B9 folate becomes THF for one-carbon transfers; and B12 cobalamin assists methyl transfer and isomerisation. A remember box gives a quick rule: transamination needs B6, decarboxylation by pyruvate dehydrogenase needs B1, and redox electron transfer needs B2 or B3. Section 17.9 then introduces bioenergetics, the study of energy flow in living systems. Reactions are classed by free-energy change: an exergonic reaction releases free energy and is spontaneous, like catabolism, while an endergonic reaction absorbs free energy and is not spontaneous, like biosynthesis; the cell links the two through energy coupling. The page ends introducing ATP, adenosine triphosphate, the universal energy currency, made of adenine joined to ribose and three phosphate groups whose terminal phosphoanhydride bonds release usable energy when hydrolysed.
537: Now, students, we continue with ATP and begin carbohydrate metabolism. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases about 30.5 kilojoules per mole of free energy, which the cell couples to tasks such as muscle contraction, active transport and biosynthesis; ATP is constantly remade from ADP, turning over many times its own weight each day. Energy is captured in two main ways: substrate-level phosphorylation makes ATP directly, as in glycolysis, while oxidative phosphorylation makes far more ATP indirectly using electron transport to oxygen, and photophosphorylation in chloroplasts uses light energy similarly. A remember box compares ATP to the cell's rechargeable battery and NADH and FADH2 to the fuel that charges it, with catabolism charging the battery and anabolism and movement discharging it. Section 17.10 introduces metabolism, the complete set of chemical reactions in a living organism, divided into anabolism, which builds complex molecules and consumes energy, and catabolism, which breaks them down and releases energy, the two coupled through ATP and reduced carriers NADH, NADPH and FADH2. The page then begins glycolysis, which takes place in the cytoplasm and converts one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules, running under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions as the universal first step of glucose breakdown. Its ten reactions fall into two phases: the investment phase, steps one to five, spends two ATP to convert glucose into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate which splits into two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; the payoff phase, steps six to ten, recovers four ATP and two NADH while turning each triose into pyruvate, giving a net yield of two ATP and two NADH per glucose.
538: On this page, figure 17.5 diagrams the ten steps of glycolysis, the Embden-Meyerhof pathway, from glucose through glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, two molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, 3-phosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate, and finally two molecules of pyruvate, with a net yield per glucose of two ATP, two NADH and two pyruvate. Three steps are irreversible and regulatory: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose at step one and is inhibited by its own product; phosphofructokinase-1 at step three is the rate-limiting enzyme, inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; and pyruvate kinase at step ten is inhibited by ATP and alanine and activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. A summary table lists key numbers: one glucose molecule with six carbons yields two pyruvate molecules with three carbons each; two ATP are consumed in the investment phase and four ATP produced in the payoff phase, giving a net of two ATP per glucose; two NADH are produced in the cytoplasm; the rate-limiting enzyme is phosphofructokinase-1; and under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate becomes lactate in muscle, regenerating NAD-plus, or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast through fermentation. An Agri Officer Lens notes that this anaerobic fate of pyruvate is the basis of fermentation industries in Karnataka.
539: Here, students, we see how yeast and bacteria use pyruvate, then move into the Krebs cycle. Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide, the chemistry behind sugarcane-based distilleries and bakery leavening, while lactic-acid bacteria convert it to lactate, the basis of curd, idli and dosa batter, and silage preservation. The Krebs, or tricarboxylic acid, cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix. Before it begins, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD to NADH, an irreversible and tightly regulated step. Acetyl-CoA, with two carbons, condenses with oxaloacetate, with four carbons, to form citrate; eight reactions then regenerate oxaloacetate, releasing two molecules of carbon dioxide each turn, and yielding per turn three NADH, one FADH2 and one GTP, equivalent to one ATP. Figure 17.6 diagrams the cycle's eight intermediates: citrate, isocitrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, fumarate, malate, and back to oxaloacetate, occurring in the mitochondrial matrix, yielding three NADH, one FADH2, one GTP and two carbon dioxide molecules per turn. Key regulatory enzymes include citrate synthase, the rate-limiting step inhibited by ATP and NADH; isocitrate dehydrogenase, which makes the first NADH and carbon dioxide; the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex; succinate dehydrogenase, a membrane-bound FAD enzyme also known as Complex II of the electron chain; and malate dehydrogenase, which makes the final NADH. A table shows the yield per acetyl-CoA and per glucose, since each glucose gives two acetyl-CoA and thus two turns of the cycle: six NADH, two FADH2, two GTP and four carbon dioxide per glucose.
540: Now, students, a watch-out box reminds us there is only one FAD-linked reaction in the TCA cycle, succinate dehydrogenase, so each turn yields exactly one FADH2, not two, and the cycle yields GTP, not ATP directly, at the succinyl-CoA synthetase step. The page then covers the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation. NADH and FADH2 are oxidised by the electron transport chain, a set of complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Complex I accepts electrons from NADH and pumps protons; Complex II accepts electrons from FADH2 without pumping; Complex III passes electrons to cytochrome c while pumping protons; Complex IV passes them finally to oxygen, forming water. This proton pumping builds a gradient that, according to Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, drives ATP synthase, also called Complex V, which spins as protons flow back through it to make ATP. Each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 about 1.5 ATP using modern P over O ratios; complete oxidation of one glucose yields about 30 to 32 ATP, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor. A watch-out box notes older textbooks quote 36 to 38 ATP per glucose using an old P over O ratio of 3, while the modern consensus from direct measurement is 30 to 32 ATP. The page then covers gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors like lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids in the liver, essentially glycolysis reversed with four steps bypassed using new enzymes, keeping blood glucose steady during fasting. Glycogen metabolism follows: glycogenesis adds glucose units via glycogen synthase, while glycogenolysis breaks it down via glycogen phosphorylase, controlled reciprocally by insulin, which promotes storage, versus glucagon and adrenaline, which promote release. The pentose phosphate pathway is then introduced, running in the cytoplasm to convert glucose-6-phosphate to ribulose-5-phosphate, producing NADPH via the rate-limiting enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
541: Let us understand the products of the pentose phosphate pathway and then move into lipid metabolism. NADPH supplies reducing power for fatty-acid and cholesterol synthesis and for antioxidant defence by regenerating glutathione, while ribose-5-phosphate supplies the sugar for nucleotide and nucleic-acid synthesis; the pathway makes no ATP, existing purely for biosynthesis and protection. A remember box notes deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the commonest human enzyme deficiency, causes haemolytic anaemia on exposure to oxidising agents such as fava beans or antimalarial drugs. Section 17.11 covers lipid metabolism, starting with beta-oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondrial matrix. The fatty acid is first activated by joining coenzyme A using ATP, then carried into the mitochondrion by the carnitine shuttle, with carnitine palmitoyltransferase I as the rate-limiting enzyme, inhibited by malonyl-CoA signalling the fed state. Each cycle removes two carbons through four repeating steps, yielding one FADH2, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA; complete oxidation of palmitate yields about 106 ATP after subtracting activation costs. An Agri Officer Lens explains beta-oxidation fuels germination in oilseed crops like groundnut, sunflower and sesame, with GKVK Bengaluru studying seed-oil composition. Fatty-acid synthesis, the reverse process, happens in the cytoplasm during the fed state, starting when acetyl-CoA is carboxylated to malonyl-CoA by the rate-limiting, biotin-dependent enzyme acetyl-CoA carboxylase, then the fatty-acid synthase complex adds two carbons at a time using NADPH to build palmitate. A remember box notes synthesis and breakdown are kept apart to avoid a futile cycle, with malonyl-CoA blocking the carnitine shuttle during fat-making. Section 17.12 then introduces protein and amino-acid metabolism, beginning with transamination, the transfer of an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid, usually alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate, catalysed by aminotransferases using pyridoxal phosphate from vitamin B6, with enzymes like AST and ALT signalling liver damage when elevated.
542: On this page we finish amino-acid catabolism through the urea cycle, then move into photosynthesis. Glutamate, having gathered amino groups, is deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase in the mitochondrion, releasing toxic free ammonium ion, which must be converted at once into a safe excretory form. The urea cycle, also called the Krebs-Henseleit cycle, converts toxic ammonia into harmless urea in the liver, running in five steps partly in the mitochondrion and partly in the cytoplasm; one urea molecule carries away two nitrogen atoms and is excreted by the kidneys. A remember box notes animals differ in nitrogen disposal: mammals are ureotelic excreting urea, birds and reptiles are uricotelic excreting uric acid to save water, and most fish are ammonotelic excreting ammonia directly into water. Section 17.13 introduces photosynthesis, the process by which green plants capture light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrate, releasing oxygen, the ultimate source of food and energy for almost all life. It has two stages: light reactions in the thylakoid membranes produce ATP and NADPH while splitting water to release oxygen, and dark reactions, or the Calvin cycle, in the stroma use that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, forming a three-carbon acid, the C3 pathway used by most plants like rice and wheat, though RuBisCO can also wastefully bind oxygen causing photorespiration. C4 plants like maize, sugarcane and sorghum first fix carbon dioxide into a four-carbon acid in mesophyll cells to suppress photorespiration, while CAM plants like pineapple fix carbon at night. A table compares C3, C4 and CAM plants by first product, first enzyme, photorespiration level, examples and climate suited, and an Agri Officer Lens notes Karnataka grows both C3 staples like paddy and ragi and C4 crops like maize and sugarcane, which are more water-efficient under hot, sunny conditions.
543: Here, students, we study plant and animal hormones in section 17.14, then secondary metabolites in section 17.15. Hormones are chemical messengers produced in one part of an organism and carried to another, regulating growth, metabolism and development in tiny amounts. Plant hormones, or phytohormones, are central to agriculture: auxins promote cell elongation, rooting and apical dominance; gibberellins promote stem elongation, seed germination and bolting; cytokinins promote cell division and delay leaf ageing; abscisic acid promotes dormancy and closes stomata under stress; and ethylene, a gas, triggers fruit ripening and leaf fall. A table lists their agricultural uses: auxin for rooting cuttings and weedicides like 2,4-D, gibberellin for larger grapes and malting barley, cytokinin for tissue culture and longer shelf life, abscisic acid for stress and drought tolerance, and ethylene for artificial ripening of banana and mango. Animal hormones also rest on biochemistry: insulin lowers blood glucose and promotes storage, glucagon and adrenaline raise it, and thyroid hormone sets the basal metabolic rate, often acting through phosphorylation. Section 17.15 introduces secondary metabolites, compounds not required for basic growth but giving ecological advantages like defence and attraction, grouped into three classes: terpenoids, built from five-carbon isoprene units, ranging from monoterpenes to forty-carbon carotenoids; alkaloids, nitrogen-containing and usually bitter, like caffeine and morphine; and phenolics, carrying aromatic rings with hydroxyl groups, like flavonoids and tannins. A table gives examples: terpenoids include azadirachtin from neem and carotenoids; alkaloids include caffeine, morphine, nicotine and quinine; phenolics include curcumin, chlorogenic acid, tannins and lignin. Azadirachtin from neem acts as an insect antifeedant for biopesticides, caffeine is a purine alkaloid in coffee and tea, and curcumin from turmeric is a phenolic antioxidant. An Agri Officer Lens begins describing Karnataka as a biochemical treasure house of secondary metabolites, with neem azadirachtin feeding the biopesticide industry and turmeric curcuminoids from Bidar and Haveri supporting a nutraceutical value chain.
544: This short page simply completes the previous sentence about Karnataka's secondary metabolites, noting that Coorg-Hassan cardamom essential oils, rich in monoterpenes, are also profiled by CFTRI, and it closes with the reminder that an Agricultural Officer who understands this chemistry can guide quality control and value addition in these crops.
545: On this page, we have a chapter mind map that ties together the entire Biochemistry chapter, so let us walk through its nine branches. Carbohydrates covers glucose as C6H12O6, starch as amylose plus amylopectin, cellulose as beta-1,4 glucose, and the glycosidic bond linking sugars. Proteins and Amino Acids covers 20 amino acids with 9 essential ones, four levels of protein structure, the peptide bond written as minus CO, NH minus, the alpha-helix and beta-sheet as the two secondary structure types, and denaturation, which unfolds a protein. Lipids covers the triglyceride as glycerol plus three fatty acids, saturated versus unsaturated fatty acids, phospholipids forming membranes, steroids with a cholesterol backbone, and lipids giving 9 kilocalories per gram, the richest energy source. Nucleic Acids covers DNA pairing, adenine to thymine with two hydrogen bonds and guanine to cytosine with three, RNA using uracil instead of thymine, the nucleotide as base plus sugar plus phosphate, the Watson-Crick double helix, and the phosphodiester backbone. Enzymes covers the six IUBMB classes, Michaelis-Menten kinetics and Km, lowering activation energy, the lock-and-key active site, and cofactors and coenzymes aiding catalysis. Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP in the cytoplasm, converting glucose to pyruvate, yielding 2 NADH, and needing no oxygen. The TCA cycle gives 3 NADH and 1 GTP per turn, occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and releases 2 CO2 per turn. Finally, the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis branch covers oxidative phosphorylation, oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and ATP synthase making ATP, while Photosynthesis covers C3 and C4 pathways, RuBisCO fixing CO2, and the overall equation of 6 CO2 plus 6 water yielding glucose and oxygen.
546: This page gives us a Key Terms at a Glance table for quick last-minute revision before the examination, followed by the start of Part B, the objective questions. Let us go through the important terms. A zwitterion is an amino acid form carrying both positive and negative charge at physiological pH. A peptide bond is the amide link between amino acids, which is planar with partial double-bond character. A reducing sugar has a free anomeric hydroxyl group, as seen in maltose and lactose. Amphipathic describes a molecule with both water-loving and water-fearing ends, like a phospholipid. Purines are two-ring bases, adenine and guanine, while pyrimidines are one-ring bases, cytosine, thymine, and uracil. The active site is the substrate-binding pocket of an enzyme, and Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax, where a low Km means high affinity. A coenzyme is an organic enzyme helper, often derived from a vitamin, such as NAD or FAD. Substrate-level phosphorylation makes ATP directly by transferring a phosphate group, while oxidative phosphorylation makes ATP via the electron chain and proton gradient, a process called chemiosmosis. Gluconeogenesis builds new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors. Transamination transfers an amino group using PLP, vitamin B6. The urea cycle is the liver pathway converting ammonia to excretable urea, and RuBisCO is the enzyme fixing CO2 in the Calvin cycle. Part B then opens with Q1, asking which biomolecule is the most abundant on Earth and forms plant cell walls.
547: On this page we work through Q1 to Q9 of the objective question bank on biochemistry. Q1 confirms cellulose, a beta-1,4 glucose polymer, is the most abundant organic molecule on Earth. Q2 tells us glucose and fructose are monosaccharides, six-carbon sugars, with glucose an aldose and fructose a ketose. Q3 shows the glycosidic bond in sucrose joins glucose and fructose, making it a non-reducing sugar. Q4 identifies glycogen as the main glucose-storage polysaccharide in animals, stored in liver and muscle. Q5 defines a reducing sugar as one with a free anomeric hydroxyl group, which lets it reduce agents like Benedict's reagent, while sucrose lacks this and is non-reducing. Q6 explains starch is a mix of linear amylose and branched amylopectin, both glucose polymers. Q7 identifies the peptide bond as the one linking two amino acids in a protein, formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Q8 tells us that at physiological pH, an amino acid exists mainly as a zwitterion, carrying both positive and negative charge simultaneously. Q9 explains that the alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet are examples of secondary protein structure, local folding stabilised by hydrogen bonds. Remember these patterns well, as they repeat often in the actual examination.
548: Now, students, this page continues with Q10 to Q17. Q10 confirms there are 20 standard amino acids coded for protein synthesis by the genetic code. Q11 explains quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits, as seen in haemoglobin's four chains. Q12 clarifies that denaturation of a protein involves loss of higher-order structure while the amino acid sequence itself remains intact, and it does not break peptide bonds. Q13 tells us triglycerides are esters of glycerol with three fatty acids. Q14 explains phospholipids are amphipathic because they have both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, a polar phosphate head and non-polar fatty-acid tails, making them ideal for membranes. Q15 distinguishes saturated fatty acids as having no carbon-carbon double bonds, so they pack tightly and are usually solid, unlike unsaturated fatty acids. Q16 identifies cholesterol as a steroid, recognised by its four-fused-ring structure, which is shared by steroid hormones and bile salts. Q17 tells us the building block, or monomer, of a nucleic acid is the nucleotide, made of a base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group; chains of these nucleotides form DNA and RNA. Keep these definitions sharp, as this section builds directly into the next set of questions on nucleic acids and enzymes.
549: Here we continue with Q18 to Q26, moving from nucleic acids into enzymes. Q18 tells us adenine and guanine are the purines, double-ring bases, while cytosine, thymine and uracil are single-ring pyrimidines. Q19 explains that in DNA, adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine through three, making G-C rich DNA more stable. Q20 confirms uracil is the base found in RNA but not in DNA, replacing thymine. Q21 tells us the sugar in DNA is deoxyribose, which lacks the 2 prime hydroxyl group that ribose in RNA carries. Q22 explains enzymes increase reaction rate by lowering the activation energy; they do not alter the equilibrium constant and are not consumed in the reaction. Q23 confirms the IUBMB system recognises six main classes of enzymes, oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, and ligases. Q24 tells us an enzyme catalysing a hydrolysis reaction belongs to the hydrolases class, which splits bonds by adding water, such as amylase, lipase, and protease. Q25 explains that in the Michaelis-Menten model, Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax, and a low Km means high affinity. Q26 begins discussing how a competitive inhibitor typically behaves, which continues on the next page.

Q26 tells us a competitive inhibitor binds the active site and raises the apparent Km while Vmax stays unchanged. Q27 explains a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme, lowering Vmax while Km remains roughly unchanged. Q28 defines a coenzyme as an organic, often vitamin-derived helper molecule, such as NAD from niacin or FAD from riboflavin. Q29 confirms niacin, vitamin B3, is the precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which are central hydride carriers. Q30 tells us pyridoxal phosphate, PLP, the coenzyme of transamination, is derived from vitamin B6, pyridoxine, and is essential for amino-group transfer. Q31 lists the fat-soluble vitamins as A, D, E and K, while the B-complex and vitamin C are water-soluble. Q32 confirms scurvy results from a deficiency of vitamin C, ascorbic acid, which impairs collagen synthesis. Q33 tells us ATP is the energy currency of the cell, storing and delivering energy through its high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds. Q34 introduces Gibbs free energy, asking about a reaction with a negative free-energy change, which we will see is exergonic and spontaneous on the next page.
551: Now let us work through Q34 to Q42, covering bioenergetics, glycolysis, and the start of the TCA cycle. Q34 confirms a reaction with a negative Gibbs free-energy change is exergonic and spontaneous. Q35 explains that hydrolysis of ATP to ADP plus inorganic phosphate is exergonic, releasing usable energy that cells couple to drive endergonic processes. Q36 tells us glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, or cytosol, and needs no oxygen. Q37 confirms that under aerobic conditions, the end product of glycolysis is pyruvate, since glycolysis splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules, and the fate of pyruvate then depends on oxygen availability. Q38 tells us the net ATP yield from glycolysis per glucose molecule is 2, since four ATP are made and two are used, giving a net gain of two ATP plus two NADH. Q39 explains that in anaerobic conditions in muscle, pyruvate is converted to lactate, which regenerates NAD-plus so glycolysis can continue. Q40 confirms the TCA, or Krebs, cycle operates in the mitochondrial matrix. Q41 tells us pyruvate must first be converted to acetyl-CoA before entering the TCA cycle, a step carried out by the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase. Q42 asks what forms when acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate, which we will see is citrate on the next page.

Q42 confirms citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate to make citrate, giving the citric acid cycle its name. Q43 tells us one turn of the TCA cycle directly yields, per acetyl-CoA, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP, along with 2 carbon dioxide molecules.
